I absolutely love this game. Easy to pick up and wonderfully addictive, with the added bonus of having lots of shiny armour, troop and weapon cards to collect. The best part about it is that, whether you're playing through the quests or pvp-ing, it's all about strategy and wits, not player level; the right combination of troop cards can be devastating to an opponent even if they're tens of levels higher than you.
I've seen lots of reviews here that claim the game is 'Pay2Win,' i.e. you have to buy things in-game with real-world cash in order to earn enough gold to even PLAY the game, never mind buy the shinies that give you an advantage. THIS IS NONSENSE. I'm now level 117 and play for an hour or so pretty much every evening, and I can honestly say, hand on heart, I have not spent a penny of real-world money to do that. All the shinies I've bought (like Epic troops and weapons, and armour that gives stat bonuses) I have bought purely with in-game currency which is EARNED BY PLAYING THE GAME. There is a very simple way to make enough gold to play as long as you want AND earn the shinies, and that's to join a guild (which is easy as pie) and help them earn trophies. Do that and the whole 'Pay2Win' thing isn't an issue.
PVP is well-handled, particularly if you're a bit timid about that aspect of the game. While the players you 'invade' or 'revenge' against ARE real players, you don't actually play them in real time; the game selects them randomly and then uses the troops they've selected in advance to play against you using the in-game AI. This removes the uncertainty of hanging around waiting for your opponent to make their move (the computer AI handles it instantly) and also stops you feeling guilty about taking a long time to make your own moves (since the computer AI doesn't care.) However, don't assume that this makes winning a pushover, just because you're 'only' playing a machine. As I previously mentioned, picking the right combination of troops can make or break a match, and with the gem-matching element being the main source of 'charging up' your troops the luck of how the gems fall plays a big part in determining both your and the computer's chances. PVP-ing is how you win trophies (and gold) for your guild, which brings its own bonuses that get better the more trophies your guild earns.
However, there's more to the game than just pvp. You can also play through the quests for each of the (currently) 18 kingdoms (you start with one and then 'unlock' the rest with the gold earned from playing.) Completing a quest either earns you more daily income from that kingdom or unlocks a Challenge, which you play through the five levels of to earn Souls (which you can use to level up your troops.) There's also an Arena option in the Broken Spire kingdom, where you're given the chance to pick three random cards to join your character and play against other players (handled the same way as for pvp, except the game AI has also chosen their random cards for them) in a series of up to 8 battles, to win trophies, gold, glory, souls and keys. And the Zul'Khari kingdom has a Treasure Hunt option, which you can use to earn more of the same providing you have a treasure map (which can be earned either through completing guild tasks, getting a super-cascade of seven gem-matches in a row or buying them with Glory points.)
In short, this game has the addictive thingy-matching of Candy Crush without the teeth-grindingly frustrating complicated extra bits (like bringing down the fruits and nuts, breaking the cages and exploding the bombs before the countdown runs out - admit it, you hate those things!) combined with the Top-Trumps-esque card battles with collectible troops and weapons. Fun on so many levels!

I've only played an hour as of right now but I have to say, I've already laughed, been emotionally moved and otherwise enjoyed the story. And that's an important note, this is a very story driven game, and it does not fall short at delivering. Another important note is that this is an adult game with the adult content removed. Despite that removal there remains a definite appeal to the lolicon, as there's a panty-shot very early and, I mean really, just look at the angel Sepha.
I actually bought this in an instant because I'm familiar with the artist's work, knew a bit about this game, didn't know it was available in English and quite foolishly assumed that there would already be the desired patch available as with when I purchased HuniePop (though that's an entirely unrelated game). Needless to say I should have read the description all the way through and now I'm a tiny bit disappointed (in myself mostly).
, it's quite interesting in how the story is advanced. Rather than dialog trees there's a sort of dice minigame where you get different kinds of "spirit" depending on what is rolled, and rolls can be messed with by "bumping" the dice as they're rolled, so it's not all chance. The different spirit can be spent to unlock spells, which gives you a scene, the spells can be used when rolling the dice to further modify results as well as being a prerequisite for quests, which also advance the story. there's more to it but that's the general idea.
, I can't believe how attached I am to these girls already. Aria's straight forward attitude and reckless behavior, Kaya's quiet anxiety and compassion; they both are very quickly established as people with life and personality that makes you want to see them succeed. Their envy of traits they see in the other girl, and their self doubt make them all the more human. The voice acting is good too. I can't help but look forward to getting to know the girls better and guiding them to happiness and success.

This is a review in-progress. I've only completed a quarter of the game so far.
In Rainbow Hero you are a gnome who finds his village has had its happy colors stolen by your stereotypically (possible a bit crazy) evil wizard. He has to go on a puzzle-solving quest through a series of magical doors in the forest to find the lost colors.
Gnome's special skill is to move platforms telekinetically over distances. The puzzles begin very basically with pushing blocks over buttons that reveal walkable tiles over the emptiness. There are also balls that when pushed will roll all the way to the opposing wall. The tele-transferrable platforms may have restricted directions to where to move.
What I didn't see yet are the levels that have several gnomes moving in unison with the base gnome, so unfortunately I can't comment on those. Also I haven't seen the laser puzzles and disappearing tiles puzzles from the trailer yet, having beaten just one world. It appears there are likely to be levels with gnomes moving separately from each other, considering there's a key for changing the controlled character.
The puzzles vary from pretty easy to really challenging. Thankfully it's often possible to skip a couple of levels if you just can't beat one and try some other level in the meanwhile. Controls feel somewhat stiff at times but there's a useful rewind key that lets you take the level back as much as you'd want or restart it if you'd like. Maybe a turbo button or a fast-mode would be useful, because when you know what you're doing, the platforms floating about can feel like a long time. Changing focused platform also feels unresponsive because before changing you have to wait for it to completely stop.
Unfortunately the controls can't be reconfigured: you can play with a controller or (like I did) with a keyboard (and optionally a supplementary mouse). With keyboard you are limited to moving with the arrow keys, which I personally don't like using. There are not many video options either: you can just change "quality", but not e.g. resolution (which was fine though, seemingly defaulting to my native resolution).
Graphics are cartoony and nice enough. While it looks like a kids' game especially considering the story, it's anyway a pretty solid puzzle game suitable for all ages. I paid some 5 € for it, getting it for a small sale (I don't remember the exact amount), for which I've been happy with even if I've only sunk couple of hours in so far.
I'll update the review once I've played it a bit more.

It's a third person hack and slashy game with a bunch of platforming where you play as a viking named Ragnar, and can fit more weapons down his trousers than Link can with max weapon slots, except these weapons don't break, but can be thrown and also easily lost. But honestly, I never had a reason to throw my weapons other than to get lizards, and I always recover my weapons. Er... until that is.. the later half of the game where you fight a ton of vikings, 3 weapon throws will take one out on normal mode, which is a pretty cheap way to deal with them as long as a ton aren't surrounding you. So I guess weapon throwing is pretty good against certain enemies.
You can even pick up a severed arm or head from a gibbed enemy, and use it as a weapon or throwable, that do about the same damage as a one handed weapon, which is quite humorous to beat enemies to death with, or even break a concrete wall with. How severed limbs don't explode into tuna chunks by breaking solid concrete with it, is beyond me.
The combat didn't age all that well, but it's fairly fun when you get the hang of it, it's kind of like a distant cousin to Enclave, or at least the melee characters in that game. You also have shields with durability, handy for blocking blows, especially when weapons do a lot of damage to you, and your main source of healing is eating lizards that are either on the ground, a low wall, or high up where you have to throw a weapon at them to dislodge them. Wander would get along well with this guy.
Speaking up upgrades, there are several health & rune, uh, runes hidden throughout the game to permanentely increase your health for more survivability and rune meter for more power usage.
Then there's the rune powers, you have a rune meter that *does not* refill over time, but instead by picking up runes of power, each weapon has a different rune power that takes varying amounts of rune energy, usually handy for taking out large groups of enemies that want to shank you with a rusty bread knife. I found the life leech on the Viking Short Sword to be one of the most useful and least expensive to use.
The graphics do glitch out occasionally, but the game ran well enough in Win 7 64bit, forgot if I had to configure anything though.
Although the game does become crash happy near the very end, when you fall down a pit in one of the last levels, it always crashes, also a cutscene in the same level crashes as well. My reviews are primarily on the silly side (because I am a buffoon), but for this game I think I've got time to sit down grab a brew and do a full review.
I got this game waaay  back when it initially released, with it's 1 monster (Lurker) and 4 maps. (Back then, I was heavily into Amnesia: The Dark Descent and the mods being created for Amnesia; so horror was my Wheaties, couldn't start the day without it). So suffice it to say, when this game came to my attention I was like "Heck yeah, horror gaming with friends! GIMME!". So I sat myself down, enveloped in complete darkness with no source of light save for my monitor, and played...

[Gameplay]
I was pleasantly surprised to find that the game plays much like Amnesia! Hell yeah! Albeit, a somewhat less intuitive version, still fun though. The game goes essentially like this, find lousy keys to open doors to find better keys that open doors that lead to a silver key that goes to a door that leads to your freedom (along the way you'll want to find a crowbar or something to unblock the escape door, meh). All the while listening for sound cues to let you know whether the monster is nearby or not.
[Conclusion]
Upon finishing a session, my friends were somewhat dismissive, whilst I saw the potential in this game and could ignore the rough edges (random crashing, Amnesia click and drag bugginess). I continued playing the game month after month, update after update, and found my experience never altering; to this day I keep thinking to myself "This game has potential". And that's where I am today, while this game has seen the additions of two more monsters (Phantom, and Mary) and is now at a total of 12 maps, has added the 'Insanity' mechanic (seeing things that aren't there), and has come out of Early Access, I still feel that so much more can be done with this game. In fact, I think at the end of this review I will whip up a list of additions and alterations that I believe would improve this game.
But before that, I would like to say,
As it stands this game is indeed worth buying if you are a true fan of horror genre gaming, and to those that ARE NOT, wait till a Summer Sale or something because the $19.99 price tag might be a little high for most people.
Overall, this game gets my stamp of approval (for what it's worth), good job 9Heads Game Studios! You proved that a multiplayer horror experience IS possible.
[Extras]
Oh good, you're still here! You're probably here for my personal Additions and Alterations That Would Improve This Game ( aka. AATWITG, working title).
1. Why Lurker No Go "Here's Johnny" On That Door?
I think that considering that the Phantom and Mary are just straight up more dangerous than the Lurker, that giving him the ability to break down doors would add to the primal terror of a vicious creature that wants your innards to be outtards. I mean his hands don't even look like they can even grasp a door handle let alone turn it.
2. Insanity, I See Goofy Faces...
Overall, I love the Insanity system, I love it to death. But the faces, those goofy looking faces are just silly! Have you ever walked around in the dark, and had a sensation that you were about to come face to face with something, like you think you can see something that is just out of sight and out of focus, when all of a sudden it's right up in your face like a deranged dermatologist! You couldn't tell what it was, you just know it gave you semi-whiplash. Yeah that, do that!
3. Insanity, Why My Legs Be Broken?
Okay, this one is a little finicky. But sometimes when your Insanity reachs the point where you can't move or see, is alright, accept when you're trying to escape a monster! I get it, you see arms coming out of the walls grabbing at you, you slow down and think about your life, but when a monster wants to push your♥♥♥♥♥♥in! I think you got bigger problems. (Disable Insanity temporarily when in danger, that's all I'm saying GG).
4. Insanity Addition: Tunnel-Vision.
Some horror games are doing it! Damned sure as shootin' can! You know that optical illusion that causes you to percieve the room or floor or what have you to stretch out further and further away. Yep that's a winner!
5. Need Me a Little Pick-Me-Up.
This just a suggestion, but how about the ability to revive buddies? Like a chance that they survived the attack from a monster and are knocked unconscious, whilst unconscious the incapacitated player engages a nightmare scenario that they have to beat in order to wake up or wait until an other player resuscitates them. However, if blood begins to pool, that is a sure sign that the victim is beyond saving.
6. More Scenarios for Success.
Escape is a fine solution, but for those more brave souls why not include an alternative. Excorsism, Slay the Monster (aka. Monster Bane), Sacrifice (appease the monster). I don't know suggest your own! I just think that more can be done here.
That's all I can think of at the moment, add your own suggestions if you want to. Thank you dear reader, for listening to me babble! You're good people.

OH THE HORRORS OF SEARCHING FOR KEYS!!  So many keys, so little time.  It's true, there has been a trend in multiplayer horror games lately, namely rogue-likes, that force you to quest for keys.
Here's an example, namely of Damned, but for this kind of game in general:
>> KEY1 - Unlocks DOOR1
>> DOOR1 - leads to KEY2
>> KEY2 - Unlocks DOOR2
>> DOOR2 - leads to.....wait, no friggin' key, are you serious?!
Backtrack a little, oh there's a key you overlooked.  It unlocks a drawer back in the room DOOR1 leads to, thereby       giving you KEY3.
>> KEY3 - Get a crowbar.... : /   and where the sh*t am I supposed to use that?! (HINT: when you finally find KEY10 which will ultimately lead you to a special SILVER KEY, then you'll find the boards you're supposed to pry off with said crowbar)
All this fetch quest madness leads to a greater sense of fear and unease in the player.  I have to admit, I found that gameplay mechanic annoying and overly tedious at first.  Since then, it's grown on me.  I realize now that if I were in this situation, with 3 strangers (other Steam players) being stalked by 1 of 3 types of monster (another Steam player; that's right: 4 'survivors' and 1 monster make up the basis of the game 'FIND STUFF TO USE ON THINGS AND AVOID GETTING KILLED BY A 'THING' ALONG THE WAY') that I couldn't possibly know where the keys were to get out of wherever it is that we're all trapped in.  So I guess you could say the fetch quest just makes the situation more realistic.
All in all, Damned is a pretty fun game and there are trading cards and achievements too. Don't worry, the achievement for successfully completing a certain number of maps goes both ways - you can do so as the monster (so much fun!!) or as a survivor.  Also, the person that plays as the monster doesn't have the advantage you'd think he/she would have.  The monsters have their own strengths and weaknesses, such as the ghoul not being able to see anyone until it's right on top of them + plus it floats around very slowly.  Mary walks slow, but she can teleport too (but even then that's only so many times until the ability has to recharge, in a manner of speaking - you get more charge/uses the more times that you see survivors) and can only go into a 'frenzy' which allows you to take them down by keeping them in your sight long enough to allow it to activate. The 3rd monster can set traps that allow it to pinpoint where survivors are, as it can't see them until it can go into a stalker/kill mode, which of course you have to wait for between each use of said mode.
So Damned is pretty balanced as far as this kind of game goes and will offer far more hours of gameplay than alot of other indie/horror games.  Even more fun if you play with friends (which I haven't done personally, but I think it would be fun).

Quick Review
Damned provides a unique spin on the Slenderman game genre of picking up keys and other objectives in order to complete a level while an evil entity chases you. Not only does it add co-op, but it adds an asymetric mechanic where the human players can work together to find the objects in order to escape the 1 player who plays as a monster, seeking to kill all the humans (can anyone say Evolve?).
The horror of Damned doesn't last very long. For the first few hours of your playtime with this game, it will be very terrifying, being stalked by one of three monsters available to the player. Moving through one of the several dark environments the game bestows upon you is unsettling and nerve wrackcing. However, the scares begin to calm down and the game loses it's horror element.
That doesn't mean the game is ruined though, as it still is a fun game of cat and mouse. The mice (humans) running around and madly collecting keys to open up more doors to find more keys is still a fun game as you try to stay alive. Unfortunately, the game is quite boring with 2 players and sometimes even 3 won't do the job. In order to experience the game truly is to have at least 4 or 5 players to play with (at least 3 humans and 1 player monster).
I'd wait till this game goes on a good sale and pick up a 4-pack to play with friends.

Ok, I have been playing this game for the last week since my internet went off. I have clocked nearly a full 2 hours into this game and still have not completed it.
I will list my pros and cons and then elaborate on them afterward.
+Good humor - If you watch the slide show for Lucid Awakening 1 you would think the two characters are nearly related the way they talk to eachother. Not only there, but throughout the whole game you will see that type of family/close friend humor.
+Great dialogue - Oh my god, the dialogue between characters is absolutely amazing, rarely in games nowadays do we see diverse and interesting dialogue(This helps greatly with the story)
+Interesting story - The story is super interesting and around every turn it changes and there is a new, exciting event happening.
+Great characters - I love the way the characters react with oneanother, each having their own personalities and reacting in different ways.
+Cool action sequences - I'll admit, when I first saw the action sequences I thought "Oh, another quick time event" but, it actually can help or hurt you. If you don't get it on time then you could fail to sneak past a gaurd. Though out of the 2 hours I have only used it once or twice, in the same level.
+Great music - Another great component to the story, the more moodworthy the music the more you can immerse yourself into what is happening, whether it be dramatic, scary, or exciting!

First and foremost, I am glad I bought this game, and I feel it has a huge deal to offer. That much should be evident from the amount I've written here.
While I don't wish to draw too strong a comparison between this and Shadowrun Returns (bearer of the infamously mediocre 'Dead Man's Switch' story), I believe it's worth mentioning that this particular installment of the franchise will, at the very least, pleasantly surprise both veterans of 'Returns' and those completely new to Shadowrun. In short, the system works, and while I'm sure they exist, I have yet to find any obvious game-breaking features that can either severely screw or enable the player. In all, while maybe not as brutally unforgiving as some players might wish, the gameplay is varied enough and detailed enough to provide both a challenge and entertainment.
For those not knowing what to expect, combat is a turn-based affair where the player's team slugs it out with various shady individuals, gang members, insane mages and fantastical creatures. Here you'll find lots of different guns, melee weapons, special attacks and spells, all of which can be helped along by shiny cyberware, drones, and various performance-enhancing drugs. It's pretty great, and the tactical options are relatively detailed. That said, you don't have to run 'n gun your way through every encounter. Don't expect to be able to use much stealth throughout the game, but a lot of fights can be circumnavigated with proper exploration, use of etiquette in negotiation, hacking various environmental features, or just plain picking the right dialogue options. After all, it IS a role-playing game.
Which brings me to where I'm really genuinely impressed with Dragonfall. Here you have a well written story, with choices that will dramatically affect you - if not so much the game (few cause repercussions beyond a serious heart-to-heart with your team). Like a lot of good RPGs are wont to do, Dragonfall offers up a buttload of non-binary morality and forces you to pick a side in a game where every side is just as bad as another. It's not all A+ in terms of originality, but it sure seems to matter at the time. The prominent characters of the game are also written relatively well, and their designs are certainly awe-inspiring at times.
It's impossible to summarise all the positive and negative qualities of this game, but also deserving of a mention is the soundtrack - which continues to be fantastic at creating the right atmosphere - and the quality of the background art, which uses some kind of devil-magic to work perfectly with the 3D character models. Finally, I should say that along with the main campaign (which in itself is around 20 hours of quality gameplay) you'll be getting access to community-made campaigns and a toolset which, as far as I've seen so far, is surprisingly easy to use.
Thus, and in conclusion, I heartily recommend Shadowrun: Dragonfall; it finally does what Harebrained Schemes so nearly achieved with Shadowrun Returns, and is ultimately an exemplary addition to the existing Shadowrun canon.

I played Shadowrun Returns and fell in love with everything Shadowrun. I love the world, I love the character classes, I love the music, I love the stories, I love the game play, I love everything about it. I did not think it could get any better, but I definitely wanted more of it.
Shadowrun: Dragonfall gave me everything I wanted and more: it is more Shadowrun, and it actually improves on an already perfect model. As RPG's go, this is right up there with Dragons Age for me. It is perfect, it is engaging, it is re-playable, addicting, inspiring, frustrating, consistent, fluid, and impossibly fun. I cannot recommend this game highly enough.
My only complaint is that you are not able to import your Shadowrun Returns character. I spent hours building up my character and acquiring skills, and yet I'm forced to drop it for Dragonfall. That hurts a little. But it's a minor complaint because, admittedly, it's a new game and with a new game you get a new character. So be it.
Otherwise, as I have said, this game is perfect. It is cyberpunk done right (and this from a guy who can't stand Snowcrash or other "classic" cyberpunk landmarks), and maybe more importantly, it's RPG done right.
Harebrained Schemes should be proud, and I commend them for bringing this masterpiece to Linux.

The DG series gets the two important elements of tower defense right: game balance & snappy UI.  A balanced TD game requires the player to think the type, order, timing, and the location of tower placement rather than just following formulas.  Finding the correct answer to the puzzle provided by the map is the fun part.  This means each tower must be unique and have its own role, which DG does well.  The crystal stealing and retrieval system adds more depth as usual, since you need to think about the order of the towers on the way back.
All this is wasted with a clumsy UI where it's easy to make mistakes or it takes time to perform actions.  DG utilizes mouse and keyboard shortcuts  (both can be used for camera pan) and intuitive indictars to show what's going on at all times.  It doesn't beat Defender's Quest's unit key assignments but it's the best out of 3D TD games I've ever played.  Being able to rewind a botched level without cost saves time so it works well as a casual game to play during a limited amount o ftime, instead of forcing players to replay the whole level.  (So many TD games these day take 20 minutes to go through a level, only to fail at the last wave)
DG2 has more content, refinment, and expandability compared to DG1, so it's definitely worth it for DG1 fans, or for those that want a solid TD game and haven't played DG1. I have mixed feelings on DG2. It's more of the same as Defense Grid, which is good, but it lost it's heart. It feels more sterile. It has updated graphics, and the environments does look good, much better than in the first game. But the same can't be said about towers and enemies. Both look awkward to me, the towers looked much more functional in the first game, and their upgrading was much better, now when you upgrade a tower it simply vanishes into a hole, and the new tower emerges in it's place. Lame imo. And the aliens look well just bad, nothing like in the first part. In the first they looked mechanized and tough. Now most of them look like a chicken had a baby with an insect.  Others simply look like insects. And some look like dinosaurs without heads.
But those are just externalities, if the game mechanics are still there there is no problem right? Sadly this is not the case. Game mechanics are much simplified now. The first game got it's appeal from the fact that the aliens were after your power cores, and the more cores you allow them to take, the less resources you can salvage. So your first aim was always to kill the aliens before they could reach the cores at all. Another fine thing was, that you gained interest for unspent resources. So you couldn't build towers like no tomorrow, because the more money you kept the more you made. This made a very interesting juggle to always have just as much firepower built that is absolutely necessary to kill the next wave of aliens, and no more. Because that meant loss of resources and less score and the end. Or on harder levels lack of resources to build enough defences for the next wave.
Now the basic principle is the same in DG2 too, the aliens come for the cores and take them if you allow them. But the fine details are completely eradicated. It doesn't matter if you kill the aliens before or after taking the cores as it doesn't influence your resources. And interest is fixed, you always have the same resource flow no matter how many credits you have. So it's completely unnecessary to hold back on building, you can empty the treasury all you want all the time with absolutely no repercussions.
To me this means the game just lost it's heart. Now all you have to focus on is tower placement that's it.
There are a few new features like upgrades to towers that give them more firepower, or disrupt shields on aliens, or give a score(not resource!) boost, but it's not enough to offset the loss of the things mentioned above. And there is one more thing missing, there are no flyer aliens anymore. All of them are walkers. Or rather there is something that could be considered flyers, as sometimes they drop a pod next to the core housing to hatch aliens right there. Frankly this I feel is cheating in a tower defence game.  It kills the purpose of the game if the enemy can appear right at the finish line.
Amongst other minor new features are self repairing aliens, that if you stop hurting them get back to full health, but as soon as you're prepared for them they make no difference. And aliens that drop shields on levels for other aliens to pick up, but with the disruptor tower upgrade this feature becomes mute too. I mean you don't have to alter your strategy because of it, just upgrade a few towers to disruptor capability and you're set.
And you have new superweapons as well, but as I found out most of them are too weak to make a difference. So you'll stick to one or two of them anyway.
Unusually for a tower defense game there is also some kind of back story, but it's even more lame than in the first game. And they went too far with AIs I mean you have these AIs whose only role seems that they spout nonsense into your ear all the time, one of them more annoying than the other. In the first game you only had one, that was fine. If they wanted more characters they should've made some real NPCs not all of them AIs. Or small cutscenes maybe to make it more personal. But there is nothing like that. They wasted money on recording half a dozen idiotistic voices in a studio.
So that's what I think about Defense Grid 2.
Mind you I haven't played all the game modes yet, only the basic campaign. But it feels lacking. If I want to score it it's a 6 out of 10.

The plot has absolutely no consistancy of the passage of time at all. Hecu arrive almost immediatly after the resonance cascade happens. The transfer between the begining of the incident the the Hecu arriving is somewhat forgivable as the game starts in the morning of day 1 and the marines come at the afternoon of that day, but "We've got Hostiles" and "Forget about Freeman" happen literaly a day apart in the game's time. Essintially 3 days pass in the time span of this 1 hour game.

Also, for whatever reason there are 3 different rifles despite them all playing exactly the same. It only comes as an annoyance as each gun has it's own ammo type. They also feel the need to flash the screen white and not give you any damage direction idecators. This makes fire fights completely unfun as you can't barely see.

Alien threat is non-existant as votragons barely appear, you only fight grunts once, houndeyes are very easy to kill and do almost no damage, and Bullsquids only charge at you and rarely use it's spit attack.

The level designer doesn't even bother to light up pushable buttons and add sound ques for buttons that don't work.
Most of the game looks completely ugly. The best looking parts of the game are parts that use mostly HL2 assets. Lighting awful and surface reflection of custom textures does not seem to be working properly.
I don't get why the mod team behind this didn't just make this a mod for Black Mesa. It would make the whole game better overall. All of the textures, AI, and gameplay would be done already.

Watch_Dogs™ is a third person hacking/shooter game that was very overhyped. Of course as many have pointed out, the game does not live up to its hype, so if you don't hype the game before purchasing you will have a very enjoyable experience. Thank god I didn't hype it because I love this game.
GRAPHICS
The graphics in Watch_Dogs™ are quite enjoyable. The city of Chicago looks very good at day and the textures are very nice. At night though, it just doesn't feel like chicago and feels like the city is sleeping, even though Chicago is a "sleepless" city. Another huge issue in the graphics is the pop-ins. These pop-ins aren't anything minor. Any object (Car, Citizens, Destructable Items) will pop in if you are driving, this is not noticable while on foot but driving at high speeds and having something pop in and you crash into in, is very irritating.
SCORE 7/10
GAMEPLAY
Being able to hack objects and interact with them is a very nice feature, and makes combat feel fresh and fun. However in the missions, the level design is boring and very straightforward. Go here, hack this, kill these guys, repeat. Since hacking is such a huge part of the game, it feels very shallow, there are around 10-12 objects that you are always hacking. I feel like if Ubisoft added more objects to hack I would've enjoyed this game a lot more than I did, although I enjoyed it quite a lot. Gunplay is nothing new, though I like how it actually has recoil, making you not able to spray at every enemy you see.
SCORE 8/10
STORY
The story is very cliche although there are a lot of plot twists that I actually enjoyed. Others said that the characters aren't memorable and that Aiden is very boring. Though I must agree on the first one, I cannot say that Aiden was a very boring protagonist. His mysterious tone made me really want to find out what this guy was all about. The ending was extremely bland and I felt like the mission before the final one was way more memorable. The story kept me interested, but not hooked.
SCORE 8/10
MULTIPLAYER
This feature was needed in order for me to get through some boring sections in the game. You can pick from a few modes, but I only played tailing and hacking. Like in Dark Souls, a player sneaks into your game without you knowing until the invader starts his actions. I hated being invaded, but sneaking into players games always had me in fear that I would be spotted, and it turns into some kind of hide and seek game. I really enjoyed playing this and had a blast.
SCORE 9/10
REPLAY VALUE
There is very little. Once you finish the story there are many activities to do, but I never got interested in them. Most of them are just more action and shooting scenes, which I had enough in the story. Maybe someone will enjoy it, but I didn't.
SCORE 6/10
FINAL VERDICT
If you don't hype this game up when purchasing it will be a very enjoyable experience.
PROS AND CONS
+Nice textures
+Aiden is a very mysterious man
+Lots of action
+Lots of plot twists
~Hacking is ok, but is very shallow
~Story is cliche but is interesting at times
-Night time Chicago looks awful
-Many pop-ins in game
-Characters aren't memorable
-Not much to do after the story is finished
OVERALL SCORE  7.5/10

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

I played Shadowrun Returns and fell in love with everything Shadowrun. I love the world, I love the character classes, I love the music, I love the stories, I love the game play, I love everything about it. I did not think it could get any better, but I definitely wanted more of it.
Shadowrun: Dragonfall gave me everything I wanted and more: it is more Shadowrun, and it actually improves on an already perfect model. As RPG's go, this is right up there with Dragons Age for me. It is perfect, it is engaging, it is re-playable, addicting, inspiring, frustrating, consistent, fluid, and impossibly fun. I cannot recommend this game highly enough.
My only complaint is that you are not able to import your Shadowrun Returns character. I spent hours building up my character and acquiring skills, and yet I'm forced to drop it for Dragonfall. Otherwise, as I have said, this game is perfect. It is cyberpunk done right (and this from a guy who can't stand Snowcrash or other "classic" cyberpunk landmarks), and maybe more importantly, it's RPG done right.
Harebrained Schemes should be proud, and I commend them for bringing this masterpiece to Linux.

If you like the Gyakuten Saiban ("Ace Attorney" in the West) games, this is right up your alley. A murder-mystery visual novel with a phase to go around examining things and collecting evidence, and a phase to participate in a class trial and present evidence, usually to disprove a red herring, and bring the true murderer to justice. If you can't identify the correct person in time, you'll be blamed and executed instead.
As with most games of its nature, Danganronpa requires a decent suspension of disblief, but it also provides a fairly thorough explanation for almost everything in the game as long you finish it. While the gameplay itself isn't necessarily challenging (except sometimes attempting to figure out exactly what the developers want you to say, because what you think should be the obvious answer isn't what they were looking for), the storyline is extremely compelling. I first played through this game on Playstation and lost quite a bit of sleep as I'd have to stay up until I finished a chapter before I could go to bed - after all, I needed to know what happened next!
I would highly recommend this game to anyone who likes visual novels primarily for the sake of story. Since there really isn't a wrong path to follow (short of presenting the wrong evidence or refuting the wrong statement during a trial, which can lead to a game over), you're basically playing through a pre-written storyline to a single conclusion. It's still highly enjoyable and is fun to back through once you know what's happening to see what you may have missed the first time through.

Vanguard Princess is an anime-styled, ecchi, 2D, indie-fighter where you fight using two characters - your point character and her assist. The entire roster consists of female characters drawn in ecchi style, so expect lots of fanservice, panty shots and heavily animated busts - if you're into that sort of thing. To top this off, the game runs at 100 fps, so everything is extremely smooth.
The game itself seems simple enough at first - the engine is that of a basic anime fighting game, there are only four buttons (light, medium, hard and assist) and the commands for the special moves are standard fare for the genre. What makes the game stand out is that there is no feature that allow move cancels - normals, throws, special moves, supers etc all have to be done separately from each other. Even basic 2-in-1 combos are only possible because of links.
But here's where your partner comes in. So one of your buttons is dedicated to performing attacks with your assist character, the trick is they can move and attack independently of  your point character. With clever use of tandem attacks you can create tricky setups reminiscent of Ultimate Marvel vs Capcom 3 - attack them high and low at the same time, sandwich your opponent between you and your assist, take turns attacking to create a chain of attacks that combos, etc. You can also create combos via counter-hits which are very important in the game, as they tend to open the opponent up for additional free attacks. There's a lot of depth to be found here but it takes some getting used to, especially if you're already into other, more traditional, fighters.
Arcade mode can be brutal until you get the hang of it and even then the AI is no slouch. It's easy to get overwhelmed by their aggressive patterns, and if you're not already familiar with the concept - the final boss will introduce you to the  SNK boss syndrome in the harshest way possible.
Other than that, the game doesn't officially support online fighting, but there is an unofficial client that you can use. You can find out how to do on
Even though the Vanguard Princess is now pretty old, I like it a lot. I play a LOT of fighting games, and I can tell you that this is one of the more unique entries into the genre. The game is cheap, works great with a 360 pad, runs on Windows 7 without problems and it's is still being supported with updates, tweaks and new content, even five years down the line.

Sorry, but this isn't worth the price even on sale. It's a resource management game that blocks your ability to manage resources. Overall, your gameplay features frustrating guesswork instead of any strategy.
PROS:
- Managing a colony is a fun idea.
- Graphics are decent enough.
CONS:
- You can only build structures on a grid, but you can never *see* the grid. You have to guess when placing structures.
- You won't know what structures build a grid either. That means you literally cannot plan your colony's growth. Instead, you just hope you're doing things right.
- You can't see a comparison of resources generated vs. used. For example, your colony depends on oxygen, but you never know if you've got plenty to spare or almost no space for expanding the colony. Same goes for food, power, water, etc.
- Occasional random disasters hit that remove resources like power. That means you can never figure out how much you generate per day or how much you use, as both numbers fluctuate a lot.
If you want a city builder experience, go elsewhere. This game feels incomplete and rushed.

15 hours in with friends, I must say that I heavily enjoyed Damned. This is coming from someone that normally hates first-person unarmed horror games on PC. The concept of the game is honestly brilliant. Each monster has mechanics that are unique to them and make all of them interesting to play as (although I think Phantom needs a bit more buffing in order to be more balanced).
As for survivors, it's interesting how the way the game works encourages people to work together BUT not stay close. That could mean immediate disaster, especially against the likes of Lurker or Mary. The sanity meter is also very neat and adds to the intensity. I also like how the doors work in this game. Makes it MUCH more challenging to escape from nasty situations.
The only thing I think needs a LOT of work is sound design. The game itself can build tension in many situations and is scary in certain ways, but sound design is very choppy and some of the sound effects they chose are incredibly cliche and immediately take me out of the game (randomly heard an Evil Witch laugh that I swear I heard on one of those Halloween spooky sounds CDs you can get at convenience stores). Mary's music is also very cheap-sounding and generic. I'd honestly turn the music volume to 0 if it weren't for the rest of the soundtrack being solid.
The game also still needs polishing. I've ran into glitches where we were unable to actually complete the stage, people would be stuck in the lobby despite the host starting the match, and Mary has been able to siphon energy off dead bodies and regain frenzy almost immediately after using it. I understand this game has recently stopped being Early Access? I still think they need to fix a lot of things before deciding that. Still, I'm sure they're working on it! Just 7 folks with a great concept, after all.
This is honestly one of the best horror games I've played in a long time. It really makes me glad someone can use this 'helpless defenseless first-person horror' genre to make something actually very enjoyable.

By the end, I had like three to four pistols, at least one revolver, two to three melee attacks (can't say weapons 'cause one of them's fists), about three machine-guns, a shotgun, and more. The animation style looks a bit like Black Mesa (which I haven't played but looks cool) which is good. The mod seems very ambitious overall. It's actually got a story to it which, while not very interesting, is better than most mod-stories. The thing is that both Blue Shift and Opposing Force were much more interesting with the way they showed different perspectives. That said, the start was quite engaging and some of the combat areas (especially before the weapon pool gets overflooded) are very cool to traverse. This is not a "video game", as much as it is a simulation that reproduces every aspect of actual, real, arcade pinball machines. The lights, sounds, backglass art, ball physics, flippers, tilt inertia, everything. These are licenced, authentic replicas of actual pinball tables like you would find in the arcade.
This is a game for people who want the feel of an actual, physical pinball table--maybe to practice and learn the rules and scoring of individual tables, or just to play in lieu of paying 50 cents a game at the arcade. If you're looking for pinball that plays like a video game, this isn't it. Some tables are unforgiving, complicated, and skills like flipper control can take a long time to master (just like their real counterparts).
Most people look at the DLC prices and go "what the hell, $120 for pinball?" It seems like a lot compared to typical games, but it really isn't for a game like this. The $30 DLC is for around 20 tables per pack, and individual tables can be unlocked for a few dollars. You can demo any table you want, with the only restrictions being a score cap that will stop play if your score exceeds the high score list. A real pinball machine is usually 50 cents a play, so it's not uncommon to spend $20 a night on pinball in the arcade. When you look at this this way, it's a steal to be able to practice and play at home for the price. Remember, these are actual, licensed, replicated machines, not something some programmer thought up in their basement. Note that if you want to buy a table pack, you can buy either the regular or "pro" pack, you don't need both, so the total DLC pricing appears as about twice what it actually is. The pro pack has no impact on the games themselves, but it does give you other options like being able to modify some of the table settings, like tilt control.
This includes "Tales of the Arabian Nights" already unlocked and ready to play. Purely personal opinion, but Theater of Magic, Scared Stiff, and Bride of Pin-Bot are great tables for brand new players--fairly simple, the production value is great, and even if you have bad aim, there's plenty to hit. Here is a IPDB's list of the top 10 rated pinball games if you're looking for some new tables to master:
#1 	Twilight Zone
#2	Medieval Madness
#3	Theatre of Magic
#4	Monster Bash
#5	Star Trek: The Next Generation
#6	The Addams Family
#7	White Water
#8	Indiana Jones: The Pinball Adventure
#9	Tales of the Arabian Nights
#10	Star Trek (Enterprise Limited Edition)

I keep swinging back and forth on whether I like this pinball emulator or not. On the negative side, features that should be included as base content are stupidly paywalled. I'm talking like freely moving the camera around to look at the tables here. You need to buy the more expensive "pro" pack to get that and the operator menu that lets you customize the game. The game can be quite pricey if you want all the tables, but I'm sure licensing them from several different pinball distributors doesn't come cheap, as well as the fact that many newer tables are franchise tie-ins and are probably more expensive to liscense.
On the other hand, this software is the best at what it does, which is emulate actual, liscensed pinball tables. Years ago emulating actual pinball tables used to be an unliscensed fan thing, and the emulators available for it were shoddy and burdensome to work wtih.
Pinball Arcade works just great. The whole reason I bought table packs for it was so i could improve my scoring on actual tables at the local pinball arcade. It has been an absolutely fantastic tool for that. The game will walk you through how to score on each and every table for it, Which is way better than
reading the  card that comes on machines or asking some snotty stuck up  neckbeard at the arcade to explain it to you. Scoring high on pinball can sometimes involve some pretty obscure methods and it is great to have this game explain exactly how it is done.
Overall, even though i am angry about the "premium" content that should be included with the regular tables (camera options!), i have had a good amount of fun with this game and it has really helped my scoring, so i am going to have to recommend it.

Pros:
Very faithfully reproduced classic pinball tables. REAL TABLES
I am very happy to play these tables on "Free Play" on my own and with my family.
Tables and physics are great. It has actually made me better at real pinball! So that is a good sign.
Turn the monitor 90 degrees, lock the camera in place, and it is almost like looking into a real table. (Note you can get a mod for this that will play on the occulous rift or at least in theory I don't have one to try out)
Good guides on how to read each table, which coming up to a new table usually takes a long time to figure out on your own.
Good controller support. I prefer running this through the controller as the nudge on the joystick seems to work a little better and the top buttons on an xbox one controller are far more responsive than my gaming keyboard.
Cons:
Tables can be expensive if you want them all. But if you are comparing to dropping quarters in one of the real tables, which I still do occasionally, they aren't bad at all.
I've bought this and tables on 4 systems (ipad, droid, ps3, and steam)... which means your account doesn't transfer tables.
Steam/PC is the best interface, most responsive, but they haven't kept up with some of the dynamic lighting and bugginess of the post processing in 2k+ resolution (AA, textures, etc) that seem to have been worked out on the iPad Version. There is a plan for a Q4'14 patch but remains to be seen.

Love pinball? Play this game. Essentially the "Rock Band" of pinball, "The Pinball Arcade" lures you in with its simple premise of accurate recreations and emulations of real life tables but then deepens your appreciation and love for this dying art. I'd played a few of the tables in "The Pinball Arcade" in real life, but the free limited trials of tables allowed me to discover new favorites that I have since sought out to play in real life as well.

Hidden Path turned the tower defence formula into a deep, complex strategy game.
Having a plethora of game mods, new interesting tower types, and multiple special powers, combined with the (expectedly) top-notch narration and an intriguing story, Defense Grid 2 is a great successor game to the equally great DG1.

I backed the Kickstarter because I was a huge fan of the first Defense Grid. For me, it was the quintissential tower defense experience, so DG2 had a lot to live up to. I'm nearly done with the story campaign and I'd say that it's lived up to my expectations in most areas and exceeded it in others.
My first concern was whether or not this would be a sufficient departure from the original. There's really only one new tower type, the boost tower. Otherwise, the missile tower has been repurposed, the command tower has been removed entirely, and everything else is the same. Fortunately, they made this work by introducing new strategies in other ways. The boost tower itself can provide buffs and benefits to any tower built upon them and different AIs can be slotted into your orbital laser, completely changing how it works. I quickly fell in love with the new temporal beam that slows all aliens on the screen as it fits my build strategy well.
My other major concern was the graphics. The first game looked decent, but was nothing special. It was, however, familiar after all this time. I could tell what an enemy was and what it could do at a glance. The new art style was a significant departure, so I had concerns, particularly in the early betas. At release, however, I'm satisfied with how the game looks. Towers and aliens have had some minor changes, but I can still tell what they are. The ability to rotate the camera is a godsend and I make frequent use of it. All in all, I'm quite pleased with the new graphics styles.
In terms of new additions, I love the ability to change the terrain of the levels through the command shuttle. It gives me even greater control of how I build my defenses. It also lets the level designers do some really sneaky things with the maps that keep you on your toes. The new alien designs are clever and also require some strategic thinking. The regenerators and suppressors are the bane of my defenses right now. As always, there are tons of other game modes, including some really interesting ones suggested by the community. And lastly, I haven't gotten to check out the level store yet, but I'm looking forward to seeing what the community creates.
Defense Grid 2 is a worthy successor to the original and worth every penny I spent on it. I see myself playing this for a long time.

Call of Cthulhu: The Wasted Land is a turn-based strategy title with minor RPG elements. As you may have guessed from the name, the game is based off of H.P. Lovecraft's works within the Cthulhu Mythos; it also features some narrative based off of Herbert West - Reanimator. Since the developer/publisher Red Wasp Design Ltd	have disband, this title has been disabled for purchase on the store page. That being said, there are keys still floating around if you truly wish to buy or trade for it.
Set in the year 1915 during World War I, you will control a team of investigators and soldiers who have been sent on a mission to investigate the Cult of the Awakened. The head of the cult, Docktor Kaul, has stolen the reanimation technology from Herbert West and he has combined it with arcane mythos magic in order to raise a powerful undead army using the casualties from The Great War. Docktor Kaul wants to eliminate all of humanity to make room for a new, superior, hybrid species; half human, half Star Spawn of Cthulhu.
I'm personally a huge fan of Cthulhu and H.P. Lovecraft in general. It saddens me to say that this game is abysmally boring; what you see in the trailer is pretty much what you get. The environments are almost soundless, the gameplay is excruciatingly slow-paced, the dialogue is uninteresting, and the level designs are dull with a good chunk of them featuring trenches. From the screenshots and trailer on the store page, you may think that you will be playing in a semi-open world, but in reality the maps are suffocatingly small. All of this makes sense once you know that Call of Cthulhu: The Wasted Land is a mobile port, one that surprisingly won a few awards.
A lot of people have had problems with the mechanics of the game, but if you take the Basic Training course at the beginning they're much easier to understand. They're still pretty awful controls, but at least there is a small tutorial. If you left click an enemy, the screen jumps to it and reveals all of its stats; you have to right click it to attack. Each investigator/soldier has a set of numbers that indicates their health, action points, and sanity. Action points are used to move around the map and attack monsters, and they can be reset by ending your turn. The sanity points go down each time the character attacks and/or gets hit by a foe that is not of the human variety.
If a character runs out of sanity, they either freeze up for several turns or go in to a manic mode, dealing a ton of damage but then they become incapacitated afterward. If you fail to revive an incapacitated team member, they die within a set number of turns; this can also be said for when all health points are depleted. If a "main member" dies, you must restart the entire level again. Some levels also have a limited amount of turns that can be expended before the level will end in a game over. In many cases, you must also wait X amount of turns for one of the main investigators to research something before you can move forward.
Each investigator and soldier can have two weapons, two items, and two pieces of armor; the further progress you make in the game, the more weapons, items, and armor that you unlock. However, you must purchase these things from the store at the end of each level. Likewise, you also spend any earned experience points at the end of a level. You only get one massive sum of XP, it is not divided up per character. Honestly, the game is made easy even on hard difficulty if you just put all of the XP into the rifle weapon for each character, and buy rifles for each of them. They do the most damage, and have the longest range. It's a huge loophole that negates almost any challenge that this title could've had.
Overall, the most irritating thing about this title is the fact that every single time you attack an enemy, the screen has to jump to center on it; even if you're just a couple of steps away. The timing isn't always the same, so while your eyes are expecting the quick motion and follow through with it, it doesn't happen, leaving your eyes to constantly want to dart all over the place. This lovely feature, combined with some of the most dry and dusty gameplay ever conceived, makes Call of Cthulhu: The Wasted Land hard to recommend even to the most avid H.P. Lovecraft fan.

First Impressions: Call of Cthulhu: The Wasted Land, looks and feels a bit clunky at first. The graphics are a bit dated and ugly (which is fair, considering that the popular imagination of World War I is fairly drab/ugly). It immediately introduces fun stock characters, and the idea of a trench based tactical role-playing game with tons in common with Chaosium's table-top roleplaying game. The biggest frustration I had when I started was that I couldn't figure out how to look around the map further than the immediate area my characters inhabited, but this was later resolved.
My 3 hours: Call of Cthulhu: The Wasted Land is divided into a number of missions, following the story of a British Company working alongside a professor of antiquities(or whatever Lovecraftian professor stock character he was) fighting against the evils of a German Cult. The missions are somewhat challenging, and often involve shifting circumstances, but basically break down into the same rhythm that X-Com players may remember. Moving from cover to to cover, setting up overwatch, covering advances, flanking, etc. This is all made more interesting by  the specificity of the setting , and the challenges of trench warfare.
Between missions, there is an interface for advancing characters, which are broken down between redshirt types and mission-critical characters, all of which can die. Their stats and skills were very familiar to me, being based on what appears to be a simplified version of Chaosium's venerable and popular Call of Cthulhu tabletop roleplaying system. (All skills are based on percentages, which stats are similar enough to how they work in D&D for most people to be able to parse it without breaking too much of a sweat.) The characters have a varied skillset, and the story that I played through seemed interesting enough. When I hit my three hour mark, I found myself honestly wishing for more.
High
My Highlight: For me, the highlight of my experience was a challenging mission that took up most of my 3rd hour of play. In this mission, my band of troops and assorted weirdos (including a psycho-analyst, professor, and martial artist(beefy white guy with mutton chops and a club) had to fight their way through trenches, poison gas, zombies and machine-gun armed Germans to a church, which we had to defend from Germans and Zombies while our professor figured something out inside. It was tense, and consistently felt like I was being pushed to the limits of the resouces I had available. Just a really well designed(and fairly challenging mission)
My Verdict: I strongly recommend this for x-com/final fantasy tactics/Lovecraft nerds like myself. For others, your mileage may vary, as the corniness or the rough edges might be a bit overwhelming.

Story:

For many of the cases, you just expect the most bewildering and out-of-the-world conclusions for the trials. Characters:
There are so many fan favorite characters in this game(Junko, Saya, Kyoto). I understand why many people would get their waifus from this game, but there are a few problems with the characters in this game. Byakuya is a character that I really like but his writing is a bit floppy. Byakuya is really sketchy with his motives with each case; the biggest one has to deal with his rearrangements of a murder scene which he makes an excuse of "making things" more interesting. This doesn't make any sense because he is placing his own life in risk.
Music:
It's okay. There isn't much of a BGM selection. You'll listen to a lot of repeating tracks.
Gameplay:
This is where this game gets a bit sketch. The problem is that the gameplay elements aren't 100% ironed out. The case trials are fun but they lack refinement. When you're making your arguments, your argument wouldn't connect half the time. The transitions between each minigame is really disruptive and slows the flow of the game. Forming the conclusion of the case trial is very fraustrating; the drag-and-drop icons are misleading and hard to understand at times. This causes me to lose health and making me wait for the transitions again.
Overall:
All in all, this game is a very solid game! The characters could get annoying sometimes. The case trials may not surprise you as much as they first did. The music lack variety, and you'll hear a lot of repeating ones. The gameplay may get a bit annoying due to the lack of intuitiveness, but this to be expected of PSP-ported games.

Dragonfall is one of the best RPGs I've played in the last five years. Why, you may ask? Well, let me ask YOU a question, what do you want out of an RPG?
Let's say you want plot. A setting. Dragonfall has you covered. This takes place in the world of Shadowrun BEFORE the tabletop. You're about forty years past the 'Awakening', an event that rocked our modern world and brought forces and creatures of magic back into it. Chief among those were the great dragons,  whom loom over both the setting and this campaign from on high. Along with magic, technology has surged forward, resulting in a cyberpunk fantasy mish-mash where your shamanistic mage can have an artificial eye, your hackers summon digital minions within the virtual world, and your drone-controlling medics can choose to fight with sword rather than gun. This strange mash of the cynical and fantastic makes a setting that is neither too grimdark nor too silly. A proper Shadowrun setting sets a perfect balance of moods and themes, and Dragonfall, fortunately, is no exception. I won't spoil the actual plot proper past what I've already said, but just know that it's full of twists and turns and has a wonderful depth.
Let's say you want party members. A good party can make or break an RPG, and Dragonfall's definitely 'makes' it. You have the dark, distant Glory, wielder of two terrifying cybernetic arms and skilled field medic. There's the aging Dietrich, a middle-aged punk-rocker shaman slightly past his prime, driven by his idol to keep seeking 'the good fight' until death. You have the professional, rigid troll marks-woman Eiger, with whom you will butt heads until you can win her respect. Aside from them, you also have Monika, team leader, local hero, and skilled decker, and Blitz, a former gang member decker/rigger who may or may not be more trouble than he's worth. Oh, yeah, and you also have a dog. No team is complete without a dog.
Each party member comes with their own backstory to explore, along with personal quests. The only thing missing is a love interest, but that's refreshing, in a way. You come to care about these characters because they're members of your team, not just because you want to get into their digital knickers.
Finally, let's say that you're willing to play literally any RPG as long as it actually plays well. Well, then I've got good news for you. Dragonfall's engine has been tooled up to be better than the one that was used with Shadowrun Returns, and there's a deep selection of character skillsets to invest in. Combat is fair and, for the most part, only punishing when you make a mistake. There was only one mission in this game that I felt was unfair, and it was mercifully brief. Levels are well designed and hold a plethora of options that are available to you if you invest in certain skills. The only real complain I have on this end is that you're rewarded experience not for combat, but for resolving quests/dialogue paths. However, this also adds a refreshing twist; this is finally an RPG where you don't have to murder everything to get ahead. At the same time, if you choose to pursue optional combat encounters, there's often a little bit of loot hidden in the area to reward you.
So, in the end, we have a game that's balanced on plot, characters, and gameplay. Not only do you have those three pillars of quality, but they're complimented by fantastic art and an atmospheric soundtrack. Dragonfall is the RPG of the year for me, and it left me feeling inspired to write and create worlds that are as deep and complex as this. If I had to recommend only one RPG on Steam, it'd be this one. That's how good it is.
... Oh, and that's only the core campaign. Took me thirty-five hours. If you'll excuse me, I think I'll be heading back to try out some of the community-made fare...

2) There's one optimal character build: Rifles, rifles, rifles. Long range? Carry a sniper rifle. Short range, grab an AR and then switch to a minigun. All the other weapon types are subpar compared to rifles. They tried to fix this by introducing weapon variety like tasers in the pistol group, or accuracy/different firing modes to some shotguns. Still, what's the point of tasing someone when you can unload full auto on him and kill him outright or in 2 rounds.
Buffs are nice but redundant when you've cyberware and stims. Mages damage output shines only for a brief moment in the mid-game and then falls behind again. Shamans suck a bit as there's only a handful useful conjuring spells and spirits are too unreliable unless you pick the creator totem (which is one of the few useful totems in the game, by the way). Deckers are plain bad and matrix segments don't really justify having them around if you ignore story fluff. Riggers scale weirdly but are still worse than other choices and if the drones are gone they're dead weight. Melee is lacklustre.
Seriously, I played through this game on hard and had a feeling all the time that having four runners with miniguns/sniper rifles/grenades would steamroll through everything there is in the game without issue. Also would feel like playing Syndicate.
3) The party system is very restrictive and, what adds insult to injury, the game capitalises on these restrictions to work around basic design flaws outlined in point 2 which never should've been there in the first place.
Ultimately I'd say the game's got lots of soul backed by great visuals, great music and a solid storyline but the PnP->cRPG translation is pretty bad which effects in a poor party system, basically non-existent loot system, poor character development and poor combat (although it did get considerably improved compared to Dead Man's Switch so kudos where they're due).
Don't get me wrong, it all works, and it gets the job done and ultimately the game is quite enjoyable - but when HBS start working on a sequel they should go back to the drawing board and rethink the way they want to do it from scratch. The whole team is there, what you need is a proper systems designer.

(Edit to respond to developer feedback)
While I appreciate the developer response it seems that my actual points weren't addressed, at all. PROGRESSION was never the problem. As I said, it's easy to figure out what you need to do. The problem has ever been MAINTAINING a colony when you constantly struggle against the AI to perform even basic duties like stocking food machines. Given the number of complaints people have made about the AI this is hardly an isolated incident.
So yes, completing achievements is quite doable. I have personally completed nearly half, 14 out of 30. What stops me from attaining more isn't a lack of understanding the game, rather it is the problem that every time I pick this game back up I inevitably hit a wall of frustration that keeps me from desiring to progress further. The number of achievements completed is an extremely poor metric for overall success, for the player or the game itself.
If you REALLY want to succeed at Planetbase sure you can study youtube vids, I guess. Want an easier method? Save scum. Just back up your game every so often (the game has a decent autosave mechanic, at least) and don't delete/overwrite saves so that when the colonists inevitably start killing themselves just open an earlier save and try to correct the issue before it becomes a serious problem. Almost invariably this is because they suddenly decide to stop performing some vital duty, like keeping up the number of spare parts for the colony, or one portion of the colony decides to stop maintaining crops or stocking machines. Rarely is it because of, say, an unlucky meteor strike or the colony is invaded by gun totting tourists. You know, the things that would actually be acceptable as challenges as opposed to trying to keep the colony from destroying itself from the colonists own sheer stupidity (it's like playing Lemmings only without the cliffs). Just revert to earlier saves until your frustration reaches a point where you give up on the game for a month or two - or forever depending on your individual tolerance level.
(original review continues)
I've played Plantebase off and on for some time now, and I feel I will continue to in the future. So would I recommend the game to someone else? Sadly no, or at least I would with some heavy warnings about preparing for extreme frustration.
The idea behind the game is solid. Build up your colony, keep your colonists alive. Expand, thrive, complete achievements, and try again on different, more challenging worlds. Once you know what you're doing you can get a base up to self-sufficiency pretty easy. The tricky part is KEEPING a colony self-sufficient because it turns out the colonists worst enemy is their own godawful AI.
The problem is trying to keep colonists doing what needs to be done. You can tell them what to build, you can prioritize tasks, and even shut down machines/facilities. There are ways to micromanage and try to dictate their behavior. The results, however, are often disappointing. They do all the work on their own, and yet they are often horribly inefficient at both their jobs and tending to their own needs. I've had colonists drop dead from starvation on the way to fully cafeterias, leaving me to wonder why they didn't decide on a snack sooner. Or why they decide to go on a long walk outside until they suffocate regardless of closer airlocks. Or you're left wondering why all of your biologists suddenly stopped tending the gardens. Prioritization seems to mean nothing more to them than a vague suggestion, and while there is an excellent system to bring in more colonists of the exact type you need there is no guarantee they'll start doing the jobs you can't get the other bozos to do. Typically more people just means supplies dwindle faster.
There aren't even that many jobs that absolutely need to be done. All they really need is food, bioplastic, metal, and spare parts to keep a colony going, but they are so inexplicably awful at balancing tasks. Something as simple offloading a bunch of resources you don't need to a passing trader can pull people from essential tasks to move supplies and once other tasks start slipping it can be hard to get them to catch back up. So yes you can actually doom a once functioning colony just by trying to free up storage space.
When everything is working fine this game can be a lot of fun. When things inevitably spiral out of control because try as you might you just cannot micromanage stupidity it's a frustrating mess. And that's the real downfall of the game because ultimately there are no real goals beyond expanding your colony and (trying) to have fun, but watching this magnificant sprawling base you built whither and die because for some reason nobody bothers to stock the vending machines or water the garden tends to be a real mood killer.

Watch_Dogs was hyped. Maybe too much and in the end this has become the game’s weak point. Ubisoft built up expectations over months and or even over years. The new character was presented as the coolest guy ever, as so special in comparison to all other game characters. Big carton figures and huge posters were found everywhere, in every game shop, on every expo. Even daily newspapers had stories about the game and its revolutionary and technology critical hacking feature.
And then there was the graphics. The early version they have shown was completely faked. Ubisoft made people believe that this game would almost look realistic. Actually that their console or their average PC, two years ago, could handle it. In the end the graphics could not hold up to the expectations. But I call this a classic Ubisoft step what we have also seen recently with The Division and they have to stop this ASAP. It is damaging their reputation and the confidence of players in their games.
And now... just imagine this game would have been shown with its real graphics? Would have been shown as a decent GTA clone with a new IP?! All of this without overhyping it. People would have received the game well. They would have talked good about it, and would even today. No doubt about this.
I try forgetting the ridiculous hype. I did not fell for it anyways and will never do. I know that the videos they show on an expo are mostly fake, pre-rendered...
Watch_Dogs is therefore for me a good action-adventure with some smart and interesting new ideas. It looks a bit like GTA, but it feels different. It is dark and without humour and yes the story is not that captivating as I would have hoped. However I like going through the missions, I like driving around in Chicago and enjoy the nice graphics and the dark and heavy atmosphere in every corner.
Therefore I would like to recommend the game to all those that like GTA and a good story-driven action adventure with a huge and beautiful open world.
