I absolutely adored this game.
The characters might come off as generic to some but I personally enjoyed the depth of each of the characters, even the ones you only see for a chapter or two.
The trials play kind of slow if you're smart enough to piece together the murders before the characters figure it out in game. You might find yourself arguing points characters make with information that you don't *technically* know yet.
The minigames run fairly smoothly and aren't overly convoluted, which is nice.
The free time mechanic is nice and adds a bit of suspense where you think twice about who you spend time with, since that time might be limited. The interactions with the characters can be pretty entertaining as well.
As for the story, I think its really interesting when you actually read into it. There are lots of themes and overtones that really do a good job of setting the mood. If you're just kinda skimming through to beat the game, you might not find it as neat.
The art style for the game is great and I must say it definitely grew on me. The animation for the executions is unique and goofy enough to either appeal to you if it was a character you wanted to see die, or make you kinda make your stomach sink if it was a character you liked. The only complaint I had was how ugly they make the characters when they cry, though it was probably intentional.
Lastly for the postitives, the soundtrack. The score for this game, and this entire series for that matter, is fantastic. Again, setting an intricate mood that makes your brain fluctuate between light-heartedness, triumph, and despair.
There's only one real downside I found with this game and it can come off as pretty minor.
The english translation is.. Well, it leaves a lot to be desired. By no means would I really say its awful, but it definitely strays from the script enough to throw you off in some cases. This is pretty common for games being localized, but the problem here is that a major gameplay mechanic is picking up on subtle cues, which of course are conveyed through text. If that cue is translated poorly, you might find yourself misinterpreting things.
Overall, I'd give the game a solid 8/10, with plenty of potential hours and some different forms of replayability. I would definitely recommend this game.
Oh, and word to the wise, if you don't want anything spoiled, don't Google any of the characters, even if you beat the first game and are only looking up a character from this game, you still might end up spoiling yourself for the other games.

My two cents. I've built a base with more than 300 colonists while, for the most part, maintaining a welfare rating of good to excellent. The problems I see posted here seem to me to be gamer error. The same errors I made when I started playing. Once I learned the nuances of the game, I didn't see any of the problems people are mentioning on the forum. Unlike many base/city builders, you have to build carefully. Plan ahead. You can't just plop down all the modules you want at one time. One new module can bring the whole base down. The thing is, you need everything all at once. Decisions decisions.
I don't see a problem with the AI. Why doesn't that engineer build the corridor when he's right next to it. He's a human. The hell with you, I'm hungry. Besides, Bob's been assigned to build it. Why doesn't he eat? You told the colonist to take inventory to the trade ship or build a mudule. This may sound contradictory, but depending on the size of the trade or the module, it can take many colonist to complete the task, which means other task like food production is delayed. I've only seen a colonist starve if there was no food to eat. Not because he didn't choose to eat. Could the AI be improved. Yes. But it is in no way a game breaker.
I've seen only one bug. The trade ship was waiting forever for one item to complete the trade. Apparently, it was somewhere on the map that colonist couldn't get too. Luckily I found this problem in the forum and loaded a save game. This has only happened to me one time.
Huge hint - save your game often. You will screw up. You will start over.
This game is loads of fun. A casual game. A perfect match for a base/city builder.
Could there be improvements to the game. Yea, without going into all of them, I think I can narrow it down to more micro-management. But that's just a personnal opinion.
Important hints for newbies.
You can't have too many airlocks.
Make sure you have enough power, water and oxygen before you add a module
Too many colonist will bring your base down. Tightly control this.
If you make a huge trade or build a huge module, give your base time recover.
Take your time. Build slowly. Have fun.

It takes patience. Yes. There are main two elements: tactical turn-based combat and text driven story. Combat is not fast, nor is it encouraged. You gain XP by revealing the plotline, and not by killing.
When solving puzzles you'll sometimes need a pen and paper to one side to (e.g.) jot down names or codes from a journal entry; as you may need that information to hack into a network later on.
Shadowrun Returns: Dragonfall is a love song to an older generation of gamers. It will appeal to people that want to read, and engage in, a story more than they want flashy graphics every time they open a door.
However. Don't play this in a hurry, or if your comprehension of written English is below par. Reading is central to the experience here.
If you like isometric RPGs, the X-COM genre and Cyberpunk you'll love this. If you don't, or you have ADHD then you won't.

Bought this game during a recent sale and tried to make it work for 3 other friends. I really wanted to like this game.
The concept of 4 survivors vs. 1 monster on a server game was very appealing to me, and for $5 a person (during the sale) how could I really say no? The atmosphere is creepy, the sound is great, and once you understand the controls it plays well. Sure the elements get reused so you can't tell a level apart from another level and THE FOREST just crashes the game, but it's not that bad design-wise.
The direction in this game is lacking, playing as a survivor is confusing and difficult. Winning as a survivor requires finding a silver key and a crowbar/hammer and having all living survivors in the escape room for 10 seconds. Finding a key can unlock a door that does nothing or unlocks multiple doors and in almost 3 hours of playing we found 1 hammer out of 5 maps as survivors. It's frustrating walking around for 4 or 5 minutes and not being able to go anywhere if you don't find the right key in the right order.
Playing as a monster has its drawbacks depending on the monster, but it's still the most fun part of the game. The 'phantom' appears to play the easiest when it comes to finding survivors that aren't careful, the 'lurker' is the most terrifying but require the most guesswork when turning on/off corporeal form and 'mary' is irritating when she isn't charged and moves as slow as she does, but teleporting can land you in the best position or set you back at the worst time.
Also creating a profile and setting up a room/finding one can be annoying, but it's not Uplay... so there's that.
TLDR: Great look and feel, confusing and unbalanced gameplay

This is a sequel done right. There's enough content here to provide new challenges to players who have mastered the original Defense Grid, but at the same time, this is still very much the same kind of game in all the right ways.
At first glance, the new content seems only modest compared to what is familiar. Almost all the old tower types and enemies are back, but the handful of new types of each and subtle rebalancing of the existing towers mean that new strategies need to be developed.
DG2 offers a plethora of choices as to how you play the game. From separate leaderboards that either allow or forbid juggling, difficulty levels from casual to very challenging, and even more game modes for each map than the first game, this takes what was until now the definitive tower defense game and makes it even better.
There have been some substantial changes to the economy and scoring system which, while I feel personally make for a more challenging game, do substantially alter the challenge curve of the basic level type. Gone is the compound interest earned from penny pinching. Instead, score is accrued independently from income. Efficiency is still rewarded, as you score more for killing each alien while you have less invested in towers. But the income from killing each enemy is unaffected, and additional income is a steady tick rather than being dependent on the amount you have banked. All this means that you can't just develop an optimised strategy for the early waves, and then find yourself with a huge bankroll. Levels can be genuinely challenging from beginning to end, and not just for people looking for pure score optimisation. I know this may actually be a bit of a disappointment for some, as the old game could sometimes be great for some uncomplicated unwinding at the end of a rough day. That is still there, but you'll have to dial the game back to easy in order to find that kind of experience.
I will say that I have yet to try the multiplayer modes, so I can't yet speak to that experience. But with that caveat aside, I wholeheartedly recommend DG2 to fans of the original and anyone even vaguely interested in the tower defence genre. If you're going to give these kinds of games a go, why not start off with the very best there is on offer?

Postal 2 won't go down in history as one of the greatest games of all time. It probably won't even make the average top 500 list. That said, I thought it was very entertaining. When it comes to Postal III, I'm at a loss for words. I'd prefer to write a positive review, describing in detail on how this game improved on its predecessor. If necessary, I could write a negative review, filled to the brim with reasons as to why I believe this product to be a disappointing sequel. Instead, I'm staring into the abyss.
The Postal Dude is at it again. After blazing a trail of death and destruction through the town of Paradise, he finds himself in Catharsis. Madcap mayhem and wacky hijinks await as Postal Dude tries to find a paying job. Will you somehow find the light of virtue within yourself? Or will you once again submit to your demons, using murder to solve every minor dilemna? Whatever the case, you're sure to be in for a great time. This game also stars Ron Jeremy and Jennifer Walcott. I'm surprised that Lloyd Kaufman didn't make an appearance as well.
This entry uses a morality system. Unfortunately, this doesn't mean The Postal Dude will be helping old ladies cross the street (or into woodchippers). Basically, if you want to be the good guy, you have to abide by the law. Naturally, this requires that you become a police officer, and make the law your own. While this doesn't give you a free pass to endanger innocent lives, at least you're doing your part to make Catharsis a safer(?) place. If that sounds like too much trouble, you can always be evil incarnate. This will result in different levels, and eventually a bad ending, if you don't change your ways. If eternal damnation doesn't appeal to you, there's always the handy taser gun. Non-lethal takedowns slowly add up, allowing you another opportunity to join the force when you complete the level. Unfortunately, the possibility exists that your morality, will be at the mercy of the game itself.
While I applaud the writers for their attempt at injecting more story into the Postal saga, things stop making sense very early on. I suppose this can be attributed to the fact that I had to skip stages in order to progress. Let me rephrase that: I had to cheat* just to complete this game. Aside from the high probability of crashes, there are numerous scripting issues. Some doors are scripted to open when an event occurs. For reasons that can surely be attributed to the troubled development of the game, these scripts frequently break.
To give an example: Shortly after I joined the force, I was tasked with eliminating the homeless that were running rampant through the police station. Eventually I reached a point where a door was supposed to open, but it didn't. I could see the enemy's guns clipping through the door, but there was nothing I could do about it. I restarted the level, which fixed it. However, there was another door later on in the level, and it had the exact same issue. This happened again in another level, where I was supposed to go to the mall, the doors simply wouldn't open.
Unlocking all of the stages in Postal III via cheats is a simple task, but that isn't the point. All that work I did trying to be a good Postal Dude? Gone. Putting difficulty aside, when a game can't be completed without resorting to cheats, that means it is broken.
Postal III tends to feel like busy-work. Most of the levels start off with an extremely boring job, which fits in with the story. After a short time, things get crazy when Soccer Moms or Savage Nerds or Eco-Terrorists or ???? show up. This is the point where you have to kill/subdue a certain number of them so that the level will end. Postal 2's strength wasn't in standard FPS mechanics. A lot of the entertainment came from using the sandbox aspects. It was a game designed around finding different solutions for everyday problems (sometimes without murder). With Postal III, almost the entirety of the product involves shooting, and it is very poorly-handled. The Postal Dude can take cover, but it's so ineffective you're sometimes better off standing out in the open. On the bright side, the enemy AI is so bad they're liable to ignore or even forget about you in the heat of combat. The levels that don't require the player to deal with x amount of enemies, tend to be really linear slogs. There are even escort missions, as if players wouldn't have enough reasons to hate this game.
Aside from severe technical faults such as long load times and poor performance, Postal III also suffers from awful mechanics. Melee is basically useless. Even the heavier weapons, like the fire ax, don't work all that well. One of the items you acquire is a laser pointer, for leading Champ (your dog) to enemies. It is complete trash. The same can be said about most of Postal III's weapons. There's no real incentive to play with them, because they either don't work, or just aren't satisfying. Typically, the average Postal III play-through is going to revolve entirely around shooting everything. It gets old very quickly. Urinating is no longer infinite either. The Postal Dude can't♥♥♥♥♥♥as much as he wants, now he has to wait for his bladder to refill. Yes, it's probably an unnecessary thing to complain about, but it's still a nonsensical change that adds nothing to the game. Everything about Postal III is worse than its prequel...Everything**.
Some of you reading this review might not care about Postal. You might even think "It's a garbage franchise anyway. Who cares?" Well, it's just my opinion, but I liked the second game. It was crass, offensive, and sometimes the humor fell absolutely flat. Yet underneath all of the nastiness, there is still a game. Postal III is broken, and is more prone to cause headaches than provide any entertainment value. The multitude of bugs, scripting failures, and generally unfun game-design, make for a forgettable entry in this controversial series.
*While I did cheat to complete a couple stages, I didn't actually try to skip any.
**The soundtrack is pretty decent.

There’s a nostalgic attraction to the concept of digital preservation - and the craft involved with an elaborate pinball table is an art. Leading the charge for commercial video pinball sim, Pinball Arcade seeks to emulate authentic tables as closely as possible.
A digital platform, the base package includes (depending on version) either 1 or 4 real life tables of historical note. New tables are added in packs of 2 as they’re recreated. Farsight has done a good job of mixing older tables with new; simple but groundbreaking boards such as Black Hole are represented along with relatively modern bombastic crowd pleasers such as Medieval Madness.
A strong aspect of the package is well-explained rule sheets with visual aids. If you thought pinball was sheer randomness, and never knew most tables have an intricate sequence of modes to activate for huge jackpots, Farsight’s respect for the game is contagious.
The only downside is a fundamentals-first ethic, leaving the presentation with the look of a cheap iOS game even in the console versions. Farsight intends to update the front end, but it’s a drag compared to the virtual arcade hangouts in the developer’s earlier generation Pinball Hall of Fame collections. Still, the play is what matters here. When at the table it’s the next best thing to owning a real machine.

This game is full of twists, turns, adrenaline boosts, and parts that make your heart drop. The characters in this game are a lively bunch, with the pronounced "normal" Makoto, the cheerful Sayaka, the deadpanning Celeste, the brute Mondo, and others make the cast and game even more bright. The soundtrack is completely wonderful, as it shows the raw emotion of the everyday school life, not to mention the changing music during the Class Trials in the game. Gameplay consists of School Life, where the students spend their lives in captivity, Deadly Life, when one of your classmates winds up dead and you investigate the murder, and Class Trials, in which you must find out the killer, which then the killer found in executions, especially tailored to them, with no two the same. After completing the normal game, School Mode becomes available, which is a resource collection/dating sim hybrid in which all 15 students live.  It makes for quite an interesting combination, as it has not been seen before, but works well. Overall, Danganronpa: Trigger Happy Havoc is a heck of a time. Just dont get caught in the despair. If you really liked puzzle quest than this game can be enjoyable provided you don't feel lured into going crazy with the PTW dynamics of the game that make a difference with how fast you progress and how strong you get relative to other players.
If you just PvE at your own pace though and non compulsively it's alright. Stay away if you can't since it's designed to drain your wallet if you let it so with that in mind I can't really recommend it.
EDIT1: It takes a while before you can really afford it but the arena mode is where it's at for free to play players. I got so much stuff out of that mode that it really helped me out with all the rest (as in improving my deck to be more competitive with the more difficult challenges and the 'fake' PvP).
I definitely recommend this to puzzle quest fans that are patient enough to get this to work without spending much if any money.
EDIT2: I played and enjoyed this game for over 100 hours (I do idle but still). I can't in my right mind not recommend the game. The game is perfectly playable for free or you can spend some money during sales to speed up your progress and get a good armor.
Basically if you play smart, you'll be fine as FTP and get a very enjoyable experience if this is your kind of game (ergo puzzle/rpg/strategy hybrid). Just check Tacet's guide for a lot of good pointers and you'll be a gem master... someday.
EDIT3: Back to negative. This game is just too much of a mind screw for those that are susceptible to that to recommend, only try it if you can handle playing and enjoying the game at your own pace and are comfortable now having to HAVE everything that there's to get in the game. I've only spent 2 bucks on the game myself and that's all it's ever going to get from me.
EDIT4: Blah... its basically a lot of fun if you like match 3 and trying out different combinations of troops and the like even with the paywall stuff but if you are sufficiently advanced to belong to a good guild... you can get everything eventually. I initially enjoyed this game quite a bit. It a match 3 combat game, like Puzzle Quest. The game plays smoothly, though the AI is not very good. The game has some RPG elements in which you acquire troops, level them up, and build your attack force before each match. It's fairly addictive, and I had fun with the game for a while. The troop management interface needs to be improved - browsing your troop's abilities is frustrating (an Xbox or Playstation constrained interface?) and there's no easy way to compare troops or compare your current army with alternatives. But the ability to build your army and attack other player's armies (the PvP part of the game) is fun and so I enjoyed this game for a while.
However, the real annoyance of the game comes after you have played a bit and start encountering armies that have troop lineups far better than you will ever obtain. I started encountering troops tougher than any I've ever obtained (able to wipe me out quickly). The problem is that you have to obtain keys to unlock chests that contain three random troops, with most troops obtained this way "common" and not very strong - very collecticle card game-like. The good troops are rare, so you can only get them by getting a lot of keys. Yet keys are also uncommon unless you spend a lot of real money.  You can't even grind for keys because every match costs you in-game gold and gold is earned on a fairly slow timer (you earn some as rewards for winning, but you earn less than it costs to play matches). Once I started encountering enemy armies full of epic troops I was toast because I'm not finding epic troops for my army. The real-money costs to buy gold or keys are stupidly high - if you want to play more than a small bit per day you'll need pay more for this game than for a premium game. Some nights I'd be playing well for an hour and then,oh well, I'm out of in-game gold.
So, as much as I like the idea of the game, and enjoy the bits I could play it, the pay-2-win design, and the decisions to intentionally frustrate players to convince you to pay, really limit how much fun you can have with this game. It's still fun, so I give it a slight positive review, but not as enthusiastic as I could be if the game wasn't pay-2-win.

Fantastic game! For Airborne being one of the only MoH games on Steam, it sure does deliver. The gameplay in Airborne was something that I had to get used to (being that you could not really move when ADS), however as soon as I adjusted to the change I felt like I was having a really good time playing. The graphics in this game are amazing especially considering that it was released in 2007. Something that really annoyed me was that in the final cutscene of the game, the graphics go to♥♥♥♥♥♥and it really sucks because I feel like it would have been an amazing sight. One of the things that I really liked about Airborne is the customization you have throughout the campaign; at the beginning of every mission, you can select your loadout accordingly based on the level (for example, you can choose which weapons that would best fit you for the situation) which is something that I really liked. Something that I have never seen before in any singleplayer campaign was the option to select which objectives you can complete in whatever order you want. At the beginning of every mission, you are briefed with the details so you can see the list of objectives you must complete, you also get a chance to preview the level which I felt was a nice touch because paratroopers would do this prior to a landing. Although the graphics were exceptionally good as well as the gameplay, I did run into a few occasional bugs. For example, for whatever reason I would get randomly stuck on a piece of debris or sometimes even a wall which would cause me to reload from my last checkpoint (luckily this happened to me maybe less than five times in my playthrough). Something that I thought was hilarious while playing, is that when you kill a German soldier while they are running, their body will completely ragdoll and fly 20 feet (believe me, I enjoyed every second of this). If you are going to criticize Airborne for it's historical accuracy, you may be disappointed. For example, one of the German units that you fight against are the "Storm Elites" which are completely fictional and look like something out of the Wolfenstein series (although they look extremely badass). All in all, this game was extremely good and I would consider it to be one of the most unique WWII shooter campaigns that I have ever played.

I have 3 big problems with Call of Cthulhu: The Wasted Land. Note that this is coming from a fan of both tactical, small squad combat games and a Cthulhu geek. I am the target market. But the phone-based origin of this game just kills it.
1. The game has issues running. The forums are pretty replete with posts about getting the game to run. I had to spend about an hour getting it to launch and I'm still not sure what finally worked.
2. The UI and controls are lacking. They simply don't seem to work part of the time. I can't explain it any better than that. The PC inputs simply fail to register or do something unintended. Again, this is a common complaint and is almost universal among negative reviews.
3. It's fairly ugly. Actually, it's really ugly. Cthulhu isn't going to be a pretty world and I like the madness mechanic but it's simply not attractive.
Gameplay it's fairly average. It's Xcom lite with few tactical options. Later enemies are overpowered. But it's the fact that the dev failed to put a working UI on the game before launching it on the PC that's unforgivable.
Unique atmosphere, easy to master but short. 30-40 hour playthrough.

Pros:

Cons:
- poor colonist AI can cause unnecessary challenge, for example, a recent loss in energy has caused all of your airlocks to loose power and thus they can't be used, and a team of workers leaving the mines tries to use a nearby airlock, but it doesn't have power so they go to another airlock, it doesn't have power, so they go to another airlock, and so they start to leave. But just as they leave the power comes back on, but do they go back to the airlock? No! they just try to enter another one on the way there but die due to running out of oxygen, and so you loose however many workers were in that team. I reccomend improving colonist AI.
- lack of filters for storage rooms, lets say you want a storage room dedicated towards storing ore because the metal processers are near it, but because a bio dome is closer to it, the colonist will put food into it, and either put ore into a storage room further away from the processers, thus making production time for metal take longer, or they'll just leave the ore outside next to the mines, having the same result, and also possibly loosing some ore because of it being exposed to the outside elements. Adding filters would be great.
- Not being able to create schedules for you colonist, not terrible, but it would be nice to set what hours your colonist will have to work, and when they'll get to relax.
Suggestions:
- adding a rover building, rovers would allow colonist to drive towards their destination when leaving the base, rather than  having to walk the whole way, and possibly dying due to running out of oxygen, the rover would be much faster than a colonist, and to use them you would have to build a rover bay, which would sort of be like a hybrid between an airlock and a production building becuase your rovers would leave using the rover bay. Rovers would cost 2 metal, 2 bioplastic, and 2 semiconducters. Like bots you can buy them from traders or build them, and also like bots they need to be maintained, but unlike bots they don't have a limited lifespan and can only be destroyed by either a lighting bolt, a solar flare, or by a meteorite.
- add meteor showers, they would be VERY RARE, because during these loads of meteors would be crashing down, but would be very spread out, however they would be even less common on frozen worlds due to the dense atmosphere, but more likely on moons due to the lack of an atmosphere.
- a little bit of a background story, maybe saying what year it is, stuff about the planetbase corporation (if you don't know in the challenges it's refrenced that the people setting up the colonies is a corporation called planetbase) and stuff about earth and why people are going out on missions to space to colonize hostile worlds where they will likely die (just a suggestion, and not at all necessary.)
- colonist interacting with each other, I don't know if it's just me but not once have I seen colonist talking to each other.

OK so let me first start off by saying i like the game, And have not finished it. im on act 3 but i felt like i wanted to address things. I can tell a lot of effort was put into the level design. Normal people can sit back and say that the levels look easy to make but i for one know how much time was put into each to make them look BELIEVABLE. The clutter, Items in places they belong. scenes that actually made me look and think, "yeah people worked here" or " this does look like a place Employees would eat"
So here are my suggestions and comments.
- First let me comment on enemy placement. I love most of them, others seem too much like a video game cliche. Its not a bad thing to have periods of space where its calm in a game. because you can work on immersion and atmosphere during them. when a player faces enemy after enemy it makes us rush through the game. it programs our minds to "kill kill kill. if im not killing im doing something wrong." I love the scenes where you put zombies in the vents and water lines. those actually were pretty cool and i was not expecting it at first. You guys obviously know what you are doing there especially when i saw one and didnt have time to react to get my gun so i used the axe. only to get hit from behind by the 2nd one. This felt cool to me because it made it look like some of the scientists tried hiding from the aliens in places you'd expect. Now i dont know how others would comment on the placement of Headcrabs. on One hand, the "jumpscare" nature of them felt cheesy. but then i began to get it. These are creatures that are not strong. They are hunters, and parasites. They NEED to infect things bigger and stronger to survive. so it only makes sense that we dont see them at the end of a hallway, but instead lying in wait, preparing an ambush. Like a real predator. so points for that.
-Now so far the Escort aspect has been interesting. At first i didnt really like it, but now i dont mind. What i think you need, is more justification for WHY we are escorting this security guard. He hasnt really done much that i feel i couldnt. he is an extra gun at times but not usually. which segways me into my next 2 points.
- You need voice acting. I know how difficult and even costly that might be, but it needs to be done. its the easiest way to advance a story without ruining immersion. but its gotta be done well. believably. I remember playing a Skyrim mod that had custom voice acting and it took me out of it IMMEDIATELY. an adult female hunter sounded like a 13 year old girl. And a big guardsman sounded like some punk teen. you dont think about it until you see it done wrong. the voice should sound like how the character looks like they would. many scars war vet? give him a rough and  raspy voice. Brooding strong adult character? something deep and smooth. There are recording studios you can go to to have this done.
- I don't feel like I'm in danger. And no amount of enemies will make it better. So here is an issue alot of games can face thats difficult to fix. some think when they feel this that they need to ramp up the difficulty. but this in the end makes the players angrier about "that ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t" than actually feel like their character is in trouble. And very few times if any have i felt this in a half life game. It usually comes down to the enemies strength, and the players weapons. The dark environments and blood soaked rooms gives off the feeling like you were going for "spooky" or even "dark" but the game doesnt go into "horror". The Axe is a nice take on the traditional crowbar idea. But an axe is too useful in this situation, and if you have some level of skill, the axe is all you need. The fists however i love. low damage, but you can fight in a pinch as a last resort. now on to the guns. This is a military research facility. its understandable the security would be well armed. but not the science team. and bullets would not be so applenty. If you want to increase the need to escort the guard, take away our ammo. not all of it, but most. I like what Resident evil did in this sense. ( early titles that is) they gave a sense of tension because ammo was scarce and you couldnt run and shoot. In this case, i think less ammo would be better. make players find different ways to kill enemies that is less obvious and more challenging. This makes the situations alot more dangerous because every bullet is precious. it makes you think  and look for different options.
-The scientists. running through i saw alot of carnage that seems to have been wrought in a very short time. dead litter the rooms but few times are their killers present until they "port" in. i think a little less carnage and more scenes OF it would be better. step into and area and watch the people die, instead of seeing them already dead and ruining the immersion with the enemies teleporting in. We've seen this all before in HL1 and black mesa. it would be a nice change of pace to SEE the invasion as it unfolds from the start. rather than black out for "some time" and wake up to destruction. show us the chaos, and for an added bonus, make us helpless to it in certain parts. with less ammo theres more chances for us to "F*ck up" and run out before a scene where we really wish we had some. ( side note, if done wrong this can make for a lot of game breaking situations. so more hidden side route options through vents would be needed for the trigger happy players) This will give the sense that the player is helpless. which is what made Fnaf, slender, and Kholat so scary. YOU CANT FIGHT THE MONSTER. you can only run. but what drives it home better, is when the player realizes the devs didnt do that, they did.
Anyway thats my suggestion/ review. ill add more when im done. And i really, REALLY hope you try some of these ideas out. it would make for a very interesting game.

(This review applies only to the single-player portion of the game.)
Released in 2000 and running on the Unreal 1 engine, Rune certainly appeals to nostalgia. It's a primitive-looking third person hack-and-slash with a combat system that's just deep enough to keep fights interesting from beginning to end.
The game plays a bit like a simplified and more forgiving Dark Souls; it demands basic situational awareness and allows for some improvisation, such as using shields or throwing your weapons or other objects (including enemy heads). Your arsenal includes an assortment of swords, maces, and axes, each with a unique Rune power that you can activate with if you have enough Rune energy. I only found a few Rune powers that were actually useful, such as unlimited throwing axes or a sword that would siphon health back to me with each successful strike.
Despite dated graphics, the scale of the environments and the overall level design still hold up today. Sometimes, finding a way forward involved some backtracking and searching, but there was only one instance where I had no idea what to do and had to look things up online.
The story is strictly serviceable. It's a standard hero's journey, but the Norse setting is still somewhat of a rarity in games.
My biggest problem with Rune is that it's slow to start. The first couple areas are just not all that fun, with boring environments and unchallenging enemies (who won't die unless you manage to chop off their heads). If you can make it through the slog, the pace does pick up and the levels and enemies get a lot more interesting.
I should note that I played through the game on Windows 10 and was somehow able to run it at 1080p without any sort of tweaks, up until the very end when the game kept crashing at a cutscene and I had to run the game in "safe mode" to let it run. Your mileage might vary.
Get this game if you're okay with older game design and production values and you want a decently challenging hack-and-slash with a unique setting. If you just want to experience the single-player portion of the game, I would recommend waiting for the game to go on sale.

Man does Rune start off slow. The other folks are correct that you'll slog though dark caves full of gnolls and sewers full of zombies. And those zombies of Hel are very tedious because they can only be killed by decapitation. You'll spend a half-dozen long levels whacking the same baddies over and over hoping for clean headshots.
It's a surprisingly linear game too, but unusual: the hidden crevices and hard-to-spot ropes that might lead to a secret area in another game are actually the *main path* here. You'll spend plenty of time getting lost and backtracking.
Fortunately, some of the levels are quite beautiful, and the game really starts feeling like the adventure you'd expect once you finally emerge from the caves/underworld.
The real fun builds as you explore snow-covered villages and fortresses taking down axe-wielding berzerkers, then trek through dwarven mountain citadels and start collecting some seriously huge weapons. The sense of power and tension keeps building through to the end, and you finally feel like some of your patience through the early levels has paid off. The game takes some interesting turns toward the end too.
So even though long stretches near the beginning can suck, the scope and scale of the journey ends up being pretty impressive. If you have the fortitude for a grand viking melee adventure, this is it.

HOWEVER I have a very important issue with this game that other people have as well. The Insanity System is literally one of the most annoying and disappointing things I have ever seen for a game. I hate horror games, movies etc, but I love it when the scares derive from the PLAYERS in the game, like in this one! But just less than an hour ago the Insanity System has caused me to stop playing due to fear.
I didn't even know this feature was in the game until earlier when I was hiding from a friend playing as Mary (who is TERRIFYING) and a CREEPY AS♥♥♥♥♥♥FACE FLASHED ONTO MY SCREEN and I think I pooped myself. Yes I get scared a bit easily but again, this had the potential to make me enjoy a horror game which I usually don't like as a genre. I play Depth, a game with sharks and the ocean, when I am terrified of BOTH, and I love it, because the scares are natural, balanced and fair.
The Insanity System saps all fun from the experience as the scares are no longer being produced from a balanced, real system. When someone is playing as the monster and you get scared, it's OK because you know they were simply using the game's features, which you understand and have the ability to counteract based on your knowledge of the monster.
Now it's not ALL bad. Some of the features include strange noises/music playing, the lights flickering, and even your keyboard keys losing response. Despite the keys thingy, I think those ideas are alright as long as they create TENSION and not FEAR. The one feature of the Insanity System that RUINS the experience are the face jumpscares (I think it's the people who have died flash onto your screen?) that occur when you have been alive and hiding for a while.
When a face flashes onto your screen, you have absolutely NO idea when, where or why it appears and it's not even controlled by the player as the monster. It's an unfair system that ruins the balance. The monster and humans have an equal environment to win. A face flashing onto your screen is random and unfair.
Overall a very fun game but the Insanity System is making me fear playing it again in case it shows up again. If there was an option to remove it, I would love this a lot more. Would love if the faces got removed or turned into an option, considering how the devs have been aware of the dislike for this feature for about seven to eight months.

NOTE: This game was given to me by the developer for review purposes. This did not influence my review in any way.
Castle Heist: Chapter 1 is an indie first-person 'pure stealth' game. You play the nephew of a member of the Cartographer's Guild who has spent his life planning a heist on the castle town of Redfort in order to steal a powerful artifact from the evil Alchemist.
Graphics - Graphics generally look nice and the game performs well. The trees in particular look very nice. There are a few weird clipping issues when you approach some objects and a fair bit of obvious popping in and out of objects in the distance, and although guard models are reasonably nice and animated well, they don't quite move across the ground properly, with feet sometimes floating or moving under the level of the ground. And for some reason your character always carries around a map in his hands, making it basically impossible for you to see anything useful when you look down. In the second area I fell off a cliff while trying to see what was down there because the map was in the way!
The game world is very sparsely populated with identical guards, and there are invisible walls preventing you from departing the action areas, but the models that are used are quite sharp and the game does generally look quite nice, if a little lifeless. When ascending stairs or navigating some of the more crowded areas (e.g. the market or kitchen) I found it was very easy to get stuck on game objects, requiring me to back away.
Sound - Sound effects are lacklustre, with loud footstep sounds that don't sound that good making any movement sound like you're scuffing your steel-cap boots through piles of gravel. There is also pretty terrible voice acting at the beginning and when you reach certain points in the game, with no way to skip it. I'd have preferred simple text instead.
The music is mostly okay, though, with a suitably medieval feel to it most of the time. I did wonder about the out-of-place jazz number in Redfort at night, though.
Gameplay - Castle Heist plays like a simple version of Thief without the combat. There are no sound or vision indicators telling you when guards might catch you, and it's not always obvious when you're hidden or not, but the basic stealth mechanic usually works well enough to make the game fun.
Controls are simple: WASD to move, shift to crouch (no option for toggle, unfortunately), and space to jump. Mouse looks around, and since there's no combat and no way to use anything, the mouse buttons don't do anything. Since crouching is the most useful action in the game and there's no toggle setting, I mapped it to a mouse button instead, making it easier to move while crouched for extended periods.
Pros:
+ Nice looking graphics with mostly very good models and textures (available from the Unity asset store)
+ Level design makes sense; the developer has made good use of the available assets
+ Stealth mostly works well
+ Mostly good atmospheric music (from Incompetech and Sleep Facing West), except for the weird jazz piece that is completely out of place
+ Two achievements (both hidden)
Cons:
- Poor sound effects and pretty bad voice acting; the footsteps in particular are annoying
- Movement and clipping issues, and objects not interacting with the game world properly (e.g. guards hovering or walking in the ground)
- There's no way to tell when someone can see or hear you until it's too late, making it more frustrating than it should be
- 'Always-on' map when you look down is a terrible design decision; it just gets in the way
- Lacks polish
I'm a big fan of stealth games, but they also frustrate me a lot when the stealth aspects are done poorly. Thankfully, that's not the case here.
Castle Heist: Chapter 1 is very short: probably a bit too short for the asking price, as it can be completed in less than an hour. It plays more like a tech. demo than a game, but it is just Chapter 1 at this stage.
Caste Heist has its glitches, but the developer has done a pretty good job of fashioning an interesting enough stealth mission from some generally very nice assets. It's not the best stealth game out there by a long shot, but it's a good start; I do want to see what happens next.
Recommended for anyone wanting a quick fix of stealth gameplay, who doesn't mind a few glitches.

Castle Heist: Chapter 1 is a short stealthy walking simulator game that introduces the plot of the Castle Heist series.
Once you start playing the game, you are immediately introduced to the story through a narrative text. At first, I felt like the voice acting of the narrative was being a bit over-acted, but after multiple playthroughs, it grew on me. The game plays as mostly a walking simulator, but with stealth aspects.
Each area has a map that you are given with notes, and marks on it of where you need to go next. If you rush through the objectives, you can finish the game in less than 15 minutes, but I suggest playing the game more like a walking simulator, and just taking your time, and exploring all the areas. Right now, there are a couple achievements you can unlock by exploring, but I would like to see more achievements added to encourage more exploration.
Right now, there isn’t any reason to replay the game, unless you missed the achievements, but I did wind up playing through it 4 times since it is such a short game. Chapter 1 is a good, but brief introduction into the Castle Heist plot, but as expected from an episodic series, you won’t get any closure, so I'm looking forward to chapter 2. If you’re looking for a game to simply play and finish, you won’t enjoy this game to its full potential. However, if you’re in the mood to take your time to explore a short, but sweet, stealthy walking simulator game for a reasonable price, it’s a decent purchase.

I think VoiceBot is a really nifty utility and may help add a new level of playability with some games and could also be helpful with a variety of software.
If deciding to get VoiceBot, as it works with using the Windows Speech Recognition feature, I would suggest to first go into the settings, click on the Speech Setup button then go through wizards for “Set up microphone” then “Train your computer to better understand you”. This can take a few minutes to do, but it can help to ensure that VoiceBot will better be able to understand your spoken voice commands.
I grabbed VoiceBot recently and so far (as I post this review) I’ve only yet made profiles to work with a couple of programs (such as my FireFox Browser and a media-player) along with trying it with a couple of games.
There is a slight delay when speaking a voice-commands and when the command is performed, but I think that VoiceBot could work great with some games or simulators (perhaps games or sims that are more slower paced, casual or turn-based) that may have a lot of key-commands and don’t require very quick reactions of pressing of keys.
And though VoiceBot can also be set-up to do mouse-actions (mouse-button clicks and mouse-movements), if a game requires quick and precise use of the mouse then I think it may be better control the mouse with your hand instead in that case.

Alright, so I got this software today and after some time playing around with it I think i'm confident in saying this.
It's good, by my guess it gets what I say right about 92% of the time
Pros:
1) it's easy to create, edit, delete macros
2) it's convienient setting it up for games where you aren't in competitive play
3) is allowed to be used without steam running
4) it can be really fun when it works
Cons:
1) when it doesn't want to listen, it really doesn't want to listen
-by that I mean, it will stay wrong for a good while, I believe it's partly the fault of my crappy mic, but it likes to be stubborn when i want to give it a command sometimes.
2) it doesn't always see a program
-What does this mean? It means that not all your programs are visible to it, meaning if you connect it to the exe file it won't work, it'll simply say you have nothing selected. I found a simple work around which is to not have any exe file selected, but that just means it'll allow you to use those commands for the computer itself.
3) definitely not competitive friendly
-By that I mean to press and release a key, the program automatically takes 25 ms or longer, no less than that, perhaps in an update the dev team can speed up the response to allow for faster response time, allowing it to better be used in shooters and mmo's.
That being said now I'll go into my experience
I decided, to test it out, i'd play an mmo, i used Nostalrius (a stand alone private server for world of warcraft) and struggled for four hours wondering why voicebot couldn't find the server, i had the exe file connected and everything, simply put, if voicebot can't find it, take the link to the exe file off, that will allow you to use the commands in game. Maybe in a later version of voicebot that'll change, but I have no idea.
After playing for about a good three hours I have found a bit of struggling, it seems because im down here in california, the voice recognition doesn't like how i say 2 or 6 and definitely doesn't like it when i have two similar words like 6 and sit, to fix this i went through the "train your computer" that's built in about three to four times, after that two worked better but the computer still saw 6 as sit, so i changed 6 to dit, after a bit longer of playing and getting used to using commands, I died three times to my own fault in miscalculating the delay, I found that 1 stopped working as a command, I no longer was able to use it during battle and for a short time after. This could be due to my microphone being a seriously low quality one, mixed with the fan in my window it could be.
Overall this product is useful, not to be completely dependent, but to make things a little easier, it can get pretty crazy with multiple bindings to the same command. All in all it was fairly easy for me to get down using upwards of 28 commands for the game when i set it up one at a time, even fun.
Overall, I'd rate this a 7/10, that may change once i get a better quality microphone and if the devs ever speed up the amount of time it takes to initiate the commands.

With so many options, it is easy to increase your overall standing in the game. And all without spending a dime.  Instead of quitting when things hit 50, fight through and take a stand.

The short: Text-heavy, but with excellent writing. Smooth combat, lots of options, extremely flexible character creation model. Recommended, particularly for RPG and tactics gamers.
The Director's Cut of Shadowrun: Dragonfall is a lighthearted, fun, and extremely playable RPG.  While visual effects are a little on the sparse side (no between-act cinematics a la Diablo here!), the world nevertheless feels like a living thing, and it's a pleasure to explore. The game's writing does an excellent job of keeping a player engaged, and develops a very solid, likeable, and extremely replayable setting. Hacking ('decking'), close combat, guns, and magic all mix together into a variety of player strategies, providing a broad set of options to get past each mission's obstacles.
The gameplay feels smooth and solid, particularly with the Director's Cut revamp of the user interface. Everything is presented in an intuitive and easy-to-navigate manner, and the combat feels similar to other successes like XCOM, Fire Emblem, and other grid-based tactical games.
The real advantage of Shadowrun Returns, as always, is the potential for user-created content. Shadowrun Returns is more of a foundation than anything else--with a handy, built-in campaign to show what it's capable of. The original Shadowrun Returns had a handful of extremely popular user-created campaigns available in short order, and I have high hopes for the Director's Cut content to come from Shadowrun's fan base. With these, the possibilities are endless. Although I have high hopes for future campaigns coming out of Harebrained Schemes, I'm sure that the game's fanbase will provide more than enough content to keep me occupied for a long, long time.

I'll review only the single player adventure.
TL;DR - the game is not terrible, but it is not worth 10$ (i got it for like 50 cents in some RPG bundle) and the 12-14 hours of gameplay is very repetetive. No wonder that less then 9% of buyers even finished it.
The game bases on some version of Odin-Loki-Ragnarok mythos however it does very bad job using the viking (or Northsmen) culture. You will spend on a ship about 2 minutes. No brutal raids on innocent foreigners, no social life at all and drinking mead is just a sad, lonely first aid kit. Its just a walking simulator with poorly designed battles.
The game mostly fits to the same category as Half Life (publshed 3 years earlier) - you keep walkin, jumping and fighting. Puzzles/jumping -> a couple of fights -> puzzles/jumping -> fighting and so on and so on. Unlike Half Life though the plot is very  simplistic and not engaging; the third person perspective destroys the illusion of every-man protagonist (who also never speeks and has no personality at all); most of the weapons are very similiar and you can basically  just hold to the latest-strongest weapon available; most of the enemies blindly charge at you (or stand in one place - the game is insanely buggy); and the landscapes are mostly grey, boring dungeons and mountain tunnels.
It wasn't a waste of time but I deffinitely do not recomment this game even though it has some great reviews on Steam (I assume nostalgia-based).

First thing I want to say is I have played this game A LOT before I got it on Steam so keep that in mind.
Now, there were a handful of games that me and my brothers played together a lot in my childhood, and every single one of these games brought many hilarious and awesome memories that I still remember.
Rune was one of these games.
My and my brothers played over LAN quite a bit, so I recommend playing this game with friends over private servers or LAN.
Its a blast to play this game with others, especially if you know the people your playing it with well. The fact that this game is so old makes it even more fun for me to play even now. It's hilarious when you chop your enemy's weapon arm off, because now thay have no arm, so all they can do is run! In a multiplayer match you can start to feel super awesome as you find things on the map with high damage and other items that increase your health, and so on and so forth.
The game's graphics and animations aren't what this game is good for. Its great because the combat is so simple, yet so hard and complicated to use at times.
Even though the game still has open online servers, no one really plays on them anymore. The people who actually play this game online is more like a community of 10-20 people who all know eachother because they met online in Rune.
Even though the servers aren't really populated anyomre, it means that you can usually find a server and play it with your friends usually without the worry of anyone else joining it.
Even if you don't like the multiplayer there's still an AMAZING storyline with a very awesome Norse setting, and it really does make you feel like an epic viking warrior. I won't spoil any of the actual storyline, but the story itself is very epic.
The story mode is also great because the difficulty of the campaign does start to get increaseingly difficult, but how does your character level up? Its simple. He doesn't.
You never level up with skill points, and you don't have an inventory, its just a hack and slash adventure going through the game. You get tougher by finding slightly better weapons slowly throughout the game, as well as items that increase your health a tiny bit and what not. But, even with those better weapons, enemies are still always gaining in difficulty, as they could still kill you in only a few hits. In the beginning of the game, enemies are no real threat and are killed easilly with your weak starting weapons. But near the end of the game, even though you have the best weapons that you can get, enemies are extremely difficult to kill sometimes and can take you out easilly if your not careful.
Overall, I highly recommend this game to anyone, especially if you like games based on a Norse setting.

This game has a really amazing concept to it. It has great horror factors to it, hardly relying on jumpscares as its main focus of fright. It also has unique types of Monsters you can play as; the Lurker (completly blind, but can set audio traps to pin-point where survivers went and manifest into a solid being), the Phantom (another blind Monster, but you can see surivers hinding behind walls or objects once you first see them) and Mary (a spectral girl similar to the Grudge spirit that is always visible, walks very slowly, but has a frenzy attack if she focuses on a surviver for a certain amount of time). Alas, this game is still ridden with terrible flaws that make it hard for me to recommened this game to anyone.
FIrst off, they made the mosters waaaaaaaaaaaay overpowered.  They can kill you in one hit and there's no life meter for the survivers. You can set how many lifes you have, but they're shared with the other survivers. Secondly, the survivers have absolutly no way to defend themselves. All you have equiped is your flashlight and whatever you find while scowering whatever place you spawn in (keys, hammers, and crowbars). There are no weapons for you to get to defend yourself from the Monsters. Thirdly, respawing is broken. There's been a few times while playing this game with some of my friends that one of them respawned right next to the Monster. Lastly, there's hidden effects that happen to you, while some are accecptible, others are not. One I think is okay is where your character will start halucenating if your flashlight's battery is low. The other is how stamina is both there and it's not. Sometimes you can run just fine, but then you halt to a walk and can only sometimes run. There's also no meter for your stamina.
If this game could get some fixes, I would recommend this game. As it is right now, I just can't justify it as a good game.

Great style, a good story, and an amazingly good set of characters. In mystery games I can usually guess the result pretty early, often just based on motives and genre tropes, but Danganronpa surprised me several times. Every murder was different and interesting.
Some fairly minor negatives:
* Although it would've increased the needed budget immensely, I can't help but wish that there were some real branching paths, maybe even ways to ensure that chosen characters never die. Danganronpa is mostly linear.
* I didn't like the trial minigames too much. Sometimes I would know the correct answer, but it'd still take several attempts to catch onto the obscure way that I needed to express it in order to advance. And the game mostly spells out the answers for you during the trial, so there isn't a lot of real crime-solving from you the player. (Note: I used medium difficulty for everything.)
* The soundtrack was sometimes repetative and grating.
* Sometimes the game likes to give flashbacks to things that happened literally minutes earlier. Some of this seems to be due to the game being structured like an episodic anime, inexplicably. There was one point where the exact same scene was shown 4 times in the span of 10 minutes. Annoying.
* Infrequently, there are quiz questions, and several of these were clearly aimed at Japanese people, asking things that non-Japanese people couldn't really be expected to know without looking up.
* The extra gamemode after beating the game is interesting, but it's sooo grindy.

So in summary, I think it's an extremely well-written and stylish visual novel, especially notable for its memorable characters. But it has only a light amount of actual gameplay, adding to the style more than it creates real challenge. Despite the flaws I mentioned, I did enjoy it immensely from start to finish, so I'd give it a score of 10/10.

The player continues where the story of

Despite the developer's insistence to continue with a mostly silent protagonist, this time there are many eccentric characters to accompany the player on their journey, whether real or hallucinatory. The level design is also much more improved, containing many differing areas that do not overstay their welcome. My favourite sections of the game are the "dream sequence" type locations where developer, Frictional Games, really begins to show off their creativity.
There are no weapons with defensive capabilities, the only way to avoid enemies is to rely on stealth or through environmental elements, yet the enemies found in

which is a welcome change. The puzzles are also not as strict or as involved and the solutions to these can mostly be found within the same room rather than having to venture across the map to find that one relevant item.
The sound design is fitting and the inclusion of additional voice actors, who can actually act, fill in what would otherwise be a dull and empty journey due to the silent protagonist trope. The directional sound for enemies is accurate enough that I was able to know when the area behind a door was clear of a patrolling monster.
Some issues I took with

Frictional Games seem to have learned a lot with the development of
as the game plays far better than

but, for me,
is where Frictional Games really hit their stride. The horror found here is far more psychologically subtle, where the player will be questioning whether the events happening right now are real or not.

Only writing this because the negative reviews of this game amaze me.  The two main complaints I see are:
1)The AI cheats.
2) It's a pay to win game.
First, the AI doesn't cheat.  There is an element of luck involved in what new gems drop into the board, but it's absolutely fair.  Making smart plays will almost always mitigate the effect of luck on a game as well.  If you're counting on a lucky gem or skull to fall in place for you, then you're the one who's put you in the bad spot of relying on luck, and there is/was likely a better play available.  When I lose, it is almost always due to poor decisions, not poor luck.
Second, I've logged over 300 hours, eclipsed level 100, gotten the second most expensive armor set in the game, and done all of it without spending one cent of real world money.  I have never encountered any situation in the game that made me feel like I hit a paywall.  I've earned over 500 gems (the real world currency) just through guild rewards.  Earning gold becomes rediculously easy after the first few hours of gameplay.  It really is free to play and free to win, I promise.

MOH airborne is one of the best games in the series. It's unique, it's fun, and it plays fairly well, but there are some problems you need to take into account:
-Weird physics. Enemies will fling 20 feet if you shoot them while they're running, and the ragdolls look kinda funky.
-LOTS of bugs. There's the infamous "video card not supported" glitch that you need to fix to run MOHA on most modern PC's, but there's also problems such as random missing models and such, or characters being %100 pitch black. These glitches can all be fixed, but nonetheless they're still annoying.
I would most definetly recommend this game to anyone that likes WW2 shooters, but be prepared to deal with the issues listed above. I give this game credit because it still holds up to today's standards given that it's 10 years old, and will always be one of my favorites.

*Its really dark.
*Enemy placement/progression is inconsistant and odd.

Other Criticism (stuff that will probably be added in later)
*Extra chapters (there are only 6)
*Voice acting/a story there are no orginal lines recorded for this mod.

POSITIVES (actual good stuff)

I like all things Cthulhu-ian.

In Call of Cthulhu: The Wasted Land, it's basically the characters you control being dropped off for a happy-go-lucky jaunt of shooting eldritch horrors and cultists in the face, learning things man was never meant to know, and spamming lots of Psychoanlysis checks.
Really though, Call of Cthulhu: The Wasted Land is what you pay for. It's a good game, but short and sweet. It has it's replay value, but for most people, once you finish it you probably won't be touching it again, save for the extra missions. As a game, it holds up well, although it's not entirely faithful to the Mythos (we all know that the invesitgators would get their s*** slapped by these things). But, relating to the Call of Cthulhu tabletop game by Chaosium? These are all characters you may very well expect to see in any other CoC tabletop campaign.
I'd say that if you're looking for a quick game with some interesting survival elements and a fun battle system, pick this one up. But if you're looking for something a bit more in-depth and drawn out in your RPG strategy collection, this is a game that wont' be satisfying you any time soon.

Fun game if you like fast advance-wars style games. Not just another gimmicky Cthulhu plot device, but rather a setting deeply entrenched (get it? It's WWI) in the style and writing of Lovecraft. Just be warned, this is exactly the same as the mobile game, which is why it has a mobile price - so don't expect too many bells and whistles, or a gamelife to match its PC relatives.
My biggest complaint is the interface is not very mouse/keyboard friendly. If you have a windows tablet then I'd highly recommend playing on that, since it's much more natural. It's also a lot more responsive than the Android version (from my experience on a gs4).

A long time ago these controls sucked hard, but with new update it is much better now. The atmosphere feels great with Lovecraftian themes, not just from Cthulhu but also from Herbert West: Reanimator. Gamplay wise its a LOT like XCOM. Its a port straight from a mobile game, so don't expect triple A graphics. Has some pretty good music in it. Overall, if you like XCOM type gamplay and lovecraft then this is the game for you.

I start with the biggest problem with this game, and the reason of the "not recommended" stamp.
It's the price. I can't believe how is that possible this game is 20€ without sale.
There are AAA games with lower price, and even indie games what are better made than this.
You can't compare this game to them. The realistic price would be "free" , but keeping in mind this is
a little indie developer team and needs money, I say 3-4€ at most. It doesn't worth more.
Well, Steam keeps it at sale nowadays, but even on 66% it's a bit overpriced IMO, and the sale is just a bait.
Now let's talk about the actual gameplay.
Pros:
-The concept is good.
-The atmosphere is spooky (at least in the first few hours).
-The three monsters are different, they are well made.
-Some interesting map.
-There's  big potential in this game, if the developers won't abandon it.
-And the biggest pro of this game is that, it's very fun to play with friends...
Cons:
-... but without them it can be horrible, because it can easily lose the "fun factor".
-As I said, after a few hours it is just not scary., you get used to it.
-It's a bit unbalanced, if you don't learn fully how the monsters work.
-Very, very unoptimized. I mean the graphics are bad, the maps are small, and the fps is horrible. Great combo.
-As a survivor all you do is searching for keys, and opening doors. That's it. Of course you run from
the monster, and hide, but to progress you only need to search, search, search...
-Opening doors, closets, drawers is ridicoulusly bad. You can fight 10-20 seconds with a simple door to open it.
Of course you can learn  to open them faster, but maybe it should be more important to make this usable, in a
game where half of the gameplay is opening doors...
-There are a lot of bugs. I mean a bug can appear anywhere. Sometimes the server just freezes. Or the game runs with 1 FPS,
or you can't load the map.  Or the chat doesn't work. Or you can't login. Or you can't click on anything in the menu. Anything
that can happen,  in this game will hapen. (Murphy's law?)
- The maps are repetitive. You can even mix up maps, because some part of them are just copy pasted from
an other map. They are not varied, they are boring.  Like there's a room full of  tables... then a room full of chairs... then a             room full of closets.. etc. (but as i said in the pros there are a few with good theme, and atmosphere)
-The whole game feels amateurish. For 3-4€ I would say it's okay. But for 20€ it's just a giant NOPE.
So when I suggest buying it?
- If you like scary games, and you have friends to play with.
- When it's on sale and it's price is just a  few € , or is in a pack with other games.

The P.R. on this game says it relies on "problem solving instead of mindless gore and violence." Maybe so, but this game makes the player work too hard to do something as simple as getting through a locked door. In fact, that's all this game is about, getting from one side of the room to the other, or finding a key to access the next locked room with another locked door. An additional problem is the English subscript. A phrase was written, "There is know way." Hmm. Might we infer this game was not created in an English speaking country? I found it boring. The price was relatively cheap, but this game relies too much on moral sermonizing and an ethical "message" as a "reveal" at the end that supposedly makes the whole (boring) adventure worth the effort (and the money). That's not why I play games. I play for the exhilaration of winning against hard opponents and difficult environments. If I want sermonizing, I can go to church. You have no weapons, (though there are lots of monsters that ought to be killed) you must solve puzzles that are unnecessarily complicated (though the pay-off for solving the puzzle is very minor) and there is no spectacular "Hurray" moment after you figure it all out and the game closes. This game ought to be a add-on or a trailer for full-fledged adventure game, but not a stand alone. It's just too deficient in its content, mode and storyline to rate all the thumbs up it has been given.

Past experiences should have taught me to steer clear of this cancer of the gaming world that goes by the label of 'Free to Play' games. Sadly, I find myself unable to resist them way too often. Thus I tried Gems of War. The wisest course of action would be to abandon this abomination and prevent further headaches. But then my Steam account would forever be besmirched by my horrible achievement completion rate in this game (30% at the moment).
I fear my pride won't let me take the easy way out.
This game has many of the usual annoying Free to Play aspects we all love. The daily login bonus, popups to inform you about the newest ways to spend your money and sure enough not only the shop button but another button which leads to the aforementioned deals. Because the popup isn't sufficient.
There are worse offenders out there. I know that because I played some of them. That doesn't absolve the developers of Gems of War. They knew what they created when they did it. So shame on them!
As for the game itself, it is a long tedious grind. Basically you assemble your army by collecting cards which represent the individual troops. Each one has different abilities, some of which are actually interesting and allow fun combinations and synergies.
But then you have to level these cards up. And that takes effort. The currency needed can be bought (of course, lol) or acquired in the match-3 gamemode this all is about. The latter method takes a lot of effort. Especially if you want to swap out your cards from time to time, to experiment or because you found a better combination of troops you want to use.
The artwork is mediocre and the dialogue is downright horrible. The protagonist mostly speaks in one-word-sentences. "Why?", "Okay." and "Hmm..." make up a big portion of his contributions. Great! I always wanted to play a halfwit who is barely able to talk.
The way you get screwed over constantly by the cheating AI is another bottomless source of joy.
Update: After playing this for quite some time now, my opinion has changed slightly to the better. Once I had a decent pool of troops and the souls to level them up to a usable level the gameplay became significantly less frustrating. But therein lies a huge designflaw. If you have to grind a game for 20+ hours before it gets fun I can't recommend it.

This game has been sitting on my wishlist for a while, and I finally decided to pick it up during a sale. Reading through some of the other reviews, especially the negative ones, there are some valid claims. This game is all about high level management, and you will get frustrated because your colonists continue to load tomato after tomato into a vending machine, instead of a diverse group of vegetables. There is no way to prioritize how many bots of each you want made, just how many bots total. And it can get rather arduous to micromanage and try and get everything running like a well-oiled space base.
But the game still plays great. I've established bases on all four of the planet types, and it's a blast getting more colonists and managing base expansion. Overall, the game feels like a spiritual successor to Firefly Studios' Space Colony, but with a much broader scope. Your ship lands, a few colonists get off, and from there you string together a handful of solar panels and plastic domes in an attempt to turn a profit. It's a great way to spend a few hours, and while there are a few frustrating points, I don't think it comes close to overshadowing what Planetbase is and what it achieves. And with a little extra polish from the developers, they could really take the game that much further.

This was my original review of this game, and I had recommended it to others:  "Fun game--great to relax to.  No need to buy extras unless you really want to.  In early play in the game it costs more to play than you "earn" by winning, but play through and soon earning plenty to play and get extras."
Now, I no longer recommend this game to others, and although I still play some, I am very close to quitting.  Here are just a few of my thoughts:
So far, I do not like anything about this new update.  The previous update was a degradation of the game, but this one has taken the game to a point where I feel like I am "slogging through" an unpleasant experience rather than enjoying an engaging fun game.  When I started playing the game it was relatively easy to understand the play and logic, and it was a nice way to relax after a day of work.  It took some thought and strategizing to improve your game, building teams for different purposes and using them to advantage under differing circumstances.  Leveling up is now too complicated, and even the "buying" rewards with earned glory or gems, etc, has now essentially become so complcated or expensive (seemingly targeted at the pay to play audience), I no longer have incentive to play enough to "earn" enough to buy a reward of armour, additional character or new weapon.
Now everything that was relaxing and casual (and fun) about the game has been taken away or changed.  I have previously recommended this game to others, however, do not believe will do so again.  The last update seemed geared towards smart phone or tablet users, and the appearance of the cards/characters changed significantly.  Most of the character/card appearance updates were not positive.
Please bring back the original game as it was--roll back to a couple of updates ago and release it as a "version 1" or "classic".  I did like the addition of new kingdoms, rewards, arena, and maps. It would have been better to have rolled out a different version ("gold" or "championship" or even as simple as "gems of war 2") to make these changes, rather than so drastically altering the play of what had been a very fun, enjoyable and relaxing game.

Has ever a franchise fallen so far as the Medal of Honor series? Once the king of first-person shooters, I know that many consider the 2010 iteration the nadir of the franchise, but for me Airborne Assault was always the worst game of the series. While the 2010 game was a cookie-cutter clone of the Modern Warfare games, it at least was competently done and halfway fun to play; Airborne isn't even that.
In fairness, the developers did try to iterate on the formula with the addition of the eponymous airborne drops; parachuting down from a plane, the player can choose where to start each level. In practice, however, this completely strips the level of any pacing and intensity. I've no love of the overly-scripted sequences of other modern FPS games, but some direction is desired. Never sure where the player was coming from (or headed towards), the level design is unexciting, with a great deal of repetition in appearance and mission goals. There's no good flow; no rise and fall of action that kept me emotionally invested. It was just one nearly identical room after another filled with a too-limited variety of enemies. Perhaps had the developers invested even further into the concept - had the game larger levels and a more open-world sandbox experience - they might have created something worth playing. Unfortunately, they were not quite so innovative and the end result was a shallow and mediocre experience.
It's an okay FPS game but the gun sounds are good since they sound like their real world equivalents. Better if you save your money and buy it during a sale for the sake of nostalgia.
