Damned has the potential to be a good game. Unfortunately there are some...damning...problems...heh..heh...Okay I'll get serious.
Damned is a 5 player COOP game. 4 players versus 1 monster. The player's goal is to escape, while the monster's goal is to kill them. The players goal consists of running around the map looking for keys to unlock doors until you get the required items to leave through the escape(A hammar or a crowbar, and the Silver Key). The monster has to kill all the survivors before they escape. Sounds easy right? Well currently there are 3 monsters, and they are pretty balanced in my opinion. Of course, you can be a♥♥♥♥♥♥and just kill everyone off the bat on certain maps, if you know what you're doing, but that's no fun. It's way better to play it smart and try to scare the players rather than just kill them. And holy♥♥♥♥♥♥is this game scary. I didn't think a multiplayer game could be scary but I was wrong. The way the monsters are designed and the atmosphere of the levels make this a very tense experiance.
Sounds good right? Unfortunatly the game is buggy. It was an Early access title, but for some reason they decided it was ready for full release.
The game runs at 25-60 FPS on my rig(Specs below), up and down constantly depending on where I am and what I'm looking at. It can be very distracting and take me out of the game. Sometimes the game will just lock to 30FPS and you have to restart your computer to fix it. No idea why, devolopers haven't explained it, they just gave the solution.
I host most of the games with my friends because I have the better connection(105Megabit down, 20Megabit up), but that doesn't stop the game from lagging. Normally in other games when someone hosts something they don't lag locally, but the people connecting to him will. Not in this game, everybody feels it, sometimes the game will just freeze for no reason. This game runs off of 9Heads servers(They are located in Brazil), meaning you have to create an account, and log in from within the game. That means whenever something happens to their servers, you can't play the game.
Now, the most damning problem my friends and I run into when trying to run this game happens before the game even starts. We all get in a lobby, select our favorite characters, select a map, start it up. Host loads in just fine, waiting for other players. The other players get to the screen that says "Waiting for the host to start the game" only...they haven't really loaded...they're still loading(At least I hope that's what's going on), but for some reason they show that screen and their game is frozen. They can't do anything until it finally loads. Loading times can be anywhere from 10 seconds to 5 minutes. We're so used to this that we routinely ask if anyone is frozen when we start the game. "I'm good" "I'm good" "Frozen..." "Alright let's wait..." When the player can finally press TAB and see the player list, they've loaded in and we can start playing.
The devolopers are kind of active on the forum. They try to help people with problems but they aren't permenant solutions, problems always come back. They say they're working on an update, but don't have an ETA on when. Only "This year". At the time of writing this review(2/19/2015) we haven't gotten an update since November 5th, 2014. I think Namco Bandai's new business model when it comes to updating its classics is one that involves respecting but putting aside some obsolete design practices such as lives (which, while still present, don't matter at all) in favor of three main focuses: progressive design ideas (dozens of ghosts), rekindling interest in still-relevant practices (points), and sensory overload. If you also own a 7th generation console that isn't the Wii, you can experience this first-hand in an arguably stronger fashion, at least in the latter focus, sensory overload, with Galaga Legions and Galaga Legions DX, both sister titles to Pac-Man Championship Edition DX and all part of the Namco Generations series that no longer exists. While the Galaga update is almost unbearably intense but still quite good, Pac-Man Championship Edition DX+ feels muted in tone by comparison but even more of a blast to play. It's clear that the design team were unafraid of implementing the new ideas in an attempt to keep a classic game fresh. Here, they throttle the gameplay forward as you use the familiar large glowing pellets to gobble up many, many more ghosts than you're used to. Gone are the days of looking out for every turn as you run and hide from the ghosts out to get you. Now, you're actively searching for ghosts to join the posse that follows you wherever you go. Some search for you, others lay sleeping in the lanes, but as soon as they spot you they abandon whatever it is they're doing and join the conga line, practically waiting for you to charge in when they turn blue. One of the most satisfying gameplay experiences one can have is saving up a DMV line of ghosts and suddenly turning on them and eating each and every one of them. The ghosts are no threat. Your real enemy is time, and speed. Once the game gets going so fast you can't keep up to make proper turns, Pac-Man careens out of your control.

If you're a living, breathing, actual human being over the age of ten, then most likely you've played 'Pac-Man' at one time or another. I wish there was a third.. "meh" option. Overall I'd say its a good game, especially given that it's free. I play a bit every day and it keeps me occupied, but I have some gripes that I need to air out here.
1) It's pay to win. Bleh.
2) It really really needs better AI. Right now the AI is pretty dumb and easily exploitable. This is the formula:
If 5 match then take it
else if 4 match then take it
else if 3 skulls match then take it
else if attack skill ready then use it
else match 3 of a useable color then take it
else match 3 of an unuseable color
3) The AI gets a major handicap in the form of free moves. Because the AI is so dumb, the AI opponent is given numerous extra moves in the form of predetermined matches that fall after the player moves. This results in the computer more often than not getting 3-4 turns for every one of the player. Sometimes these extra moves, rather than being a result of a 4 or 5 match, are simply given to the AI at random. While this certainly boosts the difficulty, I would much rather just have a smarter AI than a cheating one. Many of the matches become ridiculously one-sided after the first move by the player, which rather than being a fun challenge, is just a bore at that point.
I wish the devs would have taken all the time they used to compensate for the AI and put it into improving the AI.
That's really my main gripe. The gold limit on playtime has yet to actually bother me, given that this isn't the sort of game you sit down and play for hours on end. Heaven help you if you do.

While those with even a passing knowledge of Norse mythology may twitch a bit at this game's plot, which centers around the typical "mistaking Loki for Satan" nonsense that happens when people need to shove Abrahamic good vs. evil conflicts into pantheonic mythology, and Hel's realm is less cold misery and more fire-and-brimstone Hell, but the plot isn't what you're there for in Rune.
Gameplay wise, I would roughly describe Rune as being what would happen if you took an unpolished early prototype of Dark Souls, removed all the RPG elements, and replaced them with platforming sections. Early game is all about dodging, blocking, and timing your strikes, as even the most basic enemies will cut through you in seconds if you aren't careful. At around the mid-game point it drops "blocking" from the list as all of the weapons become two-handers and your only defense is to not be in front of your enemy's weapon when they swing.
The levels are nicely varied, going from generic nordic village for the tutorial to a deep sea cavern, the lava-filled pits of Hel, goblin caves, a snowy mountain fortress, quasi-Steampunk dwarven valleys, and finally into Loki's realm before returning to the now-charred ruins of your generic nordic village for the showdown with the final boss.
Unfortunately while most of the game is quite fun, it does succumb in the end to what is sometimes known as "Xen Syndrome," the tendancy for otherwise good games to have a sudden dip in quality towards the end as money or time or interest runs out. The enemies lose what little sense of balance they had, with even the most basic mooks able to kill you in three shots as they swarm you by the dozen and food becomes more and more scarce, a few platforming sections that could reasonably be described as impossible (eventually forcing me to cheat after the dozenth death in a row on two seperate occasions) and a final boss that is little more than a standard enemy with three times as much health and arbitrary immunity to magic.
All told though, despite the sour taste of the last few bites I enjoyed Rune, and would absolutely recommend retro enthusiasts to pick it up.

Rune is definitely a hidden gem from the early 2000s, a must-play for fans of Norse Mythology. It's basically a 3rd person hack 'n slay title garnished with some interesting jumping/crawling sections, here and there even with some simple puzzles. The action is raw and gory, decapitated enemies are a common sight too. Expect some pixel blood to flow.
The level design is pretty decent as well, ranging from mysterious, creature-infected dungeons over to goblin working settlements or viking-populated fortresses. Again, expect many severed limbs and other body parts on those premises.
The only downside in my opinion is the more or less unspectacular final section of the game and the ending. The developers could have done a better job, but some other players may have a different view on this one.
The Good:
+ Decent story and level design
+ Graphics (they were good at the time)
+ Authentic Viking setting and atmosphere
+ Fast-paced and uncomplicated gameplay
+ Gore and Blood
+ Multiplayer
The Bad:
- The latest sections in the game feel quite unpolished and rushed
The Ugly:
- Some issues on modern systems like sudden freezes. But I blame Steam for this, not the developers.
Overall a truly pleasant hackfest experience, you'll definitely enjoy it.

Fun, yet challenging, take on the dark post-apocalyptic theme. A simple concept executed with a brilliant balance of complexity and addictabillity.
Easy, mediumm, or hard, you only get 60 seconds - hence the name of the game - to collect supplies (including your loved ones) from your house, before a mad dash to take cover in your underground bomb-shelter as your neighbourhood is being nuked above.
You can perfect your gathering skills in Scavenger mode, hone your stamina skills in survival mode, or play out a complete scenario in Apocalypse mode - in which you first scavenge your supplies and family, and then see how long you can hold out in your shelter with just the supplies you've brought with you.
Quite soon you will find it necessary to go out into the radiated wasteland of suburbia for more supplies. Well, not always you ... often it's your children. You will encounter various events and make life or death decisions along the way. Things can get quite brutal.
Light humour and cartoon style makes this a great game the whole family can enjoy. Highly recommended.

Fun idea to try, was thinking early fallout kind of thing, and sounded interesting.  Here are some of my thoughts, subject to revision as game changes over time…  Please take this as constructive criticism.
Game crashes upon starting new games, frustrating especially because you have to wait for the game to synch in steam before you can restart it again.  So when you have a bad run at trying to fill your shelter from what’s in your home you can’t just exit and run a new game reliably.
Frustrating is the inability to improve your shelter, only to respond to problems or breakage in your shelter.  Perhaps doing something to conceal that large door into the ground that says ‘kill us for our supplies’ or developing a distillation system to purify water or even use random events to your advantage.  Like finding the secret door in the shelter and later using it to hide yourselves or supplies from raiders of the various sorts that come around.
Events seen random, disconnected, without common themes except negative events.
It’s expected that surviving in a fallout shelter would be mostly tragic however there does not seem to be any sense that decisions have potential positive gains.
I.e. Scavenging shortly after detonation with gas mask and suitcase could be arguably said to result in higher hauls of scavenged supplies as most survivors are not running around in the fallout.
I.e. Later scavenging with reduced supplies as things have been scavenged by other survivors already, thus leading to raiders stealing supplies to survive.
I.e. Use of a map could/should shorten timeframes spent scavenging and potentially allows for ability to get better hauls of scavenged supplies, i.e. knowing where things are in the city.  Perhaps even to try to lose pursuers attempting to follow you back to your fallout shelter.  Or using the map to try and obtain specific types of supplies such as from a hospital, police station, warehouses, etc.
I.e. You can’t obtain more than one of anything already in your shelter and bring it back even if it’s out there in the ‘wasteland’ and intact.  Who wouldn’t want to bring that extra radio, ammo, or rifle home for at least trading purposes if not the expected need for repair or replacement.  You certainly want to haul back as much food and water as possible.
More to come later…

So far, a very solid game in terms of playability, difficulty balance, and layout.  But as with all betas, there's areas that need some work, and that's what needs to be focused on here.
1)  The security guard is a complete badass.  For about half the game you really never need to fire a shot as long as you draw enemies to him.  This is particularly true for the last fight.  You can just hang out in a corner behind cover and let him do all the work.
2) If you plan to sell this game in the future, I highly recommend removing or replacing iconic trademarks like Ford, Mustang, Chevelle, Chevy, Sackboy, BF Goodrich, Heineken, etc...  While it's cool to see them in the game, if you decide to charge for it you'll be setting yourself up for lawsuits.
3) The intro info about Major Wilson is in French even if you pick English as your language of choice.
4) License plates - You may wish to contact those states for special fictitious licenses (like they use in movies) you can use as the ones in the game may or may not trace back to private individuals.
5) Road signs in the US are rectangular for the most part, not circular like in Europe.  If you're going to make a game set in New Mexico, I recommend using US style road signs.
6) The White House sign in the lobby of Black Mesa is COMPLETELY out of place.  This would never show up in a military installation unless it was in a secret presidential bunker.  If you want to put government iconography on the walls, perhaps a Dept. of Defense logo, Pentagon logo, or more Black Mesa related stuff.  Also the presidential seal carpets, while the words have been removed, are still identifiable as the presidential seal.  Therefore they have no business being there either.
7)  The seated guy at the computer on your way in turns his head and talks to you, but his mouth never moves.
8)  It is possible to get close enough to the HEV suit to put it on, but not trigger the audio and the next event.  I would suggest combining both into one trigger.  I spent a good 10 minutes wandering around until I came back to the HEV locker and walked into it.  When I heard the suit come online I knew what I'd done wrong.
9) When you climb the ladder in the corner of the flooded room it's a bit hard to get off the top, across to the hole, and crouch.  I don't know if you can improve this or if it's just a flaw in the Source mechanics, but I thought I'd mention it.
props:nice grapichs , nice sounds, an exiting adventure threw black mesa,and cool enemies . cons: confusing level desingh (not all only abaut 2 levels) stoch hl2 voices. All in all 8/10.

It's a shame that Dragonfall wasn't the original campaign for Shadowrun Returns instead of Dead Man's Switch, because this is truly one of the most engaging and enjoyable gaming experiences I've had in recent memory.  While I enjoyed DMS, it always felt like it was missing something to me.  Thankfully, Dragonfall seems to have found that certain something, because this game is something special.  I haven't enjoyed a CRPG this much since Baldur's Gate II rocked my world.
Dragonfall's story is one of the best that gaming has to offer.  The plot was engaging and the members of your team were genuinely entertaining, well-realized characters.  I found myself truly interested in their side stories, and interacting with them became one of the high points of the game.  There were several moments throughout the game that brought a smile to my face (such as, and these are very minor spoilers so be warned, the triumphant re-apperance of a previously bit character, or one particular NPC's fascination with bad TV paying off in a big way).  These little touches served to underscore for me just how much I was enjoying myself as I played.
Mechanically, the changes to the combat system and UI with the Director's Cut have finally brought Shadowrun Returns' systems in line with contemporary turn-based tactical games such as XCOM: EU and the Banner Saga.  Given a similar revamp (or at least a much needed injection of oomph) is the dialogue system.  Unlike DMS, spending your karma to beef up combat skills no longer feels like the be-all-end-all choice.  Rounding out lesser used attributes often results in unlocking new dialogue options, rewarding you with extra karma and gear, as well as increased insights into the lore (many of which come into play much later in the game as additional dialogue options).
If you were left feeling lukewarm after DMS and are itching for something more, give Dragonfall a try.  If you're a fan of turn-based tactical combat, give Dragonfall a try.  If you love these sorts of "old school" CRPGs, give Dragonfall a try.
Seriously, just give this game a try.

I originally played the PSP version of this game in 2013 (around the time the anime series aired) patched with a fan translation. The gameplay between each version is obviously the same, but this version includes both English and Japanese voice acting as well as a localized script for the game rather than a more direct translation often used in fan translations. It's been a long time since I've played the fan translation so I'm not sure how the two versions compare to each other, however I don't think the localization present in this version of the game is bad at all.
There are two game types in this game ― the standard mode and "School" mode (which plays like a regular life-sim and is unlocked by completing the main game). The standard mode follows the events known in game as the "Killing School Life," where 15 "Ultimate" students are trapped within their school and forced into a killing game where the only way to escape the school is to commit murder without being caught. This is the story mode of the game, so besides the basic plot summary, I don't want to go into too much detail about the events of the game because it is best to be discovered by playing; what I can go into detail about is how the game is played. The game consists of three phases:
There are three different difficulty settings for the game and the difficulty for action and logic are set independent from each other (much like the seperate combat difficulty and puzzle difficulty settings in the Silent Hill games) so you can change them to suit what's most fun for you.
Like I said earlier I orignally played this game using a fan translation, so I was already used to the Japanese voice acting for the game. The Japanese voice acting is great and I would certainly recommend playing with that just from a purist's perspecive. When I replayed the game after buying it on Steam, I decided to play the game with English voice acting so that I could compare the two. For the most part, the English voice actors do a good job in playing their parts and I thought the voices fit the characters well.
My only complaint is in the voice acting for Naegi and Monokuma. Something about Bryce Papenbrook's voice just bothers me. I feel bad, but I have yet to find a role he has played where I liked his voice. Brian Beacock as Monokuma doesn't feel right to me either. It's entirely subjective so maybe it won't be as off putting to someone else, but the biggest deal killer for me was his Monokuma laugh. I know it's an increadibly petty thing to dismiss an entire performance for, but Beacock's just does not come close to Nobuyo Ōyama's.
The music in the game is fantastic, and Masafumi Takada did a really good job composing music to fit the various moods of the game. I don't really have much to say other than I just really like the music in this game.
The character art for the game has a very obvious Anime art style, however the game is presented with a sort-of cardboard cutout aesthetic. It gives the game a bit of interesting visual flair, however there is no escaping the fact that this type of aesthetic gives the game a somewhat flat look at times. This wouldn't be a problem (and most of the time it isn't), however sometimes certain objects can overlap when you rotate the camera and can make it difficult to spot or click on (though this problem is extremely easy to solve as all you have to do rotate the camera again).
The dedication to the cardboard cutout look is stuck with throughout the whole game, with objects and characters falling into place when you enter a room. This can get very tedious, as you have to watch this everytime you enter a room. In cases where one room is only accessable from another room, you need to watch this 3 times ― when you enter the first room, when you enter the room you want to go to, and when you enter the first room for a second time in order to return to the school hallways. This can be avoided by fast traveling with the map screen, but you can only fast travel to specified locations.
Danganronpa is a great game. The music is great, and the gameplay is solid. Both the English and Japanese voice acting are solid for the most part, and the visuals are enjoyable enough. The story develops at a somewhat slow pace but the overall mystery kept me interested until the end. Some characters are more developed that others, resulting in some characters being two-dimensional and are only there to fill in typical anime-archtypes. The game is hurt by repetitive and tedious aspects, such as daily morning/nighttime announcements, loads of flashbacks, the room transitions mentioned above, etc., but overall it doesn't keep me from enjoying or recommending this game.

Queen of the Seas is horrible.  Calling it a platformer falls somewhere between an outright lie and creative marketting.  There is no platforming because there are no platforms.
All you get is the ground, which goes slightly up, runs flat for a bit and then goes slightly down.  And really, that's it, there is nothing to navigate.  You walk right avoid the shark and the jelly fish instances and then complete the game.  The whole thing took me 22 minutes.
There is a bit of grinding at the start to get the first 50 coins for upgrades and then once you can jump into the floating clouds of coins the other upgrades come almost immediately.  But why were there upgrades at all?  The initial slow walk and tiny jump seem pointless and aren't fun.  Although nothing in this game is fun, the inital grind is less fun than the rest.
There is no hit bar once you've bought the kevlar upgrade so if you want to know how many hits you can take.  Well, tough luck.  (And how does kevlar even work under the ocean, how does it stop shark attacks?).  Why is there no death animation?  How - in a game that only has two enemies - is the collision detection so bad?
I have so many questions and see so many poor design choices.
Why doesn't the player character duck whilst the walk animation is cycling?  Why don't any of the texture resolutions match?  Why doesn't the ground texture even tile properly?  That's seriously amateur.  Why is there no parallax effect on the background layer.  Why does the seaweed in the foreground scroll more slowly than the foreground?  Was that supposed to be the parallax effect?  If so then it's on the wrong layer.
Why do some of the sharks move stupidly fast?  Why do jellyfish pop-up out of the sand directly underneath the player with no warning?  Was this game even play tested at all?
Why don't keys work in the game menu?  Why doesn't the steam interface work?  Why do the coin based achievements not work?  I ask again: was this game even play tested?  Was this entire game written in an afternoon?  Why doesn't the difficulty ramp up as the distance decreases (what is the distance measured in? feet? meters? furlongs?).
Why are some of the "achievments" not really achievements?  Getting the hit by a shark doesn't seem like an achievement.  Getting hit by a shark 50 times is a failure not worthy of an award.
But probably my two biggest questions are: why does the player's head pop out of his diving helmet when jumping and why does the mermaid - that he is so rapturously persuing - look like Arnold Schwarzenegger?
Avoid Queen of Seas at all cost, it's barely a mobile runner and looks and sounds awful.

Originally made available as paid downloadable content Dragonfall is an all new story campaign, set in a new city with no connection to 'Dead Man's Switch,' the campaign initially released with Shadowrun Returns. In Dragonall, you'll create an all new shadowrunner to play with, but for all intents and purposes, he or she might as well be the same character with reset statistics, as his or her role in the story is that of an expat whose cut all ties to Seattle, the capital of Shadowrun, and relocated to Berlin.
Two things are immediately apparent when you start up Dragonfall: First, there is an all new save system that lets you save anywhere, replacing the checkpoint-based autosave that was a source of frustration. This really opens up the experience, letting you save your game before trying out new gear and letting you rewind in case you make the mistake of going into combat without a medic or a spellcaster.
Second, the writing is just plain better. While 'Dead Man 's Switch' isn't a bunch of chicken scrawl, it did suffer from taking a stab at too many plot threads with barely the resolve to bring them all together. Dragonfall is simply better paced and there's a greater sense of texture to the world, and not just because of the seeming foreignness of Berlin. Dragonfall evokes a world still dealing with the lingering memory of recent catastrophes and the ominpresent political, racial and economic tensions that threaten to damn it.
Characters in 'Dead Man 's Switch' tended to wear their hearts on their sleeve; you make them for who they are pretty early on. Greater attention and care has gone into presenting characters, whether it's the cantankerous Turkish coffee shop owner who also manages free wi-fi throughout the district or the race rights activist collecting charitable donations across the street. Each one has an interesting story to tell, but they won't always share it just because you ask.
The sense that every individual has layers to them is best exemplified by your crew. You inherit leadership of the group after what was originally thought to have been a milk run goes wrong. That means that although they are mostly strangers to you, they have all the group dynamics and deep histories of a pack of veterans. Eiger, the argumentative but honest ex-military sniper who serves on your crew, will bite back if you try to boss your way into authority. But try to hard in making nice with her and she will see through you and question your sincerity.
Dragonfall also presents a larger and more liberating cyberpunk playground to work with. 'Dead Man's Switch' placed the entire plot on rails, including your trip back and forth to your base of operations, and effectively dictated the pace of the entire experience.  For the majority of Dragonfall, your goal is to raise the capital to acquire the services of a highly secretive and extremely powerful information broker. Effectively speaking, that makes the middle third of the game is about going on missions to bank the money you need to keep the 'big arc' going.
That doesn't mean that Dragonfall is an open world sandbox in the mold of Skyrim and Fallout: New Vegas. Rather, Dragonfall lets the 'big arc' get out of the way in order to focus on what it is like to be a shadowrunner. You get to sink your teeth into that mean streets vibe, dealing with clients of less than honorable intent and treading cautiously in missions where complications are guaranteed. The city of Berlin isn't just a linear series of shoot outs, but a loosely connected collection of adventures centering around your safehouse in the Kreuzbasar neighborhood.
Dragonfall still has its problems, though most of them are born out of the restrictions of Shadowrun Returns itself. Precise positioning during combat is still tricky, and for all the color and detail to the maps, they serve solely as wallpaper for colorful reams of descriptive text.
That being said, Dragonfall is the campaign that Shadowrun Returns should have shipped with, as it realizes the richness of the setting even as it threatens to be constricted by the mechanical and aesthetic limitations of the Shadowrun engine itself. It simply makes a stronger case for the Shadowrun universe.

Supreme Commander Forged Alliance starts where the first Supreme Commander ended campaign wise, and sadly just like the original there is no point in paying attention to the story of the game as it is shallow and expectable. The true test of a strategy game is not its story, but its gameplay, and Supreme Commander Forged Alliance more than delivers. The amount of units in every faction from tech one to experimental can actually be overwhelming; surprisingly every unit in the game has its own unique stats and textures that will leave you in awe for hours on. A staple of Supreme Commander is the large scale 1,000 unit battles, and while fun to command such large forces the amount of micro-management is necessary but annoying. A major success Supreme Commander Forged Alliance presents is the balanced multiplayer; all 4 factions (UEF, Aeon, Cybran, and Seraphim) require unique playstyles to utilize the faction's strengths and minimize the faction's weaknesses.

First off there is the UEF which are the jack of all trades, but master of none faction. The UEF do however have higher HP than other units, and arguably the strongest tier 1 in the game.
The Cybran Nation's units are the least expensive to construct compared to the other factions' and they have the lowest HP. Their advantages lie in technologies that disrupt enemies. For instance, they have assault bots at tech 1 to disrupt an enemy's early expansion, their tech 3 aircraft have integrated stealth technology, when their Siege Assault Bots are destroyed their cores detonate powerfully releasing an EMP burst that disrupts enemy units, and they have the only mobile stealth field system. This even extends to their experimental units: The Monkeylord is the only experimental unit with a stealth capability. These attributes give the Cybran Nation a wide array of kill strategies.
Aeon units are the most effective in an even fight between equivalent units. Their HP, construction costs, speed and abilities are average, but their weapons are particularly effective. For instance, their tech 2 tanks do more DPS, their tech 3 bombers drop smartbombs that track their targets, and their tech 3 artillery does not stop to deploy stabilizers in order to fire, but also lets them have very good accuracy. The trajectories of their weapons often give them the best effective DPS and initial shot damage.The Aeon also have the best shields after the Seraphim but the highest shield density as the seraphim shields have a very large radius. Their T2 mobile shield generators have the highest shield points. This allows for a task force to be protected whilst engaging the enemy. The Aeon is widely considered to have the best navy. Aeon T1 Light Tanks: Auroras are amphibious giving the Aeon an early naval advantage, Aeon mobile shield generators are also amphibious to support the navy, and Aeon naval units are nearly all more hardy and powerful than the other factions' naval units. They also have the only submersible battleship.
Generally speaking, the Seraphim units are a combination of the UEF and the Aeon--they have a mixture of multi-purpose units and specialized units. Their units usually have the second highest HP and construction costs. Like the Aeon, a few of these units can hover, thereby avoiding the danger of torpedoes and having the advantage of being able to travel across water. In terms of equivalent units, the Seraphim carry units with high HP, high construction costs, and appreciable weapon damage and ROF. They excel in terms of land and naval units (the author can confirm killing a UEF destroyer using 5 T1 submarines without losing a single submarine), but have average air units. If the UEF/Cybran have the best land units, and if the Aeon have the best air units, the Seraphim follows by a close second on both of these. The most obvious advantage the Seraphim holds is their shields. The Seraphim is the only faction to have a T3 Mobile Shield Generator: Athanah, and both Seraphim stationary shield generators have more health and a larger radius, but at a higher cost. The Seraphim's navy in some cases exceeds that of the Aeon due to the fact that they have a T3 submarine hunter which can be used to destroy any submerged unit and has advanced torpedo defences, T3 mobile shield generators can protect a naval group easily due to their high shield points and radius. The T3 battleship is a mobile strategic missile launcher allowing for sneak attacks from different locations. The Seraphim's T2 destroyer is submersible allowing it to act as a T2 submarine as its torpedoes and torpedo defences are superior to any other factions T2 destroyers. An extension of the Seraphim navy is their naval defences which are equipped with torpedo defences which allows them to outlast any equivalent turret from the other factions apart from the Cybran's T3 submerged torpedo turret. The Seraphim Anti-Air turrets have been considered to be the worst around, but a T2 cruiser: Ithalua, having tremendous DPS for air units, is almost a compensation for this. From an aesthetic standpoint, the Seraphim take an even more extreme approach to unit design than the Aeon, especially considering their assymetrical designs. Seraphim units are generally smoother and more elegant in appearance, with few jagged angles. Their units sport a chrome-like finish, adding to the alien appearance. Like the Aeon, the Seraphim employ unusual and alien weaponry, including the Heavy Quarnon Cannon, the Uall Cavitation Torpedo, and the Olaris AA Artillery Cannon.

Here's my opinion: it's honestly not that good on many fronts. A painfully mediocre visual novel but with a criminally good soundtrack, and a fun gimmick that you'll want more of.
The premise is a restricted "battle royale" sort of a deal in an enclosed high school environment just because it would be
if there were no special rules, which ends up in it being murder mystery solving.
The writing is okay at best, there's barely any character development, the minigames are better in the later iterations (aside from Hangman's Gambit in SDR2 which requires some Ultimate Luck), every character is a living trope, but at least the soundtrack keeps it together well and the format of class trials is nice.
Talking about class trials, they are fast-paced and action-y with a time limit of several minutes (as "mean" difficulty is how every DR should be played), giving it a "panic in the courtroom" feeling throughout them.
I can recommend if you long for something akin to Ace Attorney.

This should only be bought together with SDR2 in the bundle for the fair total of 18 bucks, which is a 50% sale. Simply because you can't have one without the other. You'll get about 20-25 hours out of it if you don't count the post-game quest for underwear.
Never pay more than 20 bucks for a video game. Or a relatively straightforward visual novel. There isn't that much replayability to it, since
.

First and foremost, Danganronpa is a game you should absolutely play. The way it melds it's music and graphical style to build atmosphere is thrilling. You will never quite feel comfortable as you play through the 20ish hour experience. For a game about Despair, Murder and Betrayal; To create such a believable setting is a testament to it's quality.
While the characters somewhat fall into generic anime arcetypes, the story is what shines strongest. The very first chapter  will have you hooked and the various scenarios each add to the mystery of Hope's Peak Academy. Gameplay in each chapter is divided between exploring the school and it's class trials at the end of each arc.
The class trials are a spectacle. But to really get the experience you have to play on at least Mean difficulty. Otherwise the tension and drama just isn't there. Tutorials even require you to play on this setting before being lowered later. Unfortunately they fall short slightly in originality, despite the flashy visual effects you will be doing the same things in the first trial as you will in the last, with only minor differences. Adding more complexity to the trial system would be a great addition to the sequel (Which I unfortunately have not played yet).
However as the game progresses, more areas are unlocked and characters dwindle. It becomes very hard to find the right people to progress the plot and add bonuses in the exploration sections. Quick travel is also useless, not only does it transport you near the room you wanted to go too instead of actually inside it. But leaves you facing the opposite direction and only works if you're on the same floor as the room. This kills the pace of the game, but fortunately these moments don't last long.
To talk about the games strongest moments would only be to spoil the experience. It's amazing, even with it's faults.

I cringe a little bit calling Danganronpa a visual novel. Partly because VNs have a sort of stigma to them and also because this game is so much more. There's a lot of interaction that goes on in Dangaronpa with both people and your environment. At it's core this is a murder/mystery adventure... with visual novel elements. You play a young teenage boy, like most games who happens to be put in a precarious murder game situation. The theme is certainly not something you see everyday and the mystery surrounding the school and other students is a compelling story which takes some time to unfold.
The game plays out in roughly 3 phases. The first being the social element, where we build friendships with other students, buy them presents and get to know all their personal secrets. I know what you're thinking, sounds pretty VN-like to me but I assure you that you only do this in order to gain special abilities in the class trial portion of the game. So if you want to be an anti-social loner you can do that too.
The second phase is the investigation portion. This is where you talk to other students and gather evidence to solve cases. This usually happens after a murder. Then things get serious, actually things are always serious. It's just when you throw in the idea of getting to know your classmates and buying them gifts you kind of forget that you're locked in school with a murderous talking bear with no hope of escaping.
If that hasn't sold you on this game just yet then maybe the third phase will. This is the class trial phase, which is perhaps the most dynamic portion of the game where you decide among your peers who's a filthy murderer. This section is presented in a series of time sensitive minigames forcing you to deduce whodunit. Generally it starts out fairly easy but to perform well you actually have to pay attention while gathering clues. I will give this game props in that it doesn't always go for the clique answer and there were a number of times I was genuinely surprised at the outcome.
On that note though this game is terribly linear but because it's such a well thought out game you won't even care because you're into the mystery of your situation and the school. Also that really creepy two face bear. The only way this game could have been better is if there was an option for you to be a killer. However the game works so that the idea of losing is an all or nothing gambit. Still I had fun. And after the ending there's a little side management game. Overall I enjoyed this game so much that I bought the second one without finishing the first. Solid story, mechanics and characters make this a game you'll be satisfied playing to scratch at that murder mystery adventure itch.

First, I'd like to say I Loved Puzzle Quest One  and Two; Those two games  ate up a large quantity of my life.
That being said, I was still wary approaching Gems of War.
I had read most of the negative reviews, and in the end decided to take the (free) plunge and decide what I truly thought of the game.
As soon as I started playing it, I loved it. It was puzzle quest all over again, with tweaked mechanincs, new card/troop systems and a whole lot more content than we saw in the  previous games.
The game plays great, carried by it's solid, dependeable, "if it aint broke dont change it" gem matching gameplay. There's far more strategy this time around in the form of collectible cards called "troops" which differ in rarity.
Trying to wrangle more of these cards just added to the obsessive-addictive depth the developers put into the game.
The problem is, it's free to play, and we all know what that means. Just like most other people who reviewed this game, I reached a point in my first play session where I simplly could not play any further without paying RL money.
I mean, that's at the same time a bad thing and a good thing.
I wouldnt mind the option of paying cash to get more troop cards, or to level up your guys, but the fact that I couldnt play at ALL after a certain point was kind of discerning.
Mind you, It's not that much. 5 bucks or so bought me another 8 or 9 hours of gaming.
It all came down to me asking myself if I wanted to pay some more money to keep playing, or whether I should go to sleep and wake up tommorow when my game would have generated a small amount of currency.
I love this game, I think it's great, and I'm hooked. It's all the fun of Puzzle Quest with more features, more quests and more tactics.
The main problem is the way the developers have implemented the free to play system.
I would gladly pay 50 bucks for Gems Of War straight out of the gate it if meant I could play it indeffinately. Considereing the amount of hours' I put into the previous two Puzzle Quest's, I could easily keep playing this game for months.
Factoring in how much it will cost me to play on a daily basis, I'm not sure how long I will keep coming back.
Bottom line:
This is a great spiritual successor to Puzzle Quest. If you loved the previous games, you will love this one.
The gameplay is as frantic and addictive as ever, and you can easily lose yourself for hours in the rich quest system.
How long you will end up playing this game is up to  you; If you've got the cash, Gems of War will entertain you indefinatly. If you don't, this may be a short trip.

Next, it is NOT P2W!!!! I haven't spent a single cent on the game and have put 10+ hours into it already with much enjoyment. Sure, you CAN pay, and you'll a much easier time of it, but whats the fun in that?! Playing the game without paying just requires some patience and a love of a challenge. Like many other games.

Yes, Gems of War can be a pain to play if you dive in for hours at a time and expect Puzzle Quest-like addictiveness without paying a cent. The game does deliver the gameplay goods. But it's clearly a child of the modern "F2P" era where that "f" stands for "free", but some players will be thinking of other words that begin with that letter when they try to play in longer stretches and can't unless they dip into their wallets.
Granted, the industry's current "free" model is  broken in the first place because it's taught gamers to devalue the work of people who make these games (some of which can be good and worth paying for without the paywall nonsense). Conversely, many game studios seem to be trapped in the model because they rely on people buying into the idea of timed pay as if they're remaking the arcade experience into a more sinister version. Well, these aren't at all the same as arcade games for a few key reasons I won't get into here.
That said, when Gems works, it works quite well. The mechanics are solid and the game doesn't "cheat" as some say because you can get some pretty wild Extra Turn and Mana Surge runs yourself. This is particularly true if you're good at reading the board and not making "suggested moves" or matches before considering every gem's place post move.
Of course, sometimes you do just get "lucky". I just completed a game where the AI had a nice streak that ended when the board had no more matches and my turn came as the board shifted with a 5-skull drop and me grinning like a crazed squirrel that just discovered an overturned peanut truck. That led to a run where two of my cards were able to get in nice extra turn runs that wiped out the enemy. "Luck" goes both ways in these games. You just need to roll with the punches and perhaps think of logging out for the day if you're having a bad run. The game will be there tomorrow.
Want to enjoy this game more? Quit playing for long periods of time and game the system a bit so it's paying YOU to play it.
As I don't always have an active internet connection AND a busy life outside of one game, I'm not able to play this for hours on end like some who dislkie those annoying paywalls. So, I (somewhat accidentally) came up with a way to enjoy this at my own pace:
1. After an incident where I logged in, collected a gold bonus and my connection dropped out (boo!), I had the realization that the game pays you in-game gold that you can hoard as long as you don't use it every day.  So, I try to log in daily to collect the gold and kingdom rewards and don't touch the main game for a week or so unless I have time for a few matches. At some point, without playing much (I'm level 16 as I type this) and just from collecting gold bonuses, I had close to 30K stocked up, which was good for unlocking kingdoms and buying keys to unlock better characters.
2. When I do have time to play, I put in about 15-20 minutes then STOP for the day. Period. I have other stuff to do, so I don't obsess over not getting through events or getting certain rare stuff. My one concession was picking up a rare weapon I had my eye on because of its effects that made getting through a certain boss fight really easy.
3. I'm not a PvP guy, so I avoid it. I've been invaded and have had to defend a few times, but I don't sweat it because it's always been a much stronger enemy I lose to. But I don't sweat it because it's only a small bit of gold and I can get that back by not playing for a day or so.
Other than that, I like much of what Gems does on the game front and not much on the monetization front. That $4.99 one time offer pop-up is super tempting (and probably recommended to total newbies or those who want to pay something), but I prefer to play this completely for free as long as it's fun for me. It's too bad that it's NOT offline at all and the pay model is a bit too eager to attempt to get players to whip out that credit card. At the end of the day, this is a game I think would work better as a standalone retail product or digital download where you pay once and play at your leisure.

UPDATE
World's quickest update, I know. I put the tf2 team to shame. Anyway after some meddling with things I finally got the controls to work. Long story short my computer thought this game was malware and wouldn't let my keyboard interact with it for some strange reason. Seeing as how I have never had this problem with a game before I'll count this against the game and ultimatly assume that it is the game's fault. But that's minor.
Now to review the game on for things within it's control. Which is exactly where I'll start, controls. The arrows are what the game tells you to use for movement along with space for jump. the ASD keys work for movement and ducking while the space bar is still used for jump. These controls are alright but would be better if in addition to the space bar the up arrow along with the W key also functioned as a jump. Just so players who want it can have it. Even better would be to have an options menu to change what keys do what but what I said first is assuming that option isn't a part of the game.
Now for controls themself, they suck. Or rather they suck when you're jumping. On the ground you can dodge pretty much 99% of everything (thanks to some hits not counting at all for whatever reason) but the moment those boots leave the ground you're just floating and hoping that no sharks decide to ram their way up your butt. Or even worse one, and god help you if two, jellyfish randomly spawn underneath or behind you making it impossible to move back and away from a shark. If you plan on just floating down to save yourself then kiss your life goodbye. Recomendation, make the S and Down keys hurry your decent to the ground instead of a useless duck that I'm pretty sure actually slows down your fall. If this ability to control yourself in such away is in a boot upgrade I didn't recieve it because 1.) Jumping = death so I don't want to jump higher and 2.) When I get the 400+ coins from collecting king Triton's pocket change I have no desire to upgrade anything but the ability to take another hit from an enemy.
That is my segway into upgrades. They're horrible. They wouldn't be so bad if they didn't cost so much and if they didn't cost so much then the game would be a piece of cake instead of adding artifical dificulty. This is what they used to do in Atari games. Stop it Queen of Seas, get some help. For what it is though (and I'm pretty sure I read that this was the first game made by this group) it's not horrible. There's just no reason to let your boots leave the ground or need more speed unless you have a death wish or want to roleplay being a scuba diving Sonic.
Now onto graphics. They're meh. The enemies all look the same and get boring really quickly. Suggestion, more enemies as you go on and why not even some friendlies in the form of companions/powerups? the second one is out there so I'm not going to expand upon it but for the enemies all looking the same there are two ideas. One is beyond basic and the other one is a little out there but requires no more than a color change here and there. So I'll explain;
1.) Some sharks move faster than the others. Do something simple like coloring them brown. Boom. New speedy shark enemy that you can tell apart from the other one.
2.) This one is a little out there. Have the terrain change the further and further you walk with the same basic enemies starting to look different to match the new area. Basic but at least it's better than looking at the same great white every two seconds. This may or may not happen in the game. I don't know and I have no real drive to get that far to check if it does. The grind for survival along with the lack of anything rewarding keeps me from wanting to launch the game.
Now to the enemies themselves and if they're "cheap deaths" Short answer, no. Long answer, yes.
Okay. the sharks spawn far enough to the side and the jelly fish are slow enough that you can dodge a shark or two with a jellyfish underneath you and walk away from it before the jelly even manages to zap you for daring to cross its path. But when you play the game as intended, where you're throwing caution to the wind and risking death for twenty dollars at a time, those jellyfish and speedy sharks will pop up when you think you're safe and decide to tear you a new one.
On a side note, if you walk into a jellyfish you deserve to die. They're as slow as I am in math and just as unfunny as I me when you decide to run into them face first. Since this is a side note I want to give credit where credit is due and say good job on making the seaweed in the foreground transparent so nothing's sneaking up on you from two inches away. That comment should probably be with the graphics but I'm reviewing a game I got for under a dollar and don't feel like moving this there. Fight me.
Onto the music. People that made this, I'm sure you're very proud of your music but please. Sit down and listen to this game for fifteen minutes. I'd tell you what's wrong with it but actually listening to it is way easier. I will admit though, it sounds one hundred times better than any song I've put together. So you've bested me there. If you don't want to change/improve the music, fine, give me a mute button and we'll call it even. If there is a mute option I didn't see it but then again I didn't look.
That's a great segway into the topic of menus. For the love of god stop. The main menu looks well enough, the upgrade/starting menu is decent I suppose. "I'm ready to dive father." Is a spicy meme by the way. But please, pause menu. It's the most important menu in a game like this. I don't even have to interact with anything. Just let me pause the game. To make it better just add a pause menu with an options menu from there allowing you to adjust music and sound effects along with a "quit game" option back pack on the pause menu. When you hit "quit game" have it ask if you're sure that you want to quit yes or no? Not the automatic thing that you're delete game button does. Accidentally hit that and it was gone. Add the yes or no option to that too.
Story review! Didn't read it, didn't care, boobs. That's all.
In all seriousness though when it comes to the story there isn't any need for it. You're a diver going to give crap to a fish lady. Unless the story starts mattering at some point just let me wander under the sea with my poor controls and boots of death.
The problem with money. That's what I'm calling this. The upgrades cost too much to add artificial dificulty and minimal pockets of coins are not going to get me to risk leaving the safety of the ground to try and grab it only to spend it on improving my death boots so I can grind and gather even more coins just to get an extra hit. Short review:
This game is fun for what it has to offer, despite it's flaws. You'll get an hour or two out of it. Overall note is 3.5/5.
Long Review:
This game recalls for old school platformer (Dragon's Lair comes to mind) where some mechanics can be criticized as unfair or part of the gaming experience. The creators really got the feel of being underwater with slow, bulky movements. To some it may feel like some kind of "upgrade to win", but with the level reusing the same assets over and over again it can be seen as "choose your difficulty".
The story didn't get me involved all that much. I think telling a story using slides rather than pages of text who be more fitting.
The graphics remind me of You Must Build A Boat where it's simple, yet effective. Using a foreground for details was a nice touch, but can be frustrating if enemies are coming out of there with less reaction time than if it was removed.
There's not that many music to this game, but at least I really enjoyed the one for the level. It didn't really grow old after some time.
Enemies are repetitive and randomly generated. And there's only two types: sharks and jellyfishes. I think it can be fun to have a wider variety of enemies such as eels or crustaceans added. As mentioned before, jellyfishes can pop out of nowhere in an unfaire manner if the foreground hides their location. I found a bit frustrating having to wait for two jellyfishes to move away while an array of sharks suddenly popping out.
Controls could be better in my opinion. The spacebar is dedicated to jumping and cannot be remapped. Why not also use the up arrow as well? We already use the left, right and down for controls. Another thing is I didn't find the pause button, if it exists at all. You can be two thirds of the way there and having to do it all over again if you have a sudden poop emergency.
There's not much to say about level design, but I want to give props to the picked up speed when going down a hill as it feels really satisfying when you can take advantage of it. I also realized there's a small fall occuring when you get the speed upgrades and walk over the corners of small hills. This can mess up some of you jumps at times and make you fall on an enemy.
I don't think there's any replayability unless you want the achievements. At least you'll get to see some bare pixelated breasts.

Now, I've only played about 3 hours of this game at the time of this review, and to you, that might not seem like enough time to warrant a review. The thing is, I've literally completed the entire game twice. The game is so short that it feels like a demo as opposed to a full game. The multiplayer is essentially dead (maybe it never lived?), so let's talk about the campaign.
The campaign, however short, is actually not bad. You play as an airborne soldier (duh), and you parachute into each mission, containing a few objectives and lots of Nazis. When you jump from the plane, you can control the parachute so you can land in any area of the map, which is usually very open so you can run around completing objectives in any order you want. The maps are fun to explore and the objectives don't rely on each other to advance the mission. This makes the gameplay much less linear than games like Call of Duty. The only bad thing is that your guys are basically useless and you have to do everything yourself. Also the objectives can sometimes be tedious or hard to figure out. For example: At one point, you are instructed to kill 3 specific Nazi officers (for whatever reason), but the game doesn't give you any clue as to where they actually are, not to mention that they look exactly like every other enemy in the game.
Anyway, if you're looking for a short game for a rainy afternoon, you might as well pick this game up if you catch it on sale. You'll probably play it once and never even look at it again. But I don't get bored easily so I might actually play it later today just to see if there's anything I missed. I hope this review helped!

Medal of Honor: Airborne was one of the first games I bought in 2008, along with The Simpsons Game and Blazing Angels: Squadrons of WWII. Out of the three games, I do have to say that this is my favourite. I originally bought it on the PS3 and have played the game numerous times. Now that I'm considerably older (15 in a month, yay, I'm TOTALLY old! [That was sarcasm]), I have a more rounded opinion of the game.
Pros:
- This game is a lot of fun. The combat is very well done, and I'm constantly looking for mini-objectives (Like the houses opposite from the Mayor's Residence in the first mission) where I can kill enemies.
- For a 2007 game, the graphics haven't aged as badly as some of the game's peers (I'm looking at you, The Simpsons Game). They still tell you what you need to know, and they still look somewhat good.
- The missions themselves are quite fun. I enjoy doing most of the objectives.
- The landscapes are quite detailed, and some of the mini-objectives such as skill drops are pretty engaging.
- Weapon upgrades are quite a good system that keeps the game somewhat fresh as you go along it.
- Operation Husky (1st mission), Market Garden (4th), Varsity (5th) and Der Flakturn (6th/Final) are quite well done.
Neutral:
- The airdrop mechanic was a good idea, and breathed new life into the game. If this game didn't have it, it would be somewhat average. The mechanic was executed pretty well, but I feel that it was a bit rough around the edges, clunky at times, and could have been improved on.
- Operation Neptune (3rd Mission) was a good mission that could have been midly improved.
Cons:
- The game is really short. A playthrough will last you about 3-6 hours, depending on the difficulty.
- Not all of the weapons are well balanced. Some are pretty damn good, while others are abyssmally weak. You'll often find yourself picking an STG-44, M1903 Springfield or M1918 BAR over the likes of the Gewehr 43 or the K98K (Worst weapon in the game, don't use it). The pistols are also mildly useless, and the C96 Mauser, which is the better of the 2 pistols is only available in the final 2 missions.
- Operation Neptune (2nd mission) was clunky and boring. It did have a couple of good moments though.
- The Multiplayer is crap.
Rating: 7/10

Story/plot: The story begins with an introduction saying Odin the all father gave humanity great powerful lucky charms--*Ahem!* I mean rune stones to hold Ragnarock at bay. However the evil god Loki has attempted many times to unleash Ragnarock by destroying these runes.

This then leads to a showdown between the corrupt and evil vikings, and a village's chief and son Ragnar (you the player are Ragnar) so the village's best warriors were all slaughtered in merely seconds by magic bolts of lightning summoned by Loki's herald (I know I'm writing a review but there are no characters in this game besides Loki Ragnar and Odin so I can't remember his name currently) everyone dies including Ragnar's father.
However Odin revives Ragnar and says that he is giving Ragnar a chance at revenge if he can save the rune stones and stop Loki's return. Ragnar of course without a moment of thought accepts the offer and fights his way through monsters, demons, undead, to hell and back all the way into the mountains fighting vikings, dwarves, giants, and the list goes on! you eventually become a war lord through your journey and now you must travel to Loki's dungeon and finish the fight the gods started.
I won't spoil the rest but there is a lot to fight in this game which makes me disappointed that at the time we didn't have the proper technology to make a free roaming game. Because this universe has tons of potential! this is REAL norse mythology! not like Skyrim where everyone worships made up half naked bikini models that enjoy watching people bang. I would love to see more of this but in a free roaming world or at least an anniversary edition with new graphics and textures along with a lot of polishing.
This game may end on the very first installment but it deserves a modern RPG sequel (or prequel) anything can be done in this universe the IP is there we just need a new developer building or re-building this universe.
Multiplayer: it's fun but very competitive, there is no "help me" or "power upgrades" or tanks, there is nothing to give you an edge over everyone else in the match. It's classic skill vs skill who is the better man? (or woman) basically multiplayer is thunder dome "two men enter, one man leaves...And respawns again to get his♥♥♥♥♥kicked" so it's fun but it's not the best multiplayer I've seen in early 2000 games. The other question you might ask is: "is there customization?" yes, and a bit of no, there are skins/playermodels (however you want to call it) you can change into but there is no armor customization you can unlock and dress up in, or mix and match pieces of sets. Final verdict: I'm giving the game a 7/10 now if this was 2004 or something I would have given it an 8 but this game is extremely outdated and old. I would love to see more, a complete free roaming RPG could be adapted into this universe giving a new fresh nordic IP, hell if it has Co-op mode, free roaming, and competitive multiplayer, it might even beat Skyrim! but until then we have to wait and see.

I wanted to like this game. I really did. The concept is great. Scramble to fill your fallout shelter with supplies and save your family, then slog along through the following weeks trying to keep your family fed, watered, and healthy until the military can rescue them, in true rogue-like fashion. I am familiar with rogue-likes, so I was prepared to lose this game a lot in the process of learning how it works, because that's what rogue-likes are. However, those games keep you coming back for more punishment because one out of every ten times you play it, the luck works out in your favor and your strategies come through and you win, and that victory feels great because of how hard-fought it was.
You're not going to get that feeling playing this game though, because the chance of winning it is very, very, very, very, very, very slim, Even on the easiest mode. I've started this game 10-15 times now, and even when it looks like you're having a good game and you're finally going to win it, you run out of food, or bandits attack you AGAIN and you don't have any more weapons to defend yourself with, or you don't have the one and only one specific item the game requires you to have when the military comes calling (and each subsequent time you get a chance to do the military quest, they'll require that same item that you still probably don't have), or your entire family gets sick or injured and dies of their maladies because you've already used the 2 medkits you were able to scrounge up in the game (and ideally you probably need 4 or 5 to keep your family alive over the course of one game). And it's not even like you can change your strategy and hope for the best, because there is exactly zero strategy to this game. It's just hoping you're lucky enough to have the right items in stock before you need them, and then hoping you're luck enough not to experience some catastrophic disaster before you can win. It doesn't have the rogue-like appeal of the hard-fought victory because a win only comes through unrealistically good luck, to the point where you should never expect to win at all.
Again, I think this game can be good. Hopefully with future patches they tweak it so that winning is more in the realm of possibility, or that strategies can be utilized to increase your chance of winning, making the many losses you'll still have to endure worth it in the long run. As it stands though, I have to recommend anyone interested in this game instead spend their money on 5 dice and just roll them over and over until you get all sixes. That still uses the same "luck" gameplay element of 60 seconds, but at least the dice will be cheaper.

Classic Defence Grid
There's only a couple of levels available at the moment, but it's Defence Grid through and through. Every good thing you could say about the original can be applied to what I've played so far. The thing that sets the DG series apart from other tower defence games is the ncredibly fun and fair level design. You have a failsafe button, much like other tower defence games but it never feels like you have to use it. With strategic tower placement you should, in a good tower defence game, be able to win fairly.
What I'm really excited to play around with is the malleable levels too. The one we're given access to here pulls it off incredibly well. You're given just enough space so that when the alien horde feels like it's about to overwhelm you an addition portion of the city rises out of the ocean just in time to save you. Great stuff.
I'm intentionally not going to mention and graphics or sound because whilst all of those things are fine for now at its core Defence Grid is all about the gameplay and as I said, what we've got so far is stellar stuff. Get your money down and if you already have Defence Grid 1 and the 2nd tier goal is met, do someone a huge kindness and gift it to them. Feels very incomplete.
Very poor level design. At first I thought I was just stupid, making my way in circles in the corridors of Black Mesa, but yet another loop convinced me that it wasn't my fault.
Lots of stolen or borrowed assets. Not something I mind, it's really just really obvious in places. I can't confirm this, but I'm pretty sure the muscle cars used are from an addon for Garry's Mod. Apart from this there are simple reskins, models and voice acting taken from the Half-Life 2 games and from the Black Mesa mod.
The HUD is okay for the most part, but there is a message confirming the name of the player character and desginating the creator of the suit as the Lambda Team. Apart from the fact that "developed" is not spelled correctly, it's also mildly annoying as it blocks the top-right hand of your screen for information that is useless after the first time you read it. Perhaps in the future it can be changed so it is only on-screen when the suit is activated for the first time.
The game is incredibly lore-unfriendly. The Black Mesa incident, from what I can recall, occured roughly around 2000/2001. Unfortunately, due to this mod using assets from other games, it uses a lot of assets which would not have been available until the late noughties. The most egregious items are flatscreen televisions, widescreen computer monitors, wireless mice and keyboards. However, items that I can only assume were included as a joke or reference are also lore-unfriendly. In the very beginning of the game, a large Sackboy plushie from the game LittleBigPlanet, released in 2008, lies in a bathtub. The beginning apartment is especially guilty of this, containing the aforementioned plushie, but also the modern television and computer, as well as a sleek modern refrigerator with ice dispenser and a modern intercom. While not lore-unfriendly, I must also point out that all of Major Wilson's neighbors own expensive classic muscle cars, including wilson himself, who owns a Mustang. Judging by the fact that Wilson owns all this technology in a nice apartment with two bathrooms and a Mustang, quite an achievement for someone who probably earns roughly $3000 to $5000 a month. Later on in the game, another minor anachronism erked me, although it's one I can't confirm. Inside of a vent, the Banksy artwork of a smiling police officer has been tagged. To the best of my knowledge, this artwork wasn't being used until 2003. However, this is incredibly minor and unlike the constant usage of flatscreen televisions, is rather odd to see. Another anachronism really stands out. In the final battle of the game, a large poster is displayed with the words "City 17". For those who haven't played Half-Life 2, City 17 is a large city in Eastern Europe which is the main setting of the game. However, the city wouldn't exist in such a state for another ten to twenty years, roughly over 6000 miles away. Puzzling.
The gameplay itself is typical of the Half-Life series, but worse somehow. When you are attacked, you also blinded for about half a second in most cases, making firefights annoying. At the very least, the gunplay feels effective, which is something I cannot say for the melee combat. When Wilson enters the HEV Suit, he gains the ability to punch his opponents, although I see no reason why he couldn't punch them without it. The punching is very basic, with no feedback when you hit an opponent and the same animations and speed being used regardless of whether you hit a wall or an enemy, making the attacks feel useless, regardless of the actual damage. Later, Wilson gains an axe, with the same problems. Luckily, the melee weapons are not used often. Ammo is plentiful and the guns in Wilson Chronicles sound and feel effective. The MP5 in particular has a lovely sharp cracking sound when it is fired.
Currently, the game ends after getting into an elevator after a large firefight with Black Ops soldiers.  Despite the other flaws, I'm actually eager to see how the game ends. I couldn't guess how myself, because it doesn't seem like Wilson has an objective. In Half-Life, Gordon is attempting to reach the Lambda facility. In Blue-Shift, Barney is attempting to escape. In Opposing Force, Shephard is attempting to reunite with his team and secure the facility. Wilson has no such goals, making my gameplay experience and his in-game motivations one and the same: we're just looking for something else to do.

Wilson Chronicles was a mod that was in development hell for a long time. By my understanding it was to be a Half-Life 1 or Goldsrc engine mod. The maps that were developed were released and are available on RTSL. Before that release however, the game switched to the Source engine. Many of the Goldsrc map locations made into the current release, of course with more detail. After 8 years of development, Wilson Chronicles had one of the quietest releases I have ever seen.
Even though it is a beta, it is good. I came into this with zero expectations and I had a great time. This mod provides a pleasant recreation of the scenery of Black Mesa, just with a fresh coat of paint. Wilson Chronicles did a fantastic job at capturing the experiences that I had with the original Half-Life, both good and bad. The good consists of the variety of weaponry, the enemy models, and the scenery. The bad consists of somewhat cramped locations and pacing of environments/enemies.
With that being said, if you want an experience in a familiar setting, go into Wilson Chronicles with zero expectations, and hopefully you will have fun for a few hours. I do look forward to see the finishing of the mod and where it will go.

Whenever I play Tomb Raider (1996), I always feel a sense of exploration. I feel like I'm exploring a vast cave system, or tomb, or whatever it may be, and that there is danger at every corner, and that I must watch every step I make.
Whenever I play Tomb Raider (2013), I feel like I'm playing an Uncharted game. Which doesn't mean it's bad, but the game doesn't feel like Tomb Raider. It feels like a predictable action set piece in which I'm controlled by a story that, is honestly pretty bland. And on top of that the game is way too easy. You can pretty much just point and click. The progression system feels unneeded, because since it is so easy to play you really don't need most of the upgrades. Most of the fight sequences are kinda boring anyway, and there are just too many quicktime events. However I will say that my favorite part is the very end, where it pays homage to the original games.
Basically what I'm saying is it's not a bad game, it has it's ups and downs like any other game. But if you want to get this game expecting more Lara Croft action, you may be dissapointed.

PROS
- Excellent Storyline, plays out almost like a movie. The storyline for Tomb Raider made me care about each character and what happened to them throughout the duration of my playthrough. It never felt tedious and was excellently written. Loved it.
- Open World is a plus. I really liked how the developers made the environment open for exploration in each level, which really encouraged you to look around for secret areas, items, etc. that would spawn around the map.
-Fighting is well programmed. Fights in Tomb Raider always felt smooth, and through the style of the game, it put YOU in the driver's seat on how to engage enemies. The variety of weapons in the game match these various styles too, and they sometimes even have uses outside of fighting, which I found interesting.
- The Goal in the game is clear. Tomb Raider is a perfect example of great script writing in this sense. I never felt like I was aimlessly doing something in the plot. I felt like every action I made had some meaning that pushed me closer to the end of the story.
- The game is challenging, but not overly so. Playing my first run-through of the game, I had no idea what I was getting into. At the same time, the game can be very conducive to new players, teaching them the mechanics of each tool early off in the game without deliberatly giving you a tutorial that has no meaning to the game. That being said, I died many times, but quickly learned how to avoid the situations that had killed me in the past.
- Game Environment is gorgeous, VERY immersive. Each scene has a picturesque feel to it. You can be running through an environment and be awestruck from just looking out into the distance. You feel like you're there beside Lara Croft.
CONS
- Won't hold your hand. This game can be very conducive to new players, but I was frustrated with certain levels in the game and their difficulty. This game will not hold your hand, whether you like it or not, it'll throw you into the deep end with no floaties. Prepare yourself!
- No substantitive DLC! The DLC for Tomb Raider consists mostly of player skins, but I would've loved to see another few missions added as something a little extra. I understand the studio that made this game was planning to make Rise of the Tomb Raider and didn't want to creatively drain themselves, but I would've loved to see some post-story missions or thematic material.
This has to be one of the best games I've ever played. If you're still looking to buy Tomb Raider, it's always on sale during Steam sales, but it is always worth it to buy this game. I literally have nothing bad to say about it functionally or about the story. You WILL be amazed. 9.5/10

I've checked everything that makes sense: there are plenty of places to eat (though they'll sleep on the floor if there's no free bed, but won't sit on the floor to eat apparently), there is food all over the place waiting to be picked up, but they just stand there or mill about doing nothing. /end_rant

Cons: AI is *horrible*; zero terrain variety (you're stuck on a mars-type planet seemingly forever until you somehow manage to thrive far enough to unlock the next planet type, which of course requires colonists to choose to eat rather than *literally allow themselves to starve to death while surrounded by food*); game speed has a max of 4X which still feels painfully slow; every time you start over, you have to sit and watch a pod of starter colonists land and disembark which is also painfully slow and can't be skipped; some equipment like beds and TVs can be very precisely located in rooms, while other equipment snaps to an invisible grid that doesn't always make sense (for instance, vending machines can only be very awkwardly positioned, and you're forced to place some of them in non-sensical arrangements); trade ships are ridiculously expensive to deal with (it seems random, but many times the markup is *65%*!!); did i mention the game is really slow even on its max speed setting?

Outside of that, I would of liked to have seen a few more races, like if forty or some years has passed, since this awakening, and magic came back to world and now you have orcs, dwarves, elves, and trolls as well as humans, I would have liked to see some half stuff. Maybe again this is too much, but maybe in a future game that is continuing off where this game leaves off?
