I had to watch 57 of my finest colonists die of starvation. Meanwhile I had enough vegetation and vitrimeat to feed double that population. I'll gladly show you screenshots of this phenomenon. A large Bio Dome was maxed out on stacked food units, and all of the AI stood still until starvation or dehydration took them. There were even colonists standing right next to meals. Even my trusty robots eventually quit moving.
I don't think this was a game mechanic...because right up until this point I was doing excellent. Status on everything was green, then everybody began dying. Oddly enough, even trader, colonist, visitor ships discontinued arriving with everything open on my platforms.
This was a really fun game to play while passing the time/watching YouTube videos...but...I haven't seen the AI improve since I first bought this game a week after release...and that AI is why I don't have more hours in this game.
This had potential of being a truly great and memorable resource management game...but...the AI rekt it in the end. Sorry to see it end this way.

Okay I'm part way through Dragonfall.
Here's my impressions:-
I'm new to Shadowrun Returns but a long time player of Shadowrun in Paper and Pen format and a huge fan of Fallout 1&2 etc so this game is right down my grubby dysotopian future ally. I'm biased. Sue me.
Okay this game isnt perfection. Compared to Fallout it's a little bit on rails and not quite so open world, or at least the Dragonfall campaign is. However there is a certain degree of choice over what run's you take on, how you complete them and lots of alternate endings and moral dilema's to take different options on.  There have been a few annoying glitches where a mission cant end if you've still got a enemy active (even behind locked doors) which meant doing over in a different way (however patches incoming). I would love to be able to name save games but you can save pretty much anytime and the 'restart level' and auto saves are good.
The campaign is pretty awesome folks. I havent finished it yet...but some of the runs actualy had me on the edge of my seat. I mean for a turn based tac sim to have you watching the turn counter tick down, to have it come down to wire again and again...really got the feel of the game. Side runs to grab paydata or free innocents at the risk of the party, locked doors in the way as the bomb timer ticks down, real heart of shadowrun, your 'runners pounding the corridors of some Corp lair, the heavy responce team on your heels as you head for the extraction point.... .Decking is integrated well without forcing you into it massively...Magic seems fun. Combat works well. Blows Fallout III out of the water for me.
If you like Shadowrun or Fallout I and II then buy this game.

Then, Dragonfall happened and I wasn't delighted, but ecstatic. This is an AMAZING game. All that was good with the original was kept and improved, but this time around the story was first rate. I kept playing and playing longer than intended just to see what happened next. Here I disagree with reviews as they were 80s, and I'd say this game is a 90 minimum.
I was one of many who encouraged HBS to release it as standalone, because I felt that if someone were to buy in to Shadowrun, this would be the campaign to do it on. Well they listened, and here it is.
If you like RPGs, you owe it to yourself to own this one. The story is top notch, the art style is gorgeous, the music is superb, and the mechanics are solid. I cannot recommend it enough.

Speaking as an outsider to the anime fandom, i was intrigued at the glowing reviews and reputation this game has. Anime fan or not, as a passionate gamer, i was compelled to play it, to see what the fuss was all about. The short version is that i am glad i did.
So this is a visual novel, so lets talk about characters. It really reminded me of the Phoenix Wright games, just with the melodrama and anime trope wackiness pushed as far as it will go. It took a while for me to adapt to the over the top acting, hammy delivery and outright abstract dialogue. The characters would behave in very strange ways, playing up an extreme anime character stereotype, which initially was pretty annoying. But as time went on, i became attached to several of the characters. Some more than others, and some i never grew to like, because they were too far gone down the "playing to a very specific japanese mans fetish trope" rabbit hole. The main antagonist was delightfully obnoxious, devious and sadistic. The protagonist was too defined, because i prefer being able to have some flexibility in how you play your protagonist. The supporting cast is varied, wacky and often times has other sides to thier personality.
So next up is writing. It's pretty clever. And in the case of some of the more climactic scenes, pretty brilliant. There are many many twists and opportunities to pick up on small details and get one step ahead. Sometimes trials get pretty ridiculous with piles of evidence and confessions being ignored in favour of continuing another line of thinking. Feels liek theres a little too much meddling with evidence and characters lying for almost no reason. Sometimes though, most of the time its fine.
It's a game, so lets talk gameplay. Well, first theres the free roam sections, which are filled with story of course. You spend your time searching for objects to look at and people to talk to. When an investigation is happening, it can occasionally get unintuitive. So you may lose an hour or so trying to figure out what plant pot you havent clicked on. More common towards the end. I had to use a guide because i wasnt willing to walk through all the floors of the school for a couple hours to track down the one thing i havent clicked on.
The bulk of the gameplay of course is the trials themselves. I don't like the gun gimmick, at all. You have to aim and shoot at phrases in order to make points with a gun. You need to manage your "truth bullets" and the characters repeat thier sialogue over and over until you "shoot" the rigth words with the right bullet. Needless and adds nothing to the game. Theres alot of pointless minigames in the court system and it contributes to the surreal theme at best, and actively hurts the scenes at worst. A simple menu would have been just fine, no need to be so up your own behind to neglect the tried and true "menu". One more gripe with the court is that sometimes, it is hard to know what the game wants from you. Like, most of the time, your bullet is evidence and what you shoot is what you want to contradict. Other times, it's less predictable. Like i had three extremely similar peices of evidence that would have contradicted this one phrase, but of course the game only accepts one of them. Sometimes theres more than one logical approach to an argument, but the game only accepts one approach. So sometimes its less about "how can i refute this" and more about trying to predict the flow of the writers script.
For music and visuals, i'd say they are very appealing. With the exception of magenta blood. Yeah, in this fairly violent game, all blood is magenta. Even though in game dialogue describes it is red. Why? I mean, you're going to see alot of it, and it's going to take you right out of it as you are reminded these aliens contain fluids that belong in printers more than they do in organic beings. The executions themself i feel are free reign for the crazy ideas the author has and are really odd, but fits with the tone quite well.
In conclusion, its well worth the asking price. If I, as someone who doesnt enjoy anime or melodrama all that much can enjoy this anime melodrama, i'd say chance are high you will also enjoy it.

Okay, let's stroke the elephant in the room. Just grab on, and give it a stroke.
I honestly believe that the Russian Dev group really tried to make this a great game.

Shadowrun Dragonfall is a great improvement worth picking up. A turn-based RPG set in the cyberpunk fantasy world of the Shadowrun universe, Shadowrun Dragonfall is set in future Berlin with your team of runners after a failed run and that run's connection to a dragon killed decades ago. Unlike the original campaign in Shadowrun Returns, Dragonfall sets up the middle of the game with jobs for you team to take in which you can choose how to proceed in completing them as needed. Dragonfall also lets team members being able to handle a few things your character would normally be unable to do in the previous version such as altering drones with a rigger or using a decker to do some hacking for you. The Director's Cut also has several improvements to the game including more items, a reorganization of the HUD for easier skill and weapon use in combat, extra missions, and alternative endings that give your character more choices on how they complete the story. Dragonfall also includes a campaign editor that allows you to edit and create additional campaigns. If any of that sounds interesting, Dragonfall is the game for you. If you previously had the DLC of Dragonfall, you now own the standalone version as well. If not, its well worth the price.

While I found the "original" Shadowrun Returns fun, the Dragonfall DLC counts among the better RPGs I've played.  This new stand-alone version makes further improvements, adds in new runs, and new endings.  It's been a lot of fun to play.
If you haven't played any of the Shadowrun Returns series, skip the original and go directly to Dragonfall Director's Cut.
BUY IT

This review is written after 29 hours of playtime ("Dragonfall" campaign, start to end).
Short review:
The campaign "Dragonfall" features (imho) one of the best storywriting in the industry. While playing, you will be able to roleplay your character starting by simply talking to others in different kind of ways up to deciding major plot points. Beware, you will need to read a lot of text, if you do not like that, you will prop. have a hard time. The tactic part is really solid and with the new additions of the "Director's Cut" pretty indepth. That said, it does not quite reach the depth of other games (XCOM), which is understandable regarding the budget. The graphic is very atmospheric, but the animations tend to be a bit stiff. Thanks to the editor, you will be able to play new stories made by other players. If you like to read and influence a good story (and/or If you like pen and paper rpgs) or if you enjoy classic RPGs like Baldurs Gate, do try the game. I would recommend reading abit about shadowrun beforehand, but you don't have to. If you want to play this game: Save often, try to imagine how your character would act and read the texts carefully.

I really enjoy this game, and for it's price, I would highly recommend it. I would not pay $30.00 or $40.00 or more for this game however, because there are some issues.
I'm going to start with the positives. The game is challenging, particularly in the early going, and will be merciless about mistakes. You have to have some idea of what you're doing, and a little foresight, or else your base will fail. I highly recommend playing the tutorial, because that will give you the grounding you need. The planetary starts get more difficult not only because the environment may be more harsh, but also because you start with fewer colonists, which means less time to get the essentials up and running. Even once you have your essential base going, you will face challenges. Food shortages, long, slow production times for things that are absolutely essential, traders who will cheerfully rob you blind because you absolutely NEED what they have, and they know it. You'll find you need more colonists to speed things up, but be careful! Add too many colonists too quickly and you'll run out of food, or oxygen, or water, or sleeping space, and nothing kills a colonist's morale like his friend dying of starvation or thirst in the next corridor over.
Once you've hit "self-sustaining", then the real challenge begins. You need to juggle expanding your colony with expanding its production and its population. You start with a fairly large reserve of "spares", parts that are used to repair essential base buildings like solar panels, wind turbines and the like. Those will start to run out eventually, though not immediately. You will eventually need to start manufacturing those, which will take away your two primary resources (metal and bioplastic) from other projects such as expanding the base.
The juggling of all these considerations, keeping your food production high, and your colonists alive, plus getting them indoors during blizzards, storms, or solar flares, and treating their injuries or radiation poisoning if you're not quite quick enough is going to challenge you.
One point that should be made is that once you get to a certain point, you're just expanding for the sake of expanding. There's no "victory" condition. This may be fun for some of you, but if it isn't, happily, there are "challenges" available that give you a situation, some limits to what you can do to resolve it, and a victory condition.
I'll leave you with the one biggest issue that the game has: It has been mentioned in other reviews that the AI is something of an abomination. And it is pretty bad. I had a biologist die of starvation. She took vegetables to a meal generator. It takes a few moments to convert the vegetables into a meal. Rather than wait for the vegetables to turn into a meal, she went back to get more vegetables, and died with them in her hands. The AI will also tend to prioritize whatever it's closest to in terms of construction, so you often have to wait until your large-scale construction is done before doing anything else. (You really need that new solar panel? Well don't build any new manufacturing machines until the solar panel is done and connected, because they'll prioritize the manufacturing machine, since it's closer.) And you can't prioritize construction. I've tried. Even if one room I'm in has no priority, and one has priority they construct in the closest room rather than in the room that has priority. I haven't tried turning off the rooms, but I suspect that wouldn't help either.
That said, and TL;DR, I recommend this game. If you're really hesitant, you can wait for a sale, but I'd pick it up today at its full price very happily.

Update:  The “Game Within a Game” Award
Don’t get the wrong idea when I nominate Watch_Dogs for this one: I’m not talking about digital trips. I’m talking about the multiplayer. Not even the multiplayer – I’m talking about the META-multiplayer. See, the game itself is functionally a GTA clone with a truly universal remote and from a gameplay standpoint that’s great. The story is so-so and the writing is incredibly poor (everyone’s an unlikeable♥♥♥♥♥♥except Jordi Chin, who’s still a♥♥♥♥♥♥but not unlikeable), but I’ve gotten an incredible amount of enjoyment playing a little game I like to call Tormenting Trespassers. Here’s the deal: I’ll engage in activity likely to draw opponents into my world, either by attacking other players or getting bounties on my head. Because the game disables your profiler when you’re being invaded, there’s an audible cue when another player enters your world. Immediately after that, use any single-player option to force the game into alerting you to an invasion – this will give you a general idea of where the incoming hacker is.
After that, you have two options: The first is to drive out to an exposed location with good visibility in all directions where an incoming hacker COULD try to blend in with the NPCs and stand facing away from the direction of their approach, but with the CAMERA facing behind you. Ninety-nine times in a hundred, enemy players will think they’re safe if they’re not being watched and will give their identity away by driving erratically, running, jumping over objects and so-on. Once you’ve nailed their identity, it’s a matter of running towards their general location, forcing them to pretend to be an NPC for as long as you like, turning your back and then quickly turning towards them when they try to run or just shooting them in the face. It’s all good. The second option – and this is actually very mean of me – is to draw them into a location where they are forced to enter a chokepoint or navigate non-NPC pathways to get to you. Some people choose a specific rooftop several storeys up with a single approach and no camera visibility, but they’re just cheating to win – there’s no fun in that. My favourite locations include the back of the Merlaut, the rooftop west of the city marina and the carpark underneath Blume HQ. A good safepoint has a location you can hide with no visibility except from exposed positions and at most a single camera you can control yourself to get a better view. Make sure your profiler is still off so that you don’t accidentally target your opponent and alter them that you know who they are and in the case of Blume’s carpark, once they’re inside you can close the carpark door behind them and trigger a blackout, trapping them with you in the dark.
Yeah, I’m a monster. But I have fun.

I'd like to prefece this "review" (if you could call it that) by saying this is just my personal opinion having played Gems of War for over 20 hours overall.
It's somewhat disappointing...
I'm a fan of Puzzle Quest; not a super fan, but Match-3 games are enjoyable, low-scope games that can be appealing when you just want to play a quick, bite-sized game. At least that's what I feel a match-3 game should be. Except I found in Puzzle Quest that there was so much reliance on RNG (random number generator) as far as gems falling from the sky, that the game was: A.) swingy (you could dominate, only for your opponent to pull a victory from out of nowhere and vice versa.), and B.) time-consuming. What should have been five minutes or less was suddenly 15-20 minutes, and the scope of the game simply just does not justify the time investment.
To use a tabletop game parallel (if you like tabletop games), it'd be if like Zombie Dice was an hour long. After 10 minutes, it'd be obnoxiously boring  to the point that it wears out its welcome. Puzzle Quest is no different.
So when I stumbled into Gems of War and how it was designed by people who worked on Puzzle Quest, I was hopeful. Thematically, it appeared to be in the vein of Puzzle Quest with a brighter art style, and more appealing to me than let's say a Candy Crush. Honestly, I was thinking it'd be an evolution of the Match-3 game, where games were quick and fun, where the RNG was reduced in its impact, making the game less swingy. At least that's what I was hoping for. Instead, what I got was essentially the same game as Puzzle Quest, except the RNG is just as bad, making the game swingy as all hell both in terms of difficulty and time. Even worse, so much of the design is now blatantly micro-transaction driven. You can buy gems (which are hard to come by in-game, naturally.), which in turn can be used to by keys (to unlock troops), gold (it costs money to engage in battles), costumes (playing dress-up that affords buffs), and souls (XP to level up your troops; typically earned by playing battles.)
Ultimately, I wish I could put a 'maybe' in recommending this game. Despite my occasional anger at this game, I actually would recommend this game with the caveats I stated above: luck-driven, and unpredictably swingy and time-consuming. If you care about these things, you may want to look elsewhere for a good bite-sized puzzle game. Gems of War may be worth checking out, even playing occasionally, but nothing more. Certainly, you shouldn't pay any money for this game. Just buy Puzzle Quest / Puzzle Quest 2 (one-time transactions) and enjoy what is essentially the same experience.

Dark Matter is a potential gem of a sci-fi themed story driven platformer. I mean it oozes style and class, something that most indies dont bother with.  Unfortunately it died prematurely as a result of stillbirth, for the game was released unfinished due to a lack of funding.  After receiving alot of bad press in the steam forums the developer revisited the game and gave it a hurried cutscene ending to provide minimal closure.
If I had to describe the game it has a System Shock vibe, with story similarities and exploration style even if this game is side-scrolling. If you've played The Fall then this will feel familiar.  Its pretty short and uncomplicated but you will have to pay attention when you are navigating its levels. Some areas will need to be revisited when you have better equipment.  The fifteen or so levels provide enough of a challenge with their varying their size and complexity which are populated with respawning enemies to keep combat satisfying.  Basic crafting allows medical packs and advanced ammo types to be created.
Overall its a real shame the game is in this state because the core elements which were experienced, hinted at an excellently paced action game with a interesting story and enticing exploration, with  a fair amount of equipment to interact with.  What I particularly enjoyed was listening to the cold if sympathetic voice-over of the ships computer, guiding you on your journey to discover what happened during your time in stasis.
Dark Matter may fall short of what was promised though not through a lack of effort from the developer. I would dearly love to recommend the game but only consider purchasing if you are okay with it being essentially an extended demo, albeit a decent one and when on sale.  Otherwise I would have recommended it wholeheartedly.  Maybe one day someone will create something similar or complete the job.  I hope so! :)

Alright, so before I begin this review you need to be informed about two things. Firstly I played this game close to when it first came out on the xbox 360, so my views may be partially biased. Secondly, I have no clue about the other crashing problems that other players have seemed to experience, so beware of potential problems. Onto the review.
Pros:
-Freedom of choice in loadout and entry position, making the maps generally more entertaining and varied
-Upgrade system that encourages continued or skillful use
-Choice in capturing objectives
-Aiming (From what ive read most people dont like this feature, I personally thought it gave you more options in using cover and getting the drop on the enemy.)
-Cool maps (Last mission has a German Flak Tower, look up pictures on google)
-Alright story (WW2 war story following an airborne unit, pretty cool)
Cons:
-Mild bugs (Some elevaters flash in and out of exsistence, grenades have an unfortunate tendency of falling in front of your feet, instead of where you threw them, etc)
-Aiming (It does take some time to get used to, and controls aren't explained very well)
-Almost supernatural aiming and awareness from some enemy ai (Only from enemy snipers, id find myself being instantly shot even when it wasnt feasible. Particularly awful during the arms factory mission.)
-Short campaign time (Clocks in around 3-5 hours depending on difficulty, entry point,etc. Redeems itself with a good amount of replayability with the upgrades and map layout)
Overall Airborne is pretty solid for the price, fun shoot outs, interesting maps, and a upgrade system that feels rewarding. It has some bugs and glitches, but most are fairly minor. Mod: Wilson Chronicles
For the game: Half-Life 2
Developer: Frere d'Arme
Publisher: Frostburn Studios
Released: 14 January, 2016 (in Beta)
Genre: First-Person Shooter
Canon status: Non-canon
Setting: 5-6 May, 2000, Black Mesa Research Facility, New Mexico, U.S.A., Earth (though in Half-Life canon, the time-setting would be 16-17 May, 2003)
Spoiler-free plot summary: You play as Major Darren Wilson, an employee of the Black Mesa Research Facility. Moments after arriving at work, the Resonance Cascade occurs, and you try and find your way out of the facility.
Full review: Wilson Chronicles is a relatively short and easy mod for Half-Life 2, set during the events of Half-Life 1. This mod claims to be in Beta, so I can only assume the mod's length will be extended.
The gameplay is typical of any Half-Life 2 mod; running-and-gunning and solving a few puzzles.
Being in Beta, Wilson Chronicles clearly has a few problems:
* The Node Graph message appears at the beginning of every level.
* The checkered black and purple "missing texture" texture will appear inconsistently.
* Black Mesa employee dialogue is Civilian/Resistance dialogue copied over from Half-Life 2.
* Explosive props, such as gas canisters, don't react to any nearby explosions, such as from grenades, and must be shot at.
* The ladders are far more awkward than Half-Life 2's, which I thought couldn't be possible.
* The Houndeyes are relatively weak, and the Bullsquid's charge attack is incredibly overpowered.
* At one point in the game, after you fall unconscious from falling out of a ventilation shaft, you lose all of your weapons for no clear reason.
* This just might be me, but I think the crosshair is off-center.
As for the good stuff, there are plenty of nice touches:
* Textures from Half-Life 1 have been copied over, but have been remade in HD.
* As well as your basic melee weapon (a fire axe instead of the signature crowbar), you can now use your fists as weapons.
* A Black Mesa security guard can be your companion for three-quarters of the mod, who is very helpful in combat, though a bit useless at following you (lags behind, runs away from you when you try and get close to him, etc.).
Do I recommend Wilson Chronicles? Yes, but only if you're desperate for something set in the Half-Life universe. Being in Beta, I would wait for the full release of this mod.

I've turned around on this one. At first, I didn't care much for the old school approach. It isn't REALLY accurate. If it were, I could smack and kick the table.....and lose ridiculous amounts of quarters just to get my name on the top score. (I don;'t think that will be happening on this.)
I've found a few tables I played back in the day. That's what won me over....nostalgia.
Having said that, Pinball FX2 is modern and faster and fits the times. This one is NOT real pinball. It's a simulation of real pinball. There are things in REAL pinball that you can do with hand /eye/body cooridantion that you can't do here.
What do I mean by body? When paying real pinball,you can move, angle , shake the table, nudge lightly or hard. That's impossible to duplicate . So, to me, having been a real arcade-troll who actually played Elvira's table, and the Black Hole table, anyone who says this is real ...hasn't played real pinball.
Why do I like PinballFX2 better? It could be nothing more than the modern feel and the graphics. The gameplay is fairly similar....although Pinball Arcade doesn't alllow for a small space between lower flippers, which is accurate, FX2 makes up for it in speed and the need to be extremely accurate . It also employs video game animations and character models.
Does that mean I don't like this game? Nah. It's fine I just think the argument that it's REAL and FX2 isn't is absurd.
The other thing is, Pinball FX offers up better graphics out of the box....no need to have any special video card bs....or knowledge of how to change your video settings so you can play. THAT'S effed up.  They need to fix that and lower the prices. They want you to think they've done something special. They didn't even design the tables if you think about it. So....why pay more? I don't know. Seems like nothing more than el;itism and greed to me.

I had a few concerns where this iteration of Shadowrun is involved. I was, happily, quite pleasantly surprised. There are some differences between this game and Shadowrun Returns, but they're honestly actual enhancements. (As opposed to bugs that become features, crafted by a company that shall remain nameless......)
The first, was the UI change from Shadowrun Returns. It's much more user friendly when you enter combat, though there are some varied things that have changed in combat itself. For instance, cover now changes your chances of a critical hit.
The second is, of course, the Workshop. Mod support is the name of the game these days, especially with a PnP game translated to the computer. Who doesn't want to put some of their homemade campaigns out there and see what others say? Who doesn't want a game that has a thousand and one variations in story?
The editor, both for this and for Shadowrun Returns, is a point and click interface. There is limited scripting, masquerading as the 'trigger system.' It'is a simple interface to learn, but you can do some amazing things with it.
The content editor seems to be missing some of the props and textures that were added to the original's workshop by the devs. Still, it's an easy fix. Grab your content from Returns and Save As... it from the content editor in Dragonfall. Re-compile it, close the game, reopen, and you're good to go. Also, porting your own created information into the new format (for both storylines and custom prop packs) is just as easy.
The final concern is one that I've actually seen a lot of people asking on the forums. Do I have to play Shadowrun Returns first? No, you don't. The campaign from Returns is included with Shadowrun: Dragonfall - Director's Cut, and you can play either one first since they take place during the same timeframe. (i.e. While playing theDragonfall storyline in Germany, you'll hear gossip about what's happening in Seattle.) So, you can do one and then the other, or just do one and skip the other if you're not interested. Also, the Director's Cut includes some new sub-plots and optional quests.
If you just want the DLC for your current copy of Shadowrun Returns, you can pick up a Steam key for it elsewhere on the web. At the moment, doing so will get you both the DLC and the Director's Cut at the same time. This may change in the future.
In short:
*Better UI in combat
*Some changes to combat mechanics
*New optional quests
*Some new props and textures
*Some old props and textures have to be ported over by the modder, as the devs haven't ported them yet
*Porting custom content over from Shadowrun Returns is ridiculously easy.
*Includes the original campaign from Shadowrun Returns.
*Can get both this and the DLC for Returns for the price of a single Steam Key.
All in all, I've enjoying the heck out of both versions, and look forward to finally working all the bugs out of my own custom content for it.

It is a great title and worth checking out for any RPG fans. Great story with clever twists, interesting companions, impressive world reactivity and fun, well designed combat.
This game is one of the best rpgs I've played in years, turn-based or not.  The story is great and the characters have depth.   It's a great ride.

Initially referring to this as an expansion was a mistake because it towers over anything related to Dead Man's Switch; it's as much as an "expansion" as Hordes of Underdark was to the vanilla, perfunctory-at-best NWN campaign. It's not only 10x the game that Shadowrun Returns was originally, but arguably better than the SNES classic. I've been consistently surprised at the quality in the writing and characterization.

Shadowrun: Dragonfall is my favorite isometric RPG of a year with many other good releases. Its setting combines a cyberpunk corporatist dystopia with fantasy and magic in interesting ways. You lead a group of shadowrunners doing wetwork off the books for megacorporations while trying to combat a threat posed by a long-dead dragon. The writing in Dragonfall is excellent all around with surprisingly deep backstories for party members, interesting conversations (with choices and skills/attributes) and a story that keeps you on your toes and has multiple endings. The game takes place in Berlin with a home base in Kreuzberg (not recognizable) and missions that take you to other districts. Combat is turn-based with a system similar to the new XCOM. The missions are well paced with moments of exploration and gathering clues between combat scenarios. Dragonfall is not an open world RPG but its loose mission structure and fairly big hub (Kreuzberg) make it feel more like one than it really is.
I would definitely recommend this to any fan of isometric RPGs with good writing.
Notes: This is the improved stand-alone version of the second (much bigger and better) campaign for Shadowrun Returns. It lasts a good 15-20 hours or so. This version does not include the original Dead Man's Switch campaign from Shadowrun Returns.

I enjoyed Shadowrun, I enjoyed Dragonfall, and the Director's Cut is, without question, a solid improvement on both.
The new content is well-balanced for the timeframes in the campaign at which they are accessible, and add interesting depth to various characters (this is particularly noticeable for the Lodge mission!)
The new tactical interface is a vast improvement over something that already was pretty solid and functional, and Harebrained has patched out what few glitches I noticed within days of release.
Overall, I'd strongly recommend this, even if you were leery of the original Shadowrun release.

*****EDIT SEPT 14, 2015
I want to say upfront that I love supporting independent gaming studios – I always want to root for the little guy, and sometimes the gems they produce are the greatest products ever made.
With that said, there is a disturbing trend which has manifested within the (saturated) game development community:  the dreaded supporting of Pre-release games -- whether it be through a public fundraising such as Kickstarter or through a program like Steam Greenlight.
“60 Seconds!,” and its developer Gentleman Robot, appear to be the latest victims (or offenders depending on your POV) of this trend.
As a full disclaimer, I have not closely followed the development of this game since its early production Greenlight days, and was only made aware of its history when @beren (an apparent developer of the 60 Seconds!) posted in the comments section of my review.  According to Beren, “60 Seconds! is released on the promise that all future DLC would be free and forthcoming.”
However, I did not purchase this game in a “pre-release” state; I purchased it in an advertised “complete” state, for $10.00.  I (and many others) have learned my lesson the hard way, by supporting a game in a pre-release state, only to have the game rushed and “released complete” -- i.e. unfulfilled, buggy, unplayable, etc. etc.  The mantra from the devs is then “DLC, DLC, DLC ….”
Usually after months, if not longer, the game is somewhat patched, in a semi-stable/semi-playable state … and then basically abandoned by the developers, who have moved onto a new project, leaving the consumers/gamers burned and without an enjoyable game.  In essence, it’s a cash grab for a bait ‘n switch product, and it happens a HUGE majority of the time when dealing with independent studios.
So at Beren’s suggestion of re-playing the game with its new DLC, I gave the game a second-chance and disregarded the fact that I should have already had a completed game to play, as opposed to waiting around for DLC.  I can report, that after playing the game with the new DLC, I feel as though I have been put through the ringer of one of the most elaborate troll-jokes ever.
I was expecting the DLC to have added any type of actual gameplay or substantial level building to the almost non-existent, present content.  It does not.  From what I can tell, it has added a whopping two items (a briefcase and padlock), maybe an added music track and a few minor decision branches.
As it stands now, with added DLC, the game consists of a 60-second, item collection mini-game and then one screen with very basic, almost not existent flash animation.  Let me repeat: $10.00 game with a 60-second mini-game and one flash animation screen.
They devs obviously worked harder on the intro (which is by far the most interesting part of this “game”), because that’s the new industry norm: Make a great demo for your game idea, shop that idea around at conventions and on Steam, sell a shell of that game idea at top dollar and finally hope to produce enough DLC to satisfy the contract before moving onto the next project.
With what has been produced and released to-date, at absolute best, this is a mobile game which should be sold as an app for $0.99.  I can see it as a silly little time-waster on your phone or something, but it has no business being released for the PC.
60 Seconds! Is a great idea for a game.  The devs have caught the feel, mood, dark humor and music which perfectly captures 1950 Cold War.  They’ve sold this package for $10.00 ….
Now where’s the actual game?

This is an open forum, and I really encourage an open dialogue with the devs on these points listed.  I am genuinely interested in coming to some type of happy medium on these concerns – perhaps I’m missing something?  I’m certainly willing to listen and discuss. **********

This is a very shallow game, especially for a $10 asking price -- It's actually more of a novelty than a game.
You have three different game settings to choose from: The full game (both the 60 second scavage into and "survival" portion), and then just the scavage (frustrating and lackluster) or just the "survival" portion (the main bulk, 99% of the game)
It's ironic that the actual 60 Seconds portion is the least interesting part of the game, and I reccomend just playing the "survival" portion, since you are automatically started with far more supplies and items than you could have ever hoped collecting manually.
With that said, I use quotations when I mention the "survival" portion of the game, because there is zero substance to it.  You are faced with 1 scenerio a day, where you are basically spoon-fed which item to use.  Or, should you open up your door, because someone is knocking -- 50% chance they want to trade, 50% chance they will kill you and end the game.
Also, the journal messages you "Ted is hungry and will not survive one more day without soup!"  So you click on the soup  can, and he goes back to full health for a few more days.  That is all.
When you compare this game to another of it's genre -- let's say "This War of Mine" -- it is literally like burning a $10 bill on a game so woefully inadequate when you could actually be playing a much better game like TWOM.
You are basically paying $10 for a sorta-funny intro and a chuckle here of there.  Other than that ... you'll instantly regret parting with your time and money with this title.  Such a shame, too -- it's a very interesting concept; one which this game fails to deliver in any shape or form.

My review for Tomb Raider:
If you're looking for a game about raiding ancient tombs, full of mystery and puzzles, and maybe the occasional fight with a T-Rex, search no further. Specially, give up on anything past this point. Back up, close the door you came through, and search a different route.
This is "Tomb Raider" reimagined as "Rambo." Gone are intriguing vistas, territories you have to engage in detail with, complex puzzles... nope, instead you get to shoot things, and then for a change of pace, you can shoot things wth a different gun, maybe something will explode, then maybe you'll get a Quick Time Event where you're falling uncontrollably, and then you'll shoot some stuff some more, and then they'll get really wild and you'll shoot someone on a different team that was shooting someone you were shooting at earlier (not at the same time though, no, everyone's always going to be gunning for you specifically).
Now, if you were expecting a follow-up to Half-Life 2, this would be a pretty good game for you. However, if you're expecting the cleverness of the Tomb Raider series.. meh.
Here's the plot, I'm going to spoil it for you...
Lara & crew shipwrecks on an island. There's an ancient artifcat that lets a crazy person control the weather and keep people from leaving. All past shipwreckies have built a culture around killing eachother. You gotta shoot a bunch of them.
Starring such forgettable characters as:
- Tough guy father-esque figure who dies protecting you.
- Damsel in distress
- Pacifist noone likes and who lives up to the unrealistic stereotype of being a coward, but who will be liked more by the team when they "grow a backbone" and eventually hold a gun.
- Angry assertive black woman
- Mr. Big quiet type
- Techie in a computer T-shirt who occasionally gets corrected and acts self-consciously arrogant.

And a huge array of "memorable" villians such as..
- Mad Priest
- Russians
- Easily a city's worth of near-identical military men with a culture that somehow survives without women and children and somehow operates purely on the concept of constantly killing eachother.
Solve such ancient mysteries as...
- Discovering that the thing they told you about in the first five minutes of the game is a thing that exists in the game, and other people not beleiving you despite the fact they've been around the same kind of evidence too.
- Japanese fought in WWII
- Rusty Shantytowns where everyone will try shoot you
- A severe lack of potential allies
- The inability to affect the plot
- Random NPCs who will complain about the people you're trying to kill as being too oppressive, and then fight you to the death to protect them... repeatedly.
- The most linear "open world" game you've ever seen.
There, I just saved you a day of your life.

This isn't a BAD game. Medal of Honor: Airborne is fun for half of its campaign, and it has things that set it apart from both the other games in the Medal of Honor series, and other FPS games - especially the paradrop system, which is a neat way to try out a new approach to getting past its nasty difficulty. While it is fun, it has several glaring problems that make it difficult to recommend.
First, the difficulty. Airborne seems to be a cover-based shooter (Not with the systems like in Gears of War or other such games, but there is an emphasis on not running-and-gunning). Enemies do a lot of damage and rip through your health easily if you're not absurdly careful. This is enjoyable at times, especially when you only realize after you land that you're surrounded and manage to fight your way out regardless. Later on, the difficulty ramps from unfair to unforgiving, with juggernaut-type enemies that are extremely difficult to take down and snipers that seem to be able to fire through their own cover, making it impossible to counterattack. The less said about the sniper-accurate rocket launchers employed against you, the better.
Second, the AI. The enemy AI is fantastic, and they put up a challenging fight throughout the game. They react how you would expect a trained army to react, pinning you under suppressive fire and using grenades to flush you out of cover. Later on, this again becomes relentless, especially when you compare it to the ally AI, which is comparatively pitiful. Your allies are either gunned down in seconds, run directly into your line of fire, or take cover near you and inadvertently push you into enemy fire. The enemy AI is almost too good when your allies are held against them, because you can never count on their support. (I also encountered a glitch where having an ally even nearby would cause the crosshairs to 'x' out as though I was aiming at a friendly, when I was aiming at an enemy instead. This got old, fast.)
Third, and most damning, was the gunplay. I can only describe it as excessively slippery. Without turning the sensitivity near the bottom, I was unable to hit just about anything even when given time to line up a shot, and when scoped weapons came into play, I might as well have been hip-firing with the pistol. I'm not even bad at first-person shooters, generally. I had to grind to get the upgraded SMG and pistol to even stand a chance in close combat, and when the juggernaut enemies came into play later, it was a crapshoot whether they could be beat or not. Not to mention, this cover-based shooter seems to have infinite enemy spawns - meaning that bizarrely, the most effective strategy was to try and sprint across the flanks of the enemy to get close enough to spray-and-pray.
TLDR: Brutally difficult, shoddy ally AI, bad gunplay, INFINITE ENEMY SPAWNS. It's still aged better than older MoH games, but that's not stiff competition, and you're better off spending your money elsewhere.

Pretty decent World War II FPS. The market's pretty saturated with these types of games, IMHO, and this one's very similar in premise to, say, COD:WaW. You get a gun, you mow down Nazis, occasionally face against German tanks. That's it. The missions feel very same-y, with plant explosives at A, then go to point B and do the same, before heading to point C and repeating it again. But the unique part is that the missions are semi-open world. You can do them in any order. You can go do C, before backtracking to A and then completing B. What I like the most is the weapon progression system. Use enough of a weapon and you 'level up' your skill with that particular weapon and unlock attachments for them. For example, you get increased damage for the M1911 for example, and a scope for the STG-44 (which is a horrible attachment to be honest).
So, is it any good then? Well, if you enjoyed the simple run and gun type of gameplay of, say, the older Medal of Honours and the million WW2 shooters back then, then you will like this one. Pick it up while it's on sale though for some simple FPS fun.

The headcrabs are ugly as hell, and the Agrunt and Acontroller models look almost identical to a mod from way back that were absolutely ♥♥♥♥♥♥ then, and are absolutely ♥♥♥♥♥♥ now. No offense to the mod-creator, but those things are ugly. There's also some issues with sound, some of them are fairly low quality, like the shotgun's firing sound and some of the background noises. Lighting can also be a bit of an issue at times, being a bit too dark for my taste.
Some of the things I do really like about it are: the casual opening, the design of Black Mesa (which is closer in style to the original Half-Life moreso than Black Mesa). Weapons are punchy and feel deadly, except there's the major drawback of them feeling incredibly floaty.
Overall, good not great. It's very obviously in beta, and I'd say give it a chance!

The mod does a very poor job of leading you where you need to go, and showing you what's interactible.  More than once I had to use noclip to see where the next area I could go to was.  Weapons also feel very powerful, almost TOO powerful.  You can one-shot a Vortigaunt if you can headshot them, and most other weapons kill in just a few shots.  The game also kind of teases a story, but there's zero dialogue.  This is excusible as the mod isn't done, though.  It overall feels extremely easy, I only died once because I hit myself in the face with a grenade, and even then I lasted a while.
The maps look very good, and wouldn't be out of place as a Black Mesa expansion or something similar.  I'm also a big fan of the custom UI, the green accents are really nice.
Overall I'd say this is worth a download.  It's not a very long mod, maybe an hour, but hey it's got some neat stuff in it and it's free.

Story, from what I can tell so far, is simple, yet not bad. You play as young, 'roided up, unbearded, lad, named Ragnar, who is given the honor of being a guardian of one of the Runes that Odin placed around Midgar. Some dude, Conrack, I think his name was, wants to harness the power of the Runes to unleash Loki, and initate Ragnarok. Gameplay consists of drinking mead, beating guys to death with their friends' dismembered arms, dying, getting frustrated at your computer, and the occasional platforming segment. Combat feels like an Elder Scrolls game's melee combat in 3rd person. Minus killcams and leveling up. Left click hurts things, right click keeps things from hurting you. Enemies react appropiately to where they are hit, most of the time, such as being able to decapitate enemies with one lucky slice or destroying their shields when you happen to hit it while the shield isn't drawn. In a nutshell, while the combat is no God Of War Ascension, graphics are not Battlefield 63, and music isn't produced by Amon Amarth, you should still buy this game if you're interested in it. As I kick off my slightly longer, more detailed reviews on some of my Steam games, it's only appropriate that I start with a game that was part of my youth.
Rune is, surprisingly enough, one of the few games focusing on Norse mythology that made it into history. Not many good and consistent ones out there, and this one brings its own identity in terms of gameplay, aesthetics, and character development. It creates its own accounting of Norse cultural and religious topoi in fiction, and that does more good than harm as far as the storyline progression is concerned. You play as Ragnar, a young man whose responsibilities escalate with the killing of his kinsfolk and the dooming of his birthplace, Wotankeld. Simple name for a protagonist, simple purpose for his endeavour. Vengeance couldn't be bitterer and more predictable.
But that's where things get sharp in Rune. You're introduced to fluent combat mechanics, advanced graphics for the time (the first Unreal Engine was just starting its brilliant run), and the grandeur of the game's environmental variety. This is a videogame epic tale, with all its classic characteristics, as the protagonist rises through the image of the savior and avenger of his clan and descends into the dark realms of Helgrind, imprisoned, assuming the figure of bare life and shamanistic sacrifice - true to the Norse notion of the Cosmogonic death in order to attain the knowledge of the Runes; Wotan speared onto Yggdrasil -, to then rise again as the ultimate Berserkr who transcends revenge and defies material existence. Ragnar is ready to put it on the line at every moment. And that motif is auxiliary to the development of the game's combat system, a hack-n'-slash which is as smooth as it gets, and a map configuration that challenges the player's reasoning as well as it puts them under the pressure of claustrophobia and constant darkness.
This is an atmospheric game, and a grim one as it is. The double ending is up to you, and that's a bonus coming from an action game with tacit storytelling elements. Rune scores high in both single-player and multiplayer - which is still active, and resembles heavily the fun and flow of the Unreal deathmatches -, and the variety of weapons, as well as the distinct styles and contrast in movement swiftness that each one of them brings up, enrich the game even further.
A must-have for hack-n'-slash fans, as well as fans of games that dialogue with the epic genre.

I just finished the single player mode after a little bit over 10 hours of gameplay and what can I say?
This is the remake of a very solid  hack and slay games from the early 2000s, the graphics haven't improved much (or at least that's why my spoiled eyes see nowadays) but it doesn't lessen the fun, while hacking and jumping through hordes of monsters.
Admittedly there's not that much variety amongst the monsters and the scenes, there a few major themes, but well ... in the end they all boil down to a rather straightforward and linear design (pull a lever here, press a plate there, kill some more monsters etc.). It was still fun. Nearing the end I was wondering if it'd be better if some of the scenes would have been shorter ...
But I guess we owe this to the age of the original game, back then I had much more time to spent, today I like to be able to finish a game while it is still hot ;-)
Speaking of hot, the game provides you with a little story, which is told in various ingame cutscenes (skippable with the ctrl key). It's nothing to fancy, but it was enough keep me entertained till the end non the less, mainly with its interesting background (I used steam overlay to lookup references to the nordic mythology from time to time, very interesting and it made me appreciate the game even more). Another thing I have to mention, is that this remake is well done from a technical standpoint, I played this with a resolution of 1920x1080 on my Windows 7 64bit machine and I haven't had a single crash or glitch*, the controls are very smooth and intuitive.
All in all I can recommend getting this game if:
a) you like hacking stuff
b) you like vikings
c) you played 3d computer games in the 90s and early 2000 and don't care to much how the game looks (it's an unreal engine game)
When it was on sale you were able to get it for 2,50€ which is absolutely fair for the 10 hours of sp fun it provides (not counting the multiplayer - if you like multiplayer games like Half-Life Deathmatch, with vikings)
* (well, actually there is a problem in one of the last levels, where a triggered cutscene causes the game to freeze, if you disable sound for that mission then you're fine. If you've reached this point however, you're so determined to finish that game, that this minor hickup probably wont bother you anymore ;-) )

Danganronpa: Trigger Happy Havoc is part murder mystery, part psychological thriller. The soundtrack is fantastic and I never grew bored of it; it was easily able to give you a sense of hope or dread based on the context. The artwork was somewhat questionable; while for the most part, character sprites were very high quality and pleasing to the eye, backgrounds and backdrops were somewhat low in resolution and very pixelated. I'll assume this is because this is a PS Vita to PC port...or it could have been on purpose.
The game has a multitude of main characters -- fifteen, to be precise -- all of whom have different personalities, motivations, and pasts. Whether or not you are interested in them will depend on your own mileage, of course. Some of them were rather surprising later on down the road! The only problem with having so many characters is that it was difficult to grow attached to them, especially due to the pace of the game. You personally play as Naegi Makoto, a somewhat personable young man who is effective as a protagonist and never felt like too much of a hollow shell.
The most important part of Danganronpa is its plot and the murder mysteries. The story appears to be well thought-out and constructed; it was enjoyable to play through the game and get to the finale. Some things did seem a bit absurd, but the characters took it the same way, so that helped with immersion. All in all, the game had many twists and turns that took me by surprise, along with a few things that I could predict. The game took me around 25 hours to complete.
Most of the novel's gameplay consists of walking around and making the very occasional choice. However, the real meat of the game lies in the investigation and class trial portions of the novel. Investigations are mostly point-and-click affairs. You can't progress until you get all the evidence required by the game. Occasionally it is difficult to find everything, mostly in the beginning when you are just starting out. Toward the end you should have a fairly good grasp, however. The class trials are the most interesting part of the game -- there are multiple modes during the trials, where you can refute someone's argument, fill in the blanks to recall important evidence, shoot down someone's defenses, or select evidence out of your inventory. The trials can be a bit fast-paced but are overall fun, especially when you're trying to predict what actually happened. Most of the trials' outcomes are at least a bit surprising and it's interesting to see how everything comes together by the end. The class trials become longer as you get further into the game, but it is possible to save during the speaking portions in case you are unable to get through the whole trial in one sitting.
Of note, there is a sort of mini-game accessible after the end of the proper game, which allows you to basically spend time with the rest of the classmates in order to max out your relationships with all of them (something not able to be accomplished in the main game). This is useful for anyone who was interested in certain individuals or anyone who wants to get all the achievements. It's something I'll do in my own time with a few characters and update this portion of the review if necessary.
Overall, Danganronpa: Trigger Happy Havoc was a satisfying read with good twists and turns, and colourful characters.

Not your regular Pac-Man, Championship Edition DX+ offers a variety of challenges in a "remix" of sorts. Instead of multiple levels, Championship Edition DX+ offers a few levels with changing maps, all of which are score centric, either to do with points, speed, level memorization, and sometimes all three. Controls are tight, but require reflex, as the game "speeds up" and pushes your ability to keep up. The biggest draw out of everything, however, are the leaderboards and rankings, both of which allow you to see how well your friends are doing and compete, as well as worldwide. The rankings really draw a competative spirit in me, which gives me all the more reason to play this game.
The All You Can Eat Edition includes all of the DLC, which adds levels, songs, and skins based on Pac-Man and various other Namco Bandai franchises. At the time of purchase, the All You Can Eat Edition was $3.74, which was easily worth it, considering the amount of content it adds, however, it seems that the usual price is $15. Is it worth $15? It really depends on how much you can squeeze from the game as far as rankings go. If you just want to complete the game, it shouldn't take more than a few hours, however, if you want to A rank, or be one of the players at the top, you're looking at tens or hundreds of hours on this game, especially if your friends have a competative spirit.

Why I review Watch Dogs you ask? Or more specifically why I do it now, almost 2 years after it's initial release?
Well there are a couple of reasons for that. One of them being that I had pre-ordered the deluxe edition for about 70 bucks back then so I'd feel horrible if I wouldn't play it through at least once and since I found the time to do so, I figured why not?
That aside I've noticed that this game receives quite a lot of hate and I was simply curious how much of it is actually justified (which I'm going to address below). The game was working anything but well at release which is why I decided to give it some time and play it again someday after the last patch has been released.
Once I started playing it I got messaged by quite a few people and was asked why I decided to play Watch Dogs since there currently are many better games out there and some of my friends who just as me had not finished it back then were wondering what the the game's current state is, now after several fixes and updates. This was another reason why I've decided to review it once I'm done.
Anyway enough talking, lets get on it. I'm gonna start with a short summary as I suspect that this is going to be a long one. Also please keep in mind that while I'm reviewing the pre-ordered deluxe edition, it isn't all that different from the regular game.
In my opinion this game is very well worth 30 bucks (its price at the time I've written this review), if you still aren't sure whether you want to pay that much but are generally interested in the game then I'd recommend to pick it up when it's on sale.
Things you should take into consideration before buying it:
- Fairly buggy considering that it's been out for almost 2 years (one bug worth mentioning is that you might not be able to achieve 100% completion; important to achievement hunters).
- Good looking but not very well optimized (you'll need good hardware to run it on high settings).
- The story is decent/good but completely linear and therefore has no replay-value at all.
- Different sidequests and cool minigames to choose from but all of them get repetitive after a while.
- Multiplayer is active and fun, matchmaking works fine but most game modes are unfortunately quite imbalanced/unpolished and therefore it's probably not a multiplayer you're going to invest dozens of hours into.
- Despite it's appearance, there isn't much to do in the open-world of Chicago once you've achieved 100% completion (multiplayer and minigames excluded).
- You can expect a playtime of at least 50 - 60 hours if you're shooting for 100% completion with a few multiplayer matches inbetween (maybe 2 - 3 hours less as I had some exclusive content; other than that all DLCs and minigames excluded).
Initially I wanted to include the in-depth review into this one but as it turned out to be longer than I expected, I decided to just link the full review
(leads to a google docs document).
I find it hard to decide whether I want to give this game a positive or negative rating, being able to give neutral ratings would come in handy in situations like this.
I don't think that this game deserves a negative rating in its current state for its current price but on the other hand I must admit that it simply wasn't ready to be released back then as it was way too buggy, unoptimized and unpolished accompanied by U-Play's server issues.
Since I ultimately believe that it makes more sense to review the game's current state rather than its state from about 1,5 years ago (I believe the last patch had been released early September 2014), I'm going to give this game a positive rating.
That being said I find it unacceptable to sell an to such an extent unfinished product (not to mention that the servers were going to♥♥♥♥♥♥at the same time) for an absurd price of ~ 70€ (pre-ordered deluxe edition). Therefore I wish I could give a negative rating for the service, support, etc. to Ubisoft (as they were both developing and publishing Watch Dogs) for not even being able to fix the most obvious bugs after their terrible release of the game.
This has been the last Ubisoft game I've preordered (or even bought for that matter), which isn't going to change anytime soon unless they finally stop pursuing to become the next worst gaming company and get their♥♥♥♥♥♥together. Seeing that most of their games (currently The Division) are among the steam best sellers before even being released, I doubt that anything will change... Although... Hope dies last, right?
There will most likely be another Watch Dogs game coming out in future and I certainly hope that Ubisoft pulls themselves together until then and that it's going to be different that time around as Watch Dogs has the potential to become a great franchise/series in my view, far more than it is right now.

I was pleasantly surprised by Damned. The gameplay does get repetitive, and eventually you get tired with the constant issue of starting a game, only to have 1 or 2 people disconnect and not be able to join back.
The game is fun if you have 4-5 friends to play with. When I say friends, I mean friends you can talk to and communicate with. My friends and I would have the humans all in a group call and then the monster on their own. This made the game pretty damn fun, as we could communicate.
The gameplay gets pretty boring after 9-10 hours of playing. You basically run around looking for keys while avoiding the monster. Each monster has different abilities, meaning you have to change your strategy slightly depending on the type of monster. Currently, there are only 3 monsters.
The Lurker - The Lurker has a physical and nonphysical form. In its non-physical form, it cannot see players and players cannot see it, but it can place traps. Traps make a loud noise, notifying The Lurker where the humans are. The Lurker can then transform into physical form (if it has enough charged up) and try and kill them.
Mary - Mary moves very very slow, and Mary can see humans and humans can see Mary. Mary has the ability to teleport when charged up (also randomly teleporting if you do not for a long time). Mary also slowly gains "Frenzy". Frenzy mode allows Mary to run faster than survivors and kill them. To charge Frenzy, you have to get close to a survivor. The closer you are, the faster it charges up.
The Phantom - This one is personally my least favorite. The survivors can see the Phantom at all times, but the Phantom cannot see the humans unless they make a noise. If a survivor begins sprinting, the Phantom will hear loud music and that survivor will be able to be seen through walls. You also can't turn your flashlight on and off when the Phantom is around. Basically, the closer you get to the Phantom, the less sound you have to make, by crouching or walking.
Like I said, the gameplay is fun with friends, but over time it loses its luster and becomes very repetitive. I bought it with 4 other friends when it was only $5, and it was definitly worth it. Rarely we got to do 5 player, but 4 player is still really fun.
If you can manage to find 3 or 4 friends to play it with, get it on sale. The bugs are pretty irritating, mostly the main menu bugs that require me to verify the integrity of game cache every 30 minutes. But the bugs are also tolerable because the gameplay has its ups for a decent amount of play time.

**Disclaimer: I played the original release of this game, before it was pulled from the Steam store.**
Do not buy this game. It's an incomplete version that was tossed out the door when the Kickstarter failed in order to salavage a little cash. Whilst there is promise in what little there is, it's very short and ends abruptly (The ending has since been patched, but I gether there's little improvement.
The version I played had a tutorial level which instructed you on features that never actually appeared in the game. Obviously these were intended to be included but when the money ran out they were omitted, but the tutorial wasn't updated to refect that.
If you drop by the discussion area you can see the many complaints from those that paid for what they thought was a full game met with evasion, protests and (to be blunt) outright fibs from the publisher and developer that this was intended to be an episodic franchise, despite the fact it was not labelled as such in any description, and, more damningly, the 'final product' was identical to the demo given out when the kickstarter launched.
It's also worth noting that the publisher blamed the QA department for the complete lack of a proper ending (The original release of the game just ended when you enter a room and you were met with a couple of paragraphs of text saying you died), not, say, the developers for not actually doing things properly. It's the kind of desperate buck-passing that I might have found funny had I not paid to play it.
I have to say I'm disappointed that Steam brough it back after it was pulled. Even though the price has been slashed to refect the content, Steam really shouldn't be letting the publishers or developers get away with such shoddy practices.
TL;DR - Don't give these shysters your money.

This is a reluctant recommendation.  It's not a *bad* game, but it certainly takes some getting used to.  The control scheme, at least with an XB360 controller, take some fiddling to get just right.  It's very atmospheric (OK, not Alien: Isolation atmospheric, but for a budget indie game it does a pretty good job).
The story is interesting enough, at least enough to keep me searching for messages that other survivors have left behind.  No spoilers, but the intro video (which is one of the trailers IIRC) spells out an encounter with an unknown object which kills most of the crew, and then a parasitic/carnivorous infestation that basically wipes almost everyone onboard out.
The protagonist, a nameless Ensign, is a forgettable character that gets the job done.  The voice acting is serviceable, with cringe-worthy moments.  My wife says she walks like a dude...
Combat is simple to the point of being almost meaningless, at least in the ~1 hour I've invested so far.  Maybe it'll improve as I progress.  I *hope* it improves.
I did encounter a few glitches while playing.  One that sticks in my mind is that elevator buttons didn't work unless I jumped and hit the Interact key on the way down from the jump...  And the first time I did that, I clipped through the elevator floor and fell down the shaft.  Good thing there are plenty of save points.
On sale?  Sure, pick it up if you like 2.5D side-scrollers.  Otherwise you're better off spending your hard-earned cash elsewhere.

This is by far one of the best survival horror games I've ever played. The first Penumbra game was pretty good, the third was mediocre, but this one was definitely the best of the three. The atmosphere is chilling, the soundtrack is excellent, and the story is pretty interesting. I think it's mostly the soundtrack that made me like this game so much. The music that plays when enemies are around and/or are coming after you gives me goosebumps. It's that kind of music that you randomly remember in the middle of the night and become terrified, and it's those kinds of aspects that I look for in a good horror game. The only complaint that I have about this game is that there isn't any way to skip the dialogue that plays throughout the game (from Clarence) and sometimes it gets rather annoying hearing his voice every couple of minutes. For someone who is playing the game for the first time, I can understand why they'd want to hear the dialogue. However, for someone who is playing it again after having beaten it just to experience the atmosphere again, it gets rather old hearing his voice. Nonetheless, this is a fantastic game and is far better than any recent horror games I've played. If you're a horror fan, I highly recommend this game. You won't be disappointed.

I love Gems of War, which is no surprise since I played Puzzle Quest 1 & 2 until my daughter was old enough to snag them from me.
I started playing this game on mobile actually and unless you don't tab out (since it caused the game to restart when you come back in) or need the computer screen to see better (I had no idea how much I was squinting while playing mobile though I do need glasses), I’d suggest going with mobile. But that’s personal preference biased since that’s how I started and touch screen feels better, and I’m usually multitasking all the time so the tabbing out problem bothers me.
I don't think it's pay to win or that the AI cheats. I've gone pretty far while being a completely free player: lvl 85 with 50 troops, all kingdoms unlocked, rank 1 pvp and 41 free gems (40 from guild, one from cascade of 7 matches). You just have to pay attention to the board and sometimes switch troops around. There is more strategy than just troops (though that’s a big part of it), like denying the enemy mana, which enemies to prioritize, and forcing the enemy into giving you better matches.
Luck, of course, plays a role but I’ve only had to re-do a handful of quest battles that swung against me to beat it with the same team right afterwards. Most of the time when the AI gets huge cascades I’m kicking myself because I missed something or gave them the matches.
There was a bit of frustration in the beginning but branching out to other kingdoms to lvl and get purple troops helped solve a lot of that and really upped my PVP game. I’d also suggest joining a guild asap as the bonus help as does the task rewards. My main team also utilized every color instead of doubling up but I’ve seen some killer teams that do it differently.
As far as PVP is concerned, it’s when I have to defend against extreme higher lvls that I get decimated but that’s not a pay2win problem. I have beaten legendary teams and gotten legendary troops from iron keys.
I’ve been searching for a game like this since Puzzle Quest and have finally found it. :)

So if you love Tower Defense Games, it is a MUST HAVE!

As a tower defense fan, but not necessarily a person who goes out of their way looking for a specific game, I was rather surprised when I stumbled across DG2. Having said that, I'm glad I have. This review is taking a look at the game as it is, since I hadn't heard of Defense Grid until now and I have spent approximately 40 minutes in game at the time of writing.
Here are a few things I picked up on which I are of reasonable quality for tower defense games:
- Pathing. Yes I know that most tower defense games include pathing for strategy but this always ticks a huge box for me. Something else which was a pleasant surprise was that one of the beta levels initially started with a smaller map and it grew. I'm not sure whether or not this is new but it certainly changed the way I could think (as the initial area was tiny).
- Towers. Look, with tower defense games you're always going to be seeing the same things, but that's okay. There's always going to be how each game balances towers in terms of cost and effectiveness. I like the towers presented in DG2, however I do believe they seem a little bit stale in regards to how similar they all appear.
- Buff towers (I already forgot what they're called so I'm going to call them this). I'm sure most/all tower defense games have a tower that perform some sort of powerup to towers around it, but the way DG2 does this actually adds yet more strategy. The way DG2 does it, is that your buff tower is the cheapest tower you can build. Why might you ask? Well that's because initially it acts as an obstructor, something that can help you build your path. After you have enough resource for the tower you want to powerup, you place it on top of the buff tower and you can pay an extra 200 resource to improve the tower that's on top. Personally speaking, it's a nice touch and allows you to build more natural paths, rather than a cluster of towers next to eachother.
- Health (Cores). Nice touch with how the enemies have to take all your cores, however the fact they also have to walk back makes this relatively easy (at least on story/open/normal. I haven't had time to look at other modes yet which I'm sure are going to be a blast. Then again this is probably just me nitpicking at stuff I haven't had a proper look at), but I digress. I like how different enemies can carry a certain amount of cores (although so far without paying too much attention only the big guys carry more than 1). I certainly think this is an interesting thing and hopefully there's the possibility of an enemy that can carry a lot of cores!
- Enemies. I thought the enemies at the start were fairly standard (fast enemies, grouped enemies, large/slow/painintheass), however upon right clicking upon one (that's how you view their stats) I noticed the abstract text went more into detail about their movement, with one type of enemy being slower around corners. I found this interesting because again it makes you think about optimal pathing.
So my conclusion is this. It's a great game for what's already available and it has the potential to be something amazing for the tower defense genre. Whilst graphics aren't necessarily important for tower defense games, DG2 looks pretty, although I do wish it had anti-aliasing support. For a beta it works well, and if you go in expecting something more polished than a beta release, then you'll be disappointed, however if you can look past that and see the potential then this one is certainly a keeper and one you'll enjoy when the full release comes around.

I had actually been looking forward to playing this game for a long time, but unfortunately in it's current form I can't recommend it.  The colonist AI is frustratingly unrealistic: the ability to prioritize is very limited in this game (you prioritze an entire structure and then have to disable individual equipment within it so that only certain equipment gets prioritized), and while you'd think that colonists (being human f'ing beings) would choose to eat *when there's food all over the place*, instead they incessantly mill about *even doing nothing at all* while they're hunger meter plummets. This game's AI is literally programmed for the colonists to *do nothing* rather than feed themselves. That of course has the consequence of potentially getting really far -- spending hours getting a base going -- only to have colonists drop like flies becasue they just decide to stop eating.  I've checked everything that makes sense: there are plenty of places to eat (though they'll sleep on the floor if there's no free bed, but won't sit on the floor to eat apparently), there is food all over the place waiting to be picked up, but they just stand there or mill about doing nothing.  /end_rant
Pros: graphics are OK, nice variety of buildings and colonist types
Cons: AI is *horrible*; zero terrain variety (you're stuck on a mars-type planet seemingly forever until you somehow manage to thrive far enough to unlock the next planet type, which of course requires colonists to choose to eat rather than *literally allow themselves to starve to death while surrounded by food*); game speed has a max of 4X which still feels painfully slow; every time you start over, you have to sit and watch a pod of starter colonists land and disembark which is also painfully slow and can't be skipped; some equipment like beds and TVs can be very precisely located in rooms, while other equipment snaps to an invisible grid that doesn't always make sense (for instance, vending machines can only be very awkwardly positioned, and you're forced to place some of them in non-sensical arrangements); trade ships are ridiculously expensive to deal with (it seems random, but many times the markup is *65%*!!); did i mention the game is really slow even on its max speed setting?

This game can be challenging and engaging, or it can be relaxing and going on in the background. I've been at tough points where I kept restarting, and I've been at points where I took a nap and let my colonists take care of themselves. This game has opportunity for both.
If you like coming up with a strategy or plan and then putting it to the test, this is the game for you. Each game makes your adapt and rethink your strategy.
This is a game where you don't micromanage the colonist actions, but instead you put a put a model in place, and give plans for expansion, and hope it works out. If your colonists survive, you can modify for greater growth and production.

Tactically speaking, planetbase strikes me as a true hidden gem. Starting out you will be required to build a "moonbase" on the first planet, forcing you to juggle your colony's needs. Yes they need more air but running out of oxygen takes quite a bit longer than all the colonists getting dehydrated and dying. Since oxygen generators consume water, you may consider upgrading to more water extractors before you build that oxygen generator you need soon. Think twice about which size water extractor you're going to build too - maybe the largest one will drain too much from your power grid during the precarious night. Go big or go home you say? Build another wind turbine or power storage to offset the increased energy demands. However the more of those you build, the more spare parts you need to produce to maintain them. Spare parts, in turn, cost metal and bioplastic. Metal and Bioplastic, subsequently cost ore and starch respectively. Planetbase is a carefully crafted game of balance. By the time you have 40-50 hours in this game, you will feel like the balance beam gold-metalist of RTSs.
All in all, you don't need to be masochistic to enjoy this game. It has a decent challenge level, a good learning curve, and solid replay value.
