TL:DR It is a nice, cheap game but if you want quality your better off waiting for a similar game to go on sale.
What is the game?
In this game you start off as a Pug and then you are placed into an endless runner, not to much more to say.
World Design?
This is my main problem with the game, I wouldn't say the world design is that good.
First off in your first run you have probably seen most of it and second of all it is inconsistant.
There are some parts where it's really easy but then you have parts that require exact timing unless you have double jump, even then sometimes you can't double jump over it because behind the obsticle if you double jump you'll fall off of the map.
This would be fine but there is no progression, it seems to go on until you lose, lets take Subway Surfers, it gets faster and faster the higher score you get, this might be in Turbo Pug but it isn't really visible and only having to tap space doesn't give the same thrills.
Also it is just kinda bland, yes there are big spikes but it isn't fun to dodge, it's sort of like an army sending one man at a time against you, it is good to get used to it but eventually it's just doing the same thing over and over until one gets lucky, it would be much more fun to send two men at me, then three ect, it would also solve the problem of progression.
Unlocks.
I don't really know what to say about the unlocks, the cosmetic changes are nice but I feel like they should seperate cosmetic changes and actual game changes.
For example I think the pug in a mexican hat looks cute so I go to play him, however he feels way to light so I can't play as him, if they just seperated it then you could have comfortable controls and your favourite cosmetic animal.
That also brings me to another point, some unlocks just feel off, the mexican pug feels way to light, the frozen pug feels to heavy, the penguin is unplayable, even my favourite (pumpkin pug) feels a tad bit to heavy.
Also it isn't clear how to unlock them, I think it's getting to a point where you see red vases but the game never tells me, it also doesn't tell me when I unlock something.
However I do like how the added other animals if you don't like pugs but when it's a game called Turbo Pug it doesn't really make sense for non-pug fans to play.
Graphics
I don't have much to say about the graphics except that the art style is quite nice.
Controls
The space bar is to jump, probably the best button to jump, you can't do anything else.
I wouldn't say this is a controls issue however it's related, why can't I press space to replay? Where is the logic? If I am playing an endless runner with one button atleast let me used it to start a new game instead of having to use my mouse, it's just annoying.
Music
The music is nice and happy, I would rather play other music as with an endless runner your not doing much so listening to music or a podcast would make it more entertaining but the music's alright...
But come on I don't want to listen to the same one or two songs over and over and over again.
Conclusion
This isn't really a "game" game more just a time killer, so as much as I think it's wrong to review it as a "game", it runs around screaming "I am a game" so I will treat it as such, I would give it a 2/10.
So why recomend it? Well as much as it is said I would have liked a neutral/depends button because you know you arn't going for a rich gaming expirence but for the price of £0.79 (often on sale for £0.39) it can kill a few hours which a movie demands £5 for.
But if you like pugs why not pick it up when you have spare money on your steam account?

Just as a disclaimer, I've 100% completed the single-player campaign, but I'm not going to chase after all of the achievements because (a) many of them are multiplayer and (b) some of them are annoying. And I'm a bit burned out on Tomb Raider.
So, Tomb Raider (2013) is a hard reboot of the venerable Tomb Raider franchise. I was never really a fan of Lara Croft's adventures, though I did play partway through her previous soft reboot, Tomb Raider Legend. I didn't get far, and kept getting killed during a particular encounter. I did like the exploring parts, and the mansion. This Tomb Raider is different however. It doesn't start us off with a smug-as-hell, confident-as-hell Lara Croft, who was played by Angelina Jolie and her massive lips. This is a younger, more naive Lara, probably right out of college, and not very tomb-raider-y.
I'm going to preface this review by saying that this is a great game, and you should play it, if you haven't already. But I am going to start out by talking about what bothered me about this game, because I feel that's rather important to get out of the way.
So, this game is essentially Tomb Raider: Origins. Consequently, Lara is far less experienced in tomb raiding, far less blasé about killing people, far more innocent. And I'm fine with that. But it's rather jarring when we get past the first combat encounter, and Lara's already killed more people than Billy the Kid did across his entire career. And then at the 68% progress mark (I checked), Lara's killed more people than the bubonic plague, and she's still sobbing and whimpering all the time, and sits huddled up at every campsite.
I understand gameplay versus story separation, but this is absurd. It's exactly like this comic:
Look, I'm not saying that I want Lara characterized as a psychopath, but killing that many people should have had an impact on her. If we wanted to show how traumatic this experience was, how about just having her killing people reluctantly? Give the player a chance to sneak past encounters? But no, each kill is worth XP, and it's hard to pass up on shooting people in the head when they're each worth 20XP. And frankly, Lara by the half-way mark is a stone-cold badass... except during cutscenes.
And the bloody QTEs. I've died more to QTEs than I have to combat encounters and platforming combined. And this one encounter ate up all of my ammo because I had to keep stunning the guy because I couldn't get past the compulsory QTE necessary to kill the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.
But all of this aside, the gameplay is really good. The platforming is wonderful, with all of the different types of surfaces and jumps and climbing. The platforming QTE aren't quite so bad, and the camera is just a dream. It turns to show you where you go, but does it in a very subtle way. Combat is meaty, and improving your gear has a definite impact. And the crafting is great.
The optional tombs are fun little segments, but what annoys me is that you get XP and salvage, and an area map, you don't get any fluff on what's in the tomb. It would've been nice if they'd had that.
But, quibbling. Tomb Raider (2013) is worth your time, and you really should put in the extra effort to 100% the campaign.

I've just finished playing through for the second time, and I cannot recommend this game highly enough. Everything - the story, music, combat, scenery, tomb raid puzzles, voice acting - everything was executed brilliantly. Above all, the development of Lara from a lost and terrified child to a hardened combatant explorer is superb. Origin stories can be tricky - a Lara too slow to develop her skills would be a chore to play, but too quick would break suspension of disbelief. I felt the balance was achieved well in this game.
You can rush through the story in ten hours, give or take, but expect to put in 20+ if you want to grab all the hidden collectibles and complete all challenges. Doing so will make Lara more capable, as exploring and collecting will help you obtain all possible skills and weapon upgrades, and gives you a better chance to experience the stunning and diverse scenery.
A warning to younger or more sensitive players: aside from the violence and mild language one should expect of a third person shooter, there are numerous instances in the game where failure to properly navigate the terrain or react to specific prompts will result in a fairly graphic death scene for Lara.  This may involve being shot point blank, mauled by wild animals, or impaled on any number of things. These death cutscenes can be somewhat jarring, especially when unexpected, and may disturb some players (or their parents). This was the reason my wife couldn't finish the game. I wholeheartedly recommend this game... just not to the squeamish.

While looking down the sights pressing a movement key will let the player lean in that direction. In other word pressing left will lean left and pressing up will peak over objects. To move while aiming down the sights you have to press the sprint key. The system actualy works great for the bigger slower paced battles. What bothered me the most about the game is its lenght. the good:
+unique react to light enemies/environment
+potential for a good story
+depressive voiced ai narrator
+crew logs
+some of the larger rooms have good 3d atmosphere and detail
the neutal:
you act on a 2d plane in a 3d environment, there are several spots where it would have been good to include a shoot outside your plane rail shooter like dynamic to get background enemies
there are a few areas where some trivial stuff rolls out of your plane into the background where you cant get to it, slightly annoying, nothing important enough to be game breaking though, and otoh helps establish the environment as 3d.
the bad:
-the game was never truly completed, they patched in an end sequence on an incomplete game due to customer complaints about the game being incomplete
-abandoned by the dev, waited over a year before playing in hopes of more patches but it seems like this is it, this is also a good example of why not to support early access games, once they have the money there is no reason to further develop, instead let them take out a loan, bring a full product to the table, and have the quality of the product determine whether they profit.
-4 weapons one of which you barely have a chance to use

This game isn't what it was supposed to be.
This game aimed to be a semi-big title. ...but the Kickstarter funding failed.
The developers tried to scale back into episodic content, but if you know episodic content by now, you know that that strategy never works.
The result is this "first" episode, with episode two and three cancelled.
The developer was kind enough to attach an ending at the end, however, so we get a short budget game.
The concepts was what made the game look so promising: You had interacting with creatures through light. However, there's not much more beyond that.
...but where it falls flat is the environments: Technically they look different, but somehow they all look the same. Without any variation, the game just ends up becoming one big maze. This means that you can easily take a wrong turn and end up missing the shotgun in the game, so you find yourself asking yourself why you need to glitch-kill enemies from off-screen in order to proceed.
There's also a good amount of various bugs. It's nothing show-stopping, although you are sighing from relief when you're done evading them all. This game sure could have benefited from a few play testers.

But why is it not like Postal 2 and feels so... Dissapointing and unfinished comparing to Postal 2? Let's compare those games. First of all, the old postal two was sort of a soup made of chaos, blood, gore and insanity as a topping. And the whole soup was made in a bowl of some weak law system. That game was finished. It felt so complete and just complex enough. It was a great game and my favourite game since childhood. I was very excited when I saw this game come out. It was so promissing. If you never played Postal 2 or wish to play a cheap and good shooter with some dirtyness and black humor in it, this is the perfet game for you.
But if you are looking for a game that feels just like Postal 2, that has this chaotic insane spirit that Postal 2 had, I would reccomend you to rather spend 50$ to buy Dead Rising 3. That game feels so much like Postal 2.
I would say this game does worth it's money, but not a cent more than it's price.

Overall, I don't recommend this game. It has a lot of percieved AI noding problems (Which isn't too hard to resolve), but it seems to me that it's extremely repetitive, since I can't remember any update. While I don't think it's a bad game, the "Skill Floor" and "Skill Ceiling" are both too close together; for anyone, it seems you can thrive or at least survive, and for another, they can't seem to figure out why most of their buildings aren't being built.
Another factor, is the very limited size of all of these maps. The motive of the intruders are very confusing, and it seriously ticks me off about the inefficiency of the security guards. If I had any say, I'd make metal detectors a thing, just saying.
Additionally, I really don't like the inefficiencies in AI behavior. We can't micromanage, but I suppose that's positive. I do, however, hate the idea that colonists cannot reproduce. The goal of a colony is to be autonomous and not require immigration to maintain your population!
Furthermore, replacing buildings is difficult, and you can only have a central building, no other independent connections, absolute rubbish. I suppose that would make the noding more difficult. Additionally, the markup from the traders always was frustrating to me. The prices for things was simply too high.
Furthermore, the AI seem inefficient in other behavior. They require so much food and rest, and don't even get me started on their happiness.
For the positives, I enjoy the idea of making said colony, the most satisfying part was realizing how to correctly play the game and then having the satisfaction of making a colony that could sell something for money. Unfortunately, the learning curve was the only positive thing about this game. Once you knew how to make an efficient base to defeat the harsh vacuum of space, it's clear how to play the game. Did I mention the intruders?
If it were cheaper, I'd most definitely recommend it, but it's a very generic city building game.
Still, it's about 20 USD too expensive. Have fun if you can, tell me if I'm doing it wrong, or something.

Great initial concept, doesn't pan out and work on a number of levels.  Beyond the initial mad-dash to find and store your family and survival gear, the game basically plays out like a Choose Your Own Adventure novel, though perhaps that's a bit unfair as those novels at least had variations in the pictures from page to page.  The survival side of it plays out a bit like the choices from time to time in the "Rebuild" series, in that they are entirely text based.  Even scavenging, supposedly a life or death event in the story of the game, happens off-screen and with no input or guidance from the player.  To see something like this done right, look at the game "This War of Mine", where scavenging was a nerve-wracking, nail biting, nightmare inducing event that happened just about every night in the game cycle.  Here, you send your son out to scavenge, he never returns... something bad happened I guess?  Your daughter runs off because of lack of water and you're treated to... the same still 2d pic of your character.  No, wait, there's now an empty chair, very profound.
Look I get with the cartoony graphics the game clearly was not going for the same feel as This War of Mine, even if the underlying mechanics are largely the same.  But with the game being almost entirely text based, little interaction, the style disconnected from the 1950's fallout shelter feel the tutorial tries to invoke... all of it just misses.  You're basically playing the original Rebuild without zombies, buildings, or skilled survivors.  You're playing TWOF without the actual game.

When I went to grab Pac-Man Championship edition, I thought that what I could be getting was just the old Pac-Man arcade game with some updated visuals. I was very, very wrong. While the game has awesomely updated new visuals, and some new maps, those seem to be only the tip of the iceberg of classic gaming enjoyment in this game!
The game features multiple new modes of play, and interesting new ways of getting through them. Pills and pips aren't always where you think they are, and you can't tell where the new ones will be until you finish the last of the ones you have. And yet, the game isn't unfair in anyway. In fact, on the lower difficulty levels, the game is exceedingly fair to new players. (Or those who play like new players, like me.) The game will actually slow down in instances in which Pac-Man is in danger, giving you a few extra moments to try and figure out how to get out of the problem you're in. Can't find an escape? Drop a bomb!
While it's true that all of these things do mean that the game isn't just your Dad/Grandad's Pac-Man, I think this simply shows Bandai-Namco's ability to change with the times. Pac-Man's been updated with some really great game design decisions, and given the low cost of this game (especially during any Steam Sales), I cannot recommend it enough! You owe it to yourself to play this game, and respect how a classic game can stay relevant even today.

It's hard to make a good update to some games. While most Pac-Man sequels were basically the same thing with a small tweak, this game manages to stand out.
The focus this time is less survival, more high score accumulation.
The main game concept is still the same. You are Pac-Man, and go around the maze eating stuff. But the objective is not to just eat. The game gives you a path of dots, around which are ghosts waiting to eat you who start following you when you approach. Power Pellets are not as common as in the original game, so watch those small spaces. The game DOES have ghost repelling bombs but they do run out and are only refillable by eating ghosts. Once you eat a pattern, a fruit piece on the other side of the maze appears to replace the pattern you ate.
While this version is not so urgent and survivalistic in tone, it can be really fun, especially the faster the session gets. Plus each maze has a set of challenges with which to clear it. It may not be the Pac-Man your dad sank hours worth of quarters into, but it is still fun.
I give it a 9.5/10, because one unlockable would be impossible to get without a Facebook account as the requirement to get it is to get all the medals and achievements and post them to your Facebook feed.

Even though I personally prefer Overture to Black Plague, I have no doubts about recommending this game. Many people consider Black Plague to be the best in the series and it is clear to see why.
Overall Black Plague is a pretty satisfying continuation of the story. It has a longer runtime, more aggressive scare tactics, and better balance.
I am thrilled they did away with all combat and weapons, and the number of enemies was scaled back appropriately. The gameplay flowed much more naturally and felt slightly more polished compared to Overture.
A lot of game-time is spent searching/fetching/backtracking, but I never got lost and my progress was never really halted, so I wouldn't say the game is frustrating in that sense. Not always super fun to run back and forth through the same area repeatedly - there were times when it got old - but for the most part the story helps move everything along. If you can stay immersed, it is fine.
The setting isn't as compelling as the mining tunnels of Overture. Not many memorable environments, a lot of repetition due to the nature of the building. Considering this, I thought they did a great job with exploration and keeping things fresh.
I was missing the role of writings in this game. In Overture there was just enough cryptic information in the form of notes, newspapers, etc. It created a constant duality of discovery and horror. In Black Plague there were almost no interesting notes to find. Instead I felt like information was just being thrown at me from every direction and I was told too much too soon. There was almost no sense of mystery left.
Have to say I wasn't a fan of the many new characters/people/personalities introduced. There was a lot going on and I never felt isolated. Unfortunately it hurt the tension for me and I ran through the game mostly without fear. Despite that, there is a good amount of horror to this game in the form of some very effective and memorable sequences. Outstanding use of audio and light/dark.
A lot of decent scare tactics are used, along with some cheaper jump-scares, and it's a lot of fun. I enjoyed seeing what they came up with and when the game caught me off guard. It was kind of like a haunted house.
Complaints and nitpicking aside, I had a blast with both games. Penumbra delivered a satisfying experience with plenty of mystery and entertainment. Well done.

TL:DR Medal of Honor Airborne is a game where you drop from the sky, feed your gun souls to get attachments, and the AI team REALLY assumed every soldier on the U.S side was a private
Three downsides to address  off the bat:
1) This isn't Band of Brothers in video game form, don't take it too seriously. There's a lot of fun to be had here. But seriously, even I, a civillian can note that something is off when EVERYONE is wearing private insignias. Besides, MoH was never known for realism (well except the normandy beach level all the way back in Allied Assault, but the series as a whole generally focused on Ficticious OSS operations). However if you are looking for something more realistic. May I suggest Red Orchestra or Company of Heroes? Either will fit the bill far better.
2) Also bear in mind it is short, 7 missions. Most people I assume fighting on Normal difficulty say they complete it in 3 to 5 hours, It took me about 12 ish to beat it on hard, though if I played smarter I could have probably cut it in thirds tbh, especially exploiting the "leaning" mechanics better.
3) While the Axis AI is competent (They'll flush you out, flank you and generally try and work together, at least on hard), the U.S soldiers are complete morons, oftentimes walking and STOPPING in front of your sights while you are trying to line up a shot.Thank goodness there's not a whole lot of penalty for friendly fire.
Now time to gush! I love this series (Modern Warfare one notwithstanding), Airborne is almost a decade old and to be perfectly honest it holds up suprisingly well. Medal of Honor for the unitiated (And again, ignoring the Modern warfare one), is basically a first person shooter that plays more like a polished Goldeneye and you play as an American trooper in World War 2. In this case, Paratroopers, 82nd Airborne, and the game exploits this fact to the fullest.
The signature mechanic is the Paradrop sequences. Every time you respawn, you leap from an airplane and can land almost anywhere on the map. There's two things that make this awesome. First there's actually some skill involved with making a drop, not only do you have to measure risk vs reward (or if you just want to nail skill drops), but you also have to  actually PERFORM the landing by properly flaring the chute so you don't tumble to the ground and botch the landing. If you are unlucky, there may be an Axis troop putting bullets in you before you have a chance to fire back. Or if you are a pro at greasing landings, you can possibly get the jump on a pesky sniper that bothered you last drop!
This segways the second thing that makes this awesome, Level design. For the most part, it's less a linear run and more of an open arena. Complete with accessable rooftops, alleyways, Aqueducts, church towers, bombed out buildings, Castle-like Flak Towers, and a WHOLE lot more! Needless to say, there's almost ALWAYS a way around.
I say ALMOST because there are a few short areas where you are railroaded through some segments, for the most part they aren't terrible but they aren't nearly as interesting as the open landings, heck you don't even PARADROP in these (some of them understandably so as you are underground)
The second cool thing about this game is the gunplay, first off when you aim down the sights, you actually use WASD to lean, it's kind of annoying at first but when combined with locking it in place with shift (which also allows you to move again) it gives you a great deal of flexibility when in cover. Leaning over walkways, around corners, or even playing "Whack a mole" with germans!
Then there's the weapon upgrade, yes it is very video-gamey, but it works! Kill Nazis, get upgrades in the form of weapon attachments, for a total of three upgrades for each weapon (including grenades). They all give the weapon a signifigant upgrade, and you'll enjoy them if you are a gun geek, though they can be kind of samey at times, Still it's fun and turns mediocre weapons into some crazy killing machines.
A few other points to factor in
*For the non gun geeks, I'll let Matt Carriker of Demolition ranch break it down:
In conclusion, it's not entirely serious but it's solid! I got it at two bucks on a sale, but it's worth the full 10. At launch I probably wouldn't have paid 60 bucks due to length, but it's by no means a bad game!

Don't let the fact that this game is 10 years old dissuade you from buying it, especially now that its on sale. The game is hard to get used to as it simulates weapon recoil, so no run and gun per se (more on that later). AI can be a challenge if you let the enemy dig in, and knowing when to push is key to victory. As such, it does simulate somewhat accurately a real gun fight.
Regarding the run and gun: you can use it, provide you think it a bit through "on the spot". For example, in the last mission you have to push aggressively while maintaining cover just long enough to keep pushing, while taking out the enemy while they reload. Dig in, and they will overrun you. Push to far ahead, and you will be taken down like a shooting practice mannequin.
Expect to die a lot. Expect to curse at the game designers and their families even more. But that is the beauty of this game: it shows you that achieving victory in WW 2 required the sacrifice of many brave men, because sometimes you have to die to achieve the objective.
Pros
-Scales rather well to 4k resolution
-Land anywhere, fight the good fight from anywhere (just like a real airborne)
-Varied enough weapon set (Lugers rule)
-Simulates WW2 fighting rather well
-Scenes before you jump
Cons
-Freaking hard (until you get used to it, then its challenging)
-Graphics are a little dated IF you get pícky about it, but its not that bad (at 4K I didn't notice i that much).
-It is a little short (still, 7.4 hours of solid gameplay for what I paid is well worth it).
Buy it. You won't regret it.

This is a good, solid, fun little retro game.
My first reaction to hearing about this game was "surely a game from a magazine listing from 1981 will be too simple to have enduring appeal", and the idea of someone selling a game that's from a magazine listing seemed... well, lazy.
For anyone who doesn't remember, back in the early 1980s when home computing was first starting to take off, computer enthusiast magazines would sometimes include game listings for you to key in and play. This was back in the days before they began to tape recorded media to magazine covers.
I remember typing in game listings - back in the early 1980s - and... well, I learned two things. 1) how to type accurately, and 2) that games you type in from magazine listings generally aren't worth the time they take to type in.
The other thing is - I wasn't playing on home computers in 1981. I was three years old, and there are Atari 2600 joysticks in my mum's house with my baby teething marks imprinted upon them. I was beating my parents at Space Invaders. The first home computer game I played was "Radar Rat Race" on C64, a clone of Namco's Rally X by HAL Laboratories. It came on a cartridge. Yes, more mazes and mice! It was quite good... but my ideas of what a home computer game from 1981 are, are - "very, very basic".
So this is how I came into SPACE MOUSE. No history of playing the game any time previously in its 35 years, and with the pre-conception that it probably wasn't going to be worth my time.
It turned out that my expectations were wrong.
The default version of the game that you get to play is the "NES ARR" version - i.e. the game as imagined if it were for the Nintendo Entertainment System (Famicon), and it's been given a few extra features and enough polish to make it feel as new as maybe.... 1985! The game also includes a few other versions, including the original PC-8001 version.
The basic game is - you control a little thingie that can only move left, right, and up, and you need to travel ever upwards through a maze-like level, while avoiding enemies that flow through the level in a predictable pattern - similar to those water flow puzzles you sometimes see. There is one power up, and it allows you to bust through walls for a short period of time.
I don't know whether that simple description does the game justice. Despite being so simple, reading the flow of enemies and the layout of the maze before you gives it challenge beyond mere twitchy arcade play - you're always looking for the best route as you traverse forwards, waiting for the perfect time to move.
The NES Arranged version adds a little complexity; music, nicer graphics, helpful messages to the player, keys and extra lives to collect, and a few little hidden secrets and mechanics. Also, you can ram enemies when powered up, to beat them and earn points. It really is a big improvement to the game.
The original developer of this game went on to work for Enix and Namco, before leaving the industry to become a medical doctor. I do wonder whether elements of SPACE MOUSE were combined with Dig Dug then inverted, to influence the creation of one of my favourite games - Mr Driller. It is all vertical scrolling to the goal while racing an ever-decreasing air supply, after all.
Overall: this game really exceeded my expectations and is a lot of good, simple fun. I recommend it.

As a fan of Mindware's work on WiiWare and the DSi (MaBoShi is amazing), l had to give this a go given its rather quirky heritage.
Despite its age, Space Mouse is a product of good design, it doesn't feel as old as you'd expect it to, and instead has a timeless appeal to it much like the best games of the 80s which you'd still play today.
In Space Mouse you've got to make your way to the top of the screen, navigating floors of a building and avoiding mice which are making their way down the screen. Each "tier" of the screen is effectively a floor of the building, and there are gaps (or stairwells if you will) to move up to the next floor.
What makes this simple idea work rather well are the smart constraints applied to your character and the rules of the game. You can't go back once you've moved up a level, so you've got to plan far ahead of time. The mice which run against you either move left or right once they pass a stairwell, which introduces a constant element of uncertainty in how you tackle each moving roadblock: Should you consider a specific location on the grid a hiding place or not, or should you can quickly dash past a potential opening while it's there?
I've found myself bettering myself with every go, and subsequent stages introduce different tower layouts which further demand more from you and require better flexibility in dealing with the hazards ahead.
Despite the game's 1981 roots the default mode is a remake featuring NES/Famicom style visuals (more detailed sprites and smooth scrolling), and new mechanics. So far I've tried the NES and MZ-700 modes, I've yet to unlock the original PC-8001 version of the game. The general look of the "arranged" version certainly feels authentic to me - like a lost NES game from the early 80's, which in turn complements the grid-based game world.
In its current state I feel Space Mouse is missing one feature that'd make it feel more well rounded: high score tracking and leaderboards. I've been playing from the first level every time I get a game over and it's a shame my scores aren't being saved so I can track how well I'm doing over time. So hopefully these are added to the game at some point - it already supports features of the Steam platform like achievements and playing cards, so I'd love to see online Steam leaderboards or just local ones.
tl;dr: Space Mouse carries arcade-like sensibilities that has kept me returning to it for another quick go much more often than I had anticipated.

TLDR: A simple, but quite enjoyable little game, obviously a labour of love.
The goal is to get to the top of each level, while avoiding or killing the monsters who head in the opposite direction, but there are many little things that make it more interesting and tactical than it first might seem. For instance, while the monsters movement may appear chaotic, it is based on simple and predictable rules.
There are also keys to find and coins to grab. The keys let you unlock bonus "rooms", while the coins let you kill enemies and break walls, but only for a short while (unless you grab more coins). Later levels (in the NES-style arranged version, at least) introduce new elements that must be taken into account, such as invincible walls and walls that can be broken even in normal mode.
The presentation is quite nice (I love the little wave that the main character gives while waiting for the rocket) and authentic, and I am very fond of the music. The tune on level three is my favourite so far, I think. If you like chiptunes, you'll like the music, and if you played games in the eighties you'll definitely recognize the "sound" as well.
The added MZ-700 versions are a nice touch that adds some value especially for those of us who had Sharp computers back in the eighties and recognize the "little man" character (display codes for POKE are 202-205 on my MZ-80A ;) ). I have not yet tried the original PC-8001 version.
I think this game will appeal to anyone who like retro-style games. If you have an interest in the particular platforms being "emulated" (NEC PC, Sharp MZ and NES), you'll obviously be more partial to it, but so far I feel that it is a very well designed game that should work both with and without the nostalgia goggles.
Disclaimer: The author of the remake is a Steam friend of mine, and we have a common interest in the history of computer games. I previously interviewed him for my site:

But I bought this game as a regular customer.
I'll also add that I am a fan of the devs earlier game, Cosmic Cavern 3671.

Not too sure what to write here so heres a recipe for Pancakes instead
Ingredients:
1 1/2 cups all-purpose flour
3 tablespoons sugar
1 tablespoon baking powder
1/4 teaspoon salt
1/8 teaspoon freshly ground nutmeg
2 large eggs, at room temperature
1 1/4 cups milk, at room temperature
1/2 teaspoon pure vanilla extract
3 tablespoons unsalted butter, plus more as needed
Now to make it
1. In a large bowl, whisk together the flour, sugar, baking powder, salt, and nutmeg.
2. In another bowl, beat the eggs and then whisk in the milk and vanilla.
3. Melt the butter in a large cast iron skillet or griddle over medium heat.
4. Whisk the butter into the milk mixture. Add the wet ingredients to the flour mixture, and whisk until a thick batter is just formed
5. Keeping the skillet at medium heat, ladle about 1/4 cup of the batter onto the skillet, to make a pancake. Make 1 or 2 more pancakes, taking care to keep them evenly spaced apart. Cook, until bubbles break the surface of the pancakes, and the undersides are golden brown, about 2 minutes. Flip with a spatula and cook about 1 minute more on the second side. Serve immediately or transfer to a platter and cover loosely with foil to keep warm. Repeat with the remaining batter, adding more butter to the skillet as needed.
6. Procedure for adding fruit to pancakes: Once the bubbles break the surface of the pancakes, scatter the surface with sliced or diced fruit, or chocolate chips, nuts, etc. Flip with a spatula and cook for 1 minute more, being careful not to burn toppings.

Wilson Chronicles (2016.2844.1.0 BETA) review
Short Review:
Wilson Chronicles is a short, yet fun Half-life mod that lacks in story. But great in level design.
Long Review:
STORY: Wilson Chronicles puts you in the shoes of a Black Mesa scientist surviving the events of Half-Life 1. Sadly there is almost no story with this mod. Barely any scientists or even security will interact with you, like you're just part of the background. But because this is a BETA (from the time I'm writing this) so I hope this is fixed in the finished version.
GAMEPLAY: Gameplay is the same as Half-life 2, been there done that. But if it isn't broke, don't fix it. It's the same fast responsive fun that you've encountered in every Valve game. Using the same guns recreated from Half Life 1, it's just an over-all blast.
LEVEL DESIGN: Level's (so far) in the BETA of Wilson Chronicles are just good, but not great. Because it's in BETA  a lot of glitches can appear in gameplay which get annoying at times. But (at least for me) they didn't appear all that much.
NITPICKING/ THINGS THAT NEED TO BE IMPROVED: In the Wilson Chronicles there are A LOT of copyrighted drawings of products, bands, and even icons. Which can suck some people out of immersion, or could get the devs in trouble. Also effects and some animation is pretty bad or glitchy, I also hope this is improved out of BETA.

Shadowrun Returns was already an excellent game and I'm happy to report that the Director's Cut of Dragonfall continues that fine tradition. While the original game sported a perfectly fine UI, the DC adds even more polish and several nice new additions. No longer do you have to hunt for your weapon and spell abilities – they're now all there right where you need them.
The game was already visually stunning, but the new animations and other refinements just add a bit more polish. Critical hits are now viscerally satisfying and the new attack animations look killer. Most of the changes are small but add a great deal to the overall feel of the game.
The storyline of Dragonfall was great in the original game, but the changes in the DC really take it to the next level. The richly detailed NPCs now all have their own specific missions that meld well with their complex and interesting backgrounds. These custom missions not only give your running mates new abilities, they also give each NPC a fitting resolution to their own unique stories.
If you liked Shadowrun Returns, the Dragonfall Director's Cut is definitely worth purchasing (if you haven't already gotten it for free!). If you're new to the game,  this is definitely where you should start. I cannot recommend this game enough.

It has good physics and offers 'original' pinball machines but the gameplay, for me, is ridiculously inferior to Pinball FX2.  The 'season pass' prices are high, just like the competitors, and it will cost you a LOT of money to own all the tables available.  The same thing goes for the 'other' pinball games.

There have been a ton of awesome pinball tables over the years and Pinball Arcade is one of the best programs to come along so far to deliver the experience of digital pinball with actual table designs from years gone by. Granted, if you're not into pinball, there's nothing really here for you, but without spending any money you do get full access to one table and can demo every other table without paying a dime.
Very good (though not perfect) physics, table designs are nearly spot-on to the real machines, includes a mix of various tables from the most popular to the least popular, as well as from the most common to the absurdly rare, actual ROM data is being used so the tables have all of their hidden features and everything, all of which are documented in-game, extensive instructions available for every table to make learning the rulesets much easier.
Default configuration and camera settings are garbage for anyone looking to REALLY play the game, so you need to reconfigure everything, the "Call Attendant" feature for dealing with issues can't handle most of the problems which crop up (which are thankfully few and far between), very expensive if you want "pro" access to all the tables (extra configuration settings and options for examining the table)... still cheaper than owning just a single REAL machine. :P
If you like pinball, fun.

It’s not fair to say that the darkness consumed me, for it was I who enveloped myself in it, there was no coercion involved, only my own maddened curiosity. Another Postal game was released? Well, the second one was charming in that somewhat difficult to explain way that not very good games sometimes are, and it was on sale for a tenner, what could I possibly lose?
Sometimes in the quiet hours of the night, when it seems not even God is there to hear me, I ask myself what I could have saved had I never clicked ‘Add to Cart’. It’s more than the ten dollars, what I lost that day transcends the mere balancing of a checkbook, when I played this game the concepts of love, of faith in my fellow man, the very knowledge of any pleasures I had once known all fled from me in an instant.
I wish I could chalk my dislike of this game up to the awful controls, the movement clunkier than a 50’s movie robot or the aiming that I can only describe as ‘acrid’, like the breath of a drunken pirate manning the cannons of his schooner, the fearsome ‘Nobody Will Ever Love You’. I can’t though, much like an iceberg made of solid human feces it goes much deeper than the surface problems. I didn’t even come across anything that offensive in my two-hour waterboarding session with Postal 3, I know that’s exactly what it’s meant to do, and it succeeds with a lot of people, but it just fell flat. It's a nice game to relax to, and the desolate planets you build bases on really drives the feeling of being isolated and alone. The real challenge is at the beginning, where you're scrambling to build up a basic infrastructure as the planet's climate actively works against you.
After that things become much smoother, and the greatest threat changes from the planet itself to how well (or bad) your resource management skills are.
Unfortunately, there's not a lot of replayability. Aside from the Challenge Modes and different planet types, not much changes. You're stuck with the same buildings, the same colonists, and the same resources on each planet you land on.
Basically, the game is great for playing every once in a while when you're bored, but would have benefitted greatly from a greater variety of content.

The gameplay is quite satisfying, even though there are many quirks. It's an indie title, doesn't promise much, delivers what it set out to do to a reasonable degree and it has received constant support since it was released.
In its current state, it offers some interesting play scenarios and the way the space village shapes up eventually is really interesting and gratifying. Optimising the room placement (and workers movement) depending on terrain will make you replay the game in the same location several times.
On the downside, the behavior of the colonists feels very synthetic and although they have fixed some objective problems, they haven't fixed this. Most of the difficulty elements depends on this and on how well you start off. The game balance is very simplistic and the learning curve is not a big deal.
The survival elements are on the light side, people were expecting Banished in space maybe. I was expecting a simplistic space colonisation simulator (i.e. the tools to deal with any problems are available and if you understand the game mechanics, you can deal with all crisis eventually).
Quite a relaxing experience overall.

I have extremely mixed feelings about this game. On the one hand, the first base was quite fun, and the second, while not as fun, still managed to be enjoyable. But once you get to the harder bases, it gets extremely annoying due to the terrible AI scripting. It requires entirely too much micromanagement, and your personnel will do things without regard to the actual conditions in your base: need power, but have other projects to build simultaneously? Too bad; we're going to build whatever you ordered last. It'd be more efficient to bring materials in to storage and transport them from there? Too bad; we're going to carry everything all the way to its destination. Have something set to priority, but have connections to build? Too bad; we're going to build the connections first. Got something close that doesn't require many resources, but have other projects? Too bad; we're going to build whatever you ordered last. I could go on.
The bad AI doesn't totally ruin the game, but it does make it much less fun than it could be. It'd be nice if it was extensible, and offered the ability for users to modify it (such as improving the AI scripting, and adding new buildings).

I wanted to like this game, but couldn't. TLDR: It wasn't that much fun overall. Not really much of a horror game (not scary). I found the voice of Clarence to be rather annoying. The puzzles were bothersome at times. The ending took turn way out into left field.
Longer review:
I will start by saying that although the first installment of this series (Overture) has its flaws, I was able to finish the game without a walkthrough and the story was interesting. Black Plague on the other hand improved upon some of these flaws, but ended up making a worse game in my opinion.
Story:
Black Plague continues about where Overture left off. However, it goes in an entirely different direction by involving some organization that is apparently a gloabl order. It felt like much of what happened was created after the first game rather than having been the plan for the story all along. By the time I reached the ending, it felt like the story had gone into a whole other direction. And then there is Clarence. He is a voice in your head that (if you play you can figure out how he got there) was just really annoying. I understand the overall contribution of Clarence to the plot, but I would have done it differently myself. But perhaps his annoying voice and dialogue were exactly what the writer(s) wanted to show. Overall, it wasn't satisfying for me.
Gameplay/Puzzles- The gameplay and object interaction were pretty standard if not better than Overture. I definitely think that Black Plague was better off without combat. The enemies were not difficult to face, but rather acted to obstruct you on the way to your next destination. Overall standard gameply. The puzzles were problematic for me as I wasn't really into the game and was in a hurry to finish it, so I often would miss an item that was needed to solve the puzzle. For example, one puzzle required a book or note to tell you how to complete it, but I never saw it and thus was frustrated as to why the puzzle made no sense. Thats on me, but I probably would have liked the puzzles more if they were actually realistic.
Anyways, the puzzles were not always consistent with the objects you could use to complete them. I personally didn't find the puzzles to be realistic at times (not that this game is meant to be real of course)
Horror: There weren't any parts that I felt scared or surprised. The environment had good horror elements, but I could always see enemies coming and never really felt any danger unless I couldn't solve a puzzle fast enough. But the death trial and error system helped bme to not worry about death. Simply put, the game wasn't really scary. Just dark and spooky maybe.
Graphics: Its an older game so I didn't expect anything great. I am sure it looked fine when it came out. The graphics aren't detrimental to enjoying the game.
As I said at the beginning of this review, I didn't find the game to be enjoyable or fun. The story evolved in a way that didn't make much sense since there was no foreshadowing of it in the first game. There were some links of course such as the "infection" it self, but I think it all fell flat by the end. I guess if the game goes on sale and you don't have any better options available, it is not that expensive and will provide a few hours of gameplay. There are many positive reviews, so you may enjoy the game. If you are looking for a solid horror game, this is not it. It is important to note that the devs did make substantial improvements in these areas in Amnesia: The Dark Descent.

demonstrates an incredible story of survival and sacrifice, blended with traces of mystery, adventure, and the supernatural.
The main protaganist is none other than Lara Croft, and highly intelligent young woman working in the field of archaeology. At the start of the game, Lara finds herself shipwrecked during an expedition in search of the lost land of Yamatai, along with her fellow colleagues. As the story progresses, she develops from a helpless victim, only armed with her instincts into a hardened survivor, determined to uncover the dark secrets of this new mysterious land.
As an action/adventure-type game,
exellently mixes the two genres into a very enjoyable experience regarding combat and exploration.
Throughout the game, you will often find yourself in the middle of an intense firefight with loads of enemies. However, stealth is also fairly well-implemented into the game, and can be used when necessary.
Platforming and parkour is a huge part of the game, and the developers have done a great job with implementing it. Between jumping from ledge to ledge, ziplining through mountain valleys and climbing enormous structures, this game has it all packed into one great experience.
Initially, I found the game a bit difficult to control with a M/KB, but I quickly got used to its controls, and I don't think custom binds are necessary. Sometimes I had some trouble with WASD, especially in platforming, but more the most part, there were no issues regarding controls.
For myself to gain every single collectible in the game and complete the story, I finished
in around 20 hours, which is a decent amount. From what I've heard, the story itself takes about 12 hours to complete. Some find it a bit short but I found it just the right length.
Multiplayer is also implemented into this game and although I haven't played it, I've heard that the multiplayer is dead and no one really plays it. I played this game for the story and the action/adventure genre so I don't mind empty servers, but fans of multiplayer gameplay might find themselves disappointed.
I didn't find anything wrong with the dialogue, if so, incredibly minor. The voice acting in this game was fantastic, but there were some instances where the same voices were used for multiple people. It didn't really bother me so I won't be deducting any points for it.
Camilla Luddington's (Lara Croft) performance was arguably the best one. In my opinion, she portrayed the character perfectly through slight and major changes in her voice that created a sense of reality with her emotions. She makes Lara Croft feel real to the player, even if she
an a$$-kicking badass who probably should've died in the last scene.
Speaking of a$$-kicking badasses, Lara Croft has grown to become one of my personal favourite video game characters of all time, especially in this reboot of the series (I never played the old ones, so I wouldn't know anyway. She was probably just as good, right?).
Her character development is excellently portrayed as the game progresses, and you can clearly see the change in her character from start to finish. For that reason, she brings this rating up way high.
Other supporting characters such as Alex, Jonah, and Reyes, I took quite a liking to (although Reyes was kind of a b****, understandably one, but still).
One character that didn't really interest me much was
. As the
, I found him to be a bit uninspired. I get that his main reasons for doing what he did was for his own survival, but he stretches it...
.
This game looks absolutely incredible, and even after four years, it still looks like it could've been released today. That being said, it was probably one of the best looking games of 2013.
Every texture looks amazing from the grass and trees to the huge man-made structures. The atmosphere is captured perfectly with careful lighting while sunrays, shadows, and special effects make a huge impact on the game in the best way possible.
Along with fantastic visuals,
also showcases incredible sound effects in every single location. From caves with quiet water drops to the sound of nature in an abandoned mountainside village, the mysterious island looks and sounds like a living, breathing world.
There's a lot of things great about this game, and the soundtrack is one of the best. Even when you are just exploring the world around you, admiring the view, the beautiful soundtrack keeps you company with amazing composition.
The music in
is blended exceptionally well into the game. Whether you are exploring the world, escaping danger, or in the middle of an intense firefight, the soundtrack accompanies you, giving you specific feelings of relaxation, stress, relief, and many others depending on your situation.
One of my favourite moments in this game was when Lara
, and the incredible view paired with the epic music makes for a breathtaking moment that was worthy of a couple screenshots.
Again, the world is beautiful, all across the map. Taking place on a single island composed of luscious forests, mountainside settlements, and the ancient ruins of a lost civilization, the world feels oddly natural. All in all, it is carefully crafted with loads of areas involving platforming and parkour, puzzles, and intricate regions designed to fulfill any desire for exploration.
One point is taken off the score due to the lack of variety in the puzzles. I wish there were more ways to do certain tasks other than pull this, push that, and that sort of stuff. I was hoping that some of the puzzles seemed more natural because at times, it felt too obvious.
Nevertheless, I enjoyed the puzzles and how the world was designed. Speaking in general terms, everything looks and feels incredible.
had fantastic cutscenes, all extremely well animated involving facial expressions, character movement, and the setting itself.
Outside of cutscenes and in the actual gameplay, the animations still looked great, especially with the world as the animations for ocean waves, animals, and wind effects looked very realistic.
There's one thing that bothered me which is common in a lot of games, is how at times, the animation feels robotic when you switch between two actions. For example, when ziplining then hooking on to a wall, the character moves way too fast and it looks unnatural. Also, I felt as if though some animations were repeated a bit too often, and there should have been more variety regarding in-game actions.
Despite these issues, as a whole, the developers did an excellent job with the animations in cutscenes and in gameplay, making the world feel alive.

Been playing this game for a while now, and I have concluded that it's not really worth mentioning.
I will now explain why:
* The luck factor is a bit ridiculous. You can be CLEARLY winning a match, just to have one move by the CPU wipe out your entire side, all due to luck. This could be viewed as a fun gameplay mechanic, but it just comes across as overwhelmingly frustrating. It takes away from the fun of the game, and should be changed.
* It's good this game is free-to-play, because spending money on it would be horribly stupid. Nothing that can be bought with real money is worth it, and the whole game can be experienced without paying. Again, don't waste any of your money on this game.
* Here it is 25Jan2015, and the game still has it's Xmas theme. Music, loading screens, etc. It's no longer Xmas guys, wake up. How much longer are we going to have to listen to Xmas carols this year?
All in all, if you're looking for a simple puzzle game to kill 10-15 mins, this will kinda work. If you're looking for anything deeper than that, don't waste the space on your HDD with this throughly below average game.

I knew it had a reputation for being a medicore game when I bought it on sale, using some vouchers that I had and exactly why I didn't buy it out of my own hard earned money.
This proved to be a good decision as Watch_Dogs is the gaming definition of a missed opportunity. I'm not going say too much on this one, it's good points are that the gun play is pretty decent, I enjoyed the combat and the hacking elements of the game (not the hacking minigame though). The city they have built is detailed and pretty large and the car chases this game can pull off on the fly can be really cinematic and exciting.
That only takes it so far though, it becomes less interesting the more you play it. Each mission is exactly the same, it always boils down to going to an area and either killing people, infiltrating an area or hacking something.. often all three. You do this time and time and time again. Sure lot's of games do this but Watch_Dogs execution of these is just somehow lacking and you can't help feeling like it is just another rinse and repeat. I guess it is just a lack of interesting mechanics.
So as I say this isn't the first game to do that, but the narrative that drives it is boring and makes little sense in the world. The protagonist is mixed up, the game tries to frame him as a man doing everything he can to protect his family and gain the vengeance he is after, but in truth he is probably the games biggest villain and for me...  the motives and the actions just didn't add up. The people around him, his friends and family, who love him and who are helping him with his quest for "justuce" would have abandoned him within the first 10 hours of the game purelyt because actions speak louder than words and going off that our hero is clearly a case study in over reaction whilst armed. However of course, they don't, because that isn't what the story says and for me it was all just to jarring and ultimately too dull.
The positive points I mentioned before saw me over the finish line however there was certainly an element of perseverance, just to see what happened in the end. Regarding the games performance and how it runs, it needed a mod to make it work properly... so... yeah, thank goodness for modders but to fair once that is implemented the game looks pretty good and is a pleasant game to look at.
So yeah like I say, a missed oppourtunity but Watch_Dogs 2 has been announced, fingers crossed they do something more interesting next time.
Kinda hoping Watch_Dogs 2 pulls an "Assassins Creed 2" and kicks off the series, still liked the game very much though.

Danganronpa: Trigger Happy Havoc...this game is really good for the most part. Initially I picked it up because someone described it as a game that resembled the Ace Attorney series which I really enjoyed. However, to whomever that has read that description on other reviews that is a misnomer, the only thing Danganronpa and the Ace Attorney series have in common is a trial (and I guess murder). Danganronpa has some really dark subject matter that just seems to continuously spiral darker and darker as you get deeper into the story. A decent story that had enough twists and turns to keep me entertained to the end.
Now that doesn’t mean the game doesn’t have it’s faults. The main character is infected with the optimistic and/or stupid protagonist virus that seems to be a prevalent theme in Japanese media. This of course makes you want to punch your own character when the dialogue is incredibly naive or obnoxious. My only other complaint is the investigation segments before the trials can be a bit frustrating since in visual novel fashion the order of progression can be tedious at times.
However, other than those minor complaints the rest of the game was great. I enjoyed seeing the story progress with each new revelation defining the truth at Hope's Peak Academy to be different than I initially thought it was. The murders and subsequent class trials become more extensive and engaging with each event. Lastly and most important there was enough character development to where I actually regretted when a character died even if they were a murderer.
So my verdict is if you enjoy a unique visual novel about a dark and twisted situation I suggest you buy Danganronpa. For the games current cost of $19.99 you will get your money’s worth.

Ok, Daganronpa is a game in my favorite genre - the "visual novel + something" genre. I find it hard to make it through a traditional visual novel, and ones with a lot of branching where you have to read through the story again can drag on a bit. But if you take the general concept of making story front and center and forcing the player to read A TON; and combine that with something else, you wind up with gold. Phoenix Wright and the Zero Escape series are some of my favorite examples of this.
Speaking of Phoenix Wright and Zero Escape....
Daganronpa is basically both. With a little bit of relationship simulation and melodramatic high school tropes thrown into the mix. And it pretty much meets all of the expectations you may have upon reading that sentance. Yes, dead bodies will seem to leave a message with their bloody finger. Yes, the murders will be set up in arbitrarily stupid ways so you have to navigate a complex web of logic. Yes, the explanation behind the setup - where 15 high schoolers are kidnapped and put in a bizarre death trap - is just as much of a teast as it was in 999 (also produce by chunsoft, though it was a different director). And, yes, all of the characters have a gimmick and talk in memes.
If you like that stuff, you'll love this game! If that kind of thing turns you off, you still might get a kick out of trying to solve the mystery.
And the writing/localization is actually really good. The tone lies snugly between comedy and horror, and I chuckled or laughed out loud several times in each chapter. The humor is completely irreverent and over the top. While the game isn't fully voiced, there is enough of a vocal sound effect track to really sell each character's personality. Expressions like "Well..." "Um..." "What the heck?", and of course "Shut up" punctuate the text and make for lively reading/viewing.
During trials, all of the statements are voiced.
Speaking of the trials, I appreciate what they did to try to iterate away from the phoenix wright formula - but I found the focus on action actually took away from the puzzle aspect that I liked so much in that series. There are many mechanics stuffed in this game, and quite a few mini games. I began to wonder if it wasn't trying to do too many things? The dungeon crawl feel of navigation, room exploration with a kind of awkward 3d effect, trying to find coins to spend on randomly getting items you can give to your friends to make them like you, a super weird meta skill system, trials which consist of a "shoot at moving words" game, a "rythym" game, hangman, AND answering the questions the right way.
But ultimately, it's a fun ride. I figured out most of the major plot twists not long before they were revealed, leaving me feeling smart and not too irritated that the characters were too dumb. Monokuma, the bear villain is hilarious and creepy - but mostly hilarious.
What else do you need than to listen to a cute bear rattle off bizarre and silly phrases about despair, suffering and death?

Multiplayer survival horror is great by itself, but add in that one of your irl friends is working against you as this terrifying thing trying to kill you? 5/5 stars. Shadowrun Returns : Dragonfall is the quinetessential Shadowrun fan's game. I love the tabletop and when I thought of a game I'd like to play in the universe this game hit every point I would have wanted. The game drips in Shadowrun flavor, feel, and lore. Even if you're not a Shadowrun fan there's an intricate dark noir story to experience with compelling companions and really fun tactical gameplay. One of my favorite games.
A great improvement from the original Shadowrun Returns, the updated armor systems and companion advancements are really enjoyable, and the additional items/quests add a lot more to the game as well.

I kickstarted Shadowrun Returns. The original campaign, Dead Man's Switch, was serviceable. It didn't feel particularly engaging but it was enjoyable. The follow up campaign, the original Dragonfall, was a marked improvement. The writing, the mechanics, and the overall fun factor took several leaps forward. I said to all my friends, "Play Dragonfall first. It will definitely keep you hooked."
Now that the Director's Cut of Dragonfall has been released, I can safely say, that THIS is the Shadowrun Returns game that I had hoped for when I kickstarted it years ago. Characters and mechanics and graphics have been given an overhaul once more and it feels and plays great. A hearty recommend for any turnbased roleplaying game fan. Start here. Get this one.

I was... basically happy with Dead Man's Switch, the original campaign of Shadowrun Returns.
I really enjoyed Dragonfall when it was released as DLC. The story was way better, everything felt more polished and finished, and it scratched a Shadowrun wargaming  itch I've had ever since picking up the Shadowrun DMZ box set many years ago. I always had trouble persuading people to try out DMZ because it's a complicated setting with a lot of tactical possibilities and the rules involve quite a lot of random number generation and book-keeping, the kind of thing that's really more suited to some kind of mechanical calculator..
Anyway, this is an updated version of Shadowrun Dragonfall with a much better engine, loads of cool new gear, NPCs and sidequests. You can finally choose how to upgrade your party and resolve their personal ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t side-missions. There's a new UI. The story and setting are still satisfyingly Shadowrun.
On the whole it was well worth the zero pounds sterling the upgrade cost me. If you also got it for free (seriously, you should check) then I would recommend playing it. Otherwise you might even want to buy it, if you enjoy nerding it up with the Shadowrun setting and tactical wargaming as much as I do.

One of the best RPGs in recent years, that holds a special place in my heart.
First. What do you get, when you call your mutant hellhound while subconsciously scratching right below the smartlink implant to steady the aim of your pistol, which shoots shotgun rounds, activating you spirit guide for a movement buff while your at it - to assist the female former special ops member in your party - who is also a troll? Hint. Asking the Dragonslayer shaman behind her wont get you much closer to the answer, but most likely make you chuckle at his response. He was the lead singer in a band once...
If you haven't deduced it yet - the setting is superb. The characters well written. The story meaningful and gripping.
The best fables use magic and archetyping as set up, not to self referentially glorify the ingenuity behind it and Shadowrun: Dragonfall is a tremendous fable in that vain. The time it takes the game to draw you into the world behind the shadows - is five minutes, and it wont let you out of its grasp anytime soon.
Gameplay wise it is a round based, tactical, strategy game with a limited set of party members - in the tradition of an XCOM game, but with the added benefit of character arcs and backstories you will care about. Its accessible even for genre beginners but at the same time incredibly rewarding to master at the later stages.
The developers were able to address most criticisms of the older Shadowrun Returns release. The UI was overhauled, saving is now possible at every stage of the game and gameplay systems improved.
Dragonfall is a 12-15 hours standalone game (derived from a former DLC within Shadowrun Returns) with a unique story and a fantastical setting, whose biggest problem was the lack of marketing money to launch it into a broader market. It got niche recognition and well deserved critical acclaim - but only a few people ever played it. Lets change that. :)

Okay, after finally playing the first and second Postal games, I finally decided to give the third installment another shot. Even after learning the backstory of the game (RWS Inc. hired an underfunded and tyrannical game developer company from Russia to code the game), I decided to give it a second chance. Sure, I wouldn't get all the extra little achievements like I did with the first two Postals, but I'd at least beat the game and give it a fair judgment from that, right?
Wrong. I had completely forgotten what it was that had kept me from playing this game in the first place. It wasn't the linear levels (Postal 1 had linear levels). It wasn't the stupid jokes or the weird weapons and minigames (Postal 2 had stupid jokes and weird weapons and minigames). It was the gameplay. Yes, Akeela Software (or whatever they call themselves) had suffered through a Russian economic crash and in suffering fired their competent, cooperative developers and assigned this project to a group of Prima Donnas who not only couldn't correctly string a game together even if it was coming out of their own♥♥♥♥♥ but also deliberately altered the structure of the game against the wishes of RWS Inc. (you know, the people who wrote the game series and own the rights to them and CONTRACTED Akeela TO DO MAKE THE GAME THAT RWS had envisioned!!!). Not only that, but Akeela also refused to release the code to the general public because they didn't want those loyal gamers to make MODs or anything, even though RWS Inc. wanted them to. As a result, the gameplay is sticky, jagged, the graphics go photo-negative after 15 minutes of gameplay and glitches flood this game. For example, I had to restart a level because the game wouldn't let me open a door that was integral to the plot, and the escort mission with the segways was almost impossible. All in all, it kept me from enjoying this game not once but twice, which is a shame, because otherwise, I thought it could have been an enjoyable game.
*SPOILER ALERT* For those still interested in knowing, the game pickups where the second one left off: after detonating Paradise, Arizona with a nuke, the Postal dude drove to the next closest fictional town in Arizona, Catharsis. There, a wealthy Ron Jeremy owns and runs everything with a pretty open mind. The problem is that he's constantly being undermined or even flat out attacked by Eco-terrorists, Al Queda, God-fearing hockey moms (led by Sarah Palin...wait...why is she in Arizona?!) and other satirical and colorful characters. The Postal Dude, just trying to make a buck, is given constant choices as to whose side he is on, or at least which side he wants to flip flop to and from. While the levels are linear, your actions do choose the course of the game.   Unlike the last game, the third Postal gives you a Max Payne type of third person layout and aiming system, and you get most of the weapons from the previous game, plus a few new ones like beehives, a shopvac (filled with questionably stained tissues) and the badgersaw.
Like I said, it could have an enjoyable installment to the series, but the Russian contractors completely ruined it to the point that RWS Inc. even tells people to stay away from it.

After 70+ hours in the game I am someone who liked it allot. What this game is about is figuring out the systems, optimising and enjoying seeing your base grow and work. Unlike some other games where you can get many hours into a settlement only to discover you made a mistake 2 hours ago that is going to take it out, this is a game that once you have stabilised initially you are generally good. This is ace as it allows the game to be unfair meaning that early on you can enjoy trying to deal with the unexpected and trying to save your colony. While later on when chance comes knocking you are big enough that it is fine or have been able to deploy a solution to the issue (like big laser cannons). At that point it is about solving the next issue and managing your operation.
The game though does have its issues, the one most people complain about is that it feels like they built half a game and this is true but it is also why they sold it at half the price of a AAA game. This also has a joy to it though because you simply can not spend 30 hours on a sentiment meaning that this is about having several goes at the same thing getting better all the time. The second is that the AI can be down right stupid and this can be annoying but it also becomes part of the game because it gives you something else to optimise and design for. Lastly yes this is an independent game and it feels like it in places, particularly with the raiders who feel like an after thought.
Overall I have played this to exhaustion because I love the setting and I love the process of this game. I really am looking forward to their next game.

TLDR: I think the game needs a bit of gameplay polish in regard to progression and build options. The tutorial is rather good, but the desert planet is a lengthy achievement gauntlet that needed to be bite sized goals. All said and done, of you enjoy resource management with great moon base art--I recommend this game.
Now for the specifics:
1. Minor but annoying UX design issue once you have selected your base/challenge. The very next screen shows a string of text and under that asks you to press any key. I already selected the scenario, not sure why this screen exists.
2. The opening sequence where you watch your crew get off the ship--this needs a SKIP button. This is a game where you mess up and restart frequently and the 2 minute opening sequence serves little purpose. This combined with the issue above make restarting a bit frustrating.
3. There is a super annoying bug when trading large quantities of items with traders. The trader will occupy the landing pad waiting for the last item to be delivered (and it is never delivered). Eventually the trader will time out and fly away leaving 99% of your own cargo on the landing pad because the trade was never made.
4. I think I would have enjoyed playing this game more if game play modes weren't so difficult and time consuming to complete. For instance, if the desert planet was broken into 3 increasingly difficult goals instead of one really large grueling set of achievments. I thought maybe this was done in the "challenges" option of the game, but the one challenge that was unlocked didn't seem entry level.
5. I felt like the desert planet scenario exposed me to 90% the build capabilities, which doesn't feel satisfying. If I continue to play and find out I am wrong, I'll update my review.
6. Completing all the achievements on the desert planet felt a lot like beating the game. I'm reluctant to try other planets out of fear there will be more frustrating random environmental hurdles with the rest of the balancing act being  repetitive.

In general I like this game, but it could be better. I would give it 6/10. What I write in this review is my personal experience and view about the game, so the pros and cons may not be same you or other players.
The Good about the game:
-It has nice graphics, sound, and good game athmosphere in general.
-It is not too expensive. 20 $ it affordable for this kind of game (although I got it on 50 % sale).
-It's something different than most building games with kind of unique feel and experience.
-Lack of bugs and crashes overall + goes smooth and loading is very fast.
-I can say it is balanced overall
Things I didn't like:
-It gets boring quite fast. There is no Campain or unlockables over time to keep you interested for longer amount of time. I needed about 10 hours total (for some maybe even less)  and you can squeeze basically everything the game offers.
-Lack of tech tree - Although there are some buildings that you have to "unlock" by trading, which I find quite easy. The game would have much more dept if you had "Civilization" type tech tree.
-Lack of unlockable building over time (like most city/building simulators have - like build X amount of this, or reach X amount of population to unlock, if you choose this building you can't build this one and etc.), beside trading blueprints which are quite easy to get and are mostly just bigger version of the existing buildings.
-Milestones don't do anything really. They are something like in game "achievements" but you don't gain anything for your current game (at least I didn't notice) beside unlocking the other 3 planet types.
-Lack of political, governing aspect or deeper exonomyc system.
Mixed stuff:
-The statistics you can see for your colony are basic. No deep system to see/follow to make your colony better. For example you can see how many colonists of each type you have, but there is no way to know exaxtly how many more colonists of this type you need for the specific kind of work to go smoother. As well if you have too many of them you can't really tell.
- It feels like you are in charge of bots. Colonists have basic needs, but they don't complain, praise or tell you anythig to know if you are doing good or not, or if they need something specific/more. Sometimes out of nowhere something happens (like food is not enough) and is already too late to fix it. They start to die, new colonists stop coming and you have to load previous save or start new game if you are in the early stages of the game.
So to review in short, it is interesting in the begining but it gets boring fast. The lack of deep government/political system + lack of tech tree and different choices makes the game is pretty linear and you will be left with "nothing more to do" in just few hours. My advice - play the game, it will keep you busy and interested for couple of days, but if you can wait for a sale.
