This review comes from someone who played Amnesia before any Penumbra game, so make of that what you will. I'll try to keep this short.
I'll start off by saying that, on the technical side, the game is pretty darn good. The engine itself (as evidenced by its use in more recent games by Frictional) holds up very well to this day. Black Plague was released in 2008, so it's not incredibly old, but, in an age where I have to check whether or not entirely new games will actually run on my specific combination of hardware, I haven't had any trouble in the slightest getting the game to run. No crashes, no graphics issues, no slowdowns, nothing like that at all. The only problem that I have with it in that regard is that you can't change the FOV, but that's set
high enough for it to not be a problem for me, at least.
A lot of the game revolves around physics-based puzzles and they've definitely put enough effort in to make sure that the physics engine works as perfectly as it should do. Objects feel like they weigh as much as they should, moving objects around isn't a chore and the game knows when you want to put an item in a specific place and locks it there without any hastle or feeling like it's doing your work for you.
On the subject of puzzles, for the most part, they work well enough. The solutions are invariably completely intuative (no, you're not going to tie a balloon to a banana and feed it to a monster to get that computer running, you're going to find working drives and format them), and, on the off chance that the answer is simplified a little so that it doesn't get in the way of the game mechanics, it still makes perfect sense and there's a way to find out how to do it. As someone who frequently gets frustrated with adventure/puzzle games and has to turn the Internet off so that I don't cave and look up the answers (i.e. an idiot), I figured everything out for myself pretty quickly, save for one puzzle near the beginning which made sense in retrospect. The only problem I have with the puzzles is that many require finding multiple specific items, and, without fail, every one of them will be hidden behind a couple of other physics objects that are stacked in an odd and very conspicuous way.
Now, unfortunately, there are two very big issues that I had with the game that, while they weren't quite enough to stop me from playing, they are bad enough to me that I wouldn't personally recommend the game. The first is the story: the story of Penumbra: Overture, while not groundbreaking, was at least intriguing and subtle enough that it kept me very invested through the whole game. In Black Plague, that subtlety goes right out of the window from the beginning when it gives you a very clear and safe view of the new monster, then, sometime later, the player character develops an internal voice in his head whose main purpose seems to be to explain every plot point several times over in case you didn't pick up the hints. There were several times when I read something interesting in a note and got as far as thinking "I wonder if that means-", then he'd immediately chime in and say that that's exactly what it means, please don't try to work it out for yourself. It honestly feels like Frictional realised that they could afford voice actors for this one and just decided to throw in literally anything that they could think for them to say, no matter how dumb or obvious, on top of the quality of the voice acting giving Bethesda a run for its money. I also counted four times in the first hour or so where the player character had the
realisation about himself. Add in how, for some reason, they decided to throw in an almost constant barrage of downright embarrassing attempts at humour (seriously, one computer asked if I was sure that I wanted to do something, then if I was
sure, then if I was
sure...) and I got to the point where I just couldn't consider this a horror game anymore.
On that note, my other problem with it is that it really doesn't feel like a horror game in almost any respect. It's very dark (lighting-wise), yes, but... that's really it. It doesn't take long to realise that you're in almost no danger whatsoever. I think that I came across four things in the entire game that were able to hurt me, disregarding an obvious tripwire "puzzle", and the very few enemies that you do encounter can be outrun, avoided, sneaked around and generally outsmarted with no effort at all. I appreciate the rudimentary stealth mechanics as a massive fan of the Thief series, but the enemies in Black Plague are exactly as intelligent as the dogs in Penumbra: Overture, which is to say not too bright.
In conclusion, I suppose that, if you just want puzzles and can appreciate something of an adventure/puzzle game in first person (some mechanics actually brought back memories of classic point-and-click games, but much better-polished), and can also tune out the excuse plot for those to exist, then I can definitely recommend the game because I enjoyed those parts a decent amount. If you're looking for a compelling horror experience, then, as far as I'm concerned, you're probably not going to find it here, although I've met people with a completely different opinion to mine. I really enjoy playing this game. I like the gameplay and the idea of matching the different colored gems to attack your opponent and gaining mana to use special effects. The graphics are nice and the game is pleasant to look at. It’s easy to lose track of time while playing all the quests – if you have the coins to do them.
It’s got many nice features, but I do have some suggestions for it. Most of these are small changes or additions I’d like to see, but there are a couple of issues I’ll be addressing as well. I feel bad about giving this game a negative review (because it is a good game), but there is an issue that needs to be fixed before I can recommend this game.
There isn’t too much variety on how your character appears – 6 different races and your gender. So there are really only 12 different appearances your character can have, not including the two types of free armor and (the other ones you have to pay real money for). I’d like to see more variety in customizing your character.
The gem "hints" can be useful, but not always. Many times it's suggested that I make moves that would not help me and it would help the computer by setting up a combination for its next turn. You can turn these hints off, but I prefer to keep them on for when they actually are helpful.
There’s a place where you can type to your guild under the announcements button, but none of the users in my guild ever use it and its unclear whether that is supposed to be a guild chat or not. It would be great to have a specific place to chat with your guild that is different from the announcements so they don’t get lost in the chat. It would also be nice if we could have more than 10 members in a guild.
The coins you earn are used to unlock new content and every time you want to battle, you have to pay coins. You do earn coins every day you log on and your cities do generate coins, so it isn't impossible to play without paying (at least where I am currently in the game). So it hasn’t bothered me that much yet, but it does limit what you can do.
If there were some changes made to this game (specifically the problems I’ve mentioned), it could be very great. I understand that because it’s a free game they need to try to make money somewhere, but there are so many places, it would be better to just eliminate them and charge for the game.
The main problem I have about this game is how the computer plays against you. I've been in battles where there's not much I can do, and then the AI will get a bunch of combinations. Some of the times I don't see them, which was my fault. But many other times, the way the gems fall into place after you've made a move will cause the computer to make more combos. I've seen them get multiple in a row - like six or more - just because of the way they fall into place. This also happens with the skulls, which are used to attack. If there's an open spot between two of them, more often than not I've noticed that a skull will fill in. The way it's set up is for the AI to win.
The AI will make the best possible moves available (often that were a result of how the gems fell in after my turn).  So it allows the computer to gain more mana and attack more often. The AI also has better troops, because they want you to buy them. I’ve gotten some by playing the game, but the best troops are available by buying a magic key (to unlock the chest) to increase the rarity of the cards won, which are random. You can level up your troops by spending souls, which are won by each opponent you defeat. However, if you keep being beat, your soul count goes up very slowly or doesn’t change.
The game is set for the AI to win. It’s as simple as that. If that problem was fixed and the game wasn’t relying quite as heavily on paying, I would give this a positive review.

I honestly find it impossible to fully describe the greatness of this game in words; a playthrough is necessary to get fully enraptured by it. Perhaps the fact that I finished the main story in 25 hours total will show you how addicted I was, or maybe that I'd watched the anime first and had enjoyed the game more. However, I
summarize the winning aspects of this game into a few bullet points that should give you impetus to cash out that thirty bucks (or however much it'll cost when you buy it).
1.
Since the main tag on this game is 'visual novel,' most people go into it thinking it's one of those never-ending 'choice-heavy' simulation games. Well, actually, while this game
utilize the typical visual novel format, it's actually more logic-based. For instance, during the class trials, where the majority of the gameplay takes place, players have to select the wrong statements and put together phrases using their own logic rather than relying on 'the fated outcome.' They also have to memorize investigation factoids and know when to put them to use.

2.
I'd honestly have to say that out of this whole game, the cast of students were my favorite feature. Each of them are uniquely individual and complex- both in physical terms and mental- creating a lasting impression on the player's mind. There is no black-or-white to any character, making them so realistic and relatable. If the characters don't make a mark on you, I don't know what will.
3.
Unfortunately, I had watched the animation before playing, so I knew what the outcome would be from the start, but the writing and music definitely bring great mystery to the table. There are so many dark secrets lurking about the school that at times, despite the game being devoid of any jump scares, I was unsettled by the creepiness of it all.
4.
If you think about it, the game is pretty bizarre. You get trapped in a high school with a wide range of interesting classmates, are forced to kill each other by a 'teddy bear,' and can only graduate if you commit the perfect murder (and, if you do that, every student except for you will die). The bear creates 'punishments' that are violent beyond belief (perhaps even more violent than the students' murders), and, as an added bonus, the blood is pink. Have you ever heard of such a game, however bizzare it sounds?
5.
Simply put, the artwork for this game is phenomenal. Now, I'm not talking about the generic character anime sprites (although even those had a very unique artstyle); I'm talking about the CGs and the punishment scenes, which are literally cinematic. You can't help but be drawn to the screen as you watch the brutality go on in the form of a masterpiece.
As I said, I've only completed the main story (I'm still planning on completing the school mode), so there might be additional facts I've left off. The only real 'cons' I can mention is that there were 1 or 2 plotholes- which will probably be explained in the second installment, which I am planning on purchasing very soon- and some annoying difficulties during the class trials. Other than that, this game is truly fantastic, captivating, and downright ADDICTING and I swear that I shall never forget it!

At this point in time if you don’t know about/of Danganronpa it’s basically a crime and a sign you aren't a true weeb. Lucky you I'm a weeb with a degree (in progress) that'll give you the low down on this VN.
is a murder mystery/adventure visual novel published by Spike Chunsoft. Gameplay is through the eyes of the awkward (and possibly relatable) protagonist Makoto Naegi, who wakes up trapped in Hope's Peak Academy along with fourteen other students. The student’s captor is the sadistic, toy-like bear known as Monokuma, forcing them to kill each other if they wish to escape.
((As a side note for you newbs, Danganronpa has a anime based off the first game, and two seasons that show the time before the first game and the future after
(maybe also past V3 but I haven't played it yet so...) as well as several manga series.))
The music changes depending on the area and interactions the player activates. The opening theme and credits are the most noteworthy. For the most part the background music is fairly diverse and sets the mood perfectly.
The visuals are what really make this game stand out (and the story but that's a given). The game mixes 2-D graphics with a 3-D environment, which allows your free movement while having multiple 2-D, static characters in the same location without slowing down your computer (because 2-D is less computer intensive (duh)). This is combined with colorful art and a notable characteristic to this game series: pink blood. While originally implemented to lower the games rating in Japan, the pink blood contrasts the seriousness of a crime scene with the playfulness of the color. Danganronpa combines the linear with the non-linear, the 2-D with the 3-D, and the moods of hope and despair.
[At times I feel like the creators were on an acid trip and decided colored lights and pop art was a good idea. This isn’t a bad thing, but that’s just a thought.]
The characters at first are rather trope-y, but if you use your Free Time wisely you start to see that their flamboyant personalities are a product of their environment and inherent nature (maybe that's how all humans are?)
Monokuma's iconic half white, half black appearance characterizes the mood of the entire game, which combines hope and despair.
I like to point out how the eyes are drawn. The bold colors draw your eyes in and make you notice how distinct the art style is.
I tend to be partial toward the original voice acting when it comes to translated materials (anime, games, etc.), but I did give the English voice acting a chance...as in I watched someone play this game with the English voices. It's rare, but I find both the English and Japanese voice acting agreeable. I'm partial to the English Monokuma, but only because his laugh sounds funny as an "English" laugh.
I am one of little patience/attention span. It’s supposed to be an interactive novel, and that's just what I got. I like the freedom that the Free Time mode gives me to choose which characters I can get to know, as well as the added bonus of skills to be used in the trials. And if you get bored of talking and being social, well, if you have a bit more patience than me you'll eventually get to the game element of this VN: The trials! It breaks down into several types of gameplay that I don't care to go into detail about (go play the game to find out!)
As the game progresses and you slowly (and painfully?) kill off your classmates, the plot unfolds until you’re left with an ending that implies continuation. Honestly though if the game didn't succeed the story could have just ended it there. Lucky us there's Danganronpa 2 and Ultra Despair girls, and Danganronpa V3 (if the naming of the anime confused you, the games will confuse you further).
Too slow for an impatient person (me <3)
You'll be compelled to play all the games, read all the light novels, and watch the anime. Welcome to the cult.
The controls can be a bit weird at first, but that’s what happens when you port over from a playstation. (Note: I used a mouse and keyboard; perhaps a controller would be better?)
It potatoes well, but it's a VN so it should.
Your perception of good and evil turns into hope and despair instead.
Now you know the memes.

Pac-Man CE DX (the predecessor to DX+) is a great game. The shocker with DX+ is twofold. One, the DLC stages are as good as the older stages*. Two, the menu update that came with DX+ makes the menus less responsive.
CE DX on the Xbox 360 had simple and responsive menus. The menus are mostly the same in DX+, but the few things that they added slow everything down. There's Facebook sharing. Yuck. Whenever you select one of the special skins (Dig-Dug, Rally X, Pac is Back), everything slows to a crawl for around a second as the game loads the skin data and messes around with your settings.
Apparently Namco won't let you play with Dig-Dug characters on a Pac-Man background, or use the Dig-Dug song for anything but the Dig-Dug skin. It's a very silly restriction, and since the practical effect of the restriction is
, Namco and the company who did the port should be ashamed of themselves.
Originally, the files for this game were in an easily moddable format. But then the fun police at Namco or Mine Loader Software had to put a stop to it, lest people create custom skins or levels. Everything is now packed into one not-moddable file. At best, this was done because they didn't want people to buy the base game and then pirate the special skins. At worst, it was because they were scared that people would create new content using their intellectual property. Either way, it's bogus, and very, very sad, since it took extra effort to REMOVE modding support.
The game only runs at 720p, which if it were easier to mod might not be the case. If you use a 360 controller, don't forget to turn on vibration in the settings.
*With the new DLC stages, it seems like they only exist in 5-minute mode. The regular DX (not +) stages can be played for 5 or 10 minutes, and have more unique mazes to cycle through before you see the same maze twice.
Once you actually start playing, DX+ is the most fun you can have with Pac-Man. Pac-Man CE DX+ is a fantastic game with very unfortunate business decisions bogging it down. Yes, you should buy it. It's great. Get the version with all the DLC. It's worth it.

The Good: Decent graphics, different level design approach, fast paced, it doesn't last very long
The Bad: Botched paratrooping mechanic, ridiculously difficult, monotonous level progression, dead multiplayer, brings nothing new to the tired genre
Medal of Honor started the first person shooter World War II experience back on the original PlayStation. As time went on they redefined the genre on PC with Allied Assault. It helped put WWII shooter's feet on cinematic ground. Frontline was the series last good game, and slowly after that the series fell flat on its face with mediocrity, with EA only caring about money. Airborne continues this trend and it's dead obvious how little effort they put into the game.
You play as a soldier named Travers (like we care at this point) and you go through various WWII scenarios that you have probably gone through dozens of times before. The first thing you will notice about Airborne is how repetitive it feels in comparison to other WWII shooters. It doesn't do anything new and re-treads the same ground that we are sick and tired of. EA tried to make us feel different about this with a new approach to level design. You play as paratroopers that jump out of planes at the start of every level onto green flares. These are safe zones and contain crates of health, ammo, and grenades. Once you hit the ground you will notice that your mini-map is pointing to various objectives. No longer do you follow a linear routine and take it one at a time. Pick a direction and run, but that's when things start going bad.
Every map plays out the same, shoot some enemies, push forward, rinse and repeat ad nauseam. The enemies will keep coming in different pockets of the maps until you advance and take them out. This isn't a new trick, and just gets old quick because that is all you do. Place a charge on this AA gun, blow up this equipment, blow up these thanks. No thanks. I have done this countless times already so why do I want to do it here? The whole "non-linear" map idea doesn't really work because it makes the game ridiculously difficult and you will die dozens of times every level. Every time you die you jump back out of the plane loosing not objective progress, but advancement progress. If you just pushed back a huge group of enemies and die you have to do it again. Your objectives are just checkpoints, and this gets frustrating beyond anything you can imagine. The game throws way too many enemies at you, but there are even problems with weapons.
The game has a nice upgrade system for doing so many kills. For example, the MP40 will upgrade with a double clip, reduced recoil, and a knife melee attack. This is the most interesting thing in the entire game, but EA for some reason made the guns inaccurate to accommodate for upgrades. Guns jump around more than you are used to and no matter how well your aim is you always miss about 60% of the time. Once you hit the less recoil upgrade it isn't so bad. All the same WWII era weapons are here (except the Sten) and it is yawn worthy.
Thankfully the game is short with only 6 levels, so you can beat the game in about 6 hours. No matter how you slice it the game is just extremely hard, repetitive, boring, and unoriginal on every level. They even went back to the health pack system which is just archaic in design. You would think at least jumping out of planes is fun? Not really because if you don't grease or flare your landing you botch it and it involves a nauseating and disorienting animation of your character wobbling around while getting up and pulling the weapon out in a weird way. While this is happening guys are shooting you and you will recover with one health bar left. Nice job EA for screwing every single thing in a game up that you possibly could. Even the graphics are pretty bland and aren't anything special.
Overall, Airborne is probably the worst Medal of Honor game I have ever played. Monotonous shooting, ridiculous difficulty, screwed up paratrooping mechanic, failed level design, and a retread of a genre everyone is tired of. Do yourself a favor and skip this unless you really need a WWII shooter fix. Forget about multiplayer as well because there are only 6 maps and no one is playing online anyways.

You can build a Collosus and it can get taken down very quickly and efficiently if the other team plays its cards right. I don't think I've seen a game outside of a tactical strategy game, like Wargame, in which positioning, composition and your skill factors in so much. Between managing and micromanaging hundreds of units, maximizing resource income and keeping up with what is happening on the map, you barely have enough time to draw one calm breath. Beautifully done, masterfully expanded, and chaotically organized. By far one of the best Real Time Strategy game I've ever played, or every will play.

Planetbase is the best 3D Colony Sim I have played so far on Steam or otherwise. My total playtime in its case should speak volumes by itself. I don’t play “test” a game I’m supposed to review, for that long unless I’m enjoying it thoroughly. A game dev which has had no previous experience (and sadly, no other new titles either) has finally created the game that surpasses Startopia in my eyes, as the most comprehensive “What if?” scenario about setting up a colony in an unhospitable place. Of course, Planetbase focuses entirely on humans without even mentioning alien lifeforms.
Do not expect a storyline in the classical sense in which you may be introduced to certain characters and shall have to follow them throughout the duration of the gameplay and further discover and influence their actions. Planetbase’s campaign does feature randomly generated names for your colonists, but they never seem to stand out from one another. You should consider them as hardworking ants in your new proverbial ant farm. And you’re their Overseer, if the Fallout series strikes your fancy. Instead of a story per se, you have open-ended scenarios in which you must accomplish a strict set of objectives which ensure promotion to more complex tasks and far more dangerous planetary environments to colonise.
I strongly suggest you first play the tutorial before attempting to kickstart a space colony by yourself in this game. I shall discuss the gameplay mechanics further below and just be prepared for concepts that weren’t used before in similar titles. Planetbase aims for low-Science Fiction, also called “soft” by some fans of the genre. It’s the type of Sci-Fi which isn’t that far-fetched from the technological capabilities humanity possesses already but still represents a leap we have yet to achieve and will likely remain in the realm of hypotheses for the next few decades. Imagine 2015’s movie, “The Martian”. That film’s release date coincides with that of Planetbase and both of them share more than a few common ideas.
Despite not clearly naming its graphics engine and even if it wouldn’t be proprietary, Plantebase looks great. I’ve been running it maxed-out at 4K resolution and stable 60 fps without so much as a single frame rate dip. Couple its stallar performance with so many intricate details, from structure objects or even the colonists themselves and you will agree Planetbase's seemingly high price tag is justified. What you see in those official screenshots is also what you get to play for yourself. And it’s fully worth it.
All praise aside, there are a few pathfinding glitches in which the NPCs bump into each other (or go right through), but as long as you avoid colony overcrowding and expand at a steady pace, the effect should be of minimal impact. Just as in Planetbase’s counterparts on Steam, the astronauts/colonists are also distinguished chromatically by their designated profession. Blue for workers, orange for engineers, green for biologists, red for medics and last but not least, grey for guards. Similar color schemes for the carrier, constructor and driller robot types. Everything is neatly organized and shall run like clockwork if you keep your wits about you.
Sound effects and songs are few and far in-between. Also the complete lack of voice acting, is disappointing to say the least. Earth Space Colonies even had vague attempts at humor with its dialogues between members of your staff and an Artificial Intelligence. Planetbase is far too silent for a game of its simulated complexity and sheer entertainment value. You’ll be forgiven if you mute its sounds altogether and listen to whatever tracks you prefer.
The corporation financing your colonial efforts may not be Weyland-Yutani, yet your hands shall get dirty anyways from genetic modification. So far, only vegetables so no alien life yet. Indeed, I’m talking of GMO (genetically modified organism) tomatoes and onions. It may seem harmless enough as you’re never thinking of long-term effects when your colonists need to eat now. So you compromise and allow “beefed-up” crops to replace the more natural yet slow-yielding ones. How about some lab-grown meat? Feel free to switch the example of those 100 colonists you’re trying to save from starvation, with 7.5 billion souls. If it sounds familiar, it might just be the case to worry for our not-so-bright future. Too many mouths to feed and a “Blue Rock” that won't take the abuse forever.
Survival is your first priority and prospering is your second. You start your journey on a desert planet which resembles Mars and as you reach new objectives, you can attempt to colonise frozen or storm planets (no clear examples in our Solar System) and a gas giant moon (take your pick, Jupiter has 67 moons). In order to thrive in those hostile landscapes, you shall need to plan your first few resources very carefully. If you manage to pass three in-game days with zero fatalities, you’re on the right path towards success.
Your initial crew of 7 astronauts & colonist hopefuls, is accompanied by just two robots and the Colony Ship shall have to be stripped for spare parts, after you’ve built the first few essential structures such as a solar panel, oxygen generator, water extractor and an airlock. Apart from a few buildings that only get accessed from the outside, most of your colonists shall remain “indoors” through the modular structures which shelter them from atmospheric conditions not suitable for life. I do appreciate the valuable lesson of recycling being taught by Planetbase. Everything you build can be scrapped efficiently with almost the complete recovery of materials used initially. The robots shall eventually become damaged beyond repair and you will need to assemble more, but the resources you recover from the old go straight to the new ones. Nothing is truly lost, everything can be repurposed.
The Planetbase colonists are fairly safe compared to other colony sims I have played over the years. There are some looming threats such as asteroids or human invaders/saboteurs but both those issues can be cancelled by the implementation of laser turrets and sufficient security personnel. Every other type of sustained damage (from solar flares and sand/snow storms) can be repaired and healed, by case. As you can see, surprisingly few deaths which may not quite simulate the actual hardships of space colonization, but you can always screw things up if you expand chaotically or too fast. Human nature is humanity’s biggest enemy in the end.
While I understand perfectly that its price tag is reflected in Planetbase’s content and its quality, if you consider it overpriced, you can wait for a Steam Sale or bundle. Whenever you decide to buy it, I recommend you play it and allow those colonies to grow. It’s a game that deserves to be part of any Steam collection and it truly is the only 3D colony simulator you need for now. I would have rated it even higher if it had a soundtrack worthy of the overall picture.
+ Gorgeous graphics.
+ Steam Trading Cards & Achievements.
+ Implementation of disasters and human threats.
+ Complex colonial simulation and crafting system.
- Severely limited sound selection.
- A few pathfinding glitches.

I really enjoy playing this game. I like the gameplay and the idea of matching the different colored gems to attack your opponent and gaining mana to use special effects. The graphics are nice and the game is pleasant to look at. It’s easy to lose track of time while playing all the quests – if you have the coins to do them.
It’s got many nice features, but I do have some suggestions for it. Most of these are small changes or additions I’d like to see, but there are a couple of issues I’ll be addressing as well. I feel bad about giving this game a negative review (because it is a good game), but there is an issue that needs to be fixed before I can recommend this game.
There isn’t too much variety on how your character appears – 6 different races and your gender. So there are really only 12 different appearances your character can have, not including the two types of free armor and (the other ones you have to pay real money for). I’d like to see more variety in customizing your character.
The gem "hints" can be useful, but not always. Many times it's suggested that I make moves that would not help me and it would help the computer by setting up a combination for its next turn. You can turn these hints off, but I prefer to keep them on for when they actually are helpful.
There’s a place where you can type to your guild under the announcements button, but none of the users in my guild ever use it and its unclear whether that is supposed to be a guild chat or not. It would be great to have a specific place to chat with your guild that is different from the announcements so they don’t get lost in the chat. It would also be nice if we could have more than 10 members in a guild.
The coins you earn are used to unlock new content and every time you want to battle, you have to pay coins. You do earn coins every day you log on and your cities do generate coins, so it isn't impossible to play without paying (at least where I am currently in the game). So it hasn’t bothered me that much yet, but it does limit what you can do.
If there were some changes made to this game (specifically the problems I’ve mentioned), it could be very great. I understand that because it’s a free game they need to try to make money somewhere, but there are so many places, it would be better to just eliminate them and charge for the game.
The main problem I have about this game is how the computer plays against you. I've been in battles where there's not much I can do, and then the AI will get a bunch of combinations. Some of the times I don't see them, which was my fault. But many other times, the way the gems fall into place after you've made a move will cause the computer to make more combos. I've seen them get multiple in a row - like six or more - just because of the way they fall into place. This also happens with the skulls, which are used to attack. If there's an open spot between two of them, more often than not I've noticed that a skull will fill in. The way it's set up is for the AI to win.
The AI will make the best possible moves available (often that were a result of how the gems fell in after my turn).  So it allows the computer to gain more mana and attack more often. The AI also has better troops, because they want you to buy them. I’ve gotten some by playing the game, but the best troops are available by buying a magic key (to unlock the chest) to increase the rarity of the cards won, which are random. You can level up your troops by spending souls, which are won by each opponent you defeat. However, if you keep being beat, your soul count goes up very slowly or doesn’t change.
The game is set for the AI to win. It’s as simple as that. If that problem was fixed and the game wasn’t relying quite as heavily on paying, I would give this a positive review.

This is Puzzle Quest with actually reasonably used Mobile Game mechanics.
However, it is STILL Puzzle Quest, with all of that series' faults unaddressed as usual. The game loves to have just the right pieces fall into play after your turn to screw you over. When you do not act fast enough, the game will suggest a move. READ THE BOARD CAREFULLY. See what removing those pieces will do. These suggested moves are almost always to their benefit. And worst of all, is finding a suggested move, seeing it's not really to your benefit, and studying the rest of the board to learn it's currently the ONLY legal move on the board. You have no choice but to shoot yourself in the foot.
If Puzzle Quest could hide how it simulates escalating difficulty better, I'd forgive it. But this has been its hand from its very first game, shown to us completely. Give this a miss unless you like playing games where people stack the deck in their favour in full view.

I love seeing new Half Life mods on Steam, so when I saw this one pop up I quickly rushed to play it. Unfortunately I was kind of disappointed. I understand that this is in beta, but that does not exclude it from criticism.
Firstly the level design is awful. The levels are built in a way where the pacing feels off and you’re left spamming E on every door you find as there is no clear indication which doors can be opened and which can’t. Simply having a red or green light on certain doors to indicate whether they are locked or not would be simple enough, or having door handle models on openable doors like in HL2. The second last map also doesn’t have a changemap entity, so you have to load up the next map manually through the console.
A lot of the sound effects are reused from HL1 and HL2. I have no problem with reused sound effects, however some of them seem either out of place or placeholder. The HL1 sound effects such as the HECU dialog just sounds really off, as they sound really low quality, which again is also fine, but they just feel really out of place being used on high quality HECU models. The scientist and guard dialog is reused from HL2 which makes it seem really out of place a lot of the time. Apparently theres also an NPC that calls the player “Gordon” instead of Willson.
Another issue is that there seems to be several missing textures. Throughout most of the game I saw the purple and black checkered texture reflecting off of a lot of the surfaces, and there were some that just had a missing texture entirely. This persisted after verifying the game cache as well.
Overall I cannot recommend this mod. I understand that it is in beta, but in its current form I don’t think it is suitable for release. I think the current maps need a huge overhaul, and it just needs to be better quality before it can be fully released.

It has its faults, but it is very enjoyable from a nostalgic point of view. I'll be looking forward to the full release.
The level design is probably the shining point of this mod. They have captured the feel of HL1 gameplay without copying anything directly. There are many moments where you have an enemy pop out at you from an unexpected direction, foremost in my memory is a crawlspace under the floor with the crawling zombies.
The final fight was an epic shoutout to the Matrix, loved that.
The pacing of the entire mod is very good, over the entire story to date it builds through having no ammo and trying to hide or having to axe zombies, to finally collecting a bundle of ammo and gunning it up with a squad of soldiers.
But even within an area, the pacing is still good and in keeping with the Half Life games. Fights are interspersed with climbing sections or puzzles keeps the player refreshed to continue play without anything being monotonus.
I'll point out a few issues, but this is from beta so take as constructive critisism:
*The game is dark and some of the maps are so very dark. Soldiers seem to be able to see in the dark to shoot the player, but the HEV torch is pretty useless.
*The animation in the opening is jerky, some time to smooth that out would make it as atmospheric as it deserves.
*Several steps to progress through the game are quite obscure. Pressing a button to open a door seems obvious in real life, but it's not so much in a game, particularly if the button visually fits in with its surroundings, blending into the scenery or that the same button model has been used throughout the game and hasn't been useful until then. Most notable of these is picking up the keys; without any indication you were to do so, that's very obscure. The WORST of these was the underwater section where you need to go up a small corner bit and climb a ladder, well, I tried to grab the ladder but couldn't, so I assumed it was not the way to go and spend half an hour drowning over and over trying to work out where to go.
*I had a few issues with changing resolution; I couldn't save unless it was native (1050) but I couldn't see the HUD unless it was in it's default. Restarting the game seemed to fix this, but it might start again next time I loaded.
*Texture or effects leave pink 'spray' over gun models or the environment, particularly in wet areas.
Very well done guys, keep it up and make it brilliant!

Penumbra: Black Plague is a sequel to Penumbra: Overture, an adventure horror game with more realistic physics for more immersive interaction. It was released in 2008, year after original, and yep, still made by Frictional Games, but this time under different publishers. They say that under pressure from old publisher Frictional Games turned what was intented to be trilogy into duology, Black Plague concluding the series. It's unknown how much from planned two last episodes was fit into Black Plague, it could be possible that something important got cut. Thus some people belive the ending to be a slight cliffhanger and want Penumbra 3 to happen, while others just view it as a proper bad ending of sorts. I am leaning toward the latter.
You may notice that Steam store says "Gold Edition". It means that it includes Requiem, an expansion pack. Which you shouldn't think of as Penumbra 3, as it's just a set of puzzles that were cut from Black Plague without horror. Or big story. That, and maybe not cut, can't say for sure.
So, as far scary, it's a step up from Overture. Or step down. Now, instead of fighting it out with dogs, developers decided to remove weapons fully. Instead you will have the infected roam the corridors, who look like creepy zombies. And you will not be able to fight them directly, instead your only options is to hide and avoid them. Which is supposed to make it scarier. If forget that they aren't terribly efficient killers as you can just outrun them easily and not even bother with hiding sometimes. Oh well, always hiding would have been too annoying for me.
You aren't alone this time either, as the world feels more filled with other characters. Mostly human corpses that Overture lacked so much. But you will be accomplished by one sarcastic voice which isn't exactly enemy but not ally either. From one point it also brings in creepy hallucinations. Thankfully nothing that screams into your face. But then he and his sarcasm pop-up often enough that I can't help but to feel that at times game felt like a thriller with black humor rather than proper atmoshperic horror.
The story of the game on other hand is enough to make you play it not because of atmoshpere but to know what is going on and what happens next. It's not just about being alone and reading tons of notes. Things are happening right in front of you and plot twists around, as it finally get revelead and tells you slowly what is actually happening, while Overture was barely hinting at things. It was exciting. For horror-adventure.
Sounds and music were good at what they were supposed to do as well. Mostly tension. Sometimes paranoia. And sometimes relaxing in a locked little room, deep in a unknown.
Puzzles felt more refined as well. Or at least they felt more fitting into main flow. Still got a bunch of standard puzzles and puzzles that make you use said physics. And throwing bricks to break stuff. And combining inventory items. Even if slightly less experimental than original.
Black Plague is a much tighter dark narrative, much less about wandering in the dark alone, but still with nice atmoshpere and horror. A worthy conclusion to duology. Or main meat of it. Depends on preference.
By the way, if you find all 10 statues in the game then you will be given a password. You can use it to play a simple Space Invader-like game on one of the in-game computers. Or you can open game's folder and use it on super_secret archive to unlock bonus materials.

Beautiful artwork. Unique theme based around inscribing with ink on a book. The narrator for this game is perfect. Really, everything about this game is great.... except for the actual gameplay. I have 2 major problems with the card design. First is that there is no real gameplay distinction between the colors/factions. Every color/faction gets a heal, everyone has a damage dealing effect, everyone has the keywords: wall/portal/breach/headstrong etc. It really just feels like there is a single pool of cards instead of four unique factions. Secondly, the power level of these cards feels way too low, and this really limits the design space of the card effects. For 8 mana you can summon Lucifer, and he subtracts -2 attack from all your opponents cards. For 10 mana you can summon Netos, and all he does is heal the player for 4 every turn. You don't get that feeling of excitement after slamming down one of your high cost cards like you do in other card games. Also a combo mechanic exists in this game which as cool as it sounds, actually hinders the amount of combos you can have between your cards. Nearly every single non keyword effect is part of a combo and you can realistically only have 1 single combo effect, rarely 2, going on at the same time. I had to force myself through the entire tutorial because even though they let you try all 4 factions, every single game felt the exact same to me.

As someone with thousands of hours in Hearthstone, and nostalgia for playing Magic as a child, Rival Books hits all the good spots for me. It was very easy to pick up, as it shares a lot of mechanics with Hearthstone, but it feels VERY fresh.
The colour/combo system gives the game an entirely new spin on board control, allowing me to make trades that would look silly in another card game, but ruining my opponents ability to combo (and, ultimately, their ability to win the game).
The combo system also gives a cool spin on clocks - since larger combos do damage to your opponent every turn, games can hit a state where both players are not attacking each other, but instead adjusting their combos and boards to race each other down. As well, you can create decks with the intention of simply building combos to "not lose" instead of "winning" - you never have to attack the enemy, the ultimate control deck! It's fantastic. Also, the aesthetic and character design is phenomenal - they are honestly the most memorable cards I think I've ever seen.
I've only played the Grimoirum faction so far, but the four factions all look like they play very differently (only the Theurgia Goetia have decent card draw) while allowing a variety of decks to be built with each. At the time of writing, the only way to obtain new cards is to buy the pre-determined packs, which is fair but not my jam (booster packs are fun!).
The biggest issue the game has is... nobody is playing it! After a few seconds of searching for an opponent, the game auto-matches you against AI (which, even at the highest difficulty, still feel very easy - I've only lost 1 game out of nearly 50) - I'd like this to be changed, having a different mode for VS AI. Even with a small dedicated player base, two people would have to search for a game within seconds of each other to be matched. The fact I've played 10 hours against the computer definitely speaks volumes about how much fun I've been having with Rival Books though. I sincerely hope it gains traction, I can only imagine it will get better as time goes on.

The Good: Decent graphics, different level design approach, fast paced, it doesn't last very long
The Bad: Botched paratrooping mechanic, ridiculously difficult, monotonous level progression, dead multiplayer, brings nothing new to the tired genre
Medal of Honor started the first person shooter World War II experience back on the original PlayStation. As time went on they redefined the genre on PC with Allied Assault. It helped put WWII shooter's feet on cinematic ground. Frontline was the series last good game, and slowly after that the series fell flat on its face with mediocrity, with EA only caring about money. Airborne continues this trend and it's dead obvious how little effort they put into the game.
You play as a soldier named Travers (like we care at this point) and you go through various WWII scenarios that you have probably gone through dozens of times before. The first thing you will notice about Airborne is how repetitive it feels in comparison to other WWII shooters. It doesn't do anything new and re-treads the same ground that we are sick and tired of. EA tried to make us feel different about this with a new approach to level design. You play as paratroopers that jump out of planes at the start of every level onto green flares. These are safe zones and contain crates of health, ammo, and grenades. Once you hit the ground you will notice that your mini-map is pointing to various objectives. No longer do you follow a linear routine and take it one at a time. Pick a direction and run, but that's when things start going bad.
Every map plays out the same, shoot some enemies, push forward, rinse and repeat ad nauseam. The enemies will keep coming in different pockets of the maps until you advance and take them out. This isn't a new trick, and just gets old quick because that is all you do. Place a charge on this AA gun, blow up this equipment, blow up these thanks. No thanks. I have done this countless times already so why do I want to do it here? The whole "non-linear" map idea doesn't really work because it makes the game ridiculously difficult and you will die dozens of times every level. Every time you die you jump back out of the plane loosing not objective progress, but advancement progress. If you just pushed back a huge group of enemies and die you have to do it again. Your objectives are just checkpoints, and this gets frustrating beyond anything you can imagine. The game throws way too many enemies at you, but there are even problems with weapons.
The game has a nice upgrade system for doing so many kills. For example, the MP40 will upgrade with a double clip, reduced recoil, and a knife melee attack. This is the most interesting thing in the entire game, but EA for some reason made the guns inaccurate to accommodate for upgrades. Guns jump around more than you are used to and no matter how well your aim is you always miss about 60% of the time. Once you hit the less recoil upgrade it isn't so bad. All the same WWII era weapons are here (except the Sten) and it is yawn worthy.
Thankfully the game is short with only 6 levels, so you can beat the game in about 6 hours. No matter how you slice it the game is just extremely hard, repetitive, boring, and unoriginal on every level. They even went back to the health pack system which is just archaic in design. You would think at least jumping out of planes is fun? Not really because if you don't grease or flare your landing you botch it and it involves a nauseating and disorienting animation of your character wobbling around while getting up and pulling the weapon out in a weird way. While this is happening guys are shooting you and you will recover with one health bar left. Nice job EA for screwing every single thing in a game up that you possibly could. Even the graphics are pretty bland and aren't anything special.
Overall, Airborne is probably the worst Medal of Honor game I have ever played. Monotonous shooting, ridiculous difficulty, screwed up paratrooping mechanic, failed level design, and a retread of a genre everyone is tired of. Do yourself a favor and skip this unless you really need a WWII shooter fix. Forget about multiplayer as well because there are only 6 maps and no one is playing online anyways.
~Score: 5/10

I love this game.
I played it a whole lot on my Xbox360 years back and I thought I'd jump back in and check it out again recently. I may be biased because of nostalgia.
Good Points:
- Fun FPS gameplay with a 'drop into the battlefield from the air' twist.
- A variety of fun weapons which you can upgrade the more you use them (skipping an 'experience/level-up' mode for a simpler weapon-levelling one).
- Each mission feels unique and has its own atmosphere. Everyone will have their own favourite mission. (That being said, the gameplay doesn't varymuch from *stuff gun in hand and run into battlefield to blow things up.* But this game makes that fun, and somehow feel varied.)
- Even though it's a little old now, the graphics aren't antique; pretty good for a game nearing a decade old.
- Sniping is my jam and this game does it well. You feel powerful when you can headshot a helmet from the other side of the map. You don't complete many/any objectives doing this but it's fun all the same and is encouraged due to vertically versatile maps.You'll have lots of chances to snipe.
- Spotting a stick grenade as it lands at your feet and kicking it back into a cluster of enemies.
- The final mission is lovely. A huge AA obstacle swarming with the enemies you love to dread (you'll know the ones) that to all intents and purposes seems undefeatable. But you worm your way deeper into its machinery and ... well you'll find out the rest. You feel great when you finish the game and will want more.
- Gammon grenades. Pack a Comp-B charge into a grenade the size of a small melon and underarm it into an Anti-Aircraft turret. Just do it.
Bad Points:
- Short campaign! I could have played a campaign twice as long. (Would love an Airborne sequel.)
- Upgrading your weapons (with one or two exceptions) gives you only one of two final modifications: granade launcher attachment, or scope attachment. I guess you either have to love blowing things up or sniping things. ***SNIPING THINGS***
- Glitches. Prepare to see a fallen enemy turn his ragdoll body into a twisted knot of limbs once in a while. You get this in many games. You know the drill: don't look directly at the glitches.
- My laptop runs the game perfectly except for a little lighting bug where some characters and objects in cutscenes occasionally look opaque black. The projector image in the briefing tent doesn't show up because of this either. I know the missions so don't need the briefing but I can imagine it might be annoying for a new player who runs into the same bug.
- Parachuting is hard to control on the PC and you'll run into lots of invisible walls in the sky if you try and parachute too far. That first ten seconds of a mission isn't a detriment to the game though.
- CAMPAIGN TOO SHORT.
Overall I'd rate a 7/10.

There's been a lot of games I've played that had this amazing gameplay, but in the end were not that memorable because their story was too bent for the gameplay and fell flat because of it. Danganronpa does not take this route once. If you are craving a game with a story that will hook you, a story that will make you stop thinking about other things, a story that will make you fear loss, tremble and cry out, this is the game you will want to buy.
Its premise already had me surprised and amazed, but how this story progresses and plays with one's emotions is just amazing. There's a huge cast of characters, and absolutely none of them feel less important than the rest. They all are very unique, but in their own ways important to the overall story. In the beginning, I absolutely couldn't possibly imagine how the story, the characters, and their relations would develop.
The soundtrack is pretty long and has all kinds of songs. They fit the game very well, and especially during school life (everyday life + investigations) heavily support the atmosphere and tension. Granted, a few songs from the trials are a bit of a mess and I didn't like listening to them for longer periods, but all other songs are really fitting.
The gameplay itself I can't stop myself from comparing to Phoenix Wright. They have a lot of similarities, but there's also many differences. The games have the investigations + trials structure in common. However, once a trial starts, the differences really start to surface. Phoenix Wright is mostly about cross examinations of witnesses while Danganronpa has a round table for discussions and a few other gimmicky modes. Yes, I used gimmicky precisely because it's kind of derogatory. I felt like everything besides the discussion round was kinda implemented to be different from Phoenix Wright, and none of them feel very solid. It's not a huge issue and didn't lessen my enjoyment of the game overall, but it did always throw the atmosphere off a bit.
The discussion round itself is well done, however often too easy. Maybe I'm just used to Phoenix Wright being rather unforgiving: In cross examinations,
part of a testimony can be pressed on for more details and
evidence can be presented at
part of this testimony. In Danganronpa however, even on the highest difficuly only a selected few parts of the evidence can be presented only at selected parts of the discussion. This basically tells the player
. Now this did obviously help keep the flow of the story going, but at times I wanted to tell the characters
. They of course wouldn't have the HUD basically telling them what to present.
Now this
crying from a rather high horse. The story is undoubtedly the best I have experienced in a game so far. I'd also call the character cast the most unique and well written I've encountered, and the soundtrack is also memorable and solid. I
have some gripes with the trial gameplay, but that's really all I have to complain about here. The gameplay outside of trials is great.
I've never played a game this much in such a short time. I simply couldn't put it down. Give it a try if you want to be part of a dark, unforgiving story of despair and hope.

Though my play hours may suggest so, the game did not take me 90 hours to complete. I have just fallen asleep on the game numorous times. This isn't to imply that the game is boring by any means.
Danganronpa is the first visual novel I've ever played. It's full of shock, plot twists and a unique set of characters, with unique backgrounds. Being that this is a visual novel, I wasn't expecting this game to have much of a game aspect to it. However, the parts of the game that require user input are quite fun and interesting. The game plays with your mind in a sense where you won't always expect the outcome of certain events. So with that said, stay away from any spoilers. Otherwise, unlike most passable spoilers, the game may be ruined for you. A story driven game like this can't afford spoilers.The story may start off a bit slow, but before long, the pace starts to pick up.
You don't have to be a fan of the anime or an anime fan at all to enjoy it.

Amazingly fun game, love it, many hours, great times, would space again.

So like many city builders there is "no end".  There is "no boss".  There is only one goal: build.  Some would say, "no, the goal is to survive".  Well yes, you can and must quickly do that or your colonists will die.  They need food, oxygen, water, and a place to sleep.  But that has to be accomplished within the fist 5 minutes of getting a base or these helpless colonists die.  After that?  Well this game turns into resource mining and management with a bit of supply chain upkeep.  The key is to not have too much or too little of anything.  Essentially it is very similar to the game "Banished" in that aspect.  You need to find the right ingredients to make this "space souffle" rise.  But once you have done that all you can do is just keep building.
Games like this require a lot of game mechanics and buildings to keep them interesting.  The appeal tends to be in wanting to see what each new building does.  Sadly there are not enough.  You can get them all pretty quickly.  Oh you can unlock new buildings via trader ships, but they are just bigger versions of the buidings you already have thus giving you (or requiring) more supplies.  It tends to get a bit repetetive.  And it tends to happen pretty fast.  Emergencies are minor and an inconvenience more than anything.  The colony never evolves in some magical way.  The architecture never changes.  There are no discoveries.  No other colonies to find.  No new science.  You get the legos they give you and they only fit together in a very specific way if you want to have any fun.
The game is complete for what it is worth.  But the devs have stepped out.  They left you in the kitchen alone to make your space souffle.  Well I did.  And it rose.  But I don't want to stick around anymore as I'm trying to find more satisfaction in a complete meal.

PlanetBase offers a unique experience and has a huge potential that has yet to be unleashed. The AI is a bit buggy but it is too early to just assume it'll be like that forever. The game is definitely worth buying.

I do enjoy this game, but there is one thing that does annoy me about it. The in-game limitations. You know those techniques games use to artificially prolong their life? What I mean is paying to be able to play. Yes it isn't needed, but you need to pay in-game gold to play every time. And what can you do after that? Well you have two option, either wait for your town to generate enough gold so you can play more, or pay up. Especially annoying is when you want to defend youself, you still have to pay gold and there is no guarantee you will be able to do it succesfuly. More often then not you will fail, cause the matchmaking isn't the greatest and almost always you will be facing someone with better characters then you. When your opponent is better the only thing you can count on is the board and that luckily sometimes does help, by giving you useful combinations.
It's not a bad game, you don't "have to" pay to play, but it is definitely one of those games where paying helps, and a lot.

The game is addictive, you have a farmville like time waiting system.
You conquer towns by just purshacing them. Purshaced towns giving you a total of moderate amount gold per day. And to do quests, matches, you need to use at least 50 golds per match (it gets higher /+10 per town you conquer.
About the gameplay, it's simply Bejeweld. Furthermore, there is a ranked system which you can buy some good stuff with your ranked points.
But other than that, the game is absolutely involves pay2win factor and the RNG system sadly. You can get to unlock every town with paying real money, so means higher gold you gain per day, this leads opening card packs (which is 1000 gold). Also, there is a real money pack too which gives you a bit stronger cards compared to others. But notice that to unlock a town you also need your account to level up.
Overall, it would be stupid to blame the RNG system since here's nothing can be done about it but wish it was not that much of a limited game for non-paid users. If you are a rager type for unfair situations, I wouldn't recommend this game, otherwise, just get it, it's fun.

I want to write this review so that hopefully the developers see it.
WARNING: SPOILER ALERT!!!
First off, i want to say that for first impressions, I am very impressed that a source engine beta is this well developed. I can see all the work put into it. This is a perfect example of using the source engine to its full potential.
Some things i like:
Well one, i highly admire the fact that the developers didnt simple chop a ton of texture and weapons out of half life 2 and black mesa and call it job well done, they spent the time to model their own things and weapons and im impressed to see that.
Another thing is that there are multiple assault rifles. I always thought that the original half life series lacked a large variety of weapons and this is satisfying to me.
I love that the developers also didnt take a ton of concept of the black mesa research facility from half life and try to copy/paste a lot of the office/building styles, they made black mesa the way the wanted to see it.
The final level where you and the cops are fighting the marines is great. Although the music is a bit loud, the combat seems intense, challenging, and the layout of the room makes me feel like im in a scence of the matrix with the colums of the ceilling exploding everywher. Very well done
I simply like the fact that the developers are trying to expand the half life universe with new characters and id like to see where the story of this game will go in the future.
The levels look nice and fancy
Good textures
Clever layout of the maps
The gameplay seems very full of neat combat and keeps me interested so it makes the experience feel longer and extended.
Some things i DONT like
The game seems a little hard to manuver and it seems like a lot of times im a little lost and trying to simply find my way through on my own. Though this does make sense sense you are an employee who's aim is to simply escape the facility but half the time i dont know what im supposed to be doing.
This game doesnt seem very story driven but this is a demo so Im not gonna try to judge that.
The grenades seem underpowered
A lot of sounds seem low quality and taken from half life 1
The security guards dont talk to you nor is there a squad system or follow system.
It would be nice to know a little more of wilson's background and the whole goal in this game.
Conclusion:
Is this a bad game? Certainly NOT. Could it be improved? Yes. Am I going to get the full version when it releases? Definately. I look forwards to seeing where this is going. I recommend this game if you enjoy the half life universe and want to see an expanded universe.

Being a young teen, a fan of the half life series, and just completing this, I can say, well done! Like many other comments, there were a lot of moments where I had no idea where to go, but I still had a lot of fun. One thing that I loved from this was actually the hud. I liked how your vision changes based on damage. One thing I was expecting to happen was, after confronting a bullsquid and a few zombies, is that this was going to be more like Ravenholm but in Black Mesa. Though this stayed close to the original half life, I had no isues other than the following. The axe felt empty when it hit stuff. The animation made it seem as if it were just a regular crowbar, which it is not. The scenery and textures are amazing. However, there are indeed problems. I had absolutely no indication of where I had to go or what I had to do. Every npc seemed quiet without reason and the introduction to the aliens was poor. There was no reference to what was going on with Freeman while the intro happened. I also felt that some things were just missing or not there. Being the beta, this has a lot of potential. This is the oppertunity to do somnething new, which was done, with a few assault rifles only unfortunatley, and Wilson, the guy you play as has no depth or history included in the game. We heard a lot about Gordon and what he did was shown through the half life games, and other characters, such as Adrian Shephard or Barney Calhoun, were shown through many sources reasons to escape Black Mesa or help people. It feels likfe that here, Black Mesa has been abandoned for years. It just felt barren. I also had an idea as I write this review. Thinking back to when you fell somewhere and lost all of your items, you just wake up and all of the items are gone. Wouldn't have it have been cool, if Wilson woke up a little bit, saw Adrian Shaphard take one of the assault rifles or ammo or something, and leave thinking Wilson was just another dead scientist? Also have some kind of bullsquid or vortigaunt take wilson away after Shephard leaves or something. Just food for thought.

Please note: I've played the original expansion for Shadowrun Returns, not the Director's Cut version. However, I imagine they are similar enough to write a reasonably accurate review.
In short, this is one of the best modern day RPG's. A fantastic story, amazing turn-based combat system, great characters and real Shadowrun-atmosphere unlike in the original Dead Man's Switch campaign (here you actually do runs against different corporations and other enemy factions, many of them are optional). In the basegame (Dead Man's Switch), maps are linear and your character skills and stats are not utilized enough in dialogue, but in Dragonfall, both have been addressed incredibly well. There is also a nice variety of character interaction and optional side quests (you know, REAL side quests, not like thos in Dead Man's Switch).
In many ways, this game reminds me of the games from the golden age of Bioware: Baldur's Gate, Neverwinter Nights, Knights of the Old Republic and Jade Empire. It has similarly deep characters with interesting backstories and well thought-out story. But the setting here in the Shadowrun universe brings one unique spice to the mix: the morality is not as bland and dated as good vs. evil, but rather Witcher-like shades of gray.
Then we have the epilogue section, which, while short, fills in some background information and specifics about the story and leaves the player off with an exceptionally satisfying solution - or solutions, there are choices that matter in the game!
Couple words of criticism, though... While Dragonfall improves many aspects from the original Dead Man's Switch campaign, like adding a proper save system, side-quests, characters, shadowruns and story, the Matrix part is still just another combat system with little to no variety or difference to the "real world" combat. Luckily, there are now almost no compulsory hacking sections, so, while a bit dissappointed, I don't think this is a big deal. If you are looking for a Shadowrun game with an interesting hacking system, try the SEGA Genesis version of Shadowrun instead.
Short story short: buy it, play it! If there is even a chance that you might enjoy a good old-stylish RPG mixed with modern day UI and mechanics or turn-based tactical combat game similar to XCOM:EU, I am almost certain you are going to enjoy this one thoroughly. To me, it left such a deep impression that I just can't put into words. I used to play the SEGA Genesis version of Shadowrun, and before I played this, it was hands-down the best implementation of the classic tabletop RPG. Now it has been dethroned by Dragonfall, easily.
9/10, an instant classic and underappreciated RPG. Compared to mediocre Dead Man's Switch, this is a _huge_ improvement.

Disclaimer: This review was written when Dragonfall was a DLC and will be updated to better reflect Director's Cut in the future. If you are already familiar with the DLC version, skip to the end for my initial thoughts on the new features.
When Shadowrun Returns came out there were numerous complaints. Rather than ignore them, HBS listened to the fans and fixed many of them when they released Dragonfall. That wasn't enough for them, wanting to better address the players suggestions they re-released it as a stand alone game and freely upgraded everyone's existing copy.
In Dragonfall you are the newest member of an established runner team in Berlin. Through the course of events you end up leading the team and hunting a dragon. I could go into more detail, but the story is so well presented you are better off experiencing it for yourself.
Rather than repeat the linearity of the Dead Man’s Switch campaign, Dragonfall uses a hub approach. There are a series of missions which advance the plot, but in order to unlock them you need to earn nuyen from other sources. You have a computer which lists all available jobs and its up to you if you accept them or not. Do you do every mission possible and postpone the final battle? Or do you rush through to complete it as quickly as possible?
I recommend taking your time since this is a campaign which focuses on setting. Each of your team members has a strong back story and distinct personality.
You also get to know the community. The hub is not simply a collection of vendors and quest givers, each character has their own personality and needs. The depth of detail means you actually care what happens to the hub, its more than a means to an end (unless you want to role play a heartless mercenary).
On top of the strong story, Dragonfall is currently the definitive source for official modding assets. It includes all the assets from Dead Man's Switch/Seattle, the Berlin DLC, and more newly added for the Director's Cut. All the props can be used together yet have a distinctly different flavor. The prop selection is strong enough that I can recommend Dragonfall over Dead Man's Switch on their merit alone. Enjoy working with exploding barrels, drakes, new portraits and much more. My only complaints are that the Dragon prop is limited in its re-usability and existing fan made content will need to be migrated to the new workshop.
If you enjoyed Dead Man's Switch, you will be amazed by Dragonfall. If you were disappointed by DMS, Dragonfall fixes a lot of the common complaints people had. If you haven't played DMS, but like cyberpunk and turn based strategy, Dragonfall is an excellent place to start. I strongly suggest giving the game a try!
Edit - 5 hours in - DLC vs Directors Cut
Based on my initial impression, I am pleased with the enhancements.The combat interface has noticeably changed, making combat much easier to understand. The weapon interface is much better than the up/down scroll list in SRR and you can easily see what each attack does. Items and 'ware are equally clear.
As for the flow of combat, I now know exactly when I am in cover and when I have an exposed enemy. Each successful attack tells how much damage was dealt and why. We are told if we have flanking, if cover blocked an attack, and probably more information that I haven't realized yet. I am not yet sure how I feel about the new armor system though.
The new content seems to be carefully worked in, I am not actually sure what is an addition and what I simply missed in my previous play-through (with the exception of the new face I've met). I look forward to seeing what else is there and will update this review when I have more to say!
Lastly there is the new NPC advancement system. I'm very happy with this and hope it is easy to incorporate in my own mods! Yes, we only get two choices per level, but it is easy to understand and use, and seems to provide distinct tactics options. It also makes it clear exactly how they level up when previously it was a bit of a mystery.

In this Rival Books of Aster, a unique mechanic is the combo. Rather than combo-ing cards like in other games that only require playing on curve, the combo system in Rival Books of Aster requires you to place Simula in the right order to get additional an effect(s) off. These effects can be changing the color of your opponents cards to limit their combo ability, healing your character or other Simula, damaging your opponent or their Simula, and further abilities. Additionally, the longer chain the combo is (starting at a chain of 3, whcih deals 2dmg to the opponent at end of your turn), additional combo effect take place. In order to achieve these combos you must place your Simula in one of the 5 spots on board, however each Simula must be a different color (White, Black, Green, Red, Yellow) from any of the other ones connecting in the combo. The card on the left most side is the card whose combo effect is casted. For example, You could have Red(1) - Yellow(2) and the effect of Red will go off according to the conditions it specifies. But, if the order went Red(1) - Yellow(2) - Red(3), Red(1) effect will not go off and you will have no combo. This, I believe, adds an additional level of strategy to not just playing on curve and comboing cards that way but also setting them up and achieving their combo effect. But there are 5 spaces, so if you put your order as such, Red(1) - Yellow(2) - Blank(3) - Red(4) - Yellow(5), the effects of Red(1) and Red(4) would go off because the empty Blank(3) does not connect all 5 spaces. This maes you choose between getting a long chain combo for the additional effect or to keep a space clear to have two seperate combo chains.
In order to replace combos, cards can be placed over others, with certain abilities, such as Portal(card returns to hand) and Combine(Card being placed adds stats of the one being replaced) this allows to fix combo order, get new stronger cards out, or adjust to your opponent playstyle. This is different than other card games, in particual ShadowVerse, in that once a card is placed in one of the 5 available spots you must wait for it to be destroyed in order to place more.
So, Do I reccomend the game? A thousand times YES! And right now all the card packs are on sale so even if you don't stay around but you enjoy the game get all the House cards and play a few games everyday with the different factions.
If you enjoy strategy games and card based table top games then you'll love Rival Books of Aster.

Bought this game by accident while drunk after getting home from a party.  Played it for an hour and found it fun enough to keep, but not fun enough to play a lot.  Recently I've had some sort of a Medal of Honor itch. I really wanted to relive some of those great memories I had with the earlier games.  I tried the first game on an emulator, found it charming but dated. Frontline looks ghastly these days.  Allied Assault, which was by far my favorite back in the day, has not aged that well either.  It was groundbreaking at the time, but it has not aged the way other classics such as Half Life have.  Then I came to this game.  The main difference between this game and the others is it seems to depart from the setpieces and story focus of the other games and is almost entirely gameplay focused. There are no pre-rendered cutscenes, everything happens in game.  Each mission you choose your weapons, jump out of a plane, control your parachute and decide where to land, and start completeing objectives. You can coplete them in whatever order you want.  You can also choose your combat style, etiher you can take point and advance with an SMG, or lay back, hit the rooftops and provide covering sniper fire for your squad as they advance.   The health system is also a nice combination of regeneration and old school depletion which was done even better in the new wolfenstein games.  The graphics aren't great but they aren't terrible either. The weapons feel nice, especially the Kar98 and the Thompson, and you recieve upgrades the more you use them.  The more you play this game it can kind of feel like you are playing a multiplayer Call of Duty with bots and can get old for sure, but as far as the Medal of Hono games go, it's currently hte most fun to play.
