Frictional made some terrible decisions involving the story, how it's told, and how the player interacts with the antagonists.
Edit: I didn't want to go into a lot of detail, but people are actually reading this review so I decided to elabroate a little.  There are also very few bad reviews, so hopefully this will give people a more rounded impression of the game before they buy it.  Also, I love Frictional and I can't wait for their next game.  The first Penumbra and Soma are excellent titles.
One of the main characters is supposed to be this really omnious dude but they got someone who sounds like Bernie Sander's (US politican wish a hard Brooklyn accent) greasy brother to do the voice acting--it's completely immersion breaking.  That character is also incredibly obnoxious, it's more like dealing with an annoying child instead of.. well, what it's supposed to be.  That might have been the point, but I don't know how keeping a metaphorical fruit fly around the character's ear is supposed to contribute to suspense.
The story went out of control toward the end, think sorta like M. Night Shyamalan.  Some people might like that; I think it's poor writing.  It's almost on the same level of bad as The Village.
There's no combat in the game, which can be a positive, but all of the enemies are just really weak and slow, so it turns out to be more of an annoyance.  They also put them in your face so much you just aren't afraid of them by the end.  Of course as the game progresses more and more show up, so it's just.. more and more annoying dudes that you have to dodge and weave..
The game has boss fights.  A story focused non combat game has boss fights.  They're as terrible as you can imagine.  There are also really gimmicky auto-kill areas in the game that don't entirely make sense.  It feels really jarring to go from being chased around by actual entities then in other parts just outright dying if you don't get the puzzle right or if you're mediocre at platforming.  That's not horror, especially with how dying is handled.  It just turns into a quickload cycle until you get things right.  While that might work in something like Silent HIll or Resident Evil, that's not good gameplay for a strictly story based horror game like Black Plague.
A lot of people really really like this game, and more power to them.  The game has a really cool atmosphere and the environment is interesting and creative.  Opinions are opinions, take what I have to say along with what everyone else is saying and come up with your own decision.  A lot of the fluff/extra parts of the game are really good, but the core--the story and how it's told--is awful.  That's why I don't recommend this game.

In a nutshell, this is PAC-MAN on steroids. Visually, it's eye candy and it gives the feeling of being on a modernized dedicated arcade machine. The audio track is perfect and creates a mood of tension even before things get hectic. There are new game mechanics and powerups that add nice twists without corrupting the feel of the game. I usually hate leaderboards because I just don't care how well or badly strangers are doing, but they added the ability to replay other people's runs, which is a great way to learn new tricks. It isn't perfect, however. It doesn't support Logitech controllers, and I mean AT ALL. It's not that the buttons do the wrong thing, they do NOTHING. But even if it did work, they took the lazy road and hard-coded the controller layout, which I don't forgive even in a low-budget indie game. But despite that irritant, I still recommend the game for PAC-MAN enthusiasts.

Overall, a fairly fun game to play that I would otherwise recommend. Unfortunately, there were two things that soured the experience for me. The first was the fact that to use the classic Pac-Man skin you need to obtain all of the the achievements, as well as all the medals, which appear to be more or less a second set of achievements not tracked by Steam. The second is that to achieve all of those medals, one has to have or sign up for a facebook account and then spam your facebook followers with what amounts to advertisements for the game. While, separately, each of these issues alone wouldn't have been enough to sour me on this game enough to post a bad review, together they're irritating enough to make me regret purchasing it in the first place, even if it was on sale.

The problem with the second part, which takes up most of the game, is that it's very passive.  It's not like you actually do anything, you just react or select options in scenarios based on what items you were able to gather.  For instance, if you picked up a deck of cards, you might be presented with the option to... play cards.
An entire game lasts about 15 minutes and there is virtually no replayability because there is no strategy involved.  Just clicking through a number of pre-generated scenarios.
If this game had been $1.99 on the app store, I would have had no regrets.  However for the price it's listed at, it's just not enough game for the dollar.

Planetbase is a decently challenging resource management game, pitting you to build a successful base on a new world. Like other games of it's genre, it has "dissasters" and other additional challenges to overcome as you build your base. I have enjoyed playing this game so far. Lets go over the pros and cons:
Pros:
- Easy to understand and grasp the basic game machanics
- several difficulty settings provides a challenge for even the more skilled players
- "Challenge Mode" provides specific goals to accomplish aside from the regular "Free Build" mode.
- A decent modding community is constantly coming up with additional content
Cons:
- A.I. pathing sometimes becomes glitched out
- NPCs have to enter and exit air locks sepperatly. If too many are using a single air lock, they could die before getting safely indoors
- A.I. priorities can confuse NPCs, can randomly abandon their current tasks for no reason
Despite the few bugs this game still has, I can still proudly recommend this game for everyone to play.

Gems of War is a match-3 game with RPG and card collecting elements. If you've enjoyed the Puzzle Quest games, then this one is up your alley. It's free to play and even with the Gold "energy system", it's still a blast to play without having to spend a dime.
For every Kingdom quest line that you complete, you are awarded with the Epic card for that kingdom so no need to spend money on Magic Keys unless you really want a chance at those Legendaries.
Things will start out a bit slow since you only have 1 Kingdom and a basic team but hang in there. Once you unlock more kingdoms and join a guild, Iron Keys will become frequent and gold won't seem like a huge deal.
Read on for more tips on Gold and maximizing it.
wall-o-text inc.
In Gems, Gold is used to initiate battles and unlock new kingdoms. Each unlocked kingdom will produce Gold for you if you complete up to a certain point in their quest lines, however, you can set one kingdom as your home kingdom to give you bonus gold and mana. Your home kingdom will produce for you 500 gold per 24 hours, or 525 gold if you completed the quest line for it.
If you log in once a day, you will receive a daily log in bonus. The bonus begins at 50 gold and then maxes out at 300 gold. The day resets at 7pm EST/6pm CST.
Gems also runs PVP events that will rotate every 2 weeks. So far, the events give you an additional 200 gold per day.
My recommendation is to join a guild. The guild will give you an initial daily gold bonus of 5% and of course, the percentage bonus will be higher the higher ranked the guild is.
This is what it looks like so far on a Day 7+ log in with one completed kingdom:
1050 gold / 24 hours for just logging in
Other ways to maximize Gold is to play smart. Matching 4 or 5-in-a-row will give you 4 gold and 5 gold respectively. If you are decent at match-3 games and setting up moves for those 4 & 5-matches, you will seldom, if not never, run out of Gold. Out of my playtime on Gems, I have yet run out of Gold once.
There are also several Troop cards that give you Gold as their ability such as the Alchemist:
At Level 10, he will give you 8 Gold and then you can choose a color to change to yellow and net yourself easy 4 or 5-in-a-row matches.

Pinball Arcade is a title that has a lot of things going for it. Classic pinball tables (well mostly from the 80s and 90s) faithfully recreated for so you can enjoy these tables that made pinball a joy to play. There are some truly great tables like Terminator 2: Judgement Day, Haunted House, Centaur and Pin-Bot among others. What's more is that this game helps to preserve these tables for future generations as actual pinball machines get worn out over time and are difficult to maintain due to the mechanics involved.
BUT ... then there comes the bad aspects. Mainly, the pricing model. Like Pinball FX2, Pinball Arcade gives you one table for free in the form of Tales of the Arabian Nights which is an awesome table. If you want more tables, you need to pay. When Pinball Arcade first appeared on Steam, the only way to buy tables was through in-game purchases paid with the Steam wallet. It took awhile for Pinball Arcade to release its tables as DLC and only as Season packs. While this is fine and dandy, smaller packs can only be purchased in game. Tables come in standard and "professional" versions. The professional version only offer the advantage of giving access to operator menus and special balls, features that tables for Pinball FX2 offer as standard. And while $30 for 19 or 21 tables is not technically a bad deal, it's a huge amount to ask for as DLC and becomes even more expensive if you decide you'd rather purchase the smaller packs in-game.
This version does not use Steamworks natively to keep track of your friends' scores unless you are also logged in with your Farsight account (which I find difficulty in getting to work). This to me was one of the biggest draws about Pinball FX2, being able to easily compare your scores and top your friends' high scores. This is the sort of thing that should have been easy and automatic from the start.
The game is technically good and you can try all the tables for free up to a score cap (just like with Pinball FX2) and you can have fun just playing Tales of the Arabian Nights all the time. Unfortunately, this game's backwards pricing model holds the game back. It's far too expensive and the professional versions feel like a scam to me. But it's still a really fun game. If you can look past these flaws, I would say I recommend it.

For starters the crosshair reticle decided it wanted to take a vacation from the middle of the screen where it is usually located; to chill out and relax in the upper left hand corner of the screen and remain there.
Secondly there is no health counter, armor counter or ammo counter. So at anytime during the game; you are completely clueless as to how much health, armor or ammo you have.

As the years have gone by since 2007 its become very clear what an outstanding game this is. Game developers would do well to look at this game and learn from it. It's amazing how many times I've played through this over the years. Everytime I've found a new aspect to the level designs, or some upgrade that I was not aware of. The AI is outstanding. Soldiers flush you out with grenades and, as the game proceeds, start using increasingly scary tactics against you. Nothing is more impressive than a German soldier tactically out manouvering you and wacking you to death with his machine gun butt. Got me ! ... And not for lack of good game play skills ! This is where the true tribute to the heroes of their time is in this game. Sure you can mow down bad guys if you want, but you only get a few chances to do that and then they get THEIR chance. The weapon modelling is on the most part very good. The Sgt44 feels especially dangerous with the mag sound changing as it empties. You have squad buddies but there's not a squad command system here. But even without that you feel like they are reacting to what you're doing and are by your side. You can also go "lone wolf" if you want to. Altogether outstandng stuff and a real classic !

2- Some of the main story simply doesn't make sense. At one point a good way through, 20 mercenaries go to kill ONE unarmed person and you're trying to stop it.
Stupidity. The mission designers should NEVER be allowed to work on another main storyline; of any game, EVER AGAIN. Maybe instead it should've been a sniper and you have to chase them down?
In another mission you chase down gangbangers who... no, you're not going to believe this. They drive... *sigh* I don't want to even say it. It's THAT bad.
Okay fine, they drive a f***ing Firetruck.
Really.
Yes.
A FIRETRUCK.
It's as if the mission designers were like:
"hmmm. We need this to be really hard to kill. Let's just toss in the vehicle with the most HP in the game and say goodbye to the story! Yeah, from here on out, smoke weed and eat mushrooms the rest of the time!"
Eventually the main missions simply yank your brainless body by a chain as the player will surely question the cut scenes and phone calls wondering, why am I doing all this monkey business when a guy is holding my family hostage.
Why am I holding someone hostage the entire game? (never explained, ever.)
WHY did mission designers eat mushrooms before going to work?
3- This game in all aspects from the beginning, appeared to be capable of playing entierly without using a gun; or as a stealth play through (i.e. completely non-detected)
However, this is highly missleading. While one might assume based on the trailers and initial gameplay, that this is in fact a game with primary gameplay as 'hacking'; it is a secondary role to gunplay. (Again, at the beginning this is not apparent at all as the first few missions are sneak based)
This being said, the game rewards you for playing the good guy, not killing people etc.
Then, the main storyline is completely the opposite; indeed - after Act 2 you essentially have no choice in 75-85% of missions but to kill everyone (it is the only objective listed. "Eliminate all enemies") Yes, technically you can knock them out (usually). But, that means you cannot simply bypass them in certain places as doors remain locked until you deal with all of them.
Another issue is that; with main missions where it appears 'you are supposed to not use  deadly force' i.e. "complete mission without being noticed" - does not mean this. Kill anyone you want as long as enemies don't detect you. (i.e. shoot them in the head when their not looking)
Unfortunately, the game ASSUMES you ALWAYS do this. Why is that? Well, I played the entire game as a stealthy hacker and only used guns when absolutely necessary (almost never - opting for blackouts, grenades and stealth take downs)
The Game however, even if I silently take down EVERYONE for certain missions, assumes I did not. What's worse, it will send another 20 or 30 people after you in multiple trucks and cars and everyone will act like you can't do anything with any bit of stealth skill. Wow, so all those guys I just knocked out or sneaked past apparently let me do that and had their friends waiting outside the parking lot to ambush me. What the hell...
Ranting a little.
I still am glad I bought this game, but quite frankly I wish someone would re-do the main storyline so it feels better. Near the end of act two I was really involved and then... somewhere around seeing mechanical dragon-spider-machinegun-lighting mechanoid traps.... the missions becoming illogical, and the final mission being the most annoying thing ever because your screen tears the entire time... I just said 3 words.
F***... You... Ubisoft.

You and many other students are trapped in a school, and the only way to escape from the school is to win a murder game. The remaining students gather to determine the identity of the murderer, and to prove his/her guilty. If the students choose correctly, the murderer is executed and the game continues. Alright so everybody knows Pac-Man. I won't get into the details as what this game is about; You're some weird yellow round thing and you need to eat these small yellow ♥♥♥♥♥ while avoiding not-so-spooky ghosts that wants to eat you or something.
What's so great about this game is about how they remodeled the concept. Back in the old Pac-Man, you had to eat all the "Pac-Dots" on the stage before time runs out. In this edition, there's 4 different modes. Now the stages are dynamically changing the more you eat Pac-Dots, so the stage never stays the same. As if it wasn't enough, they added ghosts that just sleeps all over the place. So what's cool about these lazy ghosts is when you run(?) past them, they wake up and start running after you. Now you must be wondering, "Why the hell should I care about these"? Well the thing is once you keep doing it, you end up with 50 ghosts chasing you around, and trust me, once you get that shiny yellow Pac-Dots that are called Power Pellets, the real fun starts: You just turn around, stare them in the eyes, and show 'em who's boss. So at this point you "should" be eating all these ghosts, because who wouldn't, but here is a small twist. The more you eat ghosts, the faster the game speed gets. So if you think moving around a maze that dynamically changes while avoiding ghost wasn't enough, it'll just get faster and faster.
So now here is the different modes. The past gameplay parts applies to all of them, but there's 3 different modes that has it's own goal. Score Attack is basically regular mode. You have 5 or 10 minutes, depending on what you pick, to eat as much Pac-Dots and ghosts to get as much points as you can. Second is Ghost Combo, where you have 5 minutes to  eat as much ghosts as possible in one "combo", which is a nonstop "eating phase", that happens when you eat a Power Pellet. (Now that I think about this, how the hell do you call this phase). Third mode is named Time Trial. There's 30 fruits that appears throughout the map and you need to eat them as quick as you can.
On a small note, the visual effects in this game are pretty slick, they give a really good arcade "feeling" while playing, and the soundtrack's also pretty good, sets the right mood for a game like this. And as for technical matters, the game doesn't have much problems, I personally didn't encountered any crashes, bugs or lag at all.

Summary: Solid strategy card game with a fairly unique placement combo system and interesting medieval art style giving it the feel of working on an ancient magic scroll. There is a choice of which faction you would like to have for free, which is a nice change from the set starter faction of many games.
Theme:
As one of the powerful individuals of the 4 great rivaling houses you work to inscribe your will on the world through your magical scroll. As you manipulate the magic scroll you gain influence over the world and insight to the forces working against your goals.
Mechanics Overview:
There is only a single resource call "ink" which is used to cast all spells and creatures. When you start the game you have a single ink and this increments by one and regenerates each turn. There are 5 slots for creatures (called simula), and these creatures will combo together for benefits so long as there are no 2 creatures of the same color in the chain. This results in additional care needing to be placed on managing positions. Sometimes it is better to hold off on casting a creature to your available slot if it will cause the combo chain to break. Additionally the game includes cards called Snares, which act like traps you can place on your creatures, and while the opponent will know you've cast the snare they will not know on which creature it was placed or what effects it may have. This can lead to guessing or second-guessing what the opponent was trying to setup or protect.
Concerns:
While the artistic style is thematically apt, it may not appeal to all audiences. Additionally while the playing board is quite appealing you will likely want to play fullscreen or at least use using a large window lest the text in the game become too small to easily read. There were also times where I would have enjoyed being able to speed up effects or messages. Fortunately the game is being actively developed there I suspect there will be improvements that address the more mechanical concerns listed.
Conclusion:
With the game providing a free faction of your choice to play, I recommend at least giving it a try if you enjoy strategy card games. You very well might find yourself returning to this one.

This game is a mess... and let me count the ways.
1. A broken melee system: Postal, true to the franchise, offers many different tools of the trade to dispose of your enemies. And some of the tools include a sledgehammer, machete, fire axe, and something else I can't remember. But none of that matters because the only one that works is the ♥♥♥♥ing machete. It is extremely difficult to land your blow on enemies with other weapons, including your kick, but it doesn't matter because the fire axe and sledgehammer don't even do any damage.
2. Abysmal Gunplay: Would you be surprised if I told you this is the strongest gameplay element? Cuz it is. Is it because it's fun? No. Is it because there's cool weapons? No. It's because guns are pretty much the only gameplay element that functions. A headshot kills any enemy instantly. So, if you don't want to deal with the awfulness of every other tool of the trade, guns are the way to go. And don't bother with the shotgun or the MG. They're both garbage.
3. Awful Humor: Postal 2 got it's humor from satirizing both social issues and video game tropes and controversies. Postal 3 doesn't do this at all. Instead, it goes for stupid humor and shock value. Like terrorists dressing up in giant novelty moustaches and sombreros and sneaking across the US Border. Or firing man juice soaked tissue clumps at Sarah Palin in a porn shop full of men jerking it to monitors. And I'll admit, I laughed a few times, but it wasn't because I thought it was clever. Quite the opposite, in fact. I laughed because it was so utterly stupid and random that it just brought out the inner caveman. And that's the problem; Postal 3 is offensive for all the wrong reasons. There are a few times when the developers want to get tongue and cheeky with you. But it's hard to find it funny when the game keeps kicking your♥♥♥♥♥every chance it gets. Sorry Postal 3, but you can't kick me in the nads and then give me a piece of cake. It doesn't work that way.
4. What-The-♥♥♥♥ Scale Performance: Do you have a decent gaming rig? Do you have an ultra powerful rig? Well neither matter because Postal 3 is terribly built and optimized. I can run mostly anything on max settings, and yet this game chugs when things get going. And even setting it to low didn't change the performance one bit. It's amazing how you can mess up so bad on an engine designed specifically for non-high end machines.
5. It's Linear & Catharsis Sucks: The entire game has you follow a very narrow path of the dude going about his day just trying to earn some money. And, as you continue, you get to make moral choices that alter which missions you do. This would be fine, if it wasn't Postal. Or, you know, at least done properly. I wanna be free to explore the city and do what I want and attack the story at my own pace. When you beat the game, you unlock the entire city to go around and play in. But when you start it you see just how bad the direction really is. They basically took what they made of the city, and then stitched together the other set pieces from missions into the mix. There's no sense of where you're going at all. It's apparent they did not design a city and split it accordingly. They just made random crap, stitched it together with duct tape, and said, "Here this is Catharsis." You know it's bad when you walk up to a highway offramp and end up at the gay rodeo. Oh, yeah, there's a gay rodeo too. If you were expecting more there isn't. That's pretty much the joke. Gay cowboys. Harr harr.
6. Gimmicky Weapons and Assets: Postal 3 showed off a teaser many years ago featuring the Postal dude driving around the city in a segway. They showed this more in the grindhouse trailer they showed at one of the E3 conventions. Guess what? That segway they hyped so much? It's only used in one mission. Yup. One ♥♥♥♥ing mission. Besides the stupid segway, there's other weapons apart from your normal guns and melee weapons you can use to have "fun." There's grenades, the gasoline tank, feral cats with super AIDS (???), etc. And all of these suffer from abysmal controls. Thrown weapons like grenades and cats involve holding down one of the mouse buttons, and then pressing the other mouse button while still holding on to the primary fire button. Or something like that. I don't know and I don't care enough to find out. It's that bad that even after 10 hours of this crap I still couldn't get the hang of throwing♥♥♥♥♥♥ Oh, and the gas tank? Useless. Why? Because it's hard as♥♥♥♥♥♥to pour the gas out over where you want it specifically and it's even harder to throw your ♥♥♥♥ing match on the gasoline you poured out.
7. Loading Screens: This game has some of the worst loading screens I've ever seen. Not only are they insanely frequent, but they take forever too. There's a loading screen to start the intro videos. Then there's another loading screen after that to load the menu. The first launch of a map or first time loading takes 1 minute and 40 seconds (Yes, I timed it) to load. After that, any other loading screens take between 35-40 seconds.
8. The Moral System: I don't mind if a game has a moral system. What I do mind, however, is when you introduce me to the moral system mechanic, teach me what it does and whatever, and then tell me at the end of the game that it doesn't matter. They try to make it a joke towards endgame with Krotchy (who gave you the tutorial in the first place) telling you it doesn't mean anything. And then at the last level they tell you it actually didn't mean anything. So if you thought you were going to get a different ending mission, or ending cutscene, based on your actions then guess what; you don't. This isn't ♥♥♥♥ing funny, Akella. That is a huge slap in the face to your ♥♥♥♥ing player base. Especially when the moral system was one of the features you boasted about in your trailers and even on this very store page.
In short: ♥♥♥♥ this game. ♥♥♥♥ Akella for making it. And ♥♥♥♥ RWS for not making themselves and leaving it in the hands of incompetent jagoffs.

Athopiu is an irredeemable pile of junk in the vein of the Arcane Raise "franchise," only somehow worse and with less effort invested in almost every way. It keeps the conceit of "DLC" characters (really, just savegames where you start with 4 characters in your party instead of 3) since that apparently generates money, but has even less story than the Arcane Raise series, with absolutely none and no ending, the same bare minimum of mechanics (3 characters in fixed classes, all items available from the shop at the beginning of the game), is missing the ability to save the game, and is only about an hour long at best, insofar as anything that can neither be enjoyed nor completed can be considered to have a length.
To sum up the entire game easily: You are dumped into an empty "town" room with walls you can walk through, a tutorial-style popup that shows up every time you enter the town, four NPCs selling all of the items in the game, and nine exits to one-map dungeons full of obnoxiously high-rate random encounters and treasure chests full of gold. The whole "go grab all of the chests, then buy +attack items at 200 a pop / 99 for 19800, enjoy the sound of consuming items 99 times in a row" bit remains, as well, but there's no actual boss or goal, you'll reach absurd power levels after even the first area you complete, and one of the nine areas is essentially unexplorable as the game will crash 50% of the time upon encountering a random monster there.
Also, it's got a bunch of bizarre errors: two basic chest armors are called "Shield" and "Hat", Mythril Caps are accessories, Mythril Armors are helmets (yes, that's right - this game is actually pants-on-head stupid), slimes are called bats, bats are called slimes, bees are called orcs, spiders are called minotaurs, gazers crash the game if encountered, and the Cleric class gets most of the damaging spells, while the "Helix" class (drawn to look like witches, mostly) gets all of the healing spells.
So yeah, no. This is actually zero-effort enough that I'm reporting it as some sort of fraud.  <╯°□°>╯︵ ┻━┻

While I understand this is in Beta I feel it is already very troubled and going down a bad path in its development.
Its hard to classify every single flaw and why this is not worth a play-through, so bare with me as I focus on two core elements. The Gameplay and Narrative.
Its HL1/HL2 at its most basic and bland. Almost no real puzzles or physics, lacking in interesting levels to fight in. Basic polish is lacking and I find myself getting stuck on objects or parts of the world. There is a lack of logical indicators, you will turn on a button and have no clue what it did until you exhaust all other option.
The gunplay is your standard HL2 style but executed weakly. The weapons are nothing to write home about with only acceptable models and animation quality, ironsights are useless and feel tacked on as they do not have true new animations and thus your gun wildly recoils when shot. It feels lacking in everything that made HL1 and HL2 feel great as a shooter as it lacks on fundimental levels. The levels are boring and short, they lack vertical elements of gameplay, they lack loose-linear exploration, they lack interaction, they lack narrative, they lack scripted sequences, they lack any kind of "foreplay" build up to events or interesting climaxes.
Elements of the mod feel like homages to Valve's work but done in a very sloppy manner. You start on a long driving journey ala to HL2 but instead of being a driven by the player, which creates a sense of connection to the world and travel as it is YOUR journey, it is simply a very badly done cutscene using func_trains with poor animation (non-existant). The Resonance Cascade is treated like a wet-fart, you get no build up, no tension and no climax. You simply see a few pipes burst and a very sloppy recreation of the HL1 style Xen foreshadowing immediately slammed into a loading screen.
You have no build up of Black Mesa, no one really has anything to say, there is nothing to really explore or interact with, even post cascade there is just a lack of anything. The game world exists as a simple gamespace of levels for you go through, it does not convey a living breathing world. Beloved elements such as the Trams are dumbed down to a simple long hallway with dramatic music as nothing happens.
There is genuine effort here and some decent looking maps, but it fails to play properly as a game and it fails to tell a story or narrative or world. HL1 and HL2 were so amazing and gripping because they had a sense of purpose and world, meaning and lore to them. You could comb over so much in HL2 and find so many mini-stories about the world or the people around you. Dead citizen with a revolver? Perhaps he killed himself, perhaps he was gunned down. Its a level of intrique that reminds you of what this is, a world.
Wilson Chronicles does not do anything of that sort. The most connection to the world you will feel is a bunch of badly textured models and people with a generic photoshop brush blood splashed onto them. It does not engage me as a player and it does not engage me as a person. I care not for its lacking gameplay of corridor shooting and I shutoff to its non-existant narrative.
Even in a Beta State, it is quite clearly very late into development, using a myriad of content from all different games/mods/groups. I do not think it will radically improve from this time on.
Please just play HL1 or HL2. Play a classic like USS Darkstar or Poke646.

So this game is kind of like Pac-Man meets Speed Racer, or some other twitch game. The DX+ version of Pac-Man Championship Edition kindda changes the game up significantly compared to the original CE version.
In CE it was more like traditional Pac-Man. Nice HD graphics , the maze is now laid out horizontally instead of the traditional vertical layout, and the maze is basically split in half, the object is to clear one half of the maze which triggers the "fruit" on the OTHER side of the maze. When you go get the fruit the side you just cleared of dots changes and new dots appear.
Simple concept, it's basically pac-man that goes on forever without stopping (unless you get caught). For the most part the original CE version is really just Pac-Man that keeps going. It's fun/challenging and has a familiar feel to the classic game, only in HD with really killer audio and smoother animation.
So what is this DX+ version you ask? DX+ takes almost the same additional concepts from CE and turbo charges everything. DX+ gives you a similar layout, but instead of 4 ghosts you may start out with 1-4 ghosts (depending on the difficulty), that behave like normal ghosts, but the mazes also place these lime green ghosts that are stationary. I like to call these ghosts chasers. They are pretty stupid and will sleep where they are until Pac-man goes racing by. At which time they will wake up and give chase. Dots are lined up in this game so most of the time you can easily tell where you should go, at first the patterns are easy to follow.
The challenge is that all the ghosts you wake up add to this long line of ghosts "chasing" Pac-Man. it's not difficult to get 100+ ghosts chasing you around the maze. Oh, and the game speeds up as you go, at higher difficulty, it gets REALLY fast.
Obviously you want to stay alive, and the game helps you immensely in that regard. First off, there are 2 features that slow the game down to help you get out of a bad situation, though you'll get the most points if you can avoid using either.
1, the bomb, If you get stuck or the ghosts get you cornered, just press X or Space or whatever the bomb button is to basically send all the ghosts on the field (that are awake) back to the ghost pen.
2, the slow-down, if PacMan makes a wrong turn or is about to run into a ghost the game SLOWS-DOWN so you can correct your mistake (hopefully) and save yourself, or if you're desperate (you get trapped), you can fire off a bomb and get out of it.
The two saves really are easy to turn too, but in a really good game you'll use neither of these saves in order to score the most points.
I'll let you figure out the best way to score big, but this is Pac-Man, and if there's 100+ ghosts following you, that's probably the game trying to tell you it's time for a power pill. It's extremely satisfying to eat that many ghosts at once, and the game is just a sensory joy if you love nostalgic Pac-Man sounds.
So yeah, if you like old games, this is a GREAT refresh of a classic series. I have it on my xbox360 and PC, I don't think the original CE version is on Steam, but there are iOS versions and I think it's still available on XBox/PS. I'd easily recommend both of them.

Going into this review I would like to make clear that I realise this is a beta, all feedback is given as such.
So personally, I'm a pretty big fan of Half-Life games and additionally Half-Life fan-games/mods. Wilson Chronicles stood out to me in its screenshots on the store page. The somewhat varied environments and very clearly overhauled HUD drew me in and prompted me to download the game so I could check them out.
Immediately going into the game, the introduction sequence is somewhat neat but the goal of the first level in which you wake up is somewhat unclear. Eventually I discovered there were some keys on the table which allowed me to exit the apartment. The driving sequence which followed is a nice alternative to the typical train-ride sequence you see in Half-Life games and was one of the things I enjoyed about the introduction. The music begins to key in here and very clearly it does appear to fit the theme of the game.
Upon finishing the introduction it became very clear to me that the Black Mesa NPCs are crude reskins of the Half-Life 2 citizens. This game is in beta, yes, but I did expect them to at least have their own models for the NPCs, especially given that they do have their own models for other NPCs. Following the introduction you receive a weapon and the modified HEV suit. This is where the mod began to lose me. As you explore the labs and maintenance tunnels of the Military Research Complex, you very quickly begin to encounter countless enemies. Your first weapons are your own fists, an axe, a pistol and a shotgun - which is a pretty good beginner's arsenal, but you seldom get reserve ammo. I often found myself just scrambling to run past enemies due to a lack of ammunition. This isn't particularly fun when the Houndeyes attacks deal loads of damage and distort your vision, and the Vortigaunts fire almost immediately after seeing you, again dealing loads of damage.
Personally I think that the health and battery distribution is fine, but the enemies deal a ridiculous amount of damage. The ammo distribution is another story, ammo is somewhat scarce and when you do find ammo, it's almost immediately depleted as enemies attack you almost instantly after you restock.
Alright, please let's talk about level design.
The levels are pretty well constructed to say the least, but when it comes to working with the gameplay they tend to fall short. The lack of even low-level lighting makes navigating in the darkness without a flashlight pretty difficult and it doesn't help that in many cases you have to fight enemies in these conditions. I really don't like being in a dark area only to be ambushed by soldiers wearing what can only be described as all-black uniform and a black gas mask.
The detailing was a bit strange, sometimes it was on-point while others it was all over the place and kinda immersion-breaking. The quality in a lot of the environment props was quite low and it was painfully obvious.
The correct route to continue is not always clear. It is not helped by the fact that sometimes the level loops around itself which admittedly is good design as it helps sell that the facility isn't just a big single direction corridor with rooms around it. I don't think any of this is helped by the fact that a lot of doors that you can't open look like ones you can open. They need clear marking - in Half-Life the lab doors you could open were marked with a green light, ones you couldn't were marked with a red one.
The route issue is additionally not helped by the aforementioned low-lighting levels in many areas. Too many times the route has been a small ventilation duct in the corner which was almost invisible to me due to the fact that it and the area around it were in complete darkness.
Weapons.
Personally I enjoyed using the weapons provided but some felt a little unnecessary. For instance instead of just an MP5 you get an additional M4 which feels almost identical. The weapon sound design was pretty good, in comparison to Half-Life 2 whose weapons mostly sounded weak as a twig. The sound design was not perfect, however, a lot of the sounds used (for example reloading the shotgun) sounded very weird and unrealistic.
The models were okay, they could definitely use some work but they're not the worst. My biggest gripe with the weapons however were the animations. They felt very floaty and at times even moreso than Half-Life 2's.
The story; there is none. Besides the fact you're a different person, Darren Wilson, working in the Millitary Research Complex during the Black Mesa Incident, there isn't much of anything going on. I didn't feel much purpose or motivation through most of the mod as it stands currently.
Overall, I somewhat enjoyed this mod. It clearly needs a lot of work but it has potential.

You know you're in trouble when one of the best things in a game is an ON-RAILS drive through a landscape before the main action begins.  Not that there's anything remotely "exceptional" about said drive...but at least it isn't INCOMPETENT, unlike the rest of the gameplay...

The first Half-Life was released in 1998.  Since then, apparently, graphics have improved only slightly, and gameplay and story have worsened...A LOT.  I'll put it another way:  The original Half-Life remains, to this day, one of the best examples of how to make a first-person shooter "right".  Whereas this latest "entry" - I'm sincerely hoping Valve had ABSOLUTELY NOTHING to do with it, incidentally, other than allowing it on Steam - is a prime example of how to do everything "wrong".

Half-Life was a fantastically "intuitive" game.  It told you only so much, then threw you into a situation, and you had to work things out for yourself...but you could certainly manage to do so, because it all instinctively made some kind of "sense".  There is absolutely NOTHING intuitive in this game.  Not the mapping (erm...am I just SUPPOSED to be going back the way I came?  And it really does look like I could EASILY hop over that fallen debris).  Not the interactions with your environment (hey, waitaminute, I could'a sworn I already tried that door!  And as for this elevator button, guess I'll just SPAM THE ♥♥♥♥ out of it until it responds).  Not the combat (tip with the shotgun:  Aim the cursor WAY to one side of the monster you're trying to hit.  Oh, and your default melee weapon when you run out of ammo is your FISTS, and not the AXE you just picked up?  That's, erm, logical I guess).

In all fairness to the devs, though, they don't seem to have made this with any great seriousness in mind.  I mean, why the cute wicker dude in the bathtub of your apartment, and the rubber duckie in the oven?  Has this series really reduced itself to cutesy post-post-modernist humour to get a cheap chuckle out of people?  No, wait, this isn't actually a part of ANY series...IT'S JUST SOME ATROCIOUSLY POOR MOD SOMEONE HAS RELEASED ONTO STEAM.  For free, thankfully...and I STILL can't bring myself to recommend it...or even FINISH the ♥♥♥♥ing thing, for that matter...

Is this game still in alpha? Don't get me wrong, Damned is an amazing game; the 10% of the time you can actually play it. But in it's current state it's simply unplayable.
- The game crashes much more often than it doesn't. When you start a match it's VERY common for at least 2-3 of the 5 players to drop out because their game crashed. Judging by the fact the game is using 1,000,000k+ memory when I kill it, there's a memory leak somewhere.
- Upon rebooting the game, there's a myriad of random glitches. The most notable is the broken login screen. Others include sound simply not working, and lobbies not forwarding you into matches.
Outside of these glitches, there's a missing element to this game that's required for horror. There's almost no sound effects. Lurker lurches up to you and ravages you with his giant claws? COMPLETELY SILENT. There's spookity music playing, but you die without a sound. This is a huge problem with Mary, a little girl monster. If she stands near a survivor long enough she goes into a frenzy, and can completely wipe the whole party in seconds. You'd expect for there to be some sort of audio cue when she's nearby, you know to scare you, but nope. There's supposed to be a sobbing noise, but it's so faint(even with that audio maxed) that you can't realistically hear it.
The last problem I have with this game is that fact that monsters can cheese really hard if they know the map. Last night I witnessed a match where there was 1 survivor left, who had all the items he needed to escape out the final door. The enemy monster, the Phantom, was simply floating in front of the escape, slashing the air in front of the door. There was nothing the survivor could do. He had to open that door to win, and if he tried he would get killed.
The game has great potential, but until they fix their codebase you'll be fighting with the game's menus and glitches a lot more than playing the game.

I don't even know where to start.
As a lot of people already mentioned here, one of the most obvious and frustrating gripe with the game is the enemy AI. The game does not revolve around the player trying to make good matches. It revolves around the player trying to avoid creating matches for the AI. But resistance is futile, if you don't create matches for the enemy, the board will make sure to create it for you from outside of the table. You think you made a good skull match? Hah! Think again, because you just created two other for the opponent. It really downplays any kind of strategy.
Then there is the "progression system".
Your currencies are gold, souls, and gems.
Gold being your primary resource, is used to "purchase" Towns, towns which will generate you additional money. However gold is also used and is constantly being drained from you through Invasions (PvP of sorts, although still AI controlled) and Quests. A quest has multiple objectives, each objective eats up 50 gold, which ramps up as you advance.) The return of gold on the other hand is very small, always less than the amount you invested. It cripples progression and obviously tries to force microtransactions.
Your abilities from Puzzle Quest are replaced here with Cards, these are unlocked by accidentally stumbling onto a key every 10 years. 1 card/character provides 1 ability. You level up these individually for Souls. Which is yet another gripe with the game. The amount of Souls required to level cards are substantially more every time, while your Soul income from quests is significantly less. And then you are supposed to level more than one cards, but you can barely (if at all) can keep up with one. Not to mention that each levelup feels underwhelming, resulting in 1 statpoint increasing.
Oh, and the writing is brilliant. *sarcasm*
Examples of your character's lines:
"Okay."
"Great."
"Good!"
"What?"
Yep.
There are other means of getting cards, and other "currencies", but I don't think I'd have to patience to even get there.

I'm about 29 hours in as I type this, and I can definitely give Planetbase a thumbs up.   I'm enjoying my time building up my second base now.
First, the game is not without its frustrations at first.  It took me a bit of time and some mistakes (my first base starved to death) for me to understand how the inhabitants of the base operate.   My first suggestion is to go _slowly_ at first, don't expand too fast, and take your time watching what your inhabitants do and how they go about their day.  Again, don't go too fast.  Take your time and watch.  Many building games allow you expand rapidly, but this is not one of them.  Early on, especially, expansion decisions are critical given limited resources.
Secondly, don't assume too much intelligence from your colonists.  For example:  They perform their duties in fairly disciplined way.  If they're outside working too far from an airlock, they might asphyxiate doing their job; or they will go about their business even during a sandstorm and potentially die.  Build airlocks closer, and pay attention to time periods when you need to order everyone inside the base.
Thirdly, pay attention to what types of workers do what types of jobs - that can be a hidden clue as to bottlenecks in production.  (For example, growing alot of food is in-and-of-itself not sufficient to keep everyone fed.  There are more steps done by different kinds of workers, and how you design your base matters.)  Use prioritization when needed to focus on specific type of production.
Fourth, things became much more fluid for me once I got a good number of robots buillt (or purchased).  Robots of all kind can take the stress off your colonists and make for a much happier environment.  I think it also helps to prioritize the essentials (like air, power, water) with considerable excess capacity to avoid emergency surprises that can result in a quick downward spiral.
Anyhow, I'm enjoying this game much.  Highly recommended for a _patient_ player who likes builder sims.  The sci-fi setting and systems are more appealing to me than some historical settings I've played in other games.

Don't be fooled by the fun premise; Planetbase is a tediously shallow experience that lacks any strategy or excitement. Whereas so many other city building games allow for a sense of freedom and discovery in how they expand and develop, here players are forced into following an extremely strict build order if they wish to survive the game's many poorly designed pitfalls.
There is little choice and certainly no variety in how to approach the construction of a base and the second you encounter a challenge, whether it be running out of materials or being invaded by an enemy force, your entire colony will frustratingly die in seconds with no opportunity to recover or repair the situation. Tough luck sunshine, just quit the game and start again.
I won't mention the very weak A.I that seems to direct your colonists in every direction than where you need, nor will I mention how you have access to the entire building set within the first few seconds of the game, eliminating any sort of excitement of discovering something new. It's a very by the numbers approach which goes against the idea of strategy since there is no option for thinking outside the developer's own rigid build order. It's a shame, the game actually looks nice on a simplistic level but the execution will leave you wondering why this isn't a budget mobile game at best.

60 Seconds is an interesting adventure in decision making. Some days you get the carrot and more often than not, you get the radioactive Commie Beating Stick. I love the aesthetics, I love the 1950's scare of nuclear war, the mad dash you need to make to get your family into the shelter, to slowly watch as the bunker drives everyone into the dirt. I love it all as a game, but my biggest draw, and unfortunately this was the thing that made me refund it, was the fact there is so little to do.
The game looks good, it sounds good and it plays well but it becomes boring just clicking the same menus after each day. I appreciate the craft made to show things both being damaged or used such as a torn gas mask, ripped up map or having Timmy wear a colander and holding a squirrel (if I remember correctly). I just don't recommend buying this for 10 dollars.
Maybe if a few minigames or a few other features were thrown in it'd be a lot more fun. But the mad dash at the beginning is the biggest core component of its gameplay. Sure you can play the tutorial, practice getting supplies & eventually running the full game and seeing where you stand. My longest streak was 40 days and when I played for the first hour, it was a lot of fun but I noticed it was very repetitive. Maybe that's part of the point, and if so, sorry I missed it.
Sending people out is about the second funnest part of the game aside from the overall decision making process. I just wish there was more control over it. More to do. I'd like to pick the place I could go maybe, maybe pick the actions I make or what supplies. The game is very text intensive, and I apprciate that, so I don't see why we couldn't have some more prompts out in the field or handling situations.
I felt bad refunding this game, because I really like the idea but $10.00 for something like this, compared to say a game like LISA, it kind of really draws points against itself for $10.00. If this game had a little more, just some more decisions, maybe a bigger house, maybe a smaller house, maybe just a few more options to really make it your own experience, with maybe a bit more gameplay elements, and I'd have kept it wholeheartedly. I'd like to maybe rename the Wife and Kids and Ted as it were. It'd make me feel more involved.
I mean I could feel their plight, being stuck somewhere for a long period is no fun. So if I missed the point, again I'm sorry but I feel like this would make a good game to give a kid in his younger ages like maybe 11 to 13 and say "here have some fun with this" and it'd satisfy their desire to make decisions, but for me, it didn't hold my attention long enough combined with the price point.
I'll be honest, I'll pick it up again when it goes on sale probably because I see hope for it. I just wish I didn't have to feel like I wasn't getting my moneys worth.
The design? Good.
The sound?  Satisfying.
Gameplay? Lacking, my biggest point against it.
I hope this game grows and the people who made it continue to add to it, but as it stands I don't recommend it for the combined price point and lack of overall variety

Hard for me to not reccomend this game, but it has a 3 very serious issues that set it back from being a wonderful game.
Firstly, the energy system is completely and fundamentally broken. Basically, it costs you gold to play missions, whether you win or loose. That would be bad enough, except you usually don't even get a net positive in gold when you win a mission. That's right, it costs you more to play and win than it would to not play. There is this tax system kinda thing with the kingdoms that lets you get more eventually, but when taken into account that you're suppose to be buying new units and unlocking new kingdoms with this same currency, it's difficult to even get enough to play, and keep in mind, this is the basic currency, not the premium currency. I really can't think of why they would do this either, as nobody in the world is going to buy the currency for IRL cash, since you need it so often and in such bulk, and that there's really no way to make a net positive. Which keep in mind, breaking even is simply being able to keep playing the game.
Secondly, The AI cheats. No, i'm not just bad at the game, to give you some backround, the game plays like a combat trun-based bejeweled, 4 in a ro or an alligning row of 3 gives you a free turn, and lining up attack tile or collecting enough of one color ball will fill up an energy bar you can use for abilities. If you get 4 or 5 in a row, or two connected rows of 3, you get a free turn before your opponent can do anything. The AI will regularly get 4+ tiles in a row 4+ times in a row. This leaves you just frustrated watching it get stupidly lucky while you're helpless to do anything but watch, just hoping it will be done at some point. This is especially frustrating when considering the jumbled mess of a currency system, and that when you loose, you loose the money you put in just to fight.
Finally, and this one is only really an issue in light of the other problems, it wouldn't be that bad if it weren't for the energy system, but there's no way to really grind missions. Every time you beat a level, from what i can tell, there's no way to do taht level again. This means you're going to be going up against a lot of things you might not be ready for, and with the energy system, it's pretty much a hole you can't dig yourself out of.
If at some point these issues get resolved, the game will be great! Apart from those issues it's quite fun and if they'd just fix these glaring problems, i'd reccomend it to anyone in a heartbeat.
Edit: march 10 2016
All these issues have been fixed! Which is great. There is the problem now that it's impossible to get above green cards with gold now, whereas before you could get legendary cards, but overall it's an improvement, and i think the game is worth reccomending now. Still, it would be better if they could include at least a small chance of getting at least blue rarity cards, or have some way of getting rarer cards with regular income.

This game.  I've lost countless hours to it on the Xbox 360 version, and when I found out it was coming to PC, I was excited.  I really only ever got my 360 out to play this, and having it on my computer instead would be far more convenient.  Pac-Man CE:DX is the sequel to the first Pac-Man CE, something that, I believe, is still limited to consoles and handhelds.  That game was quite fun, and DX took that and gave it a serious make over, both visually and gameplay wise.
This game captures the arcade feel of Pac-Man quite well, minus the sense of endlessness.  If you’ve missed the Pac-Man boat until now, you play as a yellow circle that eats dots and avoids ghosts in a maze.  Why?  That’s a good question.  But, all of that aside, DX is comprised of a couple maze types, all of which have differing qualities that set them apart.  For instance, one called "Spiral" features designs that mimic a spiraling shape, and has you constantly looping around.  "Junction," as you may expect, has a variety of entrance and exit points that allow you to traverse all across the screen in a matter of seconds.  The big draw of the CE series of Pac-Man, is that once you clear a side of a maze (it's divided in half), a fruit will appear. Once eaten, the other side of the maze morphs into something else.  This goes on and on until time is up.  What DX does that the original CE didn't, is that there's now a train of ghosts that follows you around until you gobble them up.  There are ghosts scattered around the maze, sleeping, and they wake up and join the ghost train once Pac-Man passes.  There are also bombs that reset all the active ghosts on screen to the ghost pen in case you get yourself stuck.  Lastly, some ghosts will be carrying bombs or power pellets, so that when Pac-Man is able to eat them, he’ll collect that power-up.
So, basically, the gameplay is: eat a bunch of dots, gather some ghosts to follow you, get a power pellet and go to town.  The maze patterns eventually repeat, and this goes on until time runs out.
There’s a few different gameplay modes, with the big two being 5-minute and 10-minute runs.  These two modes are what you’ll be coming back to, and they are the core gameplay of doing what I’ve already described in the time limit.  The other modes are:
*Ghost Combo: Eat a power pellet, and consistently eat ghosts for as long as possible.
*Time Trial: Complete the course as fast as possible
*Darkness: Complete the maze when only the dots light up the walls; everything is hard to see
*Free Play: Do what you want in the maze without a time limit
The visual style of this game is fantastic, and is something my friends frequently joke about being something that would be wonderful to watch while under the influence of something.  Namco-Bandai kept the charm of the original game, and then smashed in some dubstep and trippy visuals.  You can also select different visual styles of Pac-Man (from the iconic arcade type, to the design seen in Pac-Mania) and colors for the maze.  Overall, they WILL NOT detract you from the game going on, but people watching may get a bit hypnotized.  (I will note that there are a few visual styles that make things a bit more difficult, but you’ll find what works best on your own.)
The music is hit or miss for me.  Some tracks stand out, others are boring.  The annoying thing about the music in general, however, is that as time runs out, the music reaches a quickened pace to mirror the dread of "you're almost out of time, better hurry up and get that last bonus."  If you're like me, this can easily put you on edge and screw up where you normally don't.  I usually just keep the music off and listen to something a little more slow and/or peaceful (it's helped me numerous times when I tried to beat my high scores).
You can breeze through most of the mazes in an hour or two, and you’ll be coming back for more to beat high scores and get on the leaderboards.  It’s important to note that you are paying for a game that you’ll play the same couple levels over and over again, aiming for a high score.  So, if that doesn’t sound like something you’d like, then I’d say not to bother with this game.  But, if you like arcade games, then this is absolutely perfect.
However, there are a few small (or big?) issues with this port:
This game suffers from random frame rate drops very frequently during normal play.  On consoles, this is unseen.  I don’t know why this happens, and it isn’t just my computer.  It can happen when there isn’t much going on screen, and also can happen when the screen is filled with activity.  This has been reported in the Steam community for this game, and I have a couple friends who have purchased this version of the game and they also experience random FPS drops.  Being that I already own this on the Xbox 360, I’d much rather play that version of it, since I know it’ll stay constant.
The other issue I’ve found is that the textures in the game are definitely not as crisp as those on the console counterpart.  There are artifacts in the images (the “READY?” message before each game is where it is highly noticeable).  Why this is, I have no idea.  Apparently, at one point, this game was more mod-friendly, allowing file replacement for different sprites and textures in the game.  However, now, the game is grouped into one large file that you can’t edit.  I’d imagine this might have been fixable, but, I have no idea.
The biggest problem, however, is the frame rate issue, since that has tripped me up a few times while playing, and I don’t understand why it’s even happening.  Other people have experienced this, and you probably will to during playing.  This game requires quick reflexes, and if the game drops a few frames during those times, it can make you run into a ghost when you meant to turn.
Despite all of that, the game isn’t bad on the PC.  If you don’t have a 360 or a PS3, this does get the job done.  However, if you have an easily accessible 360 or a PS3, I’d recommend getting it on there instead of Steam, since the game doesn’t have any issues (and the leaderboards are far more populated).

In short:
You can barely interact with anything. There is not enough content. Haven't noticed any update. The game is way too simple. Once you complete the initial tutorial the game has nothing more to offer.
How do I spend most of the game time?
- The speed of the game is almost always at maximum, yet still have the bored feeling of having to wait for way too long (half an hour?!) for anything to happen.
- Turning on or off structures to reduce electricity usage.
- I can even ignore emergencies as I can't really interact with them and a redundantly built base just survives anything.
- Counting the pixels between dorm room bunk beds when placing them in order to be able to achieve 100% bunk bed count per dorm room - pretty annoying and boring.
- Interface for colonist hiring should have a disable colonist type option as I have been setting one type to 100% so many times to avoid random spawning, it would be easier to block the ones that I don't need actually.
- Sometimes I want to see the base, but can't. The camera is way too restricted. You can only have a hint of the nice sky above your planet as the game doesn't let you to change the view angle at all.
How are the challenge missions?
They turned off most of the game features and made you wait even more. The challenge is about patiently waiting to stockpile the resource needed to win. Very boring.
How is building?
Way too restrictive. You can't have separate bases on the same map, it has to be a single supercomplex. Half of the buildings can have only one entrance - otherwise will loose its purpose - making layout planning too annoying. Also buildings have to have a giant gap - distance between buildings is very restricted, taking any creativity out of the layout planning. The variety of buildings are way too low, some of them are even redundantly useless as the 2 types of recreational rooms can be substituted by the tv in a diner.
AI bug for biologists:
Biologists are not prioritized during starvation, making it a chain reaction. So if you don't have enough biologists or a meteor hits them and don't act fast by hiring biologists before the stockpiled food runs out, your entire colony dies out slowly, you wont be able to hire new colony members (biologists) once the starvation hits in as low morale prevents colonist ships from landing - in the meanwhile the few remaining biologists will work on producing food for others until they stupidly starve to death. Trading for food might save you if it's not a megabase over 100 colonists, but ironically trading ships always randomly don't bring the stuff you might need - there is no option to call for help or anything.
Trading?
The way trading works is just highly unprobable. In a real world scenario a trader wouldn't land on your planet unless he is absolutely sure that you will trade with him. They just land with a bunch of useless material so many times and its about WAITING for the right trader to come. Or spending your resources on another landing pad, so you can WAIT LESS.
The game is terribly overpriced. I would only recommend it to anyone under 1$.
You can get AAA games with 100000x more content for less.
Room for improvement?
Certainly yes, the core idea is great. Is there any developer reading these?
- different weapon types (machinegun, flamethrower) that can only be used by professional soldiers
- native Aliens on the planet randomly attacking you in lategame would give a thrill; they could even enter the base via creating an opening on any room with their acid and leaking oxygen from that room until you repair it.
- points of interests on the planet that you have to visit with your ships, kill aliens or humans, claim loot, level up, etc
- raid/attack/capture/enslave other colonies, interact with other colonies, setup regular trades with other colonies
- campaign of conquering hostile planets with multiple bases to support establishing colonies on more hostile environments (ex: trading with your own other colonies go at a better rate, you can get limited stuff for half of the price, etc)
- buildings that regulate heat of very cool or hot planets giving a new dimension of problems to be solved...
- terraforming tools/buildings to actually have a GOAL, making the planet hospitable
- buildings that are for glory should attract better paying visitors
- recreational buildings should attract better paying visitors
- new luxury buildings for even better paying visitors
- underground buildings to be protected from meteors & save space and more creative base building
- direct orders for people or first person control of them (fight intruders in first person)
- different mineable/tradeable minerals
- trader ship building & managing your own traders
- more needs for colonists (ex: bladder - fixed by bathroom, social - fixed by chatroom talk with relatives on home planet, etc...)
- unusable bot recycling to save all those precious materials
- more bot types to eventually replace all colonist functionality (biologist, medic, combat & mechanical robots)
- ability to order colonists for money
- have traders with better prices time to time as they are extremely overpriced
- being able to sell bots to traders, this one is pretty much the most annoying thing that you can only buy them at ridiculous price but can't sell them at all... what?! no trader wants a droid?! are you serious or just trying to annoy the hell out of your players?
Music:
Some people complain about the music - I actually do enjoyed the music a lot, but I ended up turning it off as it is a neverending repetition. But this is a minor thing, I don't expect games to have complete OST's, anyone can put on some background music for their own liking...
In overall I'm very sad that a good idea is sinking in the toilet for the lack of content.
And yeah, it has decent graphics - that doesn't help being the game terribly boring.

Bought the game at said date. Early on a Saturday. 7 hours straight for reasons I barely can explain other than it hooked me so fast. Like a hot, random chick that introduces herself by telling you she wants you "right now" and you don't know what the f*** to do.
It feels like a mix of Banished, Astroneer and some other game I can't recall. Sim City in alot smaller scale maybe?
It's all about survival and the difficulty vary dephending on your preference. Personally when it comes to the AI (behavior and visually), I feel it looks like a polished game from 2004 or older (which is a good thing for me). The gameplay is gentle if you are, but if you are harsh then the game will torture you slowly in return.
----------------------
You start off by landing on a planet and need to set up vital buildings that will keep your colony alive. Electricity, water, oxygen and biomes for food production.
- Your settlers need somewhere to sleep, a cantine for them to eat, drink and have fun.
- You'll need to build a landing zone to further increase the population, as since that's the only way to do so at the moment.
- There are different professions that you'll need: Medics, Engineers, Guards, Workers and Biologists. You can also buy/build drones to help carry, build or mine.
- The settlers do not die naturally (old age), but traumas, sickness and random events like meteors and solar flares do occur.
- There are "enemies" in the game that aim to take control of your base once your prestige have reached a certain point. These tend to "hide" along new colonists or visitors that drop by.
It's so many great features in this game but also have a few downsides:
- Strange distance-restrictions between buildings (should be closer)
- Can't remove pathways/buildings if that result in not being connected to a powergrid
- Colonists are easily displeased after a certain population milestone
- Choosing loction on a planet to inhabit doesn't affect anything
- Needs more content. The achievements and ingame milestones are great, but the game do get tedious once population rises. Maybe do more random events? Visually or in gameplay? E.g colonists get mental breakdowns, bigger meteors, new form of storms/blizzards with lightning? Character editor?
- Zoom in closer. The characters are actually really good looking, but the details are easily missed since there's a zooming limit. God knows why..
- And that's all I can think of....

The game has some serious issues when it comes to simulating people('s logical behavior) and in consequence general behavior patterns, plus medicine.
People just starve to death when there's no food, instead of becoming letargic and sleeping more and becoming sick first.
Apart from that, the player doesn't care about the people, which makes the player not care so much about the game. Because the people don't age, they don't have any personality, they don't differ at all other than their clothing and name. Instead of those gimmicks, it'd been better if the devs would've focused on at the very least a basic stats system and perhaps traits / buffs / nerfs, randomized within extends from the start and increase / decrease over time, based on how well they're faring (increasing health, work and movement speed, ... and in effect morale and don't get sick so easily / don't retire so quickly because they're doing well).
Speaking about retirement - people don't retire. Because they don't age. Also, it seems that they're working for free (other than being given food, medical treatment and a place to sleep).
Following are a few more issues:
"recycling" an object or structure is instant, doesn't require a person or bot; yet building isn't.
Then the weird connection system between structures and the spacing between structures - you can't make connections intersect and you can't place structures right next to each other, instead they can only be placed on some arbitrary grid.
There's also no way of tunneling into the ground or at least burrowing wires and pipes (for electricity and water respectively).
And although people have a sleep and work cycle, other than that and food, they don't have a needs system (such as restrooms). The devs should have a look at Prison Architect, which implements those quite well (yet even there is still lots of room for improvement).
Then the morale... for it to get improved, you can put down plants and TVs (mainly in dining places). For people to improve their morale, they have to be standing still in front of those morale-boosting items; they can't seem to find happyness watching TV or look at plants while they eat.
Conclusion:
It seems like the dev focused on winning people over with graphics and sounds / music (both which aren't mind-blowing but ok) rather than logic and actual game elements. Instead of putting in more graphical elements, the dev should fix the logic flaws and add planning elements to the game.
That said, it's still in development, so hopefully the dev reads this review and tips on how to improve the game so it can truly stand out, just like Prison Architect does, because Planetbase has a lot of potential given that the dev is smart enough to implement those things.

I was
close to recommending this game.  I had one mission to go and I figured I might as well finish it before posting my thoughts on it.  It turns out the game's last mssion was effectively unplayable for me.  The rest of the game was just fine.  The last mission was a glitchy, stuttery parade of pain and frustration.  I gave up and uninstalled the game with extreme prejudice.
The game is like a generational bridge between the old Playstation 2 Medal of Honor games and the more modern Call of Duty games.  If you have never played a Medal of Honor game before, you will probably be saying to yourself "COD does this so much better" as you play.  And it is largely true.  But those of you who have played Medal of Honor since the series started will find some nostalgic fun factor here.
The game also introduces a unique element to the series; verticality.  I don't mean wall-running or double-jumping like modern shooters.  But landing on the battlefield via parachute means you can go land anywhere.  On roofs, scaffolding, etc.  and you can also leap or climb to places that was not possible in the classic MoH games.  Enemies can be placed in high places as well and this adds a subtle new twist on the series.
EA took a bold but awkward direction with this game.  They invested time and money into new (for the time) rag-doll physics technology.
it's pretty impressive.  Most of the time.  Enemies you kill may stiffen and then fall backwards, or they may lose all motor control and slump over.  When I compare this to the death animations in Call of Duty: World At War, I like this better (most of the time).  Yeah, COD:WaW has dismemberment and more blood, but in this game they have a better sense of weight.
But then there are the
times...  Times when the rag doll simulation isn't so natural.  Maybe 5% of the time it just looks weird.  And then there is that 1% of the time where it just gets
Bodies will pop five feet in the air, or shake violently.  One time I saw the enemies gun got stuck in a wall and the corpse's hand would not let go of it.  Other times a dead enemy's body part will get stuck on... nothing.  It will hang from the air.  It can get pretty ridiculous and you will get a chuckle now and then.  Sometimes the derpy physics will even effect YOU.  And you don't have to be dead for it to happen.  I was walking along and I was suddenly tossed 15 feet to one side like I was hit by an invisible car.
Like all of the classic Medal of Honor games the enemies seem to get more durable as the game progresses.  On the last mission I was using my sniper rifle almost exclusively because the other weapons seemed to do very little.  Some enemies required more than one hit with the sniper rifle.
The game starts pretty slow but it gets pretty fun in the middle.  Operation Market Garden was quite fun.
But the game went completely crapular for me on the last mission.  Wildly uneven and stuttery frame rates, graphical and audio glitches constantly.  Controlling the player was difficult and laggy with each stutter.  When things started moving again I would find I had completely oversteered or walked farther than I intended.  I use a 6-core i7 and a GTX960.  There is no reason a game of this age should suddenly act like this.  The crazy level of difficulty on the final mission combined with the glitch fest was too much for me.  I tried for several hours to complete the final mission but just gave up and uninstalled the game after it had depleted my very last drop of resolve.
The game is quite fun in the middle.  But I can not recommend it.  2 or 3 fun missions is not enough to warrant a purchase.  Esp. if it decides to break down on you for the last mission.  Maybe get it if it is dramatically discounted in price.
