This game is a great game to play with friends.  It is very fun being a monster, moreso when you mess with the survivors rather than trying to kill them every chance you get.  Playing as a survivor will get your heart racing and wake your roomates.  The ambiance adds a serious chill to the air as you desperately look for items to aid in the escape, all the while being on your toes looking out for the monster.  Swinging your mouse to open doors and cabinets like the Penumbra games gives you more control, and more chances to make mistakes trying to slam doors on chasing monsters.  Sounds like a game to give a whirl right?
Not so fast.
You might want to rethink that purchase.  This game is absolutely loaded with problems, mainly with nuances in the design and the framework of the game itself.  Right off the bat, this game is written in Python, meaning you will have to install Python first, however Damned will install Python for you.  After installation you may have to restart your computer to fix any initial problems you run into.  Restarting a machine to get a video game to work is unacceptable in this day and age.  This game is not optimized very well.  High shadows, lighting, or AA will tax some machines more than it should with unremarkable differences in the quality of the graphics.  Connection issues can be spontaneous, and freezing can at some times be common.  This game has moods.  One day it will work relatively fine, the next it won't.  Hope you like verifying your game files, because you will be doing that a lot with this game, and you will almost always find at least one file missing.  Even after reacquiring that missing file your game may still not work properly.  It's not uncommon to spend more time than should be necessary just to get everyone to join the game proper.
This game has horrible balancing issues.  The monsters are quite powerful, with some maps making it just downright impossible to win as survivors.  There are no limits to setting traps as the monsters, and there are loads of things that can be trapped.  Many maps have narrow corridors with overhanging lights that can be trapped and impossible to avoid.  Survivors also have no way of knowing what is trapped without springing it.  In order for the survivors to win, they must find the silver key, hammer/crowbar, and the actual escape door, all while avoiding the monster.  The key and tools however are usually behind some locked door which requires some other key to open.  Of course there is no indication of what keys open what, with some levels having many locked doors and you will find yourself running back and forth looking in every nook and cranny for every key you can find and testing them on many doors until you can open one.  Insanity, the condition set upon survivors as the game drags on, is designed to keep survivors moving, but uses cheap jump scares and annoying hands to do the job.  Also darkens the screen or flickers the flashlight sometimes which is actually nice.  The maps are dreary, abandoned, gritty, dark places, a staple of horror.  But they can also be confusing and tedious, especially when trying to find that one key to open that one door.  Of the 11 maps, 3 are in an asylum.  Sometimes items may glitch out and cant be picked up, or cabinet doors that's shouldn't be locked won't open.  There are also jack-o-lanterns all over the place.  Is this a halloween or horror game?
Even after all this, I would still recommend the game if not for one thing:  The asking price.  $20 USD is highway robbery for a game in as bad a state as this.  Maybe the developers believe they put in effort worthy of selling for $20.  I don't see it.
Buy this game?  No.  Sit on it.

I would like to start this review by saying that this is not an easy game. F##king something up, will most likely break everything. And by everything, I mean absolutly everything. The game requires planning and planning and planning. I'm great at these types of games. Building difficult economics and manage the growth of a settlement. But this game doesn't have any margin of error. And I love the game for it.
Having a challenge is amazing but let's be honest it isn't for everyone. The economy is fairly straight forwards, 2 food types, 2 raw materials and everything else is build out of that. Nothing special about that. What is fairly special about this is that the escalation is amazing. The two raw materials are neede to build spare parts, all buildings, and all sub parts of everything else. Failing production of one will break your economy.
During this, you constantly have to work to get sufficient power and water in the system so that you can produce O2. Failing that, and you'll kill everyone.
So you'll have to manage the exact growth of your population and keep track of surplus so that you can react as soon as possible. This game isn't for the meek and the puny. Not if you want to manage a constanly growing population.
While I recommend this game, I can only recommend it to people lile myself builder, micro-managers. For anyone else, buy caesar 3.

This game has no depth or replay value at all. After 1-2 hours of game time you are in the "end-game" which consists only of expanding your base in order to get more colonists to move in. There is no point of the game, and no victory condition as far as I can tell.
In addition to there being virtually no content in the game, you have to deal with incredibly stupid AI and obvious features that are missing, such as:
-Designating what kind of goods that are to be stored in each storage (workers will often carry food all across the base to a different storage than the one right next to the biodome)
-Setting individual landing permissions for each landing pad (you can't decide to have traders land close to where you store your supplies and visitors/colonists land close to where you have your security centers)
-Setting priorities for the workers tasks (sometimes all my telescope consoles will be vacated at the same time, so that my base fluctuates from 100% intercept chance for meteors to 0% in the blink of an eye)
This game seems like a beta game at the moment. Stay clear and buy a good base building game instead!

Postal 3, a third sequel to the cult classic, POSTAL franchise. This game, developed by Akella, NOT Running With Scissors - sees the Postal Dude rigth after a Nuclear Bomb goes off in the previous city, crosses a zombie infested bridge and is now forced to find a job in a new city, Catharsis, where a matter of chaotic events occur.
The game features a branching Storyline System ala Mass Effect's Paragon system, but more black and white with it's execution, it does make the game differ greatly with it's content and is a highly welcome addition imo - the rest of the game however... is terrible. It is a third person shooter that barely plays at all, it was built on Valve's Source Engine way back in the day, this game pretty much controls terribly and loosely,  has music falling out of loops, AI bugging out occasionally and much more that just scream unfinished.
I should mention I do enjoy this game for what it is (a fan of the POSTAL franchise and the kind of macabre humor it uses) but from extremely buggy set pieces (Doors closing on you halting chapter progress.), horrible performance issues (Game is NOT enabled to properly run on Multi Core PCs and PhysX feature do a LOT more harm than good), spotty AI and just overall terrible loose mechanics, the game is most definately a skip to those whom are not willing to put up with the game;s shortcoming - those being dang near everything else - considering the game is buggy to the point of it being borderline unplayable.

It lacks the spirit of Postal 2 and is fairly unstable for many.

This mod made Half-Life not fun. That's an achievement.
1. The hud is garbage, there's no health or ammo indicator, which is supposed to make it difficult, but it's just annoying. If you even get a nick on your pinky finger, your screen gets blurred and starts flashing red, and you'll see this for pretty much the entire game.
2. All the custom assets look like garbage. The animations are mediocre, the textures are out of place, and there are supposed to be little "easter eggs," but they're just random garbage, like Sack Boy from Little Big Planet sitting on a couch right in front of you because... Well I dunno, ask the developers.
3. It is extremely linear. See all of these doors? Only one works. See all these buttons? None of them work. There is no exploration, and the game doesn't make it clear where you should go, resulting in you running about the place, spamming USE until you progress.
4. Nothing makes sense, like, at all. Things will just happen for no reason, no explaination, nothing.
Overall, it feels like one of those poorly made saves on the Garry's Mod workshop, which is just you fighting a load of zombies with CS:S weapons. This game is a waste of time, and while I was skeptical about all the bad reviews at first, now I know why.

-Some nice graphical effects (grenade shockwave for one)
-Levels look pretty nice (design is another matter)
-I like the throwback use of some Hl1 sound effects
-Music is good (if a bit overdramatic at times)
Cons:
-Level design is just not good.  Leaves you wandering around too often and expects you to backtrack a lot without any prompting.
-Too much enemy spawning right around/behind you and in the last room you cleared when you have to backtrack.
-too many enemies placed in 'jump scare locations' (top of ladder, behind you when you go into sewer, behind door, etc).  Not scary, just annoying (ladders hare hard enough lol)
-Weapon sounds are hollow
Overall: It isn't "Black Mesa" and plays like how you might expect a older HL mod to play (don't know about one developed for 8 years but whatever).  It is missing some polish and still has some bugs/annoyances that can be fixed.  The biggest problem is the level design...you have to fight it the whole way.  I think it's worth a play if you can put up with some bugs and just want to relive a little half life.

Save your money, folks. It's better off spent on another game, just not on Watch Dogs.
Right off the bat, some issues about the game need to be addressed:
The main character, Aiden Pierce, isn't particularly interesting. The story that unfolds feels mundane and unsatisfactory.
Some game mechanics are rather flawed in practice. There are many instances of pathing-prevention where it looks like you should be able to walk through. Attempting to clear out a gang hideout for a mission (where you are dispatching of the bad guys) leads the police to become alerted but come after you instead, which can easily frustrate a player.
You might think that the hacking in the game is really interesting and is worth a try. Sure, its a new take on stealthy combat of sorts, but it feels lackluster as well. You can manipulate nearly everything in the technologically advanced city of Chicago, but it feels just like a toy rather than a hero's secret weapon.
Plus, I still have personal gripes from playing on release day to be welcomed with terrible stuttering and graphics issues on my high-end PC. It is thanks to this game that I learned that you should generally not pre-order games, ever.
So yeah, don't buy it.

Its another day of school, where you can enjoy the time with your friends.
There is only one, tiny problem:
You are trapped and can only escape when you kill someone. This is the awesome start of the battle Hope vs Despair.
The Danganronpa series is best to imagined as a combination between Ace Attony and Detectiv Conan.
Someone get killed, you search for clues and hints who done it for the upcoming class trail. If you are unable to find the culpit all other besides the murderer gets executed, so the stacks are pretty high.
Gameplay:
You have "Free time" which is basicly an opportunity to interact with other characters and get to know their backstory.
After some dialogs the main story progresses.
As stated above, the biggest part is the detectiv work. After a murder case happened you search every nock and crany to find the evidence the killer has left behind. But dont worry, you dont have a timelimit. The trail always starts when you found all the clues you need.
In the class trail itself you try to reconstruct the case and argue with your schoolmates, always with the danger of being killed if you are wrong in the back of your head.
The story itself is such a good mindtwisting piece of art, everybody should enjoyed it. When you think you know what happens next, the game throw you a curveball.
Since its impossible to get to know every character fully in the main game, there is another mode after you beat the game. "School mode" feature a slightly different premise. You have much more free time and no killing whatsoever, so you can get to know your favorite chara (you will have one, trust me) alot faster. The goal in this mode is it to build statues for Monokuma. You get the ressources by searching areas in a simplyfied fashion.
Pros:
-One of the best stories by far with alot of plottwists
-Clever trails where you need to remember the facts about the case to find lies or contradictions
-Different modes, minigames and collectables keep it fresh for a long time
-If you replay a chapter the fast forward/skip option is a blessing
Cons:
-Some of the classtrail minigames are not that enjoyable
-You need several playthroughts for the school mode to get all character endings/ filled report cards
- After one time the school mode is just a grinding
-The replayvalue is pretty low because the game lives from its plot.
Overall verdict:
Get it! Danganronpa and Zero Escape are the kings of visiual novels. Best get it as a bundle with Danganronpa 2: Goodbye Despair. After that watch the anime conclusion "The end of hope peak academy" and thank me later.
If you love "Zero Escape" then you need to get this game!

This game can be infuriating. But it can also be a lot of fun.
It took me 12 hours to beat the game and then go back and get all the weapon upgrades for every weapon and the grenades.
The enemy AI is extremely dumb and very spastic, they will hunker down against an object and keep repositioning themselves so they become impossible to shoot sometimes and they can straight up teleport because of the AI's cover system. They move around so much even when un-alerted, they give us sufferers of ADHD a bad name. They can shoot you through walls and the tiniest cracks in them and other objects. They never miss a grenade throw and some single enemies can chuck EIGHT grenades at you in a split second. They've thrown grenades through tiny cracks in the walls that are impossible for the grenades to fit through and yet they still manage to go through.
Your teammates are just useless cannon fodder but amusingly they'll sometimes band together and run at the enemies and all of them melee a single enemy at once running this devilishy satisfying fist train on them and insta kill the enemy sending their body FLYING. The enemies do this too, even to you, they'll come around a corner while you're reloading and ONLY ever do it while you're reloading and run the train on you and instantly kill you. Your teammates WILL ALWAYS get in your way and probably get you killed, they can softly push you around and block your ironsight peeking and they'll do it all the time. They'll run through you and in front of you and sometimes they follow where you're aiming and do nothing but follow your crosshair to be shot, like no joke, seriously.
The enemy AI are also aim-botting ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s. No matter what weapon they're using, they'll shoot you from a far distance and get a headshot and take 50% of your health. And other times, they're super dumb and miss every shot, but most of the  time they land every shot even if their gun is aiming at the ground and they're running the other way. Their bullets can apparently eject out of their barrel at a sharp 90 degree angle and they can blindfire around any object and ALWAYS hit you. It's never missed me once, even when I'm behind cover. And a common problem, you'll enter a new area before there's any cover and you'll be shot by every enemy there at the same time instantly killing you.
Your teammates will almost always cause the RPG enemies to hit you, they'll run across the battlefield and the RPG enemy fires at them and it completely misses them and hits you even if you're behind cover even when the RPG enemy has no clue where you are, thanks to your useless cannon fodder buddies. I died more times because of this than any other means of death in this game. It happens with the tanks too. I've walked through a door my buddy ran through only to be hit in the face by a tank shell and insta-killed.
Enemies also have infinite clips and randomly reload even if they don't need to and RPG guys? They can fire as many rockets as they want without reloading and then all of a sudden they decide to reload the rocket launcher only to fire it at you again before they've even dropped the rocket in the launcher, and they can be facing the other way and then just turn around and fire instantly exactly where you're standing, all enemies do this though so it's to be expected, even snipers can one shot kill you like this as well.
And mind you, this entire time, I'm playing on NORMAL, not HARD. I tried hard and it's almost exactly the same, but their weapons do more damage, that's the only difference, you can be shot twice by an MP40 and die but it can take a whole clip from a Thompson to down a single enemy. And even in normal mode, most enemies can take more bullets to their face than you can but a grenade at 20ft away or rocket of the same distance is insta death to them but not you if you have full health.
Your buddies will also almost always fail their grenade throws and it bounces back right on top of you which can damage you. Your grenades also kill your buddies, so if you throw one, your buddy will 99% of the time try to play fetch with you and be blown clear across the sky where he is truly part of the Airborne now.
This game has no option to adjust FOV and I had to adjust it using the fixes provided on PCGWiki. It's a normal problem with UE3 games and you need to adjust the FOV every time you start a new level, with the fix you just hit Page Down to make the FOV accurate. Also, get rid of the sprint effects if you don't want to get motion sickness.
You can get stuck in the map, especially on stair cases or closed quarters, normally you can just crouch, jump or sprint out of it but sometimes you need to kill yourself.
Parachute landings are borked? My landings always range from terrible to perfect and the drop points are kind of dumb, they're really hard to even see because of the super restricted camera angle while parachuting and you need to apparently play a level five times just to get each secret drop location and they're not highlighted once you find them on foot either even though it tells you "Secret Drop Discovered!" and sometimes they don't even work or are really wonky, I've landed the exact same way on multiple secret drops and it's a 50% chance I'll succeed in the exact same method.
Game uses some kind of mouse smoothing that causes your crosshair to move over objects instead of directly on them. And for the love of GOD, do yourself a favor and turn off the motion blur. There are also bugs with the DOF in this game too, it takes FOREVER for it to accurately adjust to where you're looking and sometimes if an object near you is close to your crosshair it won't adjust at all, your teammates can cause this to happen too if they're inside you.
But despite all that? I really like this game. It pisses me off, but the gunplay, graphics, audio, controls and especially the ragdoll system all make up for it for me. It's an incredibly short game, only ten missions that you can beat in twenty minutes each. But for some reason, I really liked this game. I've played all the Medal of Honor games and even though this game feels like it's missing polish and feels rushed, I enjoyed it for some reason. It feels like a good productive time waster that doesn't require hundreds of hours to beat or collect everything. I feel the length was perfect.
Game looks nice if you could get past all the bugs glitches and the makeing of a EA game.

Puzzle game, tower defense, minimalistic, short, resource management like in an RTS game (the resource management from M.A.X. is the most similar I've seen), some army management.
Nanuleu focuses on the formula at the core of some tower defense and most realtime strategy games: Balance economy with warfare. Invest too much in your economy and you'll get overrun, invest too much in warfare and the opponent will eventually out-produce and overrun you.
Everything is reduced to almost the absolute minimum: graphics, sound, variety in the gameplay mechanisms.
The game is pretty short, with only 7 maps, and the first 4 are just tutorials. Still, at a $3 pricepoint you get more than your money's worth with 4-6 hours of engaging gameplay. The difficulty goes up sharply on the last three maps, with ever fewer strategies working and a dwindling margin of error. The hardest goal, beating map 7 within 15 minutes, turns this realtime/tower defense hybrid into a nice little puzzle game.

I remember as a kid putting my first quarter in to play Pac Man in a dark and noisy arcade and feeling a sense of panic as the ghosts chased me around the maze, and delight when I was able to finally eat the power pellet that let me get my revenge on them.  Does this live up to the name?  Well.... no not really.
It feels like it has more in common with the game of "snake" for your cell phone than it does with Pac Man.  In this game, you start in a mostly empty maze with a couple of sleeping ghost sentries guarding the maze.  As you pass by these sleeping ghosts, they wake up and start chasing you.    As you clear dots from the maze, a fruit reward will open up and more ghost sentries and more dots appear in another part of the maze.
The only thing that stands in your way of a humongous score is a time limit (5 minutes to start) and a set of lives you probably won't lose (unless you're a 5 year old). As you eat, you slowly pick up speed, going faster and faster until you die (which slows you down a bit and wastes some of your time).  If you feel threatened with death, well you've got a bomb that will clear the ghosts out of the way and send them back to the "home base" to give you a little breathing room, but this also slows you down a bit (but not as much as a death would).
You continue clearing the dots and fruit with a long string of ghosts (growing ever longer as you continue) chasing you RIGHT BEHIND.  At no time do these guys break off to try to surround you or leave to wander the maze on their own (at least not at first).
Eventually you're given a power pellet to eat and now you get to turn around and eat the ghots that were chasing you...and again, they pretty much keep going straight for you anyway so it's not hard at all. Additionally, some of these ghosts contain extra bombs or power pellets so you can keep that chain a goin' for as long as possible.
Also, it seems like the game doesn't want you to die, because if you should find yourself running head first into a pile of enemy ghosts somehow, the game speed suddenly slows to "bullet time" allowing you to reverse your direction and get the Pac out of there, or maybe you can see it's merely going to be a close call and you can continue.  Maybe this effect is lessened as you go up in levels?  It doesn't seem to change between novice to expert mode.
Eventually though the difficulty does sorta ramp up a bit, and in later levels you get some ghosts wandering the maze, some ghosts trying to head you off at the pass, etc.  Up until that point it doesn't really feel like Pac Man, and considering that you'll still have several lives and bombs at this point, there's no fear or thrills to be had.
There are all sorts of special game modes for each level including: 5 minute time attack, 10 minute time attack, and ghost combo (how many you can eat in a row) to name a few, and each level has a theme around the dot patterns, like spirals, highways or whatever.
If you're a social media junkie, it also integrates with facebook so that you can tell all your friends about how you cleared a level without losing any lives OR using any bombs; basically you get to share your achievements to facebook (I'm sure your friends will be thrilled).
Lastly, if you're a big Namco fan, you'll find there's a bunch of in-game skins for the characters so that you can play as dig dug, or change the look from classic pac man to a more neon looking pac man, to the "PacMania" style 3D Pac Man.  Sadly Namco doesn't believe you should be able to mod the game and they removed the ability to do so in a recent patch.
So to recap, the main focus in this game is to eat dots in a pattern while growing a long "tail" of pursuing ghosts so that you can eventually eat them all in rapid succession for mega big bonuses, and to move as fast as possible so that you can amass the highest score before the time runs out.  It's not EXACTLY like "Snake" but it does have a lot of similarities.  Sorta like if Snake, Pac Man and a puzzle game got scrambled up into one game.
It's not classic Pac Man but it's still fun enough to play.

Classics Remastered.
We all know, that sometimes, re-makes of classic games are mostly a way to earn more money on old names.
But in case of Pac-Man Championship Edition DX+ we get remastered classics, which has a chance to become a classics of its own.
Fluid and fast-paced gameplay, crazy visuals and some really great gameplay solutions, which original Pac-Man was missing turns this new game into really great arcade game, which is fun and competitive.
Totaly awesome.

Pluses: More of the same hyper skill-based gameplay that the original Pac-Man CE provided.  Although a slightly worse game than the original, there's still many interesting levels to master and built-in leaderboards for nearly everything.
Minuses: The game STILL tries to ding you for several pieces of DLC that amount to nothing more than new skins and mazes, and has the nerve to disguise those pieces as if they were ordinary unlockables.  For such minor content, the costs are simply too high.  Because of this, it is best not to play this if you're the type who typically tries to "unlock everything," because if you aren't willing to pay for the DLC those locked skins and mazes are going to gnaw at you.

PAC-MAN Championship Edition DX+ is modernized version of the classic Pac-man with more features, frantic gameplay and flashy visuals. You're still eating dots and avoiding ghosts like usual. What is new is now the stages change without interrupting gameplay and you find sleeping ghosts sprinkled seemingly randomly around the level. Also, the scoring emphasizes finding the fastest route around the maze and leading a train of ghosts behind you until you manage to find a powerpill and score lots of points for clearing the ghosts.
Playing is genuinely fun in small doses and you can compare your scores alongside with your Steam-friendlist and all the players globally. On the other hand this "social integration" has gone downright ugly considering several of the achievements require you to announce some of other miniscule accomplishements in the Facebook! You want the retro Pac-Man visuals? Then you need to share over a dozen of varying achievements which gets embarrasing really; most of them aren't even any real feats, they'll just end up cluttering your FB profile. How awkward.
Which leads to the final verdict: Would I recommend this game? Yes, unless you for some reason have always hated Pac-Man. The actual gameplay underneath the needless bloat is fun and you might even appreciate the techno soundtrack. There are ample customization over the visuals and style (some of them are DLC) and a few different game modes. You won't 100% clear this game in a couple of days. There's a demo available so give it a go. I'd say it gives you the very best impression of the game and does it's best to leave you hungry for more. The Facebook integration might be (or not) a negative factor to you but I'd rather not give a damn about it.

This game might not be for everyone. It's similar to titles like Gnomoria or Banished in style. It's production system and tech levels are not very deep compared to for instance Gnomoria. It is however a great game to kill time if you do not have unlimted amount of the latter to spend exclusively on gaming.
Compared to Gnomoria or Banished, this game focuses more on optimized placement by forcing some strict limitations on the player. In Gnomoria you can simply digg another level up or down, and in Banished you can at least place buildings freely and connect them with roads. Dooms in planetbase are more restrictive in placement. Depending on the doom size and available space, you can only connect so many other dooms directly to it. Also, airlocks are slow, and can become a bottle-neck. In my oppinion, the main fun in this game arrise from this restrictions. It's your job as base designer to deal with the restrictions to achive an efficent base! All you realy need to remember is this: The less time spent walking. the more time spent working!
If you have a lot of time on your hand though, and want a deep game, you could get a lot more for your money if you buy a game like Gnomoria or Factorial.

TDG might not be early access anymore, but it sure doesn't feel like a finished product.
The music is great and atmospheric, and of course the world looks as stunning in-game as it does in the screenshots - but that's about the only positive feedback I can give. After a while it feels like you're just running in circles while waiting for the game to start being fun.
You start out by watching a scene that implies there’s going to be a story, and it actually sounds like a good one to begin with; You’re a man reborn as a deer as punishment for hunting them, and you have to redeem yourself by aiding both deer and men in various ways.
It becomes clear after playing for a little while that 99% of what you'll be doing is just running through the same 4-5 or so areas on repeat, double-jumping, headbutting critters, and solving puzzles that require no thinking or effort. Bosses don’t make sense in any way either, as there doesn't seem to be an obvious way to defeat them (even as an adult buck that can shoot fireballs and use temporary invulnerability). Die too many times and you'll respawn at the beginning as a baby (assuming you’ve been playing the game as intended), and you have to repeat every tedious action all over again.
Being reincarnated is the whole point of the game, but it all feels way too grindy for it to actually be enjoyable. The karma system is fairly interesting, but will probably screw you over in the dumbest ways. I killed a fellow deer and turned into a fox after dying later on, and ultimately got stuck between two cliffs since you can only double-jump as a deer. Accidentally killed some other non-hostile animal, and turned into a snake that fell off the map and didn’t die (I just kept falling until I closed the game).
The Deer God is a cutesy game with a cool concept that will punish you as promised, but mostly because of the *bad* gameplay, and the fact that it feels buggy and hollow. It’s aggressively dull and poorly executed, unfortunately.

UPDATE 2: Same old, same old......
UPDATE: Not much has changed since I posted this review. Frames keep dropping, game keeps crashing, and the game breaking bugs are still present (to me at least), where you have to enter line of codes to fix it. The developers website hasn't been updated since 2015, so my expectations for this mod to be finished are very low.
ORIGINAL REVIEW: At first, I was confused why does this mod have so many negative reviews. The screenshots look nice and the first level was promising. However after finishing it, and looking at the development history, I can see now why many people feel unsatisfied with this. I'm one of those.
Short review:
Pros:
1, It's free.
2, At some points, the game changes it's genre from action to survival to hold players interests.
3, Weapons look decent and have nice reload animations for a mod.
Cons:
1, Zero story.
2, No original voice acting.
3, Extremely short (about 2 hours in first playthrough, less than a hour in second).
4, Not the most interesting level design (at some point it feels like a point click adventure game, where you touch everything, until you find the specific item, that let's you proceed further).
5, Buggy ( While I haven't encountered that many bugs, but the one I did range from enemies standing still to changelevel trigger not working at the end of Chapter 6)
5, Runs abysmally in large areas (from 30 to 11 fps).
6, Chapters can last from 20 minutes to 2 minutes.
7, Terrible cliffhanger (reminds me of Residual Life)
8, Feels like a giant Gmod map, and not a good one.
Verdict - I can only recommend this for the most hardcore half life fans, but even then, approach this one with caution.
Long review:
What looks like at first as another good half life mod inspired by the Black Mesa mod, turns out to be the poor man's version of it. The game is free and still in beta, but after finding out that this was in development for 8 years (as claimed by the devs), I don't think it's gonna get better from here.
The story begins, and I'm quoting the description :" With Major Darren Wilson, one of the employees of the military research complex at Black Mesa. Your objective is simple: get to the surface an escape from this mess at any costs. ". And that's all the story you will get. If some of you thought Gordon Freeman was bland, then after this you'll change your mind quickly. Unlike Gordon, this "Wilson" guy, has absolutely no background, there's no way to know his personality, nobody talks to him, if fact, almost nobody talks to anyone or reacts to anything at all. There's no original voice acting. All of the dialogue is taken from Half Life and Half Life 2 NPC's, so they feel like out of place. What also feels like out of place is Sack Boy from "Little Big Planet" (It may sound like nitpicking, but I have my reasons). In the first level, he's in a bathtub, so most of us thought that this is just an easter egg, but in the second chapter, you'll see him driving a Truck and working at Black Mesa, and that's were I was confused. Was this a joke, that got old the second time I saw it or something else ?
Once the action begins, you'll notice the odd level design. Areas look nice and are packing with detail, but once you try to find a door or an elevator that works, it honestly feels like a Point And Click Adventure Game, so prepare to mash that E button. Now I support games that encourage you to find the path yourself instead of the game telling you where to go,  and honestly I didn't mind it at all, but for some this migh make them angry.
There's not much to talk about the gameplay itself. It Half Life, it functions. For some reason, sprinting is absent, so dodging lightning and bullets will be harder. There were at least 2 moments, where I was low on ammo and health, so the game kinda turned into a survival game, since finding them was hard, but it quickly became action game in the next chapter, kinda reminded me of the F.E.A.R. series.
Going back to the levels, the game sacrifices performance over detail and that is unacceptable. In larger areas, the game sometimes drops framerate to 11 (I don't know about other players with this issue, but a 2013 laptop with a Processor - intel core i7- 3630qm 2,40 GHz; 16 GB RAM and a GeForce GT 650M video card should not run Half Life 2 mod at max settings with problems.)
Bugs aren't such a big problem, but at the end of chapter 6, you'll be stuck in limbo, since the changelevel trigger won't activate (if it's even there). To fix this, R mouse click on the game in steam library, properties>general>set launch options and type in "-console". After that, go back to the game and in console type "map wc_08". This should get you to the last chapter, but it's not worth it. I beat it in 2 minutes.
Speaking of length, it's just 2 hours. It took them 8 years to make an unfinished single player mod that lasts only for 2 hours. and 1/3 of the game, you'll be spending to find a pathway, so playing it again will take you about an hour if not less. Chapters can last from 20 minutes to just 2 minutes. Why did they make them seperate chapters I don't know.
Again it's still in beta, work was put in here and maybe developers will take these negative reviews to the heart and fix this mod, but for now, I have my doubts. Overall, this is not a good Half life 2 mod. At least it's free.
Verdict - try it out for your curiosity, but don't expect to find much enjoyment.

As an aspiring writer, I seek various forms of inspiration from various different sources. I wanted to write a story where "x character is thrown into a deadly game housed by a god-like entity" and as I was discussing with a friend about this, he recommended me this game. Trying it out now, I find that the game is very well written.
In Danganronpa, you are thrown into a deadly game by an iconic *teddy bear*. You encounter many notable characters, but in this game ANYONE can die. With a little deductive reasoning, however, you can determine if characters have plot-armor or temporal plot-armor. With a little guess work, it is also possible to guess "who's gonna die next" but at the time of writing this, I guessed correctly twice.
The fun of the game is derrived from the story that unfolds, the main "gameplay" comes from the court room cases. Basically, it's like Phoenix Wright, but anyone can die. The soundtrack of the game is just as righteous when you find out "No! That's wrong!". It's just as satisfying to find a flaw in someone else's testimony.
If you like Phoenix Wright or like a good story, Danganronpa will not only hold up in that regard, but it excels. I wouldn't recommend this as a "game" with "gameplay", so only play it for the aforementioned reasons.

NOTE: This game was given to me by the developer for review purposes. This did not influence my review in any way.
Nanuleu is a casual strategy / tower defense game of trees and warriors that has been out for some time on mobile devices, but is now available on PC.
In Nanuleu, you fight for the side of light on seven stages across three different difficulty levels against an invading enemy, by planting trees to fend off the darkness, and eventually sending out your own warrior force to repel the invaders.
Graphics - Graphics in Nanuleu are simple and tidy. Each level is made up of squares which can be used to grow stylised trees of different functions. Friendly and enemy warriors are small sprites with basic animations.
The interface is basic, too, but functional and smooth, and suitable to the minimalist overall style of the game.
The game is played from a fixed isometric viewpoint and features essentially no graphics options, beyond screen resolution and window/full-screen options, and the typical Unity single detail setting from 'fastest' to 'fantastic'.
Sound - Sounds are minimal and relaxing, with quiet tones alerting you when events require your attention and light sound effects in response to your actions, or the slow battle being played out.
Music is subdued and minimalistic as well. It sounds nice and for some reason it reminds me of Monument Valley. I can't imagine anyone finding it annoying or off putting, but you might prefer to play your own chillout tracks to suit the mood of the game instead.
Gameplay - You begin Nanuleu by selecting the one available mission. This takes you to a semi-randomly created map and introduces you to the basic game concepts as you play the mission. This first mission is easy; as long as you've paid attention in the tutorial, you should have no trouble. Upon finishing the mission you're given a score and proceed to the next -- again, there's only one choice. But here things become much harder.
Each mission starts you off on a small map with coloured squares that make up the world. Squares are either empty or have one of a number of resource symbols on them: water, minerals, or life. You start with a certain number of points of each of these resources, which are used to create roots, which expand your area of influence, or trees of a number of types. At the beginning only water and mineral trees are available to plant, but you'll quickly have protector, life, and, later, war trees as well. I didn't encounter any more than this during play, and the nature of the interface suggests that this is the limit of your planting abilities.
Water trees can be planted only on water icons, and each one increases the rate of your water resource generation. Similarly, mineral trees can only be planted on mineral icons, and increase that resource generation rate. Life trees are treated similarly, but the life resource icon is much less common, with only a few on each map. Each tree you plant uses one life resource and a certain number of water and mineral resources. Roots are automatically planted to connect new trees to the existing root network, so the farther away you plant a tree from your existing growth, the more it will cost in water and minerals.
Protector trees are planted to protect your territory, and act as the base defense tower of the game. Any enemy coming within the tree's predefined attack radius will be targeted by the tree, which shoots out a little bolt at it. War trees can only be planted after you've planted the requisite number of life trees beforehand. These act as a barracks, growing little warrior units that move towards the closest enemy units or trees/towers and attack them.
While you're planting your trees and collecting resources, a progress bar near the top of the screen gradually fills up. When it is complete, an enemy tree is planted at one of a number of pre-set positions on the map. The longer you take to reach the point at which you can grow your own warriors, the more enemies will be spawning to attack you. The core mechanic of the game, then, is simple: balance resource tree planting with protection until you can grow war trees and fight back.
The game includes some more fine-grained tactics, but these aren't described in the tutorial at all. For example, planting a life tree wipes out all enemy units currently on the map, which can be very helpful, and trees take damage when roots that connect them to the rest of the root network are destroyed, which would have been nice to know. Also, each level includes four stone altars that are also enemy targets, but I don't know if these hold any particular significance, other than contributing Achievement goals.
Controls are simple, as you'd expect for a port from a mobile game. If you have a touchscreen then the game should support it, otherwise the mouse is used exclusively, and only one button is required for everything except zooming in and out (which uses the mouse wheel).
Before I finish up, I'd like to offer a warning: Nanuleu is hard! I'm generally pretty good at tower defense and RTS games, but for a long time I just couldn't get the hang of Nanuleu. The first level was a cakewalk and took less than 10 minutes. The second level took me about 90 minutes to finally work out the one strategy that worked, and that same strategy kept working for the next level, and was looking pretty good for the level after that, too, until I got bored and turned it off.
Pros:
+ Nice minimalist graphic and sound styles
+ Steam achievements.
Cons:
- Minimal tutorial; no discussion of roots, light and dark control, or anything but the most basic tactics.
- Very difficult unless you use the one strategy that works, which seems to be the same for every level.
- Minimalist gameplay: very repetitive, even with only seven levels to beat.
- Poor grammar that otherwise ruined a very polished presentation ("The enemies are multiply rapidly.")
I'm on the fence about Nanuleu; it's another game that makes me wish Steam's review system had a 'maybe' option for recommendations.
While Nanuleu has a lovely minimalist art and music style, its minimalist approach to gameplay is not quite as endearing. If you're an achievement hunter who enjoys a challenge, it's probably for you. Personally, though, once I got the hang of it, I realised it wasn't really for me.

I actually played this at PAX East 2017 and bought a key. It was really fun, especially with multiple people.
Basically there are 2 modes as it were. Apocalypse and "Sports" mode.
"Sports" mode basically involves either basket ball or some kind of collection/ capture the flag type game. It's actually quite fun for what it is, but it requires people to really make it something special.
Apocalypse mode is one that see's you and your friends trying to survive 1 of 2 world ending scenarios. A meteor and a zombie pandemic. Each features a barrier that will OHKO any players that are too slow to complete the level. Both level types requre players to use tetrominos to build bridges or platforms to advance. The goal is to reach the Helicopter and fly to safety.
In the Meteor level the barrier comes in the form of laval. This level is verticle so you'll be doing a lot of climbing. Occasionally small meteors will drop from the sky and strike the stage. 1 hit will kill you.
The Zombie level features a wave of destructive energy advancing from the right side to the left. The main obsticles are the Zombies. every time you brush against one they take a bite out of you until you're dead. Use tetrominos to block them off and advance towards the helicopter.
For a party game it's great, but on the same token that is it's weakness. You really want to play with friends to get the most out of it. It's also pretty liniear, once you've played the levels it's all pretty much the same. I do hope they come out with more vairence in the future. Having different Apocalypse scenarios would be a great start as I feel that is where the game shines most. It would also be really cool if characters had special attributes of some kind. As of now they're only skins and they all behave the same way, even if they are refferential in nature. An element like that could elivate the way the game is played, especially for the basketball game mode (sort of like a super mario strikers lite).
Anyway, the game is good as of writing and I look forward to seing more people pick up the game.

Blockpocalypse is a platform-based game deliberately trying to look like something designed for the NES littered with pop culture references and unique characters.
Blockpocalypse is the story of a post apocalyptic lava world after a grimacing asteroid collides with the planet. There are four game modes where you and other payers either work together to build ever higher in order to evade rising lava, work in teams to score baskets, fight as individuals to maintain control of cake or simply throw each other off platforms into pools of lava.
One thing that comes across is while all the game modes are simplistic and the graphics unassuming there is great enjoyments to have, as the skills are easy to learn but difficult to master.
On the whole it is an engaging game in which a rudimentary core game play is used with a surprising degree of variety without compromising its simplicity.

The Deer God is a fun, tight horizontal platformer with a beautiful look to it. I'm not usually much for pixel art styles- they begin to feel overdone and lazy after a certain point- but The Deer God manages to impress with its graphics.
That said, the game can at times feel poorly thought out, even sloppy, and definitely unfinished. There are a great number of glitches, nonsensical puzzles, or dead-end situations that force the player to wait several minutes to starve, respawn, and try again, an unwelcome interruption to otherwise fast-paced gameplay. The story, voice acting, and dialogue also leave much to be desired. No updates have been made to the game to address technical issues in over a year, which is unfortunate.
That said, it is fun in the moment, when you're leaping between platforms with cervid grace, solving puzzles to gain magical powers, or battling hostile creatures in breathtaking environments. My personal advice would be to wait for a sale and pick it up for cheaper; a full price for a game that could hardly be considered complete isn't reasonable, in my opinion, but it's an experience worth having if it's available to you.

Gems of War is an interesting and rather fun twist on the Bejeweled-clone formula that so, SO many puzzle games (Candy Crush Saga, anyone?) copy. Like all Bejeweled clones, Gems of War is a match-three-gems game at its core, with a bonus if you match four or five. But the goal of the game is the kicker- the shell around the match-three-gems field isn't that of a puzzle game, but instead, that of a turn-based RPG with attacks and spells! It seems extremely polished gameplay wise, and is extremely engaging- and FUN.
And then you get into the rather confusing system- er, systems- of currency.
First, you have gold. You get gold pretty easily in game, even getting small amounts for small things like matching 4 or 5 gems- but it, as far as I have seen so far, goes absolutely nowhere, and has zero uses. This confused me to no end when I checked out the store to see if I could get a new costume.
Then you have the ACTUAL first in-game currency, souls, which are used for leveling up your allies- and that seems to be it.
Second, you have the real-money currency, gems. And it's used for buying EVERYTHING in the shop, except for itself- you, of course, need real money to buy gems. And the thing that irks me the most is that although you have no use for gold, you can buy it with gems- and although souls are pretty valuable as they're used to train allies, you can't buy them.
And fourth, there's Glory, the event-reward currency, used for buying extremely rare items.
Finally, as far as I could tell, there was no way to let my character try on a suit of armor before I could buy it. If a suit of armor is only for looks, let me see how it looks! (Even if I can't buy anything at all with gold.)
However, it IS a rather new game, so the stellar gameplay takes the cake here. Upvote with little hesitation.

Since it reminds me of Underhell, I'll start off being nice instead of starting off with a whole bunch of hate (as I said, that will come later).
This game's saving grace is that it performs decently when it comes to human to human gunplay. The AI for enemy humans is surprisingly well done and they all have custom models. They take cover, throw grenades, run away from grenades, and aren’t aimbots and hit every single shot they take or Stormtroopers and miss every single shot. They feel nice and rounded. However, I have a sneaking suspicion that the AI is only good because it's copy-pasted from HL2's Combine Soldier AI. I’ll give this a pass because it’s not really detracting from the gameplay. Next are the guns. As to be expected, the gunplay is similar to Half-Life 2. But what I didn’t expect were all the guns they added. There's a large variety of guns (at least relative to the Half Life series), and there’s an even larger amount of guns not in the game but still in the files (you can spawn them in through console commands, e.g.: “give weapon_gauss”, “give weapon_mortar”).  It feels like there’s been effort put in these gun and enemy models (if they haven’t been ripped from another game or someone else’s work) and it’s a lot better than the other crap that Valve lets flood the store. As I said before, this
be a good game if the developers put more time and effort into it.
All good things must come to an end, so now we move onto the cons/things the developers need to improve, starting with what I hated the most. The story is absolutely non-existent. From what the game tells me, you're some ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ named Wilson who drives a bright, red Mustang (straight past a man stranded in the middle of the desert at one point), arrives at Black Mesa 5 minutes before Gordon unleashes Armageddon, after which he survives and somehow finds an HEV suit, and starts beating/shooting the living♥♥♥♥♥♥out of everyone and everything that even so much as looks at him funny. Oh yeah, there's also some guard dude that follows you around for a few levels before eventually you get split up and I guess you find him dead. I don't know what makes him important. He just starts following you around, teleports to you when changing maps, is completely invincible, and calls you Gordon every now and again. That's right! All the NPC's are default HL2 NPC models and use the default NPC dialogue. All this put together makes sure that you have no idea what the heck is going on and makes it feel somewhat like the devs made the game in G-Mod.
This only scratches the surface of what is wrong with this game, but hopefully I can help identify some of the things wrong so the devs can fix it. Un-inspired level design and obtuse progression through levels made it so that I had to rub my face on every door in order to find the right one to open, and in some instances, I had to noclip through some levels in order to find the right way to progress. Reused assets were all over the place with the same rooms appearing in different places, the 4 or 5 scientists that climbed into a vent with a shotgun and died in the exact same way, and always with Xen Creature and Vortigaunt ambushes around corners and Headcrabs and zombies in vents. Xen Creatures and Vortigaunts are a pain to fight since they spawn instantly (usually a couple feet away from you giving you no time to react), ignoring their teleportation animation and do a large amount of damage even on normal difficulty. And finally, for the piece de resistance, the second to last level in the game does not have a load trigger for the final level, meaning that you have to cheat (go to advanced keyboard settings, enable console, type "map wc_08" in console) in order to travel to the final level and watch some friendly NPC's fight enemy soldiers to get "TO BE CONTINUED" and a big anti-climax. To be completely honest, this game feels like it should still be in alpha with all of the problems it has.
I know this is a beta/early access game, and from my perspective, it has a lot of potential (it kinda reminds me of Underhell when it was first beginning), but I sincerely cannot recommend this until the creator fixes/improves the level design at the very least. If they fix this and they'll get my recommendation.
thats all there is to it.

A fairly decent experience that recalls a lot of the pulse-pounding adrenaline of the original Half-Life. The maps look beautiful, albeit terribly designed from a gameplay perspective (unless I'm just an idiot, you'll spend a lot of time hunting around for doors that'll work. Expect to press "E" a lot.)
Story is thin as thin gets. You are man. You work at Black Mesa. You get HEV suit. You get gun. You shoot soldiers and aliens. Rinse, repeat. Dialogue is clumsily recycled from HL2 in a way that would have been excusable during the early days of modding for this game, but now just comes across as lazy and incompetent.
The penultimate map (a clerverly redesigned version of the Hazard Course from the original HL) fails to link up properly with the last map, which itself is a tonally inappropriate gun battle against hordes of soldiers. It's a masterstroke in losing player confidence, and I was rolling my eyes as the "to be continued" blurb flashed across the screen, as if I should be waiting with baited breath for the conclusion of this shoot-man chronicle.
I'm honestly not sure what compels mod makers (and hell, even studio developers) these days to release buggy, half-finished products. Is it a lack of discipline? A need to drum up hype among players? Why even release this as a beta when they could have had a slam dunk with more fine tuning and patience?
Anyway, all of this may seem to contradict my assertion at the top that this is a decent experience, but I'm going to hold myself to that. The gun fights are solid, the difficulty is appropriately slanted against you (at least on hard mode,) every gun you hold feels solid, just waiting to spit hot lead into aliens or soldiers, and the map aesthetics successfully recall the Black Mesa of old - aside from a few rather baffling anachronisms and pop culture references. I'm lookin' at you, Little Big Planet dolls.
It's just... kinda disappointing, in the end. But hell, for the low-low price of free you can do a helluva lot worse than this. My humble recommendation is that you wait until this is actually finished before playing, but you wouldn't be wasting your time if you played it now.
Still, give 'em a few months, I say.

There’s not a lot you can do in 60 seconds.
Boil a kettle, nuke something in the microwave, maybe have a wee, of course if you’re Nicolas Cage then could hot wire a car, but that’s Hollywood for you.
But what if your future and that of your family depended on the decisions you made over one short pressure filled minute?
Imagine a situation where you’re sitting at home.
Glancing around you can see all sorts of junk begging to be tidied away; maybe if you leave it long enough your wife and kids (who are around the house somewhere) might get around to doing it.
As you idly wonder who left a crate of bottled water in the corner of the living room a screeching noise shatters the silence.
You’re filled with dread as you realise that it’s the sound of the early warning system wailing outside.
We knew politicians would be the death of us and it seems that day has finally come.
The bombers must already be on their way, carrying their payloads of nuclear Armageddon,
The world is about to end...
... But don’t worry, you’ve prepared, unlike most of the other saps who are about to take a crash course in nuclear fission you had the foresight to install a nuclear bunker under your house!
You smile smugly to yourself, all that time playing fallout was well spent after all and in a few seconds you’ll be sitting safely in your cosy vault as the world above you turns into a radioactive wasteland.
Moving for the shelter your eyes again drift to the crate of bottled water and an awful realisation washes all traces of smugness away.
You might have had the foresight to build a fallout shelter, but you never did get around to filling it with supplies did you?
Cursing your laziness you look desperately around the room, what items are you going to need in your shelter?
Food, Water, maybe the wife and kids to keep you company?
The alarms are still wailing outside, how much warning do they give you?
60 seconds?
Dashing towards the bottled water you trip over a can of soup, stumble and crash into a chair, if only your house wasn’t in such a mess!
Which room are the kids in anyway?
... tick... tock...
This is the premise behind the first part “60 Seconds” a unique little survival title developed by Robot Gentleman Studios.
I say the first part, because “60 Seconds” is split into two very distinct yet connected games.
The first part of the game is a quick and frantic “treasure hunt” around your house.
You’ll control your character as he runs and stumbles through the various rooms searching for supplies to take down into the bunker.
You’re given a few short seconds to explore your surroundings before the sirens blare and the countdown begins, this time is vital to quickly scan around the layout of your house and look for the locations of useful items. (This changes every time you play!)
Before you’ve had chance to complete your stock take the countdown will begin, it’s time to start grabbing those supplies and dropping them down the hatch into your vault.
It’s not as simple as grabbing everything in one go either, you can only carry so much at a time,  this leads to a frantic dash through the various rooms with armfuls of tinned food or bottled water.
This is 60 seconds of sandbox physics mayhem.
Furniture will go flying, objects will get in your way and you’ll be looking for one thing and get distracted by something else.
A radio might be useful to keep in touch with the outside world, maybe a good book would help stave off the boredom, there must be a first aid kit somewhere, etc.
These are the thoughts that will go through your head as you crash passed tables and fall over chairs in the rush.
It’s an ultra intense supermarket sweep and it’s as fun as it is frustrating!
This is just the beginning, after diving into the bunker yourself, you’ll get to experience vault life and ration out those precious supplies to prolong your existence (and that of your family if you got around to saving them) for as long as possible.
Of course, if you got distracted by something shiny and didn’t make it into the shelter in time then you’ll be dead and need to start a new game, so let’s assume you did make it, because it’s in the shelter that the real fun starts.
The game changes pace in the shelter and becomes a short tongue in cheek survival adventure.
You’ll spend the remainder of the game looking at a static screen of yourself and any rescued family members sitting in the vault along with whatever supplies you managed to scavenge.
Each day this screen will be updated to reflect any changes in your little vault, including the ever dwindling supplies sitting on the shelf behind you.
Your food and water will almost certainly require rationing if you’re to last until help arrives, keep someone hungry or thirsty for too long though and they’ll get sick and die.
Other items you threw into the shelter could well prove useful too, you see, strange things happen when you’re cooped up in a vault.
A board game might be enough to stave off madness and a can of bug spray might be handy if you don’t want to share your bunker with some new scuttling friends.
Like a post apocalyptic Adrian Mole, you keep a diary in the vault, but there’s more to write about than the dwindling water supplies.
Vault life is more eventful than you might think, random events happen every day and it’s these events that drive the narrative forward.
Each day you will go through food and water rationing, deciding who (if anyone) gets something to eat or drink that day.You’ll then read through the vault diary,
it’ll cover the health and moods of your surviving family members and report on any interesting events that occurred that day.
Mutants, bandits, a nice game of scrabble, anything could happen as you wait out the apocalypse and most of these events will require you to make a decision which will impact the narrative as the days progress.
There’s a banging on the vault door, It could be a post apocalyptic mailman delivering some goodies, or it could just as likely be a gang of bandits fresh from the set of Mad Max, do you answer it? Well that’s up to you.
The outcome of many of these events will depend on the salvaged items from the first part of the game.
If a radioactive bug bites a family member, you’d better hope you bought a first aid kit with you or the consequences might prove surprising.
Your first play through will give you an idea of the importance of the various items you ignored whilst foraging for cans of soup to bring down into the vault.
This game will quickly teach you that no matter how innocuous an item seems, it could well prove useful in the vault.
60 Seconds is a refreshing and quirky little game but It definitely feels like a tablet conversion.
It’s quick to play and immediately addictive which is great, unfortunately, like most mobile gaming ports, it can feel a little shallow and become repetitive pretty quickly.
Having said that, it’s priced to reflect this short term appeal and there is no denying the hours of entertainment you’ll get out of playing it.
60 seconds isn’t looking for a relationship, it’s looking for a fling.
Its fun whilst it lasts, you’re going to enjoy it but you probably won’t remember it in the morning.
It’s the one night stand of post apocalyptic gaming!

I wanted to like this game, I really did. I went in with an open mind and an open heart and I left 40 hours later severely disappointed. Watch_Dogs has everything I love in a relaxing game: a big open world for getting lost, driving, stealth gameplay, cyberpunk, all sorts of elements. For as big and complex as the game world is, however, Watch_Dogs is incredibly empty.
Watch_Dogs has you controlling Aiden Pearce, master hacker and parkour enthusiast, as he hacks his way through a futuristic security network linking all of Chicago. The game world has, by far, some of the best object modelling and NPC generation I've seen to give the urban environment of Chicago a living, breathing feel. Yards and sidewalks have clutter that changes with the socio-economic level of different parts of town and as Aiden free runs through back yards or across apartment complexes, it's not unlikely you'll trip over barbeque pits or shopping carts reasonably placed in real world settings. NPC's look varied and react differently to your actions and, after a while, the environment does feel sentient.
The fantasy stops there, however, as the graphics, which you've no doubt heard by now, have been so watered down from the E3 demo that they look almost cartoonish. The color palette is off with a base-level shade spectrum you don't see in the real world, and the textures are clean and flat to the point of almost appearing two dimensional. Shading is apparent but thin, debris is minimal, and even in hot and heavy gunfights and car chases, everything just looks so mild. There are a lot of objects being rendered and maybe that's why the textures are so muted, but when Grand Theft Auto 4, 2008, and especially Assassin's Creed, 2007, look better than Watch_Dogs, one wonders why it was released at $65.
The driving, a major part of the game, is just absurd. Almost all of the cars are modeled the same way, poorly. Whether it's a 70's muscle car or Euro exotic, they all have back ends that float away on the corners and send you crashing left and right. I stuck to the same motorcycle throughout the game, wasting some beautiful artwork crafting dozens of useless cars. Collision detection was almost non-existent except for head-on impacts, and body damage on vehicles seemed almost random at times, with odd dents appearing on places where the car was not touched. Very poorly done.
The gameplay mirrors the graphics with a dull story that ignores the surrounding elements of advanced technology, privacy, illegal searches, totalitarianism, and even human trafficking, and settles on a simple but convoluted revenge story. The voice acting is decent but story elements are for naught and some are just stupid, like a main character dying in an odd setting for no reason, and a plot twist at the end that bears no consequences. I'm curious if the people that wrote the plot were even shown the game they were supposed to be following.
The game is divided into several smaller missions that almost play out exactly the same almost every time. The same objectives, the same enemies, it's just tedium after a while. The "hacking" is non-existent as checking people's phones or activating cameras is done with the Q key automatically. Breaking into a system uses the old water pipe puzzles from Flash games you could play for free on the Internet. PC Gamer reported in 2013 that the developers were utilizing real cybersecurity experts to consult for the game, and I really can't see where their tutelage was utilized. At least the gunfights were fun, which they better be considering you can carry an obscene amount of guns and explosives on your person. The worst of all this, however, was when the objectives were completed and I was given the option to kill all the enemies or leave the area. I walked away almost unchallenged, and I did this repeatedly on the hardest difficulty setting. After doing what I was supposed to do, I just ran from the area with maybe a short car chase or helicopter pursuit, but in the end I truly just left the scene unchallenged. There's a "bullet time" mode for when the going gets tough called "Focus". I made it through the entire game on hard without having to use it once.
Watch_Dogs offers no challenge, not as a game nor as an intellectual topic. I put 40 hours into this game feeling like I had wandered about a beautiful, yet flat, setting for no reason whatsoever. It saddens me because I know the painstaking detail that went into developing the game world, but in the end there's no reason to go back to it after finishing the story. I could go wrap up the massive amount of side quests and secondary objectives but why? If you played one you've experienced all of them. Watch_Dogs is a pointless trip down busy streets, and in the end I felt less of a hacker and more of a digital tourist.

While writing this review, I found it hard to write it without just saying "It's Penumbra: Overture, but without the hit-or-miss combat system and with more reasons to be frightened of the world." Because that's precisely what Penumbra: Black Plague is. It's the example of what a successor should be. It sticks to what worked in the original and removes what players didn't like. For example, Penumbra: Black Plague maintains the terrifying atmosphere and adventure game elements of Penumbra: Overture, but removes the (overly reviled) combat system. There was also some new additions, with one specific addition being a character that constantly messes with Philip's mind (and by connection, the player's mind).
Anyway, continuing without connecting it to Penumbra: Overture, Penumbra: Black Plague is just a excellent horror game, and the clear step toward Amnesia: The Dark Descent. The game starts off immediately, with only a brief cutscene explaining the prior events. From that point, Penumbra: Black Plague is practically a nonstop horror show of twists, turns, evil science, hallucinations, and an ancient evil. As cliched as I'm making it sound, the whole of the story is highly creative, with an increased atmosphere as well. It's just as terrifying as Penumbra: Overture, if not slightly more. The removal of combat helps, along with enemies that won't give up the chase and hallucinations that constantly make you question reality. As for the gameplay, the removal of combat makes Penumbra: Black Plague feel identical to the classic adventure games of the 1990s, such as Tex Murphy and Myst. It's a change that is highly welcome, as it becomes amplified with decent exploration, hidden collectibles, and great puzzles. It's a very tense and terrifying game with a great story and more than decent visuals.
Penumbra: Black Plague Gold Edition also gives you Penumbra: Requiem, a small expansion pack to Penumbra: Black Plague. The expansion is decent for the most part, trading the old-school adventure approach with gameplay more akin to Portal. The puzzles do mesh well with the gameplay, creating some intricate, multi-part puzzles.  However, the atmosphere is pretty much gone here and, while still occasionally eerie, it's not nearly as terrifying as the original two games. The story does try to tie up all of the loose ends, which it does reasonably well, thanks to two endings that are up for interpretation. It's a short stint, but worth looking into if you want to see Philip's story to the end (or ends).

The Bad:

Not your traditional MoH, but still a great game nonetheless. What sets Airborne apart from previous MoH games is that you are not a single agent sneaking behind enemy lines; instead, you are a paratrooper dropping into a large scale battle. The “one man army” feeling is nonetheless preserved, for better or worse. Fellow NPC paratroopers accompany you throughout each mission, though their combat effectiveness is questionable. They neither help nor hinder you very much in gameplay, though they at least provide cinematic backdrop for sense of a larger scale ground battle.
Perhaps the biggest difference between Airborne and past MoH games is its nonlinearity. At the beginning of each level you (as the title might suggest) jump out of an airplane and land on the battlefield. During this jump you can steer your character towards anywhere you want to land (to an extent). Upon landing you are tasked with completing a number of objectives which are spread throughout the map. You may carry out these objectives in any order you please before a new area is unlocked through which you will complete the finale to the mission. This is a far cry to previous games of the series and in some ways it is therefore lacking. There are much less cinematic moments in Airborne that the series has been known for (like running across a family having dinner in Frontline), and entire missions take place in relatively the same battleground. In this vein, the game is somewhat disappointing. However, this it makes up in replayability. The singleplayer campaign clocks in around 5 hours long on normal (which is a bit short), however the freedom to start missions (almost) wherever you want and complete objectives in any order you want allows for exta hours of gameplay in comparison to MoH’s generally more scripted level design. In addition, there are various unlockables and collectibles such as weapon upgrades (unlocked by killing enemies) and “skill drops” (marked places on the map where you can land).
If collectibles aren’t something you’re particularly into, the gameplay itself is a blast. Each weapon is punchy and satisfying to use. At the start of a each mission you can choose your own loadout, allowing for multiple playstyles. Want to land on a rooftop and pick off your enemies with a sniper rifle? You can do that. Want to run and gun through the streets with a thompson? You can do that too. To that end, the game allows you to choose your own pace. You can race through the mission if you please, completing objectives as quickly as possible, or you can simply take your time, picking off enemies one by one. In gameplay, Airborne truly does feel a lot like a MoH game, yet more open to different playstyles. One unique feature in Airborne is a Ravenshield-esque leaning system. Whilst aiming down the sights you can press the WASD keys to lean your character to and fro in different directions. Unfortunately, whilst doing this, you cannot move from where you are standing (unless you hold shift as I later found out). It is by no means a bad feature, but its implementation is strange and makes movement in the game awkward sometimes. The game would certainly benefit from the ability to toggle this feature but alas, there is none.
Airborne offers a new experience for MoH veterans, perhaps not one they may have hoped for, but a fun one nonetheless. Hardcore fans may have trouble accepting Airborne as a true MoH game, and maybe it isn’t, but it is by no means worth passing up.

Edit:  Since writing this review long ago, the devs have put a remarkable amount of work into improving the content and gameplay.  I now feel this review was too negative.  However the feedback provided may have helped them to improve the game.
I have played this game more than all the reviewers listed on the front store page combined at this writing.
I give this game a thumbs sideways -- theming and setting are good, gameplay is not.
The majority of gameplay consists of quickly paging past daily status updates of who hungry or thirsty, and assigning rations accordingly.   With only rare exceptions, it is a foregone conclusion how to assign rations, it usually doesn't feel like you are actually making a decision that you might have done differently to result in a different outcome.  So most of what you are doing in this game is a kind of mindless make-work to see the next random result.
You might have a person who is sick or wounded -- but usually you will not have a medikit available to do anything about it, and if you do you will almost certainly use it right away.  Again, it's almost as if there is no true decision to be made that will change the result.
Perhaps once a week you might send the healthiest out to explore and find supplies.  You only choose who to send, not where they go or what they focus on finding.  It's random where they go and what they bring back.  If you need a medikit or radio you can't focus on finding one, you just have to hope you get the random event result that makes it happen.  This can be frustrating when you have someone dying of starvation or disease as your explorer comes back with a discovered flashlight.
Also once a week you might have a decision of consequence -- for at least half of these you quickly figure out which choice is best and it no longer feels like a real decision in future attempts.
There is a fatigue system which can affect your characters, but there is nothing the player can do to avoid fatigue or mitigate it other than hoping for different random results.  So how interesting is it to read status reports about how fatigued each character is when you have no control over it whatsoever?   You can't assign them rest, and according to the devs exploring and rations  have no effect on it.
Ultimately, the game feels like a random result generator.
Some of the events and outcomes are interesting and amusing enough that you want to play more to see more of them.
And you do sometimes learn over time which decisions are better for certain events.
But for the most part the game doesn't feel like one where you have significant effect over the outcome.
Maybe that's actually realistic in an odd way, when you've got a family in a bomb shelter and starving neighbors, there is an awful lot that is out of your control.
It doesn't make for compelling gameplay however.
The devs promise to add a lot more event content in the future.
I hope as the game evolves the players feel like they have more of an impact on the outcome.
