Boil a kettle, nuke something in the microwave, maybe have a wee, of course if you’re Nicolas Cage then could hot wire a car, but that’s Hollywood for you.
But what if your future and that of your family depended on the decisions you made over one short pressure filled minute?
Busy Doing Nothing
Imagine a situation where you’re sitting at home.
Glancing around you can see all sorts of junk begging to be tidied away; maybe if you leave it long enough your wife and kids (who are around the house somewhere) might get around to doing it.
As you idly wonder who left a crate of bottled water in the corner of the living room a screeching noise shatters the silence.
You’re filled with dread as you realise that it’s the sound of the early warning system wailing outside.
We knew politicians would be the death of us and it seems that day has finally come.
The bombers must already be on their way, carrying their payloads of nuclear Armageddon,
The world is about to end...
Don’t Worry, Be Happy
... But don’t worry, you’ve prepared, unlike most of the other saps who are about to take a crash course in nuclear fission you had the foresight to install a nuclear bunker under your house!
You smile smugly to yourself, all that time playing fallout was well spent after all and in a few seconds you’ll be sitting safely in your cosy vault as the world above you turns into a radioactive wasteland.
Tick Tock
Moving for the shelter your eyes again drift to the crate of bottled water and an awful realisation washes all traces of smugness away.
You might have had the foresight to build a fallout shelter, but you never did get around to filling it with supplies did you?
Cursing your laziness you look desperately around the room, what items are you going to need in your shelter?
Food, Water, maybe the wife and kids to keep you company?
The alarms are still wailing outside, how much warning do they give you?
60 seconds?
Dashing towards the bottled water you trip over a can of soup, stumble and crash into a chair, if only your house wasn’t in such a mess!
Which room are the kids in anyway?
... tick... tock...
Pre-Apocalypse
This is the premise behind the first part “60 Seconds” a unique little survival title developed by Robot Gentleman Studios.
I say the first part, because “60 Seconds” is split into two very distinct yet connected games.
The first part of the game is a quick and frantic “treasure hunt” around your house.
You’ll control your character as he runs and stumbles through the various rooms searching for supplies to take down into the bunker.
You’re given a few short seconds to explore your surroundings before the sirens blare and the countdown begins, this time is vital to quickly scan around the layout of your house and look for the locations of useful items. (This changes every time you play!)
Supermarket Sweep
Before you’ve had chance to complete your stock take the countdown will begin, it’s time to start grabbing those supplies and dropping them down the hatch into your vault.
It’s not as simple as grabbing everything in one go either, you can only carry so much at a time, this leads to a frantic dash through the various rooms with armfuls of tinned food or bottled water.
This is 60 seconds of sandbox physics mayhem.
Furniture will go flying, objects will get in your way and you’ll be looking for one thing and get distracted by something else.
A radio might be useful to keep in touch with the outside world, maybe a good book would help stave off the boredom, there must be a first aid kit somewhere, etc.
These are the thoughts that will go through your head as you crash passed tables and fall over chairs in the rush.
It’s an ultra intense supermarket sweep and it’s as fun as it is frustrating!
Take Shelter
This is just the beginning, after diving into the bunker yourself, you’ll get to experience vault life and ration out those precious supplies to prolong your existence (and that of your family if you got around to saving them) for as long as possible.
Of course, if you got distracted by something shiny and didn’t make it into the shelter in time then you’ll be dead and need to start a new game, so let’s assume you did make it, because it’s in the shelter that the real fun starts.
Post-Apocalypse
The game changes pace in the shelter and becomes a short tongue in cheek survival adventure.
You’ll spend the remainder of the game looking at a static screen of yourself and any rescued family members sitting in the vault along with whatever supplies you managed to scavenge.
Each day this screen will be updated to reflect any changes in your little vault, including the ever dwindling supplies sitting on the shelf behind you.
Your food and water will almost certainly require rationing if you’re to last until help arrives, keep someone hungry or thirsty for too long though and they’ll get sick and die.
Other items you threw into the shelter could well prove useful too, you see, strange things happen when you’re cooped up in a vault.
A board game might be enough to stave off madness and a can of bug spray might be handy if you don’t want to share your bunker with some new scuttling friends.
Dear Diary
Like a post apocalyptic Adrian Mole, you keep a diary in the vault, but there’s more to write about than the dwindling water supplies.
Vault life is more eventful than you might think, random events happen every day and it’s these events that drive the narrative forward.
Each day you will go through food and water rationing, deciding who (if anyone) gets something to eat or drink that day.You’ll then read through the vault diary,
it’ll cover the health and moods of your surviving family members and report on any interesting events that occurred that day.
Kevin Costner or Mad Max?
Mutants, bandits, a nice game of scrabble, anything could happen as you wait out the apocalypse and most of these events will require you to make a decision which will impact the narrative as the days progress.
There’s a banging on the vault door, It could be a post apocalyptic mailman delivering some goodies, or it could just as likely be a gang of bandits fresh from the set of Mad Max, do you answer it? Well that’s up to you.
Valued in the Vault
The outcome of many of these events will depend on the salvaged items from the first part of the game.
If a radioactive bug bites a family member, you’d better hope you bought a first aid kit with you or the consequences might prove surprising.
Your first play through will give you an idea of the importance of the various items you ignored whilst foraging for cans of soup to bring down into the vault.
This game will quickly teach you that no matter how innocuous an item seems, it could well prove useful in the vault.
Keep Taking the Tablets
60 Seconds is a refreshing and quirky little game but It definitely feels like a tablet conversion.
It’s quick to play and immediately addictive which is great, unfortunately, like most mobile gaming ports, it can feel a little shallow and become repetitive pretty quickly.
Having said that, it’s priced to reflect this short term appeal and there is no denying the hours of entertainment you’ll get out of playing it.
60 seconds isn’t looking for a relationship, it’s looking for a fling.
Its fun whilst it lasts, you’re going to enjoy it but you probably won’t remember it in the morning.
It’s the one night stand of post apocalyptic gaming!

I can understand the positive reviews. There is the promise of a good game here, which promises to be a lot of fun with friends. It's just not that playable at the moment. The game should not have been released in its current state, since it is glitchy to the point of being impossible to play. Your game will crash, your voice chat will not work, you will be unable to connect, you won't be able to perform certain actions, etc. (At one point, I asked if it was still in beta, because it's absolutely unacceptable as a final version.) Even if those glitches were fixed, there are some serious design flaws. The stages are extremely dark and murky, which may create an atmosphere but makes it hard to see the tiny items that the survivors need. This decision might be okay if the game wasn't already so imbalanced. The survivors don't have enough options to get away from or defend themselves from the ghost, who has a one-hit kill. They also aren't given any indications about what keys open what doors, so it becomes an exercise in trying every key in every door. Worst of all, the ghost and the survivors are in the same voice chat, which makes it impossible to coordinate with the other survivors without the ghost hearing all your plans and knowing where you will be. So, in its current form, I cannot recommend it to others.

My honest opinion(V2 edited after more play time):
The game plays very well, reading a few reviews set me on edge about the required pay to proceed factor.
Needless to say I finally received a single free key which allowed me to open my first chest! I have learnt since then that Rare cards can sometimes be better used than epic cards! It all comes down to deck dynamics.
There are very varied skills which allow one to customize their decks to their own play style which I consider a big plus.
Now for a bit on the down side, after a few hours of playing without a single new card i decided to sponsor them $5, so yes it has already become a pay to proceed game for me. I received very very nice cards in those packs and as mentioned I dont even use the upper tier cards (I am top tier ranking number 1 as I type this) so if you do happen to get a hold of even some other card options you are not limited by encountering uber god cards that will insta kill your entire team on turn 1!
I did notice I only started finding keys after I purchased a $5 bundle, this may just be random luck but 0 keys for the first 4 hours and 4 keys for the following 2 hours post paying $5.
The normal keys gave me an epic card (Which from what Ive seen is the highest rarity that may be obtained. Thus even free to play has access to this tier.)
the game.
Final note / tip, using a unit that can add orbs to the board, allows for many multi matches giving you gold each time. Using one of these characters almost guarantees that I actually make a bit of gold per win, so spend 60 per match gain 72 back etc.
All in all I  am enjoying the game, it seems the $5 was a good investment for me, however if it turns out that one cannot get keys frequently without paying I would be very very disappointed with this game. All round Im enjoying it, I would recommended to the developers to give one or two low level boosters to give players a head start.
(V2) (Only read this if you need more insight and have been playing a bit) After a considerably longer period of play, it seems key drops are very rare, daily one can expect to accumulate a passive 1000 gold  +-500 from your castle and the rest from login/rank bonuses.
Only 1 castle purchased and used as your home base will accumulate gold for you per day. However normal quest progression that adds a daily +5 gold per day will accumulate daily on castles that are not set as your home base.
Questing generally always costs you gold and you dont make a profit on these, however defences and invasions (Invade button) if you win them frequently always more than double the cost of the match at higher levels. Thus running these can fund your normal questing indefinately.
Once one reaches the top tier ranking you can no longer lose that rank ( As mentioned in game ) This will give you  a considerable amount of free gold and feathers for stuff in the shop every new day.
For me persoanlly I use a mixture of cards that use all the types of energy, this allows for any match to work out well for me. For instance to have 3 cards that all use brown would mean that random matches of other colours would not go to good use and further if you needed to use your 3rd brown allies skill you would first need to fully charge brown allies number 1 and 2!
I like to use at least 1 ally with some sort of random spread damage, this allows for enemies with just 1 or 2 HP remaining to get sniped and the rest of the spread damage not to go to waste as it is allocated to other enemies.
I do hope this "tiny" review has helped you a bit. Kind regards :]

At least implement a system where you permanently lose a heart if you fail a trial. (Maybe even permanent throughout the game)
Anyways, the game is finished and these ideas are useless.
Extreme suggestions, but again...
they are just random suggestions.
Honestly these cons are trivial, as I believe the game is perfect on its own.
I'm also not a game developer or have any experience making game concepts in general.
So forget everything I just said.
Buy the game.
It's a good game.

Short version: I love the heck out of this game and think if you've made it as far as looking at reviews in your considerations to buy it, you should buy it.
Longer version: I love mysteries, and am always disappointed when you can easily peg the correct answer or who the bad guy is before you're remotely close to the end. This game does not have that problem in the slightest, and I often found myself going to trial with ZERO IDEA what I thought had actually happened. Danganronpa has an interesting story that unfolds in an amazing and hilarious way, successfully dancing the line between fantasy and realism in my opinion. It gives you the tools you need to do what the game asks you and never pulls a trick on you. It's fair, logical, and drives you down the rabbit hole of "what if" constantly. Love it, and the sequel!

A decent single player FPS that's a refreshing change from Call of Duty and other more linear titles. I particularly love the large maps and numerous ways to complete your objectives, which you can usually complete in any order you want. It is however really buggy, but despite this, I enjoyed the campaign a lot!
Pros:
- Alternative level design, lots of choice (e.g. freedom of movement and gameplay style, sniper or assault)
- Gunplay is reasonably satisfying
- Music is great, very John Williams
- Simple but effective weapon 'xp' system
- If you die, you parachute in again and pick up from your last completed objective; nice and fair
- Each mission can last a good half hour if not more, depending on your gameplay
- Fair health system. Regenerates, but split into four quarters, and you'll only regen the top incomplete quarter.
Cons:
- One of the buggiest games I've played. Things disappear, the physics are broken, grenades sometimes just stick to you, you can get stuck in walls, you bounce back from objects like small stones or ramps
- On some missions it's easy to get lost
- Friendly AI is poor
- Campaign is sadly too short
- Not enough guns
- Graphics aren't great
5/10, worth playing if on sale!

The key thing to understand about 60 Seconds is that it is a game driven by a random number generator. All events, big or small, are a dice roll in regards to good fortune or bad fortune. Sometimes, you'll survive for months...other times you'll be lucky to last a week.
The biggest problem with the game is that, regardless of what you do or what supplies you take with you, there's very little you can do to affect the overall outcome of the game. Yes, Bug Spray can be used to make a replacement Medkit, and the Boy Scout Handbook is overall the best item you can take with you, but their value hinges on you getting the events to use those items...preferably before you get one of the fundamentally unfair disaster events, which forces you to choose between three supplies and you can only save one - nevermind how many people are in your shelter at the time.
60 Seconds is a game that has its charm. The art style is excellent, the humor witty, the writing is engaging (Until it grows stale from repeat views). Even the RNG aspect of the game can be engaging, if one is drawn to chance-based gameplay.
It's just that same RNG can quickly take the charm out of the game. Beyond the Boy Scout Handbook *always* being the best solution to any problem, there's actually very little you can do to influence the course of the game. Indeed, you can have all the pieces needed for rescue available, only to have it snatched from your hands by one of the aforementioned disaster events.
TL;DR Version: The game is flawed, but not without its charm. Wait for a sale, and give it a go. Just don't expect to win.

This is pretty much Deer Simulator where you play through the life of a Deer. It sounds really interesting at first as it's a platforming where you play as a deer and fight for survival... however it is poorly executed and here's why.
Pros:
♦ Graphically Stunning (It has some pretty amazing graphics for what it is)
♦ Controls just work (Most peoples biggest complaint in a platformer/fighter is hitbox or jumpbox is off, but in this all controls seem to run smoothly when using a keyboard)
♦ Has nice number of Achievements (Not too many not too few)
♦ Has Trading Cards (It doesn't say it on the Store Page for some reason, but it has trading cards, which is why this will also be a con as it's misleading)
♦ Great intro Cinematic with Voice Over (It was one of the best cinematics for an intro, I've seen in a long time)
♦ Ingame sound/music is eargasmic (Really fitting and relaxing ingame sounds and music)
Cons:
♦ No full ingame options menu, only the Unity outside game one (This is annoying as the outside game Unity options menu is limited and normally buggy, from experience with most games that use it, it normally is buggy. Therefore, it's really annoying that you can't remap controls or fully change graphics or resolution options from within the game itself)
♦ No Tutorial to explain what is going on (This is weird as I just seemed to be running right the whole game not knowing what is going on, at some point it told me I had an inventory and I never even knew until like 15mins in. Also nowhere explained to me what I do with items)
♦ No where to fully explain controls (Only the unity input menu shows limited, not all of the, controls. This is annoying as I can't view the controls again within the game)
♦ The Storyline seems Misleading due to intro cinematic (I say this because after watching the intro cinematic, I thought I'd be playing to get revenge on Poachers, but in the time I played... nothing like that was happening)
♦ Doesn't state it has Steam Trading Cards on the Store Page (This is weird as some people factor that into the price of the game, therefore, it should state whether or not it has Cards)
♦ Weak Platformer (I say this as it was very, very weak platformer as all jumps could be made easily and nothing seemed challenging. The only time I died was when jumping from above to down below, where I couldn't see and landed on Spikes, I never missed a jump)
♦ Puzzles don't reset and are hard to grasp (There are pushible blocks everywhere and half the time they don't make sense at all and if you push them in the wrong way, they don't reset, so if they become stuck... then that puzzle seems uncompleteable)
♦ Many weird blocks that seem like they should be reachable, aren't (I found this weird as I saw many things that seemed as though they should be reachable but aren't. Even if they were reachable with powers, at the time I saw them I didn't have powers as the game had just started)
♦ Baby Deer that follow you are glitched (These are suppose to be where you respawn and you can tell em to sit, however if you tell them to follow you they will for an extent and then stop or not jump up to the ledge to continue following... really weird)
♦ In game it gives you a sprawl of text when talking to NPC's (I find this weird as the Intro Cinematic had epic voice overs.. I would have assumed all NPC's would have some kind of voice over as well)
♦ Days don't seem to be do or mean anything (Nowhere explains what days are for, if they are there for a speed run or something, it makes no sense as there are no highscores or anything)
♦ Dieing ruins the game for me (When you die it seems you become small again and lose all your progress, this concept is good for people wanting a hardcore no die game, but when it takes ages to grow your deer up and you have no idea what you are doing because the game doesn't explain it at all and then you die and become a baby deer again... it just feels as though it ruins the game as you have to basically grow your deer up from scratch again which is repetitive and takes ages)
Overall, I know I am nowhere near finished this game as I've only played 35minutes of it. However, in that time, I just seemed to be running right, killing things here and there and jumping through days with no real goal other than to fully grow my deer up in the most repetitive way possible. Therefore, I found this game to be very confusing, have little to no explanation of anything, puzzles seem to be there but it's hard to tell if it's just a random block or if it's a puzzle and overall seemingly very, very repetitive running right doing the same thing over and over again for the 35minutes I played. Hence, for a $15 game it is graphically pleasing, like very pleasing... however as it is very repetitive and not very well explained, I wouldn't recommend this game. It however, does have Steam Trading Cards and Achievements so if they outway repetitive unexplained gameplay, then by all means do buy this game.
PS: Will I finish the game? One day if I want 100% of Achievements I will, otherwise unless someone can explain what to do and explain that it's not repetitive to me, I probably won't.

How do I even start reviewing Supreme Commander: Forged Alliance? I think I'll start by telling about something that happened earlier today while I was playing a multiplayer match, an experience that quite well describes several of the qualities of this game. It was quite late into the game, about 30-40 min in and everyone had grown quite powerful. My Armored Command Unit, your most important unit that you use to build your whole army and whose death means you're out of the game in most cases, was under heavy attack from a swarm of Gunships and a Heavy Artillery Installation firing away from the other side of the map. I managed to bring my fighter planes in to take care of the enemy Gunships but the ACU was really low on health, another devastating artillery shell was incomming and if it hit I would be out of the game. The shell was going straight for it's target, I was going to lose. But I did not, straight above the ACU the shell hit an unfortunate fighter passing above and destroyed it. An artillery shell from the other side of the map hit a ridiculously small and fast moving fighter plane, I could hardly believe my eyes.
There is an unbelievable attention to detail in this game, every projectile is calculated individually which adds great tactical depth. Good micro and smart use of the lay of the land can have a significant effect on the outcome of a skirmish as shots might miss,  impact hills, rocks or units they where not intended for. This combined with the games truly epic scale brings one of the game's few minor drawbacks, seven years after release even the fastest computers have to slow down when literally thousands of futuristic aircraft clash.
The scale is another thing worth mentioning, the size of the maps range from quite small 5x5km maps to the enomous 81x81km battlefields that it take several minutes for even the fastest units to cross. So no matter if you want to wage war for hours against 7 opponents or if you're interested in intense StarCraft styled matches Forged Alliance will provide.
There is also a great variety of units, from small land scouts that take seconds to build to colossal experimental units that could take hours for a single engineer to construct but are able to singlehandly defeat huge armies. The balance between units is good, all four factions are viable and almost all units fill some role during some part of the game without any unit standing out as particularly overpowered which is quite impressive as there are hundreds of them.
To summarize, this game is a polished gem. The gameplay, both single- and multiplayer, is great, the design is amazing, the sands of time hardly seem to affect the game at all and the replay value is close to infinite. I'm a huge fan of real-time strategy games and I honestly believe that Supreme Commander: Forged Alliance is the apex of the genre.

Nice solitaire game similar to Faerie Solitaire.
If you're played Faerie Solitaire or Three Towers (as it's sometimes called) then you are familiar with the idea of this game. You have to clear all the cards in the layout by clicking on a card that is numbered one higher or one lower than the card in the deck. For instance, if your deck card is a 5 you can click on either a 4 or a 6. It's easy to get combos by going up and down the numbers, like 4-3-2-3-4-5-6-7-8-9-8-7-6, etc. depending on the layout and luck.
As the story goes on you gain 4 helpful allies with special abilites. There are also amulets you can purchase in the store with the gold you gain in the levels.
The story is kind of silly, but it's just a card game so who cares. Bad guy in black robe and holding a snake staff wants to conquer the world. You and your allies have to stop him. You travel the land of men, elves, dwarves, and mermaids (though you only get to see a merMAN, no maids unfortunately). In each place you have to restore the temple that has been desecrated by the bad guy, and restore the elemental crystal.
In addition to the card playing levels there are also occasional hidden object levels. That makes for a nice break from just cards, cards, cards all the time.
The gameplay is solid. It's fairly easy to get good combos even without using bonuses. Though, I was playing on casual difficulty, so i don't know if the gameplay is harder on the harder difficulty or if they just give you more things to accomplish to win.
Graphics are nice, with soft colors fitting a fantasy world.
Music is nice background music. It's sort of like classical music, just nice background music that does not intrude on your thinking.
There is also voice acting in this game. Each character has a voice. They also print the dialogue in boxes.
Length of playtime for me was 12 hours. However, I tend to keep replaying levels if I don't get a perfect or near perfect. So it could be less for someone who wants to just rush through the game.
tl;dr version:
Similar to Faerie Solitaire (Three Tower, etc)
Hidden Object Levels
Easy to get combos
2 difficulty selections
Full voiced audio
10+ hours of gameplay for first time through
It's Cheap!!!

You're the only hope of the world even if you're just an apprentice of a mightful magician. During your journey, you'll improve your skills and meet new allies!
If anything, this scenario is quite common in a fantasy game. So, I will not expand myself on it.
As it's a solitaire game, you're dealing with cards. The gameplay follows the suits rule: to get a card out of the board, you need to have a card of the value just above or just under in the pack. However, be aware that the game doesn't always let you win: I've stumbled upon levels where my board was full because the needed card to start appeared in the last ones of the pack.
When you understand that gameplay, you can look at the bonus. Each upgrade of your magic level will improve a skill: temporary money on a card, return 2/3 cards on the board, add cards to the pack, etc.. However, you can also buy (hence the money) amulets that will raise your experience, add cards to the pack at the beginning, show every possibility, etc.. Even amulets for characters will be available to enhance their skills.
Four allies will join you: the human can change the displayed card on your pack (with the upgrade of having a card that will always match one on the board), the elf can shoot a card down (two when improved), the dwarf will return cards on the board (3 if improved) and the mermaid will help to remove cards that are displayed.
Obstacles will also be present in levels : from flooded cards where you need to find the scoop to remove the water to the stoned ones needing a hammer to break the rock, you'll even be forced to sacrifice cards for those on fire.
After 10 levels, you'll go to another one, however, between these stages, you'll have a sort of hidden object scene: you will have to find 10 items (beyond objects, you know, those who are changing appearances, animals, parts of a bigger object, etc...).
In other words, The Chronicles of Emerland (the free-to-play game with the name Emerland is also set in the same universe, with the same gameplay by the way) is a classic solitaire game with some nice bonus. If the graphics are quite reminiscent of a heroic fantasy game, I largerly liked the soundtrack, very fitting and very nice.
Anyway, for 4 bucks, your wallet isn't robbed. If you like solitaire games, go for it, I've spent many hours in it because I wanted to have a lot of perfects - so if you're anything like me, you'll spend also hours to run after the evil wizard while asking yourself why they didn't make the dwarf more interesting than returning card....

I'm writing this now, still a little stressed and in the throws of an adrenaline high caused by my friends. First and foremost, play this game with a group of friends who are bad at the game along side you and can get better with you. Playing with randoms online will not help you learn in this HIGH stress environment and the current how-to guides online are only so helpful.
Here's what you get:
You're one of the survivors in the haunted hotel/asylum/hospital, and your on a scavenger hunt for keys to open the various locked doors on the map. As you creep around, you deal with randomly generated hauntings that do aweful things like make the dark screen darker, mysterious spooky noises play in your ear, or keyboard keys can even be disabled. All temporary.
And thats all before your friend takes control of one of three monsters and attempts to murder you before you get the silver key and escape.
The keys and tools are all hidden in obscure places, anything from in drawers of desks to the garbage can in the woods. But never somewhere completly random like the middle of the floor of a ball room. They are hidden well, but not unfairly at all. The rest of the challenge is finding what doors they unlock. Eventually leading out.
The Three Monsters:
As of now there are only three creatures to threaten you and they all garner a different approach to avoid. Here's the long/short;
Lurker sets traps to try to pinpoint your location and materializes in a blink for a few seconds at a time. You pretty much just run from him like an old monster movie. Bracing doors and sobbing until he's gone.
The phantom is 'blind' and only sees players who make a lot of noise. People complain about him being Overpowered but  thats mostly because they run around and get slapped instantly. You need to be sneaking when this ghoul roams the halls.
Then there's mary. She randomly teleports around the map, and if she fills up her spooky-meter she frenzies and can run at you rather than her usual trundle. Think the Witch from Left 4 Dead, popping and locking through the dining room looking for victims.
The Good:
-Very different kind of game play. If you have a group of friends you dont mind never wanting to talk to again, team up and go scavenger hunting.
-This is a HORROR game, not an FPS. When you see the monster you run. There are no guns, just a flashlight. This might sound like a negative, but it really helps amp up the FEAR
-Atmosphere. This might be a little generic, but they really do try to use your less obvious senses to pick up on the creepy factor. You get trained to listen for traps and musical queues, little details, that when you finally do see something. It hits hard and helps you scare.
The Bad
-Crashes. There seems to be a lot of crashes between my friends and I. Hardware capability dont seem to be the issue, and if someone drops midgame, they wont be able to get back in. They'll only be able to spectate.
-Genuine stress level. It might not be a problem to everyone, but I get genuinly stressed out. Legs tight. Hands sweating. Worrying about ever little step. This is why you play with friends. Let the strange monster creeping on you be your pal. Not some mook on teh interwebs.
Final Verdict:
Love it. Go in on a 4 pack with your friends. Maybe hope it winds up on a sale. Hopefully the crashes get patched out and new features like new monsters and  different playable characters get added. But this is not a game I can compare to any other experience very well.
If players could jump back in if they were kicked and the crashes were resolved I would say full price is worth it. As it stands now, $19.99 is a little steep for what feels like early access material. However I still love the experience. And few things are as satisfying as hearing your friends fill their diapers over skype as you pop out around the corner.

This game is still early access, so this review is subject to change/additions
Damned is basically what it says on the Tin. A survival horror game for 5 players (Maximum) where four play scavenger hunt Point A to point D item findings, and one player plays one of (Currently 3) monsters to murder your friends. Fun for everyone, especially if you have friends who enjoy screaming very loudly at your music-cue arrival. Lets get down to it.
Gamplay involves item-based problem solving. Simple stuff. Find key, key goes to Locker, locker goes to safe, safe goes to kitchen, kitchen goes to crowbar, crowbar goes to wood over door, escape through door. Not always that simple, but basically always that formula. You have to find keys, unlock doors and safes, and escape out of the final door while eluding the monster player. Not always so easy.
The Monster player has 3 monsters to choose from (At the time of this review) being Lurker, Phantom, and Mary. Lurker is your tall and gruesome skinless hulkbeast who spends a majority of the game in "Phase mode" which is where the player will move around quickly, phasing through doors (Cause you cant see them) and players (Who you also cant see) and setting traps. Since you can't see players, you need to use the traps to figure out their locations. Once they set one off, and it lets you phase in, you pop in and slice them to ribbons.
The phantom is like a satanic stevie wonder. A floating torso who is completely blind to anyone unless they make a lot of sound. This means running, and clicking your flashlight. And getting too close. Make too much noise, and you'll show up in his vision as a white life-form that he can go maul. It's a fairly simple system, and I've nearly had it gotten around when I played him.
Mary is your near-typical japanese-horror esque girl. Similar in design to popular ones like the Ring, or grudge. For a majority of the game she moves slower than a 95 year old man walking through hot tar. She also randomly teleports as a way to balance and make your life easier. You might teleport in the same room as the players, might not. You can also manually teleport, but we'll get to that in a second.
Mary has the ability to enter a /frenzy/ mode when her meter (Which you dont see) fills. Stare at the players enough, and you can activate frenzy mode. a 10-15 second burst of quadrupled speed in which she screams violently, goes all scary faced and comes bullrushing you. You can also exchange a bit of the frenzy meter for another teleport, if you dont wanna wait for the freebie random one.
There are about 12+ stages right now, with the most recent (At the time of this review) being a forest/camping area. The game does have some flaws, like optimization issues, data leaks, and minor coding bugs. Updates are also somewhat slow, but when they come around they are very nice. Running on my toaster I get about 25-30 frames in a map. Apparently a high-end gets about the same, due to optimization issues. It happens.
I can't really rate it with a number right now, but I am giving it a yes. It's a nice game, for a beta.

Note: I am an early adopter and played the alpha also and that was an exe file oustide of Steam, so my playtime shown here isnt accurate.
Deer God to me is a pretty game lacking interesting gameplay. Due to the pretty pixel graphics I adopted quite early a couple of years ago and I played the alpha. Now that I finally found the time to play the finished product I am quite surprised how little has changed since the alpha, but I will expand on that in a second.
Playing the alpha (or was it a beta? I cant remember) was playing a prototype where you are shown certain elements of a game to come, so I had nothing to complain about but was just curious of where the game would be heading gameplay wise, as this was the most lacking aspect in the alpha. Visuals were pretty already then. As mentioned, this was fine to me and I trusted in the game developers having much more planned for the game.
Now that I see it wasn't so, I can only wonder how much thought and planning went in the gameplay mechanics. There are basic ideas, yes. But the implementation of them into something compelling and fun to play hasn't happened. Most of the time I am running around through random levels without a clear goal and it's simply put not interesting.
When designing a game the core of the question of what will define the game and how you play it is the gameplay mechanics. What do you actually do in this game? What is my interaction within the game? On a moment to moment basis and on a grander scale of things. What makes it fun to play?
Shigeru Miyamoto of Nintendo always is quoted to be telling his designers when they approach him with a new idea for a game Yes but how does it play? What am I doing as the player and is it fun? He says, ideas for a story of graphic style don't matter first, you need to build on solid gameplay mechanics and if you have those you can use any idea or graphic style. If the gameplay is boring, story and graphics wont save that much and otherwise too, good gameplay maybe doesnt even need a good or deep story (see Super Mario series) or elaborate graphics to be perfectly enjoyable. With Deer God I feel the former happened, a game build more on a pixel style and ideas than  properly developed mechanics.
For instance the game orients its worlds on traditional platforming, you are constantly jumping up and down on platforms but there seems little reward in exploring areas off the main trail (which is going further right in general). An example would be there is a small gap in the wall in the ceiling above the main trail. I manage to jump into it and it leads me on top of the ceiling rocks, but when exploring them there is nothing there. And these kind of things are everywhere. It feel like they were meant to make the world seem big and explorable but with platforming as a base and lack of rewards it doesnt fit for me and I see no point in it. So the game worlds feels rather random than immersive as maybe intended with this design choice.
What doesn't help with the feeling of randomness is the quick change of scenery or worlds. While not a critique on the style of the worlds itself, the fact that they change so often and then are repeated plus the lack of significant level design differences between the worlds makes the changes much less impactfull than they could and should be.
Another aspect too undifferentiated are the enemies. There are plenty but the way the encounters with them are set up they feel too similar. Battling them usually boils down to the same experience. Also it is too easy to avoid them and just double jump over them, so they don't display a threat.
Also I encounter seriuous bugs, for example a rock wall you need to overcome jumping from the back of a huge turtle. The turtle itself walks in the direction the player is facing and sits on a platform from which it can fall off to one side and there is no way to get the turtle back up other than a checkpoint reset. When you reset to the previous checkpoint the turtle isnt sometimes not there at all, or it walks off the platform while you are respawning despite you facing the other direction that it walks.
Apart from this, the solution executed in this part of the game is also a good example to show how the game doesn't lead the player to naturally come to understand what you need to do. There isnt another turtle situation prior with a simpler and fail-save puzzle to understand the newly introduced turtle as a gameplay element in itself before moving on to use this gameplay in a more challenging situation. Here I have to cite Nintendo again and the gameplay masterclass that games like the Super Mario Galaxy series or Super Mario 3D World represent. In these games a gameplay mechnic is first introduced in a simple and obvious situation so that it is clear what it does. Then later you get a second situation where you need to apply the mechanic in a more standard situation. After that the culmination is a third part in which you have a more challenging setup that might require you to improvise or use the mechanic in a slightly different way. Usually these three steps are done in one level  and they assure the player understands the mechanics without much need for explaining but also understands how the mechanics progress or can be advanced. Which may be required to do in future levels but there the player will already understand what to do.
Closing with the positive aspects, the game does look really nice with beautiful pixel art landscapes and front and background grafics creating a welcome depth effect. The world and it's inhabitants, despite being naturally low poly pixels, looks all coherent and beautiful as a whole. Also the music felt fitting and unobstrusive to me.
So in conclusion I would like to encourage the developers to revisit the gameplay mechanics and level structure concepts and invest more time here. Real horror is a connection with the audience. It taps into our insecurities, plays on our weaknesses. Real horror is scary because, simply put, it feels real.
This game didn't feel that way.
Don't misunderstand; I enjoyed it. There's a lot to love about the title, the least of which is the well-integrated physics systems and the "realistic" puzzles. Don't expect doors to start opening just because you found a note somewhere. Not that kind of game, which is a relief.
But for all that I felt it was more "sci-fi romp" (romp... why do critics and reviewers always use that word?) than "survival horror." At no point during the game did I actually feel that my life was in danger. The conditions are right. The execution is close to right. So what's lacking here?
I think, in the end, the baddies just aren't imposing enough. They're slow, and forgiving to the point that if you run thirty feet away and turn a corner, they give up on you. That and they run simple patrols. Makes this feel more like a stealth mission than a life-threatening escape scenario.
But do play it, because (before the weird end sequence), the writing is just too phenomenal to miss out on. Seriously. It's weird too see a game where the writing outshines everything else for once. It's like they took someone working on a bestseller and said "hey, forget the book. Come write journal entries for our game." Pretty astounding, really.
3.8/5 for me.

60 Seconds! is a combination of an action game and a text-based survival game. You play as Ted, the air raid siren has just sounded and you have 60 seconds to grab supplies and family members and get down to your fallout shelter before the bombs hit. Once in your shelter you begin a fight for survival as you ration food, try to make contact with help and venture out into the radioactive wastes.
+Great art style, really feels like it's in the 1950's
+The 60 seconds portion of the game is rather unique
+Each run has a different story but it's always interesting
+Early on in your run it's a real struggle to survive and the game provides you with a good challenge
+As well as food and water you have a number of other resources to manage which can be used in certain situations
+Some situations have rather amusing outcomes while others have outcomes which threaten the survival of the family
+The appearance of the family members changes as the longer they stay in the bunker and appearances also change when they become ill or similar
+Most situations can be approached in different ways, for example if there's a dark, unexplored room you can use a flashlight to see what's in there or use your gun to scare off possible hostiles
+If, like me, you aren't so keen on the 60 seconds part you can start from the bunker and you'll be given a random selection of resources and family members making it feel like a rogue-like
+The writing, until it gets repetitive, is great
+Great humour
+Great tutorial
-The controls for the 60 seconds in the house aren't great, they're very insensitive and sometimes the control for picking up an item doesn't work even when you're standing next to it which is very frustrating
-After around Day 60 it just becomes a case of clicking through the text to get to the next day without doing anything
-Sometimes the game presents you with situations you can't actually do due to you not having the right item which is also quite frustrating
-The writing gets repetitive quite quickly, in my first run I got to Day 78 (before my save got corrupted) and I saw some situations four or five times
Verdict:
Worth Purchasing (7.5/10)
An interesting idea combined with great text-based survival with a great art style, interesting stories, good humour and good writing.

is exactly what the title suggests, a solitaire game. The most basic of games and one of the few that has come already installed on PCs for years is now given an updated look with updated features. There are many games like this on the market, taking a simple card game and adding bells and whistles to keep the interest of the player and attract new ones. However, in my opinion this game got it right and created something that’s more than just a game of solitaire.
One aspect that
has going for it is that it has a story. Your character is an apprentice under an old gray bearded wizard and things are going fine until an evil sorcerer attacks and makes threats against the world. It’s up to you to travel to the four kingdoms to save the elemental stones and gain the power you will need to defeat the forces of darkness. The kingdoms are basic, you have Humans, Elves, Dwarves and Mermaids, but you also get a companion from each kingdom creating a sort of party like in a role playing game. Together you and your team travel the land and try to save the world. It’s a pretty simple fantasy story but enough to keep a player entertained.
If you’ve played regular solitaire then you should have all you need to get into this game. The board has cards laid out randomly and you have a draw pile, your goal is to stack cards in order from your drawn card to create combos and score points. If you’ve played modern day solitaire games then you can expect to see some added features to spice things up. Roadblocks, a common one, come in the form of ice, vines, bricks, etc. Each one requires you to unlock the roadblock by finding an item like a sword hidden under another pile of cards. This adds more of a challenge, especially in later levels, as you have to plan your moves precisely to continue on and sometimes may not get the draws you need to even get past the roadblocks. Each level has ten stages to it and in between each level are small hidden object scenes, which I enjoyed.
I mentioned earlier that the game gives you four companions, each character helps in a different way, the archer for example can shoot down one card off the field which is useful if you have a lingering card and want to get a perfect rating. You can also power up your companions by buying certain amulets! There is one amulet for each party member and then other amulets to add bonuses to the game such as getting more gold or experience or even seeing every possible move on the board. The last aspect is leveling up, when you do this new perks are added that can pop up randomly on cards that are on the board and each perk has two levels to it so instead of being able to get two extra cards you can then get three.
To top off this fun game are some great visuals. The cards are all beautiful though I would have liked an option to change the design of the deck. The scenery is wonderful and fits the mystical theme of the game. Bright colors along with lovely character designs help round out the visual aspects of the game. The music is also great, if you play the game long enough you’ll notice that the tracks tend to repeat quite often, I think there are maybe three or four unique ones. I didn’t mind this but the music was so lovely and soothing I wouldn’t have minded more. The game is also fully voice acted so every time a character speaks you will also hear them. The acting is not the best but it’s passable.
+ The game is cheap.
+ Offers a good amount of gameplay for the price.
+ Overall presentation looks good.
+ I love fantasy so this was a personal plus for me.
+ The game has two different difficulties.
+ It has trading cards and achievements.
- Levels can get repetitive, so it’s best if played in short bursts.
- There is a bug in the game, if you’re playing a level and want to exit the game, the game counts that stage as a failure for some reason. This has been addressed on the Steam forums but the developer sadly cannot fix the issue.
I personally loved this game and would find it perfect except for the bug. I’ve played quite a few solitaire games but this one is definitely a favorite for me. I loved the fantasy theme and I enjoyed having party members with different helpful skills. The game can be a little challenging even for solitaire veterans but the game gives you plenty of perks and ways to power up to help level the playing field. Plus, all of the achievements are relatively easy to gain if you simply just play through the game. If you want to play alone with yourself I recommend this title, as a great card game of course.

this is a great solitaire with nice graphics and good music, there's even voiceovers in the cutscenes. the gameplay is nothing new, there's a store where you can buy amulets and wildcards that make your life easier, but there are a few unique things, like wildcards not only covering numbers and there's even a joker, but you can only have 6 of them at a time. you'll meet companions with special abilities that are really useful and you also gain levels, which unlock random bonuses while playing, like bonus xp, more gold, etc. there are also hidden object scenes, which I'm not a fan of, but they included both hint and skip buttons, so I can't complain.
there are two things you have to take into consideration before buying and while playing, and they basically mean that the 'I'll just play a few hands before bed' approach won't necessarily work, which is unfortunate for a game like this. first of all, the 24 stages each have 10 levels, but you can only replay individual levels before moving on to the next, otherwise you have to replay the entire stage and you can't restart them either until you're finished with one. if you're not going for perfect levels, it's not really an issue though.
the other thing is related to this: make sure to only quit during hidden object scenes or right at the beginning of a level, before you click on anything, otherwise you're risking failing the level because the game marks the incomplete level as failed. I always made sure to perfect a level before moving on, just so I can safely quit at the beginning of the next one, which sometimes meant spending more time than I wanted with the game.
to be honest, after reading a few reviews and the forums, I was worried that the game would be really frustrating, but once again, 'knowing is half the battle' and keeping the stuff above in mind and setting aside a bit of extra time, just in case, did the trick and I had a great time.

*OK, I'm changing my review to not recommend this game because of the level replay issue everyone else mentioned.  At first, I didn't know what they were talking about because it hadn't happened to me.  Now, it has, and I'm so annoyed I'm abandoning this game entirely. You can't replay a hand unless you're on the stats page at the end of that hand.  Once you move on from there, you have to replay all of the 10 hands in a level if you wan to replay only one of them.  That's horses**t.  It's far too difficult to complete a hand the first time to then force me to do them all again.  The game warns you you'll lose your progress on the level if you quit the game mid-way, but that's not an accurate warning.  What it should warn you about is that it will record a loss for you, and you'll have to replay the entire level to fix that one hand.  The thing is, if you quit the game on, say, Hand #5, and it records a loss, you can't simply start over at Hand #1.  You have to complete the remaining 5 hands until you've complated the level then you can replay the entire level to fix Hand #5.  Screw that, and this game.
On another note, it's glitchy as hell.  I had a hard time even getting it to run.  At one point, it was in windowed mode, or what they consider fullscreen mode, and the game prevented my mouse from moving anywhere beyond its borders, even when it wasn't the active window, until I went to Process Explorer, and killed it.  I didn't say anything about the technical issues originally because I thought it might just be me, or my computer, but now I'm convinced its the game itself.  Nothing in this game works as you would expect it to.
Just to further complain about this game because it deserves it: why is the title written "The chronicles of Emerland. Solitaire."  Shouldn't "chronicles" be capitalized?  Why is the word Solitaire its own sentence?  This should be a red flag as to the level of care, and attention that went into this game as a whole.

Danganronpa: Trigger Happy Havoc - Rating 8/10
Danganronpa is a series that takes a lot to get into. Going into this game you are not told a lot of things about how gameplay works or progression of these games at all. So I wanted to review that in a style that will help the every day buyer decide if they would like this game.
Gameplay - 5/10
This is a bit better than your standard Visual Novel for the actual conversation points. There are character sprites shown with text in a box and a set number of pre-recorded lines for each character.  It is not very riviting or visually interesting and as such looses a lot in this field.
However for the trials, this game really shines! Turning 2D into three and making the idea of litterally shooting down someone's arguement come to life. I think that the minigames (Bullet Time Battle, Hangmans Gambit and Rythm Attack) are all fun and unique in their own way. They make the trials refreshing and fun to play. While they can be tedious I think the trials are worth the investigation.
Story - 9/10
This is a unpopular opinion but I think the story in Danganronpa: THH is way better than in DR2. It's not the most amazing thriller on it's background plot. But it does something amazing in... it let's YOU decide the story as you go in a way. You are only given hints as to what happened outside of the school you are trapped in for all of the game. Never once do they tell you for sure what happened and it's not frustrating because you have much more to think about. Like your friends all dying... Speaking of which.
The trials are predictable. The keen player will be able to spot who the killer is easily by text presenting in the investigations. However... The characters intreactions still make it worth the time you spend investigating them. Plus there are some loops thrown in here and there that will mislead you.
The place where the story is actually important and worth talking about is the final trial which I will not spoil. But when the story you've been waiting to hear finally gets revealed and things start falling into place. It is very much worth it. It makes you feel a sense of uneasy dread but also a sense of... Satisfaction from everything snapping into place so easily.
Art Style - 4/10
The art style is good on it's sprites but i'll be honest with you. I do not like the way the school looks. I've never liked the art style for Danganronpa's enviroments and I don't quite understand why.  Maybe I am just used to higher budget games or something but the enviroments make me annoyed more than anything. The second game somewhat fixes this and the anime makes it much better.
The sprites are good but more variation in some characters would've helped make them feel more alive before they died.
Besides that the art style is pretty cut and dry. Not much to say..

Recommending this with a big BUT...
Pac-Man Championship Edition DX + is everything the reviewers said it would be. It is the most perfect traditional style Pac-Man game to date. Words can't describe how satisfying the experience of playing this game is.
But here's where the BUT comes in...
I paid $9.99 to get this game complete via pre-order. It came with a bunch extra simple modifications to the game in the form of mazes, skins and extra background music. Pretty fair price for a complete package. However, once the game launched, all those extra options got taken out of the game and sliced up into various unnecessary DLC packs. Let me just say this is a complete insult to Pac-Man fans everywhere! There was no reason (except for greed) to separate these features out of the game when it launched. Let's take a closer look at this crock of sh... I mean smelly chocolate pudding.
For $9.99 I got the game plus all of the below. Now if you plunk down your $.9.99, you'll get the base game and have to pay extra for each of the items listed. I'll put the price beside every piece, so you can see how it adds up. For heaven's sake, these are just modifications to the game; maze configurations, skins, and Background music:
$1.99 Mountain Course
$1.99 Big Eater Course
$1.99 Championship III and Highway II Courses
$1.99 Dig Dug Skin
$1.99 Rally X Skin
$1.99 Pac Is Back Skin
$.99 Pac Steps Music
$.99 Reentrance Music
Buying these individually is insane and I'm sure no one will do that. But Namco thinks its doing you a favor by giving you an "All You Can Eat" pack after the fact for $14.99! That's the base game and every item listed above. But still, that's 50% more than what I paid for the game with all its content! Billy Mitchell would be rolling around in his grave (if he wasn't still alive).
All I can say is, for the love of Pete, DO NOT BUY THIS GAME until comes on sale! And I'm saying wait until it's no more than $5, AND includes the game with all it's DLC packs. Namco needs to get the message that gamers are sick and tired of being nickel and dimed. I am glad I preordered it, and that I'm enjoying the experience, but I'm really angry that so many companies think that this kind of BS is acceptable.
What's next, a bow attached to Pac-Man for another $1.99 so I can play as the Ms's?

For a while I thought I was just playing this game wrong. It turns out it's just a poorly designed game. The main problem is the AI. It's extremely dumb. One of the major things that can cause a game over is starvation. When the AI get hungry, they tend to gather near the dining hall, even if there's no food there, when they should be tending to the hydroponics. They also  sometimes walk forever to get from place to place, and the starvation timer is so short that they might starve before they get there. This makes large bases simply not possible. Also, the airlocks only let 1 person in or out at a time, so a lot of productivity losses (and starvations) are caused by trading too much cargo at once.
It's a decent concept, but the implementation is sloppy, and the AI is inadequate once you get to a medium to large size base. There's not much sense of fulfillment to be had either. In the end, it's a rather painful experience.

Let it be known that my total number of hours in Steam for this game is misleading. I've played Supcom/Forged alliance since 2008 off and on and spent most of my time on the 1v1 ladder. This review which reflect that time and SupCom's merits as a competitive RTS. I won't touch on campaign (Good but not great) nor the story (just there to get you to the next mission) in any great detail.
Supreme Commander is a game whose origins can be drawn to Total Annihilation and it from the Command and Conquer school of thinking more than the Blizzard school. Units exist outside of the movement speed/attack rate/damage mold that has served those games so well over the years. Total Annihilation's contributions to the genre were twofold: Its scale both in map and unit sizes was unparalleled. Its units also existed in three dimensions. Aircraft didn't hover, rather they made bombing runs, or engaged in dogfights, or VtoL craft swayed back and forth as they unleashed their payload. Long range artillery countered any turtle tactics forcing them out of the comfort zone and the sound design supported the entire package. I dare say that none of those who fell in love to TA have forgotten the first time they heard a Big Bertha fire.
Supreme Commander is the natural evolution of that game but in a bigger and more user friendly package. All of the aforementioned features still exist. Units have weight as they turn and massive units don't feel like smaller ones except they are scaled to be larger. If you have an experimental (a very expensive endgame unit) plan its trajectory carefully because you won't be turning on a dime to get it out of danger.
The in Forged Alliance is simple, unobtrusive, and effective. The hotkey system leaves a lot of be desired and is quite clumsy but there are mods to fix that into something more elegant if that is you inclination. Individual buildings can be upgraded as can your ACU, which acts as the King and Queen in chess melded into one units. Absurdly powerful but also the victory condition.
Perhaps SupCom's greatest innovation is its strategic zoom. One can use to to go from looking at the rivets in a tank to a satellite image of the entire map in a flick of the mousewheel. It cannot be understated the effect this has on gameplay. You can see more, plan more, and execute more complex strategies because of this feature alone.
On release this game was far too demanding for most computers and limited its install base. Now I would say almost any decent machine can run in without much issue. It is worth noting that the initial multiplayer client, GPGnet, was discontinued several years ago. What remains are steam's matchmaking infrastructure, which is about as bare-bones as it gets, and the community built client Forged Alliance Forever ( which can be found here:
). I strongly recommend FAF as it is still undergoing balance patches, the client is still be developed, and the greater portion of the game's user base resides there.
This was a long and rambling review that is mostly clouded by nostalgia and a love for what I believe is the most strategic RTS on the market.
TLDR: Recommended

A nice atmospheric platforming puzzle game with just enough to keep you going through the game to it's natural ending.  It's roughly a 1.5~2.5 hour run-time for one clear but requires at least 1 more new playthrough for an achievement completion.  The narrative is jumbled at times with some very random quests from characters but the new abilities and items keep things interesting.  There are quite a few boss fights and enemies in the game as well which take some cunning to win over. Once you figure out the rules of the game and that you can basically speed up the run by running past most enemies makes the clear bearable.
Now for the many downsides to this game is how they handled game overs, bugs resulting from using certain combinations of items/skills at certain times, unclear puzzle mechanics that require some tedious trial and error rather than intuition and extremely dull repetitive running sections as you move to the next progression point (quest, puzzle or location).
Overall the game gets a passable recommendation from me if you are able to get the game at a discount or free during a promotional event because it's a solid enough crowd-sourced indie game.  Yet it's missing a few key elements that push the game into a must play.

In Orbt XL you control a planet-sized object, whether it be our lovely planet Earth or the Death Star, orbiting a black hole as other asteroids and objects are hopelessly sucked in. You are gradually pulled in, but with the tap of the mouse, you can bump planet Earth slightly away from the black hole in order to avoid being sucked in entirely or to avoid colliding with other objects. You gain points over time and earn extra points by skimming other objects. The closer you are to the black hole, the faster points are accrued.
The graphics are nice. The music is soothing. The Gameplay is simple.
The nice thing about this game is that it can be picked up for however long as you desire. A single round, from start until finish, can last anywhere from several seconds to a minute or two if you're pro. I won't say how long I typically last because that would be embarrasing. Ok, I typically last about 30-40 seconds assuming I didn't die within the first 10 seconds. But oh boy do I get a rush bringing the Death Star and it's occupants as close to a black hole as I can without dooming everyone. The urge to beat my own time (let's not fool ourselves and think we can actually enter into the learderboards) is addicting and it's hard to say "no" to just one more round.
To Summarize, this game is like an endless tasty bag of potato chips. You can eat however many you want, but, really, who can eat just one.

This game is not bad. I had fun playing through the game, so why be a negative nancy?
Well the last stage ruins it all. It's riddled with bad decisions and 'bugs' (hard to tell which one it is) kind of like a pr0stitute...
Firstly, you cannot replay levels within the stage at your leisure. The only time you can replay a level is straight after or after completing the stage, in which you have to start back at the first level and go through one by one. This isn't too bad throughout the game as the only thing you really need is a perfect stage (if you're a completionist like me), which means completing at least half of the levels with a perfect score. You can easily do this by just replaying any levels straight after if you do not have a perfect score.
This is a minor inconvenience... until the last stage. The last stage, you have to beat a big stone by collecting gems hidden behind cards. You have to collect 60 gems in 10 levels and obviously it's not 6 per level, as a normal, levelled game would be. There are a varying number of gems on each level and it doesn't state how many you have to collect, so it's near impossible to know whether or not you should replay the level unless you perfect it (It's hard to perfect every level of a stage, especially the last stage).
This isn't even the worst part though. Replaying a stage at the end until you get perfect on every level isn't a massive challenge? Just a bit laborious... Well, there is a bug/feature where in after you play the level, any replays wield no more gems... Therefore, unless you collect all the gems on the first playthrough of the level (which you don't actuall know how many are on each level), you can't get any more gems and therefore if you've missed one, you have to go through all 10 levels to complete the stage, fail and then start again. Basically, if you don't perfect (or very near perfect if you're lucky) every level of the last stage, without fail and with incredible luck, grabbing all the gems, you cannot complete it... oh and also you can't quit levels half way through (otherwise you get a fail) so therefore you have to play the stage all the way through in one go otherwise you 'fail' and due to the nature of the last stage, that means failing the whole stage...
This seems ridiculously complicated for a 'casual game' and one that is fairly relaxing and simple throughout.
This is supposed to be a relaxing experience and the last stage turned into something that frustrated me so much, I had to go on super meat boy and dark souls to relax me. I hope that big boss stone gets kicked by a kid into an old persons window or something where it feels forever guilty to the point where it never shows it's fiery self again...

Danganronpa: Trigger Happy Havoc - Rating 8/10
Danganronpa is a series that takes a lot to get into. Going into this game you are not told a lot of things about how gameplay works or progression of these games at all. So I wanted to review that in a style that will help the every day buyer decide if they would like this game.
Gameplay - 5/10
This is a bit better than your standard Visual Novel for the actual conversation points. There are character sprites shown with text in a box and a set number of pre-recorded lines for each character.  It is not very riviting or visually interesting and as such looses a lot in this field.
However for the trials, this game really shines! Turning 2D into three and making the idea of litterally shooting down someone's arguement come to life. I think that the minigames (Bullet Time Battle, Hangmans Gambit and Rythm Attack) are all fun and unique in their own way. They make the trials refreshing and fun to play. While they can be tedious I think the trials are worth the investigation.
Story - 9/10
This is a unpopular opinion but I think the story in Danganronpa: THH is way better than in DR2. It's not the most amazing thriller on it's background plot. But it does something amazing in... it let's YOU decide the story as you go in a way. You are only given hints as to what happened outside of the school you are trapped in for all of the game. Never once do they tell you for sure what happened and it's not frustrating because you have much more to think about. Like your friends all dying... Speaking of which.
The trials are predictable. The keen player will be able to spot who the killer is easily by text presenting in the investigations. However... The characters intreactions still make it worth the time you spend investigating them. Plus there are some loops thrown in here and there that will mislead you.
The place where the story is actually important and worth talking about is the final trial which I will not spoil. But when the story you've been waiting to hear finally gets revealed and things start falling into place. It is very much worth it. It makes you feel a sense of uneasy dread but also a sense of... Satisfaction from everything snapping into place so easily.
Art Style - 4/10
The art style is good on it's sprites but i'll be honest with you. I do not like the way the school looks. I've never liked the art style for Danganronpa's enviroments and I don't quite understand why.  Maybe I am just used to higher budget games or something but the enviroments make me annoyed more than anything. The second game somewhat fixes this and the anime makes it much better.
The sprites are good but more variation in some characters would've helped make them feel more alive before they died.
Besides that the art style is pretty cut and dry. Not much to say..

What a ride...I'm a sucker for detective games, and this one is a strange yet enaging detective game. A mix of Ace Attorney with investigating cases, and Persona with interacting with the students. You and 14 other students are trapped in Hope's Peak Academy with a sadistic teddy bear named Monokuma being the warden of the school. The students either have two choices: live together in the school for the rest of their lives, or escape by murdering another student and getting away with it. This game is weird, but it's still enjoyable and has a really good story to it with every case being different and unique. When my brother and I sat down to play it, we ended up staying awake till 4 AM completely engaged.
PROS:
-Great story
-Great game performance
-Catchy and yet fitting soundtrack
-Every case is different and engaging. You never know if the student you just hung out with is gonna get murdered the next day
-Every character is memorable and (to an extent) enjoyable

CONS:
-Most of the students aren't the sharpest tools in the shed, so sometimes there can be some really stupid arguments that completely waste time

-The bullet time battle in the class trial is...meh
To conclude, Danganronpa is one of the best visual novels I have played. It knows the story it wants to tell and it tells it damn well. If you love a weird but good story and a good detective game, get this game

TL;DR version: Hesitant yes, if you're an intelligent player that paces their games.  A no if you're a one-sitting gorger.
As far as a game goes, I find it a nice and interesting take on the Puzzle Quest concept.  The art is clean, the mechanics are smooth, and things are for the most part labeled as they should.  It's still a question of how much mana of a color you need for a certain card, but considering it's fairly recently come out it's not that big of a gripe though.
In regards to the reviews of "Getting stuck after 4 hours" because of coins and souls, I have to say this:  There's more to this game than the storyline.
In regards to coins: Yes, you only get 500/day, and battles do cost 50-60 coins apiece, but this is to try to help you limit your playtime.  You're not supposed to gorge on video games for 12+ hours at a time.  The game does seem to be formatted like a mobile game, and one of the logos on the title splash IS a mobile department.  So the micropayments for additional playtime/content seems normal, yet I haven't spent a dime on the game and am having fun.
In regards to souls: Don't hoard cards.  Look through what you have, chuck the crap for souls.  Along with this, also do Challenges.  Broken Spire's Stone Wall and Fortress Siege can be done really easy with a lot of cheese tactics, and they give large amounts of souls for completing them.  So it'd be a win-win, no?
The one gripe I have, and is starting to become a wall for me, is the RNG in the game.  Far far far FAR too often will gems fall perfectly for the AI to combo off of (since 4+ strings give an extra turn), or will drop down skulls at the perfect placement for them to push them into damage.  It's almost too coincidental, and feels more like fluff difficulty than an actual challenge, which without this luck of the draw for the AI, would be a general pushover.

This highly emerssive game, in my opinion gives the greatest of simulations of what it would be like on the surface of a planet that is newly explored. While you may know of such things as astroids and blizzards, it leaves you not knowing what the outcome will be. The AI of the colonist it rather intuitive to real people. They work less when depressed and hungry and wish for simple things outside of work. You have some that seem they spend their entire day in the bar and others that walk in just to watch the news. You can't make them work hard, you can't force someone to replace them, you can only watch as they do their jobs how they wish no matter who is watching. It isn't for the easily enraged, it will constantly deliver a unwanted situation just at the peak of "doing good". The trade system serves as an excellent way to get stuff you need, granted you have what they want. However, it also serves for an outlet of habitual mistakes that could cost you. Each planet having it's own circumstances that effect your overall gameplay while there, it goes to show how a few mistakes that seem minor/unnoticeable effect a community over a long period of time. One of the greatest proofs of this are within the early trading. It doesn't seem like a big deal to take your "Spares" and trade them as they have the most value, assuming you have plenty by leaving a couple for yourself in exchange for a fair amount of food. Once, you start to gain momentum suddenly you see your power and water sources need repair, while almost simultaneously seeing the notification "We have ran out of spares" pop up on screen. The rush is on to resolve the issue. This is one of the greatest simulation I think have ever been built. Now, for a touch of bad news! Well..... Not really bad more of a "I wish it were a thing!". If I had to suggest improvements I would request, that they allow you to assign workers and shifts for each place. Such as your agriculture is the staple of your colony and it would be nice if you could create rotating shift for them for maximum effeciency as when you are in late game and you start allowing visitors and more colonist to join sometimes you loose up to 10 simulataneously so it would be beneficial to be able to assign shifts, it would allow for better management of the resources you have so you are pushing out as much steel as you are bring in ore. This is without mention the fact it would be nice also, due to you could see what you need instead of hoping you have enough to manage your food. Overall, I love this game. You can see I quickly got a addicted it, it didn't take long after purchase to rack up over 12 hours of play. Thank you to the developers for this game.

The entire 'Doorways' series should be at the top of the list for ALL serious horror/adventure enthusiasts. The gameplay, graphics, atmosphere and story make the saga one of the best PC gaming experiences currently available. I never thought I'd be impressed again after finishing Outlast, but Doorways delivered in a big way, and now I'm waiting for the next 'aha!' gaming moment to come along.... these games won't be easy to top. Also, prior to playing the Doorways series, I always felt it was 'wrong' or somehow a 'copout' to have to rely on hints or walkthroughs in any way. The dynamic problems one must solve to complete Doorways gave me a different perspective on this; even if you need help with some of the tougher puzzles, once you solve them they certainly seem more than fair, and getting a bit of help didn't make me feel one bit like I hadn't played a rewarding or challenging game. Seriously, check out all three, as they're each masterpieces in their own right.
