Oh boy, where to start of with Observer_
I'm a huge Cyberpunk fan, I've played, read and seen a great deal of it by now and Blade Runner happens to be my favourite film of all time, it's safe to say that the Cyberpunk genre is a bit of an obsession of mine.
I'm no stranger to horror games either, having contributed work to games like Amnesia:AMFP and Frictionals SOMA, I'm a pretty big horror nerd.
This game, scratches neither of those itches for me, but let's start of with where the game has a glimmer of shine.
WORLD BUILDING_
World building is always an important task when dealing with Cyberpunk, and here the game does a decent job, with some pretty generic but effective backstory as to why the world has gone to crappers and some pretty alright voice acting ( for the most part ). Grungy detectives and people so hooked on body mods they might as well be skinjobs, this game certainly has what makes the foundation of a good cyberpunk world.
Now for those of you out there who have played Layers of fear you will know exactly what you're getting into with this game, mood, atmosphere, zero gameplay and lots of corridors, emphasis on LOTS. Admittedly I did not get more than two hours + into this title before deciding it was not for me and the above example is one of the many reasons.
Now having gone over pretty much all good I have to say about this title, it's time to get into why I would not recommend this game, to neither horror fans nor fellow Cyberpunks.
GAMEPLAY_
The game is set in an apartment complex stuck under lockdown with seemingly something skulking around in the shadows, the actions you will be taking as a player is enabling different visual filters from photoshops cartoon filter section to identify key items in the world which you need to click on to progress the story.
You will be selecting various dialogues to respond to people with during conversations which seem to have no impact on the gameplay whatsoever and the feature really appears to be in there for no other reason than being able to claim it as gameplay instead of making cutscenes for the dialogue.
A few puzzles are present in the game here and there, such as the bog-standard “find the combination to the keypad which we hid somewhere in the room you’re in” puzzle, and “find your way through a series of corridors that loop if you turn the wrong way” copy pasted straight from Ocarina of Time.
Other than this, there really is not much in terms of gameplay, hold W down and watch the flashy effects appear on your screen as you dive into peoples minds.
These sections are part of your job as an Observer_™ where you jack into the memories of various individuals you meet up with. They consist of previously mentioned lost wood puzzles and holding W for about 5 minutes whilst you learn things about the characters that hardly have any effect on the game at all.
What I’m trying to get across here, is that the game is padded with content that is completely pointless to anything that goes on in the game itself, the camera zooms in, zooms out, shows you blurry effects and then makes you walk through corridor number 2048 whilst your character has an epileptic seizure, these sections if designed right could have taken 20-30 seconds at most and gotten the exact same information out to the player.
Speaking of presenting information to the player, the game again fails here, forcing you to jump in and out of menus to figure out what to do, stumbling around without much of a clue on how to advance the story and failing to communicate with the player about items that you can pick up and have to use whilst playing the game.
Did I mention the clunky controls?
Steering your player around is a bit like going ice skating whilst riding an especially reluctant horse, opening doors and cabinets uses the physical version that amnesia popularized of pushing your mouse in various directions to guide the objects, only here they completely forgot how to implement the feature correctly resulting in the game often leaving you fighting of a feisty door instead of imminent threats.
And that, is honestly all I have to say about the gameplay section of Observer_.
HORROR_
Now! Onto the horror aspects, the horror in this game is very much reliant on jumpscares, turn around and POOF! There’s a character standing there saying hello to you.
Turn around the corner and POOF! There’s a spooky effect showing up in your face as a pigeon flies away, all of this accompanied by loud string effects to try and startle you.
For fans of horror who enjoy games like Amnesia, Silent hill or Resident evil, you will most likely not get anything out of this, as the scares are lazily implemented and the ones that are there, you’ve already seen so many times before.
SOUND_
I’ve not much to say regarding the sound design of Observer_, it was acceptable and didn’t bother me much, with the exception being two parts of this games audio, specific voice acting, and the obnoxious strings that try to scare you constantly even though nothing is really going on.
Being the huge Blade Runner nerd that I am, I was absolutely STOKED to see Rutger Hauer take up the role of the player character in the game.
Now I don’t believe I have to express my disappointment when I launched the game and realised that pretty much every single line spoken by Hauer is slurred, at many times to the point of needing to rely on the subtitles to understand what he was saying, plain and simple the man sounded like he had managed to bite his tongue before every recording session.
The other voices in the game are perfectly fine and never really bothered me, with the exception of one or two characters whom I could swear was the same voice actor, but that might’ve just been my imagination.
ART/GRAPHICS
Okay, so here’s another one of the games massive missteps, the art.
Being a graphical artist myself I am sure I’m more sensitive to these things than the casual player, but there were a lot of things that really bugged me about how this game was designed art wise.
Observer_ runs on Unreal Engine 4, a game engine known for being a graphical powerhouse.
So to look at this game and see how much the art team has failed with basic things like shaders and Physically based material rendering brings a little tear to my eyes.
Extremely low polygon models that appear close to the players vision and certain objects throughout the game world that seem to have been squashed, flattened screw models, flat lamps. Lamps shining through walls, reflection captures not being present where they should be causing completely wrong reflections to appear on shiny surfaces and the level designers simply failing to attach objects like lamps properly to the walls and placing various clutter on the ground, leaving them floating in mid air goes a long way to ruin immersion and breaking down the atmosphere which is the only thing that is really holding this game together.
Adding to the annoying screen effects that the developers took a step too far there is also a sort of matrix effect being rendered over entire areas, this effect makes large areas of the game look like a digital simulation, which could have been cool if done in moderation! But just like all the other effects present in this game, it was taken too far to the point of me stumbling around the environment not being able to tell what anything was.
Performance wise I ran everything on maximum quality and encountered no issues on my GTX 1080 TI card, which is to be expected.
FINAL THOUGHTS_
The game is an absolute mess, with gameplay that is hardly gameplay at all, slurred voice acting, lazily implemented horror and artwork on the level of a university student on top of clunky controls.
Get the Westwood Blade Runner game, play the classic “Snatcher” by Kojima, watch the blade runner films, get lost in Neuromancer or play a session or two of the“CYBERPUNK” dnd style classic.
Overall, this was a disappointment.

Solving the cryptic puzzles and mysteries is great once you get into it but there are so many frustrations throughout, I struggle to say if it's worth it.
There's terrible hitboxes on the bosses, which are insanely difficult without getting the extra secret upgrades and weapons (even then they're still really difficult).
The jumping mechanics are weird and imprecise, which wouldn't be so bad except a lot of the levels and enemies/bosses are designed in such a way that you have to be precise.
And the game loves to throw insane annoyances at you, like how about a room which is really hard and annoying to get to even once you've worked out how to get there, so every time you need to go there you have to spend ages trying over and over to get in there. Then let's have a really hard mini boss in there so every time you die you have to go back and do it all again. Then once you've finally beaten it, have an insta-kill trap in the next room. There's a fair bit of that in La-Mulana, and I get that the game seems to pride itself on dicking you over but you can do that without necessarily feeling unfair.
I don't even mind most of the insta-kill traps. You can usually see them coming and avoid them if you're cautious and pay enough attention, and they're usually close enough to a save point that you can just laugh them off and continue.
If you think you can put up with all that and you really enjoy big adventures and cryptic puzzles that'll have you taking lots of notes then it might be worth it for you. Despite that I'm not recommending this game, I did enjoy it well enough, it's just a deeply flawed game that really isn't for everyone.
If you do decide to play it, here's some words of advice:
The game has a manual (you can access it by right clicking the game in your library), you'll have to read it to solve a puzzle early on because as far as I'm aware, the solution isn't even alluded to in the game.
I would of course recommend avoiding using a guide as much as possible but you'll probably end up needing a guide at some point. I recommend "Cheshire's Hint-based Guide" on the steam guides as it'll allow you to get hints to parts you're stuck at without having the solution outright given to you.
After you've beaten the first boss you'll be able to gain access to three separate bosses without actually having to beat any of them. You should get to that point, and then use the previously mentioned guide to help you find the Axe weapon and make sure you've gotten as many life orbs as you can. Without those you're going to have a really hard time with the bosses.

A pretty good visual novel + point n' click.  Most of the game is basically a visual novel where sometimes to advance the story, you have to click on objects and examine them.  There are also sections of the game where you can move your character around in first-person, which is cool. The other main parts of the game are these "trial" sections where you listen to characters' conversations and then present evidence to point out contradictions in the dialogue. There are also parts where you play little minigames (there's a hangman game and a rhythm game). The trial sections are the parts with the most actual gameplay as opposed to just reading text.
The best part of the game is definitely the characters.  All of the characters are interesting, the translated dialogue is natural, and I found everybody likeable (even the antagonists). The game introduces all of the characters literally at once, but I didn't have any trouble remembering who was who because they're all extremely distinct.
The story was okay- it was definitely interesting enough for me to play the whole game. Unfortunately most of the mysteries weren't that hard to figure out. I had a solid guess for who the murderer was for the first four cases before the trial began, and I was right about all of them.  It's kind of frustrating when you know what the answer is, but then you have to watch your character being really clueless for thirty minutes. The last two were more mysterious though, and I geniunely wasn't sure who the murderer was in those two cases until the "big reveal".
One thing I wasn't a huge fan of- the difficulty in the trial sections seemed to be all over the place.  Sometimes the answer is super obvious and then it's way too easy.  Then there were also the times where I got stuck. The thing is, most of the parts I got stuck on, I knew exactly what the contradiction was. I just didn't know which specific piece of dialogue the game wanted me to present my item on. I get that they're just having a conversation so it's more unclear than say, Ace Attorney (where the characters are giving a testimony in court)... but yeah, it's frustrating to know the answer but then have to guess how to convey the answer to the game.
Overall, I definitely recommend the game. It's a great value since the game is pretty long, and you'll be so attached to the characters that you'll want to play the whole thing to see what happens to them.

Wow. This game falls nothing short of "utterly fantastic."
You play as Makoto Naegi, a boy who gets trapped in a school with fourteen other students, and they're forced to live their entire lives there forever. There are multiple rules and twists over the course of the game, but that's the main premise overall. Just know that the story has EXCELLENT pacing.
When an inevitable murder happens, the gameplay has you investigating crime scenes, questioning students, and searching for clues for the class trial, which is where the meat of the game lies. There's three different minigames that take place during a trial, all of which are fun in their own way and make perfect sense storywise.
Whenever you're not trying to solve a murder, you're building friendships with the students, which unlocks skills for the trials (and learning the backstory of the characters in the progress).
ABSOLUTELY worth the hype, and EXTREMELY recommended. A must-own.

After a long line of disappointing games in the Medal of Honor franchise that just never could recapture the magic successes of Allied Assault, we finally get Medal of Honor: Airborne that combines high presentation values and good, fast-paced fun. While there's definitely some good entertainment value here, the campaign is short, and the multiplayer isn't incredibly deep. Still, it's a good game overall and the best game in the franchise in some time.
Medal of Honor: Airborne takes a different approach to World War II shooters. Instead of starting players out in each linear level on a path where there's no variation, EA LA decided to let us choose where to start each mission by throwing us out of a plane. Once floating in the air, it's a matter of steering the parachute to the best location to start the fight. Where the best location is depends on how you want to play the game, a mechanic that certainly is useful if you want a challenge or find that it's more fun to start out in a certain place on a map. It also provides an opportunity to drop into a new location if the previous one was a little too difficult or even complete one of the five different skill drops (drops in very specific areas).

The atmosphere makes this game.
The sound and graphics capture the grandness of it all and is uncompromising- no tacked on comical relief thank god, just plain interstellar survival. Immersion is almost complete, randomly generated environments and realistic movements and interesting machinery makes this game a lot of fun to play, and keeps replayability high. You will find yourself wanting to try "just one more time" to get it right, and it feels good achieving development goals. The game makes you feel taken seriously when you manage to establish self sufficiency, or expansion states. Graphics zoom out, you get an acknowledgment, and it boosts your morale to keep going.
There are a bunch of different planets which all come with their own dangers, and the graphics truly make you feel like you're on another planet completely, whether it is the moon, Mars, or some icy moon.
Starting a new game kind of feels like starting a game of Civilization- what have we here, ok, let's make the best of the situation.
While random, the way to achieve victory is fairly linear, but you are never forced to make decisions by the game. Storms, solar flares and meteors provide a constant sense of danger, and hearing the station alarm go off does feel important enough to raise your pulse.
If you're a fan of space, space colonization and pretending you're on a different world, this one is for you. The game isn't perfect, but for what it is, it's worth every single penny, and I love it.

I've seen a few reviews on here that were a bit too critical. "I don't like the way the heal spell looks" is one of them, which is obviously just nitpicking. Anyway, I absolutely love and recommend this game if you like JRPG type games. I've listed what I liked and disliked, and will update as I get further into the game.
Good features:
+ Stylish graphics, switch between HD or classic 16 bit look
+ Great music, also able to switch to Sega Genesis sound
+ Quick to get you into the game, very fun upbeat story
+ Compatible with many controllers, even my SNES one!
+ Adjustable encounter rate: fight more or no enemies at all
+ Adjustable combat speed: great for when you're just training
Unappealing features:
- Steam overlay is bugged. Will move/select when typing.
- The controls can be strange. Not game breaking.*
* Holding a directional key seems to disable the use/talk button in the middle of dialog. When using a heal spell out of combat, there is a strange quirk where I have to hit the up button to scroll left, but the right button to scroll to the right. This is incredibly minor.
ALSO if you do have controller issues, right click the game on steam, go to properties, set launch options, and write dxjoy. This might make your controller more compatible. Be sure to map buttons once ingame of course.
I'd like to add that games of this nature are very rare. The HD graphics have incredible, well-detailed environments with some classic 16 bit sprites mixed in. It's a timeless work of art; these visuals don't age and are very pleasant to look at. Give the demo a try if you are interested, and take into account that the bad reviews are only from a handful of people. If more people decided to try this game out, the ratings would likely go way up. In an oversaturated indie market, where some of the most lazy looking, blocky games are highly praised, I find it hard to accept that Pier Solar gets hardly any attention; it provides beautiful visuals, great music, a lovely story and classic RPG mechanics that are both intuitive and pretty satisfying.
- Sarah

Too much dialogue at the beginning, not able to skip. For some who want mainly Role-Playing aspects, meh, fine. But you should really make it versatile to allow skipping so people who don't care about the story can skip it. Even being forced to read all of the dialogue, the controls are gimmicky and probably one of the weakest choices for assignment I've seen, paired with nothing but story line to go off of for early progression. You don't need a tutorial, just literally like one minor hint as to what to do would be enough, rather than just hoping to accidentally figure it out.
I am only interested in combat, so my review is based strictly on that. As of yet, I have experienced no combat in the first 15 minutes, which instantly makes me lose interest. There are two kinds of players, Role Players and Combatants, and some are both. Your game is too based on Role Playing that you lose 50% of your player base simply because you don't introduce combat early on. Many RPG games such as this begin the game with a Role Play scenario of a combat scene, giving both players a taste of what they're interested in. But, this game, you forego that and completely lose us Combatants by a slow and bland story line that we cannot skip to hope to get to combat sooner. I really want to see how combat plays out, but it honestly is not even worth getting there with how crappy the story is. If it was able to be skipped, and gave a quick 10-second hint at how to play, then it would be golden. About one day of work and you effectively increase your player population by double. But, obviously that isn't worth it, or the developer's didn't care enough and just wanted a Role Playing game.
TL;DR:
If you enjoy slow Role-Playing story-based games, you may be interested
If you enjoy combat in RPGs, save your money, but more importantly your time. 15 minutes into a game and no combat is too long. I feel like I just read the Terms and Conditions for a game before I even logged in.
15-minutes of play Rating: 3/10
Not worth swallowing the bile to go farther, save your money.

Men of Valor is one of those rare first-person shooter titles that takes place during the Vietnam War circa 1965. Many of the reviews for this title on Steam are negative, primarily because of the hard difficulty of the game, as well as the fact that this title has some problems getting started. Before we go any further into this review, Men of Valor will not appear when launched, you must press CTRL + ALT to get the window to show, and then CTRL + Enter to go full screen. There's also a handy guide in the community hub that will help you eliminate the stuttering issue that the game has by simply editing out the vsync option in the .ini file. If you can handle those minimal tasks then read on, as Men of Valor is a pretty decent FPS overall.
You play as an inexperienced African-American Marine named Dean who has been assigned to the 3rd Battalion of the 3rd Marine Division. It's important to note the main character's skin color, as given the year that the game takes place in, it's a prominent and recurring theme. All in all, you will battle your way through sixteen missions in total, through a number of locations that range from dense, thick jungles, to underground tunnels, and urban landscapes. Men of Valor is laden with true-to-life historical locations and battles that took place in Vietnam during 1965, including what happened at the height of the Tet Offensive.
Now, as far as difficulty goes, this game can be frustratingly hard at some points. Though there are three difficulty settings outlined in the menu, for some reason only medium can be played; this is most likely a bug in the port that the developer never issued a patch for. The damage that you take is high, and going toe-to-toe with any enemy is almost always a guaranteed death. A death is almost always a guaranteed restart to the beginning of the level as well, as checkpoints are few and far between and there are no manual saves. Luckily, each mission is rather short, so when you are forced to give it another go from the beginning it isn't detrimental to your overall progress.
Some more elements that add to the difficulty factor of Men of Valor are the health and healing system, as well as searching bodies. Your health is indicated by a medical sign in the bottom left corner of the screen, and when you are hit you start "bleeding", any blood lost will then become permanent damage, which is indicated in a dark red on the same medallion. To stop the bleeding, you have to bandage yourself by pressing F; the sooner the better, as the more blood you lose, the more permanent damage you incur. To recover permanent damage, you have to find med-kits and canteens on dead bodies by searching them, which requires holding down the spacebar for a length of time. It's rather time consuming, and in some cases can put you in more danger than it's worth, but that's just another ingredient that makes the title more realistic.
For a game from 2004, the graphics aren't half bad. The character models are a little blocky, but there's a good variety of enemies and your squad-mates are easily defined from the generic soldiers that are scattered about. The environments are very well detailed, with lush forestry, reflective water, devastating fires, and atmospheric mist. In particular, the final level is extremely graphic, as bombs that are going off in the distance look like lightning strikes. The soundtrack is also decent, as it's heavily cinematic and ensures that your heart stays racing from the very first battle, to the very last.
Even though it has some issues getting started on more modern systems, Men of Valor is an excellent FPS title. Moreover, it adds to its already unique setting by centering around an African-American Marine, which was uncommon back in 1965, when every minority was heavily discriminated against. The historical accuracy of the battles and locations is just another added factor to the in-depth care that went to crafting this title. It's a tough one, but if you don't mind the challenge then Men of Valor will be sure to scratch an itch that's been unreachable for a long time.

Straight off the bat, Men of Valor is a great game. Though old this title holds up in its authenticity, variety of levels and gameplay, as well as a basic but good score with a couple of classic tracks from the era thrown in for good measure. It even features a graphics option for 1920x1080 which is nice and not always seen on these older games. Men of Valor does a good job at narrating the period of the Vietnam War it covers from the soldiers perspective, highlighting and cutting through some of the media lies and ill-advised public perception of the war. It does this though narration between levels but also through a set of letters which are read in-between missions between the main character and primarily his farther back home. It also does not dance around the vulgarity of soldiers and portrays African American marines of the conflict well without really crossing into the area of the laughable stereotype.
The game puts you in the boots of a U.S. Marine, fighting through the first few years of the United States' involvement in the Vietnam War. A period which will see you completing a varied set of interesting missions ranging from jungle ambushes and search and destroy missions to running retreats through misty marshes at night. All offering a change of scenery (though obviously mostly green) and in some cases tense situations where you are constantly looking around for Charlie in the bamboo, though all are enjoyable.
To complete these missions you are given an equally wide selection of small arms to play with which range from the M16A1 and PPSH-41 to the M79 and M134 minigun while serving as the door gunner in a UH-1 Huey Slick. The weapons in the game are for the most part well represented and all come with alternate 'firing' modes, such as 40mm buckshot for the M79 or the folding spike bayonet of the Type 59. For the most part though this alternate mode is the option to switch between semi and fully automatic fire. This is a very nice feature which allows you to make the most of your weapon’s firepower in close range engagements or its accuracy when trying to engage targets at a longer range. It is also very useful for conserving ammunition.
In terms of aiming mechanics the game does show its age a little as there is no aiming down sights, unless you are using a scoped weapon. Personally I did not find this an issue however. When you use what the game calls 'precision aim,' you merely zoom into the centre of your screen a little and focus on a crosshair. When in this mode however you cannot move, though the game uses this aiming mechanic as an opportunity to allow for a separate leaning mechanic which is only accessible in this mode. A little strange to get use to at first, it was easy to adjust to and I had little problems with the system after a few minutes.
Another notable mechanic is the way health works in this game. Though based on a health pack system, when you are hit you will generally bleed out and have a chance to bandage yourself to regain health you may otherwise lose. This however cannot be done while in the precision aiming mode. While this slows combat compared to a regenerating heath system, I prefer it as it promotes intelligent movement and taking cover to preserve your life in the long-term. This being said however most dead enemy bodies have small health kits on them, so you are never far from heath if you need it. This scavenging feature also allows you to pick up enemy weapons and resupply ammunition for these weapons. Something which becomes necessary in lengthy missions out in the Jungle.
The friendly AI is relatively intelligent and while they get in your way now and then, I have only encountered one instance where I could not get him to move by walking into him. Eventually he walked away of his own accord after a minute or so. They are also fairly capable and are no slouches when it comes to knocking off Mr Charles. The enemy AI is a bit of a mixed bag but I generally found them to be fairly competent. Sometimes they will get stuck outside of the map but still shoot at you, this isn't too much of an issue though as you can still kill them by firing back at their tracers’ origin. On other occasions I felt quite confident sitting short distances from the enemy as in many cases them proved themselves rather incapable of landing shots. Still, often this was not the case. As I say, a mixed bag but not really an issue and while they displayed inept behaviour at times, in general they were far from push overs, requiring you to use cover wherever possible.
Unless you are really put off by the graphics, I would definitely recommend this game to you if you enjoy games set during the Vietnam War. Delivered through a unique and interesting perspective, Men of Valor amounts to an excellent Vietnam FPS with a wide range of diverse and interesting levels, environments and weapons.

One of the best games I've ever played in recent memory, and one of the most challenging. Excellent mechanics, ideas and most importantly the incredible amount of mind-bending and incredibly well thought-out puzzles that await you at every turn.
If you're looking to pick up a game that will really challenge you, La-Mulana is a must for you.

There are a lot of things I love about La-Mulana: the soundtrack, the world-building, the fact that it has the gameplay of a metroidvania with the puzzle solving of a point-and-click adventure game.  The reason I would recommend it, though, is that it's a passion project, made by gamers who loved a certain kind of game so much that they made their own, and did so well.  You can feel the love they pored into it.  No Indiana Jones or Tomb Raider game can match this level of Action Archaeology.
This game is unfair, deliberately so.  If you take pride in beating puzzle games without consulting hints or walkthroughs, you will probably be turned off by La-Mulana in the end.  Still, I would highly recommend it for the experience, frequently soul-crushing though it may be.

La-Mulana has an heir of nostalgia to it. It has a lot in common with games I grew up with. Very fun Metroidvania game if you like exploring and stumbling around trying to figure out what to do next. It's a game that requires some note taking to get through it and even then I still was stumped two or three times to the point of looking up what to do next. Some may call that a flaw but I enjoyed trying to figure it out on my own. The combat in the game is pretty good, although it takes a little getting used to the character's jump since you can only change it's arc a certain way. All in all a fun game that I've sunk plenty of time into it for what I originally paid for it. I'll be looking forward to it's sequel when it finally is released.

Extremely satisfying 'vania game that refuses to pull punches and demands effort in exchange for success. Expect tons of exploring, difficult puzzles, hidden upgrades, backtracking, and the occasional progress wall. Be prepared to fall through hidden trap doors, compulsively whip walls, use fast travel to escape spike pits and lava, and die often.
You may find it frustrating or overwhelming at first, but beyond that is a rare and memorable gaming experience that satisfies a craving you may not realize you had. In short, La-Mulana will challenge you, even if you're used to other games of its type, but you'll want more when it's over.
This game is awesome!

La-Mulana is often considered a 2D Dark Souls, and for good reason.
This is a game where puzzles are so difficult to solve, it's almost impossible to solve them without reading a walkthrough, and considering it is a Metroidvania, its nonlinear gameplay can make them even more confusing than they should be.

I'm on the fence on recommending this game or not despite how many things I dislike about it. I'm not attempting to damn it by faint praise; I'm praising it, but only faintly, because that's what it deserves in my opinion. tl;dr at the last paragraph
The first playthrough takes about 22 hours. There's a new game mode of sorts that opens up at the end but I didn't look much into it, it doesn't seem to be my thing.
The story is very interesting overall, and the mystery behind it is the reason I  played the game to its end.
You may or may not like the artstyle, depending on your tastes.
The soundtrack... is just kinda there. There's like only four tracks or something. It's sort of repetitive and while most of the tracks are alright none of them really stand out.
The gameplay is alright, even though BTBs kind of threw me off at first: they don't fit that well with the rest of the game, but they were okay after all. However, in most chapters you are basically hand-lead through the investigative section and through any actual reasoning you need to make to solve the current case. Also, many times you'll enter the 'trial' phase without all the evidence, so if you were hoping to guess who the culprit was before starting to throw accusations around, you often won't be able to do so.
So if in the investigative section for each case you are guided by the game, when do you need to reason on your own? Well, I mentioned before that what makes this game good is the story. While investigating, some stuff you'll find and some sentences you'll hear won't be that relevant to the current case, but will allow you to make hypothesis on some other mysteries, and I think that's where the fun of the game lies.
The characters... My god, the characters. Almost every character in the game is unremarkable, uninteresting, unrelatable, unrealistic, and/or unlikeable. You'll feel bad for them because they're in a really ♥♥♥♥♥♥ situation, of course, but you'd feel bad for anyone in their situation anyway, so that's no excuse for me to overlook the fact that most of them suck.
On a few occasions, the game progresses the way it does purely because the main character makes stupid decisions without allowing the player to intervene.
The game treats very oddly, I'd even say in a dangerously superficial way, concepts such as masculinity, femininity, truth, and mental health.
In the end, the game does have a confused but positive message of hope. However, it also teaches you to bottle up your emotions, never talk about how you feel to anyone, and to lie constantly. There's more than that: you are expected to feel thankful and grateful towards the character that teaches you this. That character is presented as an exclusively a positive model. That character is never wrong, never does anything wrong. That's absolutely unbelievable and ridiculous and I hate that character with all my heart.
Let's talk about the bear, the mascot of the game. I don't mind that it's a bear, or the bear puns (which are actually fairly rare, I bearly noticed any of them during my playthrough). However, one of the first thing it admits itself is that nothing it says makes sense. So why should I, the player, have to read what it says? Therefore, I skipped every Monokuma Theatre section (which is basically just the bear spouting utter nonsense every in-game night) and some other lines as well.
That said, if you can stand the characters' inanity, there are a very interesting mystery story and a very passable gameplay behind all of this. If you get this, try to get it on sale.

Turbo Pug is a 2D, one dimensional forever runner that has you jumping over pits and spikes across a single level. You keep running forward until you fall into a pit or hit an object. This is a game that lives and dies by how addictive you are to clicking your mouse and its cheap one dollar price tag. After about five minutes in, I felt like I had seen everything. At fifteen minutes I had unlocked the twelve playable characters. Its worth a dollar, but if you're looking for something deeper than a mobile game on your computer, then look elsewhere.
The game does have a few things going for it: graphics and charm. The charm of a goofy little pug and unlockable chocolate pugs, rainbow pugs, cats, space cats and Santa hats adds a lot to a baron and starved game. The graphics have a great style and it fits that retro style. To make things more interesting, the day and night will cycle, and you'll see rain or snow happen. Its all random so it feels like the single level is dynamic and changing.
This single level throws patterns at you. One pattern has ramps and two boxes, another has two pits, there's one with a large pit and two floating boxes. Later patterns start having giant spikes and saw blades. The saw blades are dark, so seeing them at night becomes an issue. I will guess there are a mere ten or so patterns.
The control is simple; mouse click or use the space bar to jump. The space bar is less strain on your wrist, but then if you fail, you still need to use the mouse anyway to click play again. It would just be nice to have a keyboard work the menu, but why do that when you can throw a game out the door and make money? There is no support for controllers, which is never an issue, but with a game as sparse as this, its tough to think of anything to say to fluff out a review.
Every frame that you stay alive, you get a point. Then there are pug pellets for lack of a better term where then you get either fifty or one hundred points. Oh my! Puggles getting pellets getting points. Yes you is. Who's a good pug wagging his tongue while he runs? You is!
With each failure, you see your points, your high score and your overall accumulation of points. I assume the overall points unlock pugs, because the game never told me I had unlocked anything. To the game's credit, each of the playable animals does feel just a bit different. It seems like the lunar kitty has less gravity and other animals seem to run faster. Without a description of how they're different, you just need to play. I prefer the default two pugs that the game comes with to any that get unlocked.
To keep you in the game there's a leader board, but that's it. The game could have had more leader board integration such as challenge your friends or even online multiplayer where you compete on the same course. When someone loses you keep going and they drop out.
As I ran, I noticed a few glitches here and there. Nothing game breaking, but sometimes the hill terrain has a line. I've also noticed seems between the background where the background loops.
Turbo Pug is a game that kept me occupied for a good ten minutes. There are better games out there that do the same thing, but Turbo Pug just looks better and has a better flavor than other forever runners. Its too simple to be played on anything but a phone when you're waiting for something else, but hey its still fun.

>Observer_ is a game which excels in worldbuilding and creating atmosphere, but heavily suffers in terms of pacing and technical problems.
The cyberpunk world here is among the darkest (literally and figuratively) ones I have seen. The world and the history behind it feels dirty and hostile, creating incredibly heavy atmosphere. Exploring the building complex know as the "Stacks" is where the game gets it right. Talking to tenants, investigating locations in detective mode and discovering side quests is where the game shines. I just wish there was more of it.
Where the game fails however, is pacing, especially during the "dream" sequences. These parts of the game tend to go on for too long, and mostly without story to keep you hooked or gameplay to keep you interested. Lot of screen flashing and fever dream like imagery for 30 minutes can be very jarring, and its a shame. I feel like if the craziness of there parts were turned down to 10 instead of 11 and shortened by half, it would fix the core problem.
The main story itself is what people expect out of games like these, mind bending investigation that leaves you saying "Wait what" by the end. However, pacing is also bit messed up around here, the game gets quite infodumpy near the end, answering all of your questions in span of few minutes.
The horror element is mostly created with the great atmosphere and few non offensive jump scares. There are few parts that include sneaking, but once again suffer from the pacing problem, being more boring than scary.
On technical level, the game looks great and the art direction is perfect for the world they have created. Framerate however is very unstable on a system (GTX 1070 i5 4670k 4.0Ghz) that should handle indoors areas just fine. Also the lack of FoV setting is bit dishearthening since the default setting caused eye strain for me, and I had to do some .ini file editing to increase it, but this sadly makes the computer monitors hard to read. Patch is absolutely needed here.
I might come off as bit negative here, but I absolutely love games that get my brain running and take me on a wild ride. >Observer_ gets cautious recommendation. There are so many great things going on with this game, but I wish the execution wasnt so rough.

Observer starts off well enough, and at first plays like a unique interactive detective game. Using your biological/technological scanner to inspect and examine clues, searching cupboards and opening drawers. But there is a radical shift early on, a descent into madness. Its hard to describe, you get thrown through a series of psychedelic and confusing sequences. Some have you fumbling around a dark room waiting for god knows what to trigger the next scripted sequence, others are relentless flashes of disturbing images accompanied with terrifying sounds.
If your like me, on paper that sounds pretty awesome. Sadly, it loses cohesion and becomes a confusing mess. It seems the entirety of the game takes place in a cramped and claustrophobic apartment building. To say that the building is a maze would be a great understatement... Every hallway looks the same, everything is so damn dark and theres flashing lights everywhere from the cyber punk techno contraptions. I spent the first two hours bumbling around confused and not knowing where to go or what to do.
There is little in the way of guidance. You get a little log menu you can pull up that has vague and brief descriptions of your objective and what to do next. Everything is difficult to see due to the incessant darkness, and the night vision and scanners arent any better, as they are intentionally blurry and grainy to give it that cyber punk style. Sadly, it turns what should be an exciting detective game into a frustrating mess of struggling to just see your surroundings.
There are auto-fail stealth sequences, in a game with no combat. I love stealth games, when you actually have tools or gadgets or skills to present options. Observer has the WORST type of stealth sequences. You have to evade some wierd monster thing, that will insta kill you when it spots you, forcing a reload from last checkpoint, which hopefully wasnt too long ago. Now add that in with the stumbling around in the dark and ridiculous and confusing lights and hallucinations constantly shifting and changing, and it turns into a total crap shoot.
There is such an abundance of psychedelic crap, its a complete overload. I get a headache everytime I play it. There comes a point when your done seeing surreal and spooky stuff like a chair balancing on one leg on its own, or a creepy man shaking convulsively standing in a corner. The flashing lights and hallucinations get downright irriating. Theres only so much crazy I can handle. In the end the game boils down to a spooky walking simulator, when your not walking down hallways looking at all the wierd stuff and flashing lights, your fumbling in the dark struggling to find clues in a pitch black room. It gets old FAST.
The skull-jack sequences, when you plug into someones neural implant to interogate their memories is much, much worse. Again, what could have been a brilliant concept and experience, falls apart into overwhelming stimulus. Its difficult to describe this game, because its truly unlike anything Ive seen or played before, which is its greatest strength.
Observer is a very unique game, and has some very compelling concepts. Thats the long and short of the games upside. I get the perception that this is the kind of game where you get it, or you dont. It will click with some, but not others. It didnt click for me, and I fail to see why Gamespot gave it a 9/10 score. Personally, I give it a 6/10.

This game was one of those few where my opinion, changed several times while playing it.
At first when i started, of course i had a positive opinion, i was...interested.
Observer is a science fiction cyberpunk type of game, where you play Daniel Lazarsky, a detective of sorts, who is in fact working as an Observer, a special force capable of hacking into your mind, looking into your memories. This can become specially usefull when looking for the truth after the fact.
Here comes the cyberpunk part: you are not only able to hack into the minds of people (thanks to your wrist device) but also you have within yourself, several augmentations upgrades,  for example you are able to scan all kinds of devices, look for general structures and machines, model, build, you can also scan for biological elements in a scene, you have also night vision, and you can hack computers .
It is without a doubt that i was interested in this game, the setting to me was excelent, but the story was also promising...
At first you arrive into this house complex, (looking for someone) many people live  here and suddenly the building gets a lockdown after something happens and everyone is trapped. (they can't even leave theyre appartments because there's the possibility of a plague.)
So you start investigating and here comes the first dissapointment (at least for me) to be honest maybe this was me not knowing what to expect from the game. I thought it was going to happen on different locations, or at least a few of them. But it turns out it is  only one, the house complex and tons of rooms. It was sort of like a haunted house but in the future.
So, thats not necessarily a bad thing in itself, if its done right; it just that, it seemed to be presented as a type of thing that it really wasn't.
So then it starts to become repetitive, but then the story starts to develop somehow and you also do your first brain hack. So it turns positive to me, i am invested story wise (again) and the game.
The hack sequence at first its a little weird but thats ok, it is how it is supposed to be.
But then you start to have more of these  brain hack sequences, and the more you have the more they become ... random. It is a part of the story, what happens to Lazarski in those brain hack sequences, but... at the end of day ,although shocking and very appealing in principle, they become more of an exercise in figuring out what the developer (of the game) wants you to do here and then there, and less making some sort of sense...the sequences are hard to understand not in story but in gameplay mechanics. Its like the game is more concerned in shocking value and being emotional than in functioning as a game.
An then the story starts to drift off a little. The game presents itselfs as cyberpunk horror. And soon it becomes mostly horror. I dont mind the horror part, i like that, but its just that the cyberpunk setting seems wasted. There's so much background world and... it is absent a good part of the game. At one point it seems you are going from one horror scene to another.
The game itself is not really all bad, it has good things, like the setting, (pretty much wasted), but still a very good place to start, a very interesting world  and then the graphics are really well done here, and have very good photography.... but then the game ultimately fails in many other things so it is not a good experience on the whole.
The so called hack sequences although frightening and beautifull at first, they become more like white noise later. Just a lot of screams but not  so much content.

tomb raider is probably one of the top three games i've ever played. the graphics are beautiful, the story is rich and compelling, and the gameplay and fighting mechanics are smooth and feel totally natural. the gameplay is intuitive and fun and the optional tombs are a challenge that help to fill in time in between main quest objectives. although finding gps caches, documents, and relics is not a required part of the game, it's fun to look for them and they help to flesh out the story even more without taking away from the tense action. it's an incredible start to a new era of tomb raider, and i couldn't be more in love with this game.
the game does not take an especially long time to complete, so it's possible to knock out a good amount of the story in a few hours, but given how interesting it is and the amount of collectibles you can find before and after story completion, tomb raider does have a lot of replay value. the environment is also absolutely gorgeous, which makes exploration fun when you're trying to go back and get everything you missed.
it runs very well on both my current non-gaming laptop and my old clunker, and i've never had any issues at all with random crashing or bugs. i would recommend this game to anyone, whether they're a new gamer or an old one, and especially if they enjoy games with both strong story and action components.

There is quite a learning curve to creating them, but there are hundreds of cards others have made already and have done the hard work for you. Even entire sets!
Modded decks/cards even work online. Though ONLY if you and the other player have the same exact files. So really only useful for playing with friends and not randoms.

Patience.
A virtue so absolutely critical to playing this game "correctly", that I gave it its own paragraph, to emphasize. You have a colony at whatever stage of its growth. The first thing that you do is make sure nothing explodes, figuratively or literally. Is there enough oxygen? Food? Medicine for the casualties of the maw of industry? Is there spare power and water to expand with? You look at global charts, storages, individual colonist indicators, search out and mitigate bottlenecks in the flow of goods. If all this (and more) comes out okay, you build a few additional buildings, maybe just one. And then the process starts again.
And I don't know why, but I find it utterly addictive. I admit the flavour of the game (what the gameplay is packaged in) works really well for me here, because colonization of space and hard sci-fi are both major turn-ons of mine. It plays a bit like Settlers 2 meets
. A little bit like Dungeon Keeper (minus the combat and the humour). There are some annoying bugs. Even worse, the user's quality of life has been neglected and some obviously important interface/building features are not present. The game feels very rough around the edges at times, like a typical indie, however it won me over with its intangible charm and a vision of a spacefaring future.
Of note, there are user translations provided for most major languages by now, via the Steam Workshop. Yours truly is the author of
. And the savefiles are in plain text, editable with Notepad. Which helps with the few asinine achievements (the majority of them are reasonable).

Medal of Honor: Airborne is a fair game, well worth buying. It presents fictional battles during WWII that nevertheless play off of the main storyline. You take the place of an American paratrooper, who works to eliminate the Nazis. Airborne presents a useful upgrading system, where you can improve several weapons based on the number of kills you receive for each. The controls are familiar, but present some new functions that work like a charm, once you get used to them. I did see some small blood puffs, but took a keen eye to place them. The graphics for this game are fairly good, doing a very good job of using the environment and lighting to generate an atmosphere that, along with the soundtrack, fit Airborne like a glove. As for the gameplay itself, I want to say this--Casual is Casual, Normal is Normal, Veteran is Veteran. I highly suggest getting used to the game before advancing to higher levels. The enemies are also class-based--they certainly get tougher later in the game. This is perfectly exemplified by the deadly Nazi Storm Elite trooper, who wears a bulletproof vest, a gas mask, and walks calmly along while carrying a mini-gun. I will never encounter anything scarier in a game than walking around a corner to find myself face-to-face with this horror. All in all, Airborne is a good game, and is definitely worth buying

Quick review to start: Holy cow is this ever fun to play!  The only caveat to recommending the Pinball Arcade is that, naturally, it's all about pinball and maybe that doesn't float your boat.  I do believe that pinball is universally entertaining however if you accept the inherent gameplay mechanics and so if you play this game you'll find happiness.
This is the second major pinball system on Steam now, but I will rate it unquestionably the best.  Why?  Because it *feels* perfect.  All the physics involved has a very satisfying sense of weight to it... the ball accelerates believably, the timing of when you strike the ball with your flippers affects the trajectory properly, and the rebounds from bumpers and sidewalls fits your expectations just *right*.  This is absolutely the best playing pinball experience you'll find on Steam.  There IS still room for improvement however but those are fiddly details that you'll hardly notice (the ball never leaves the table surface making certain actions reliably consistent compared with reality, the flippers are rock-solid and don't have any "spongeyness" that happens with real tables, and the friction of the table surface and steel rails is constant which again makes the ball behavior suffer no random deviations).
I've been familiar with pinball games, but I'm not a nut for the genre, and so I'm not bothered by the lack of absolute authenticity with the real tables.  Each game that's recreated here scores high by replicating a faithful experience.  You probably won't be able to "train" on these virtual recreations and expect perfect knowledge about how to work the real thing, but you WILL get all the entertainment that was built into the original games.  And on the note about those original games.... WOW!  The variety of tables to play is astonishing from truly old school pinball experiences from the 1960's to classic 70's and 80's table complete with early arcade sounds (I *love* those sounds!) to the zenith of pinball evolution in the mid 1990's.  The Pinball Arcade is truly a museum piece approach to the genre that shows no favorites for any one time period or manufacturer.  The breadth of choice is very, very nice!
Some other things to note: all the tables present in this game are recreations of the originals which were designed to eat your money.  This is important to remember because even though there's no longer any quarters being spent to play there can be a lot of frustrating moments where your game ends prematurely because happenstance physics will cause your ball to drain no matter how skillful you can play.  It's possible to "nudge" the machine in multiple directions in an attempt to coax the ball into a different trajectory but I can't count how many times I've had terrible games because the ball just dumps itself down the drain prematurely.  Another important thing is that the game is going to be receiving a visual upgrade in 2014 when the developers release a DirectX 11 patch that adds much more modern lighting support and (hopefully!) texture map resolution bumps.  The game looks great already but these two additions will make the experience even more lifelike and exciting.
I do have some gripes to make about the game however.  Currently there's no support for Steam Friends in game, which is something that Zen Studio's "Pinball FX 2" supports and I miss it.  You are encouraged to make a FarSight Studios account in order to have your scores ranked against other people, but there's something mighty satisfying about seeing your scores compared with people you actually know on Steam, and that's just not present right now.  Another complaint is that the Steam release still shows heavy connections to the Pinball Arcade releases on lower performance hardware (tablets, iphone, Android, etc.).  The game still PLAYS fantastic, but there's a level of spit and polish to the user interface and camera controls that's just not right for a PC game and cheapens the experience.
The last thing I have to say about the base Pinball Arcade experience concerns the Free-to-Play nature of the title.  "Free-to-Play"... eh.... it is and it isn't.  When you download the game from Steam you will be downloading ALL the tables which you can play as long as you want UP UNTIL THE FIRST HIGH SCORE.  This is actually rather generous because it means there's no time's-up-and-you're-locked-out-until-you-buy penalty, and in practice I found that the minimum high score threshold is high enough for you to play for a good amount of time in a single game and it's only when you really start getting your skill up that you find yourself hitting that ceiling.  Once you do starting bumping up to that limit you'll likely have found some favorite tables to play and you can then purchase them individually or all at once via the Season Packs.  There's even one pinball machine you can play forever (Tales of the Arabian Nights) that is extremely fun and definitely not a "throwaway bone" for the FTP monicker.
For all that this offers for free I say check it out right away and see if it finds a place in your heart... there's a lot to love here and I daresay if you're not a pinball fan when you start playing you will be when you're finished.

Always wished there were more RPGs on the Genesis.  I'm glad the guys at WaterMelon shared that opinion so strongly that they made their own.  While the game suffered through development hell (the original Genesis version from my understanding... as well as this HD version which I feel like I waited a year after the scheduled release date to check out), it finally came.  It managed to captivate me in the way RPGs did in my youth.  I honestly didn't think I was going to enjoy it that much.
A few notes:
- Battles are reminiscent of Lunar both in the way of style and challenge.  Areas can seem gimmicky and lack variety in fights up until a boss or change of region, however.
- Sound is wonderful and fitting of the game's environments and mood.  Perfectly done in Genesis style.  The HD music is even better.
- The options to swap between original graphics and HD, as well as original and HD sound are nice.
- Without listing all the reasons, I feel the game has some replay value (I can see 1 or 2 more playthoughs in the future for mehself).  Obviously I'm not looking at it with nostalgia goggles either.
- The characters are likeable, which is good due to the fact you'll be spending quite a few hours with them.
Overall, I'd give it an 8 out of 10.  There's not too many great RPGs on the Genesis, so this game is  welcomed by me.  I'd even go as far as to place it at my number three spot of favorite Genesis RPGs, falling short of only Phantasy Star IV and Shining Force II.  If you're a fan of those titles and also Lunar, then definitely try to pick it up if ya see it on sale, and give it a shot.
Happy Gaming, friends!!

So I held off on reviewing this game until I was completely done with it so I could give a fair and proper judgement, this review is long and will cover mostly things I can't stand about the game. As a JRPG and RPG fanatic in general, I just can't justify telling people to go out and purchase or bother wasting their time playing this game because frankly, you're not missing out on anything at all.
I'm not going to spoil any plot points in this review, but I will be spoiling elements of the game play and areas so you'll understand my frustrations.
It's a fairly standard JRPG plot, it doesn't do anything remotely new or interesting and brings nothing to the table. Same old tired cliches you've seen before but I suppose they were just trying to recreate that nostalgia and archetype's from the golden years of gaming. The three mains are likable enough but the rest of the cast is just kind of there and I didn't really connect with their personalities or designs. The villains are standard garbage stereotypes, not even going to bother getting in to it... They rip off just about every Final Fantasy game in existance, which is just another testament to how unoriginal and uninspired it is.
This game's structure and pacing is a bit of an oddity as it just decides to switch up the formula about half way through. For the first half of the game you basically choose destinations by pressing left or right on the d-pad and it will cycle through the available locales. At about the half way mark the developers just decided to start linking all the dungeons and towns together so it all becomes one giant cluster♥♥♥♥ of a maze.
So you'll get a formula of Town - Dungeon - Side Town - Dungeon - Main Town - Side Dungeon Under Town - Warp to an entirely unrelated area with no way of going back - rinse and repeat for the rest of the game.
It becomes rather tiresome at the 90% mark when you have to walk through previously explored area's just so you can backtrack to pick up items you couldn't access before. There is a warp device given to you late in the game but it doesn't really help, it just allows you access to the previous "chapters" of the game that all seem to be separated by islands that are no longer linked together and must be accessed separately.
The worst feature of the warp device is that you can't just call upon it whenever you feel like, like the airship from Final Fantasy or the Flamme Drum from Secret of Mana... No you actually have to walk ALL the way back to the device and touch it on some arbitrarily placed square on one of the sides of it (it's different in each area) in order to continue on with the game.
This is what I'm talking about when I say the game requires A LOT of polish... Something this important shouldn't be overlooked... It's an essential part of the gameplay and it's confusing and obnoxious as hell to figure out due to lazy programming.
If you're one of those people who enjoy getting 100% completion rates in RPG's... just forget it. There isn't a solid guide on the web because this game is such a sleeper cult game... I can't even use the word "hit" in there because I don't even think it reached those kinds of sales numbers.
Either way, all the secrets in this game are cryptic and obnoxious, invisible walls with zero tells... just start walking in to everything and hope you find something. There are treasure chests in unreachable places that MUST be opened with a spell from a distance... I found this was a major design flaw because some chests I didn't even bother walking to, I would just open them through walls. I found this to be incredibly lame and lazy.
There are hidden dungeons and items, most of which are missable and you can never return to. There are side quests hidden all over the place as well and some won't even open up until certain points in the plot which can be rather annoying... You could talk to everyone in the city but after you trigger a main plot event, the people you talked to could have a quest for you to embark on but you've missed it under the assumption those characters were just background objects filling the cities.
There's also a side quest and a main quest in this game where they place an important NPC against the same coloured backdrop so it's nearly impossible to spot it unless you literally stop in your tracks and scan the area with your eyes... It's probably because of how quickly the game moves when your characters are running... The Genesis was notorious for creating blurred backgrounds due to it's "superior blast processing" >.< LOL.... what a joke.
Just be warned that you'll most likely never find everything in the game, I know I missed a dungeon and I couldn't return back to it because they give you a single opportunity to access it. I missed a side quest some where as well... and quite possibly a shop... even though I was incredibly thorough.
I found all the master keys, never got the achievement for doing so... even though I opened all 8 treasure chests with the ultimate gear. This leads me to believe the "Shop-a-Holic" achievement is also glitched, among some others. Again, more polish required.
Terrible... just a terrible battle system. You have to "charge up" like Goku from DBZ so your characters can multiply their pitiful damage output and you have to have a full "gather" meter to use some of the best spells. If you so much as get hit before your turn comes up, you lose 1 gather and the spell is rendered ineffective. Your character will then miss their turn and spin around like a jack♥♥♥♥♥as to symbolize that they're confused. AWFUL DESIGN.
There's still hope though, you can give away your gather to other party members to help them use their OP attacks but at the cost of missing another characters turn for that round and what's worse, it's all or nothing... You can't just give away 1 or 2 gather... NOPE, you have to give away ALL of it...
So for example, a character requires 5 gather to use an ultimate special attack but the character only has 4, you can then request gather from another party member. However in the likely event that the member that you're requesting from has 5 gather... well you then proceed to steal all of it instead of just using some basic math... because apparently in this game 5 - 1 = 0.   :/    DUMB.
You'll get in to fights every 15 steps... Considering every dungeon in this game is a convoluted maze of eye tricks and illusionary walls, it's just an awful and frustrating mix. There's a spell that helps you avoid fights but it's literally only for about 45 steps and BAM, another fight. This means every 40 or so steps you have to recast the spell and watch some obnoxiously slow spell animation taking place... It becomes clear to me why this game drowned when it first came out in 2004. I wanted to love it, but here is why I couldn´t:
I play on my Win XP rig for authenticity reasons so I can´t give any insight of what issues this game has on modern systems.
Let´s start.
It´s pretty short to begin with if you play it quickly and don´t die too often. You have 13 missions which I each finished in roughly 30 mins. If you have good aim and know your FPS games, you run through this pretty quickly.
Graphicswise the game was ok in 2004, it had all you wished for, a nice jungle environment for example, but I gotta say the animations in the cutscenes are bugged and break immersion, as well as the sound design. While the animations are too fast or too abrupt and buggy when transitioning stances, the sounds often are of different quality, sometimes high quality sounds and then low quality appear next to each other in the effects or voice department, such as marines shouting or explosions. Gun sounds are beefy and done nicely, obviously with most of the sound budget going in there, the rest doesn´t stand out and often even falls too short in terms of quality and atmosphere. Between missions you get characterization in form of letters written from your dad to you and you to your parents with reports of thoughts and what´s going on. Typical war letters which explain situations at home and with your characters streams of thoughts. You play the generic black marine called Dean Shepard. A real story as in cutscenes or plot doesn´t exist. You simply play missions as experiences of an marine. I wasn´t immersed enough to care in terms of story sadly. Vegetation is thick and animated and it feels like jungle even though the corridors are quite obvious. Vietcong gave you a more open feel, sometimes literally being semi open world compared to Men of Valor, and you can feel vietnam shouldn´t be treated to much like a corridor. MoV is straight up widened up corridors and sometimes straight up corridors leading to your objectives. Cutscenes in between chapters are historical flicks presenting information about the vietnam war and your next area of operation. From Khe Sanh to the Tet Offensive. Loading screens are presented with president´s quotes etc. It feels pretty pretentious given that the characters are uncanny valley.
Your squadmates can shoot and move. That´s about it. They have names you forget as the presentation and story can´t keep you thrilled enough to give a s  h  i  t  nor should you. The enemy AI is artificially difficult. They often run past you or keep an blind eye to their path finding or they straight up aimbot you. It happens only occasionally but can get annoying in the worst scenarios, same goes for your squadmates. I´ve seen that hodges guy run past enemy lines too often to care anymore. You can´t give em commands like in vietcong, taking control out of your hands in this game. The guns feel different from many other corridor FPS´s and are fun to shoot with decent animations and models for the time. Objectives are repetitive and barely change from what you see in the first few missions. There are a few decent missions where objectives feel fresh and so does level design, but that is done in the first third of the game and barely ever comes back.
At the second half of the game most spawnpoints in the world are set to solely make you ragequit. You have to carefully advance otherwise you trigger enemy spawns and enemies just spawn all around you and you are cucked without the support of your squadmates. Some buildings have collision detection issues, so do some rocks and enemies themselves. Thankfully barely any trees have. Meaning even when cowering like a   m  o  t  h  e r  f  u  c  k  e  r   behind your rock while you can see the enemy, you can´t hit him as you shoot the rock instead. Sadly you don´t notice it easily, because of the lack of decals such, as bulletholes, which make it hard to get bullet feedback. The enemies themselves give feedback when hit, such with animations and blood, except when in a running animation, in which they barely react at all to your shots but still get hurt.
Another issue is movement speed. You either snail walk or you jog, which is your standard fastest speed and it´s infuriating in dire situations! Make sure you play by the games rules as you can´t jump either and looting enemies takes 2 secs if you can even reach them without running into the enemy directly. You can run out of ammo as well, which means reloading the last checkpoint. You can´t quicksave! So you have to rely on these quite widely spread checkpoints. Which isn´t bad, but not good either.
Some guns have different values as others, the most effective ones are semi auto high caliber rifles such as the SKS and M14, while the M16, CAR 15, Type 56, AK47, RPD, M60, Scoped Mosin and M21, Thompson M1, PPSh 41, are mediocre at best. Many guns are low in terms of accuracy when standing and require you to shoot from a crouching or lying position to enhance your chances of survival, but the sad thing about that is that due to the jungle environment, crouching and lying basically renders you an idiot, as you can´t spot any enemy anymore deu to the high grass! DUH. So using the semi auto modes on those guns is key to survival generally. A deep cut in fun by stupid game design.
Another stupid game design was the aiming and leaning feature. If you aim with your gun you can´t strafe, instead you lean left or right. There are no iron sights, just a zoom with your crosshair. If you manage to adopt to that system, congrats, otherwise you will curse the game designers. You have an option for enabling loose aimpoint, aka rail shooter fixed camera with moveable gun and crosshair, but that´s just for personal preference anyway.
You can´t choose anything besides medium difficulty unless you played the game once, or at least I think that was a bug in my game... I really can´t figure it out. In terms of difficulty balancing the game is f  u  c  k  e  d either. Headshots gets them down pretty easily while everything else is basically the same damage multi. 3 shots in the toes is the same as 3 in the back with most machine guns. Only semi auto only guns with higher caliber are different. They are often 1 hit headshot or 2 hit body shot depending on enemy type. Damage inflicted on you however is broken. You either take small chunks of health when hit or half of it directly which leaves you swearing again and most enemies have the same 7.62 ammo or guns. For health you collect canteens from looting enemies and rarely you find medic kits laying around. If you are hit you need to hold the bandage button so you don´t bleed out too quickly. You can basically restore most of the lost health from the gunshot by doing that, as it fills up the medicus that serves as a health indicator on the left down corner of your screen.
Repetitive, mediocre, flawed designs, unimpressive vietnam game by the leftovers of the game stuiod 2015. It´s more of an Original Xbox diamond than a PC diamond. A decent shooter with a nice promise but mediocre execution. I can not recommend it to anyone who isn´t an FPS veteran, or someone who loves vietnam era games or does care for the things said above.

City of Brass is a first-person action, rogue-lite game set in an Arabian Nights-themed “City of Brass”. Working your way through rooms filled with enemies, traps, and loot, the aim is to complete the 13 levels and get all the treasure. I don’t know what happens then, as I’m nowhere near good enough to succeed as of yet. I’ve played for 10 hours so far and only succeeded in getting halfway through and even that was a struggle. This is a fairly consistent theme for me when it comes to reaction based games.
The gameplay is fairly smooth, with movement consisting of running, jumping crouching and sliding, but alas, no real parkour of any kind. Combat is swift, responsive and satisfying, with a melee weapon, ranged whip and limited throwables. The whip is a lot of fun to use, with the ability to hit enemies in different locations for different results (hit the feet to knock them down, hit the face to blind them etc) as well as the ability to pick throwables up with it. Enemies are fairly diverse, with different strategies required to defeat them. There are lots of different traps, although perhaps a few too many, as sometimes it does feel a little bit like City of Traps. There’s a lot of fun to be had in pushing and pulling enemies into traps, kiting them around and triggering the traps with your whips. Watching them get crushed, spiked, impaled and blown up is always good for a bit of morbid entertainment.
I enjoy the equipment system, as it seems quite varied and can make progression different. This is RNG based, as all the levels and shops are procedurally generated. You pick up loots as you run through the level and then spend it at various shops (genies). There’s a good variety and it does actually make a difference what you buy. Although the levels are tile-generated, they sew together seamlessly and look very natural. It’s not quite the quality you’d get from handcrafted level design, but it’s surprisingly clever and very well done. The random generation is of course what gives the game the majority of its replayability.
It’s described as a rogue-lite, which usually indicates progression upgrades but there aren’t actually that many upgrades that carry through. For someone who is not particularly good at this sort of game, but still enjoys playing them, this really upped both the challenge and frustration level. I like to feel like I’ve achieved something, even if I died. The only thing I’ve discovered that carries through is that every 3 levels you can unlock a portal which allows you to start at a later level in future runs, and there are a few consumables you can purchase which will carry over to 1 future game, but not permanent additions. If I was going to find a complaint with this game, it’s this. My main suggestion for improvement would be more permanent upgrades, even if that’s attached to an “easy mode” for people with granny reflexes, aka myself. Every death was my own fault due to not seeing a trap, not dodging, or simply not reacting in the best way and I’ve not encountered any bugs so far.
The game is Early Access with no release date at present. Priced at £18.99, it is quite a big ask for an early buy-in. However, it’s incredibly well polished, with beautiful graphics and feels quite frankly, fairly complete to me with a respectable amount of playtime available. The daily timed challenge with leaderboards is certainly an incentive to return, but more interesting and unique challenges could make this something people return to even if they’re pros who can complete the game every run. You do unlock “divine burdens” as you play and gain achievements, which make the game even more challenging to complete.
It could certainly have a bit more depth with more items, more enemies, more traps and more rooms and it looks like these are all planned for the future anyway. If I’d played this and been told it was a full release, I’d still be giving it a thumbs up, so I’m pretty satisfied with the Early Access experience here.
I would recommend this game to fans of rogue-lite and one-shot games, but it’ll be of special interest to those who enjoy speedruns and timed challenges as well. Right, I’m going back in for one more try…

More progression would be great, obviously more weapons and abilities, maybe more uses for the whip, and this could be GOTY material. This game has vast potential and is currently great fun to play, and if the developers keep adding new content it could be seriously great.
Short list of things i'd like to see:
More uses for the whip! The whip is already your best friend, but after a whille whipping every enemy's legs becomes the dominant strategy for most encounters. Leg whipping might be a little too powerful in its current state, perhaps two whips and it knocks an enemy down, otherwise it simply staggers them... I also feel there's a lot of potential for HOLD moves, such as holding the weapon attack to charge up a powerful swing, and perhaps you can pick up items from the genies that changes that move to a different move.
HOLDing with the whip could maybe grapple an enemy at a distance, and pressing the alt-fire for the whip could execute another move that can be changed at genies as well.
The combat feels great currently and is interesting, but there's so much potential to add to the depth of combat by varying enemies further and adding additional moves (jump attack, crouch attack, Mouse1 hold, Mouse2 hold, etc..)
Overall i'm very pleased to spend money on a GOOD Early Access game with a bright future
