A rather interesting concept that we don't often see. Works well with 5 friends, not so much with random people. Unless said random people all leave their mics open or join a teamspeak server and share in good laughs when they get freaked out by a monster appearing in front of them or tearing them to pieces.
Ultimately though, this game is lacking variety right now. It is an Alpha, so I will give it that. The gameplay is simple, find the keys or codes to unlock doors or safes to find more keys and codes. Eventually, you'll find a tool to pull wooden boards off of a door. After that door is unlocked you escape from the monster. There are a few maps so far, so it does get repetitive eventually. Withut any dynamic events happening, I don't think it will ever stop being repetitive. Anyways, there are only two monsters aka creatures. One of which is not as fun as the other.
There's the Phantom. Which is the not-so-fun monster. As the Phantom you float around as a half decayed torso imbued with some evil magic or something. You float around decently fast and are allowed to pass through closed doors. Which is the only thing scary about this monster. From only a few play attempts it was clear to me that it was pretty overpowered and did not provide that great of an experience, both for the monster player, nor the character players.
The second and so far final monster, the Lurker is a rather intimidating piece of work. Though when I think about it, I find that it also resembles the Phantom in a way as they share a common trait. They both can get through closed doors. The Lurker is a little more difficult to get through though. There are two phases to this monster. Your "ghost" phase, and your "flesh" phase. In the ghost phase you are unable to see or hear the players, but you're allowed to set traps. The traps range from pianos, to kitchen timers, to creaky boards. Unfortunately there are no visual traps like falling chairs, chandeliers, or candles that would blow out or anything like that. Then if you are near a trap you set that goes off, you click and change into your flesh form for a limited time. In this time you are to chase down and kill the player near you.
For the Alpha that it is. Damned is definitely entertaining. If you are a streamer, this is a good kind of game to play with friends while live. Especially if you're easily scared/really jumpy. But don't play it too much or you'll get bored!
For the Alpha that it is, I give it a 6.5/10.
It definitely needs some updates to add some more fun to it. More creatures, more maps, and hopefully eventually some more dynamism.

A legendary game. I'm not usually the kind of person to pick up a game I played 5+ years ago and play it through again with much enthusiasm, but this game is one of the exceptions. It had been over 15 years since I originally played this game yet I was very excited to start playing Commandos: BEL again. And it managed to keep my motivation up from the beginning until the very end. It's a great mix of stealth/tactics/suspense with some action. The controls still felt good (remembered a lot of the hotkeys too!) And I like that it's not too short and easy as many games of the same type nowadays tend to be, the difficulty and length are just right. I even still loved the graphics (something that I can't usually say about old games).
The only minor negative thing that comes to mind is that you can't enter the last mission unless you got good enough ranks from the other missions. As I liked to take my sweet time to indulge myself in nostalgia and often planned the missions perfectly, I didn't manage to get the ranks needed to enter the last mission. And as much as I loved playing the game, I wouldn't have had the motivation to start playing through the missions again, so it's good that there's a cheat code for entering the last mission. Minor issue, otherwise the game is 10/10 in my books. Get it when it's dirty cheap on sale with the other Commandos games.

The second installment of the Penumbra series that picks up immediately after the end of Penumbra Overture.  Right off the bat, the mere menu screen with it's dark, grimey visuals and it's deteriorated, darker music fills you with the dread of the horrors that await you, making you realize that everything is getting worse and more hopeless for our main protagonist.  Not much has changed gameplay-wise, keeping the scares high as ever, except now, that terrible combat system in Overture has been completely removed.  You will also find yourself meeting a new support character and an unexpected antagonist that evolves psychologically in the player's mind that not enough games have been able to pull off with their bad guys.  To be perfectly honest, I enjoyed this game more than Amnesia and I hope anyone who has played Amnesia will feel like this one will stack up nicely to it.

First of all, I'm biased - the Tomb Raider games have always had a big place in my heart, but from "Angel of Darkness" to "Underworld" I had been a little crestfallen that objectification had taken over a little (don't get me wrong I enjoyed them too but not as much as the originals).
This game more than redeems the franchise for me - Lara is a believable character with intelligence, faults, fears, realistic measurements (for once) and only ever oversteps the line into violence when people she loves are in danger. I can never watch the beginning with that VERY painful drop but it showed a strength of determination in her refusal to give up that you just don't get when you have lots of guns and plentiful ammo - and even though you do grab a gun and fight, it's purely in self defence. This time you have to survive against literally all odds with whatever you can scavenge.
A little more on her character: the backstory with her friends and the expedition was a poignant backdrop the entire time, wondering if you can actually save everyone, or even yourself. Her grief and self-doubt can make her appear a little mary-sue-ish at first glance when you don't know her character, but you sharp realise that when nobody else can or will, Lara steps up and would (and does) risk her life for others without hesitation. Lara is strong willed but doesn't have to sacrifice her femininity or warm personality during the unfolding of the story - you start the game as her, you end the game as her.
Not only has this earned my respect for story-writing, feminism, and playability, but this game should literally be held as a true classic that can be mentioned in the same breath as the original games proudly.
Also, plays on Linux - more of this please!

Imagine if Flappy Bird had even fussier controls, an environment where hitboxes make less sense, and an energy meter that exists only to inhibit the player's progress. That's this game.
The bird is so fat that flying it through some of the incredibly narrow, forested areas is like driving a dump truck through a grocery store aisle- it's just not going to fit.
The game's tap system is very erratic and if you tap too quickly, you will find yourself rocketing 30,000 feet high, it'll make some stupid noise and it'll be game over.
A speed system is incorporated via every 8 coins collected, your speed will increase by a tenth, which then makes it like driving a dump truck through a grocery store aisle at 100 mph.
There are several glitches that I had the fortune of coming across, but the one that stood out the most was: sometimes when you hit the ceiling or the water, the bird will land and keep sliding through the level, endlessly, but the timer will have already ended; there is no in-game restart button, so your only option is to restart the game itself.
I happened to actually enjoy the music for the most part, though it can get a little too analogesque at certain points, and the atmosphere of the game is very pretty, but the good qualities, unfortunately, do not redeem the game of its bad qualities.

Orbt XL is not just Not one of the worst things that ever happened; it’s actually quite good.
In Orbt XL, the player begins as the Earth, orbting a black hole. And when the player doesn’t hold down the game’s one button, the Earth orbts in towards said black hole; while when the player holds the button, the Earth orbits away from the same, big, naughty black hole.
I like black holes, for the record. Holes in general.
And because it may seem like my taste for holes may be coloring my opinion, I want to take this moment to emphasize that that’s not why I’m recommending this game. Though, if you like holes the way I do, then there’s that.
The game also features an excellent scoring system, and various deadly objects hurtling straight towards that beautiful black hole. Meanwhile, said scoring system works by awarding you points at a faster rate the closer you are to said hole, which is in the center of everything, the screen that is. And, ratcheting up the thrills, is that orbting close to the hole is dangerous, if you know what I mean ;)
I mean that you could get so mesmerized by the hole’s beauty that you fail to hold down the button, and thus get sucked in, ending your run. Plus, when you’re orbting close to the hole (which is the center of all that matters) you have less Space to dodge incoming Space Matter, with which near misses award you extra points, but with collision destroying the Earth.
And all this is brilliant, both in a gameplay sense and in a meaning sense.
For the Earth is our home. It is our existence.
It is fragile.
Yet, it’s imaginable that we and our Earth might be special enough that the Apocalypse gets postponed. And we can go on enjoying holes for a very long and hard time. Orbt XL is saying that, if we focus, and get good, we can perform some amazing hole action (a high score) before the end finally arrives. Simultaneously the game is saying that, if we want to have fun in our finite lives, well we're just going to have to orbt close to that black hole, and flirt with the planets and comets and other space matter, who themselves exist so dangerously that they plunge straight into the hole without delay, lacking all self-restraint when shown the amazing, throbbing hole, that is black.
[Speaking of throbbing, there’s a space object in the game that I particularly like, which temporarily enlarges the hole! And then it gets tight again! Neat stuff!]
So Orbt XL is charged with meaning, meaning about both existence at the cosmic level, and at that of the individual’s. And on top of this, it really sucked me in, and not just into the hole, which, again, expands when a certain object enters it; I got sucked into the gameplay itself!
All thoughts of my life left my mind as I tried to increase my score, and see how often I could barely pass by space matter, and see how long I could orbt the hole.
But, what keeps Orbt XL from being a classic is that I laughed zero times while playing it; and I smiled just a few times. The game often had me in a state of Flow, and had me think about the ultimate purpose of life, but not much more.
And that’s fine. As Orbt XL is really good, and most-certainly worth half-an-hour of your time. It certainly is a great step forward in the development of its developer (Adam). He’s clearly on track towards making a great game. And though his previous game Bit Blaster XL may have been like seeing your pet python eat your dog, it was definitely effective practice, much like a first child. And though I feel like his not including other colors of holes (such as white, brown, and asian) is an obvious missed opportunity, I have no difficulty awarding Orbt XL a score of:
8/10

I just got this game from the sale, paid for the deluxe edition, and so far the game is awesome, I only have a couple complaints about the game but that is about it.
Pros:
Great graphics (not much to really talk about here)
The character movement feels nice and intuitive as well as immersive, walking through the city listening to music while I hack passerbys is surprisingly fun
The city itself is immersive, the city feels real, stores, builboards, advertisements, people holding their own conversations, (saw a guy get tossed out of his home by his wife because he was watching porn, kind of funny to see the fight and her throwing his stuff at him) there are minigames littered all over the city which are fun to play, I walked into a park and there was a guy playing a shell game calling people over, it was surprisingly difficult, but there wasnt any cheating done by the devs to make it hard, your able to follow the ball once your eyes adjust to the speed. Also as a hacker your able to hack peoples phone calls and texts, can lead to some pretty funny stuff, or some pretty cool equipment.
The controls feel good, after a few minutes of messing around I was running through the city parkouring and hacking like I had been doing it my whole life. The controls are completely customizable, but I haven't found a reason yet to change anything.
Performance is good, I am running everything on max settings, no frame drops, hiccups, or other irritating things.
Online mode is nice, so far I have had a couple of encounters and they all were entertaining, trying to chase down a player after he tried to hack me, or I in-turn having to hide because I tried to hack someone else, I ended up getting chased through the city and had to escape by boat.
Story is decent I have not really gotten into it, I am still in the first chapter of the story (got sidetracked by all the cool stuff in freeroam) so far, the characters are enjoyable, the story itself is your typical revenge story, however, the writing and characters have made me feel deeply saddened one moment then cracking up the next, so along with freeroam the story completes the game and makes it extremely fun.
In freeroam there is a ton of stuff to do if your willing to take your time and enjoy it, I think you will love this game. There really isn't any downtime in freeroam, unless you ignore everything, there is either a crime going on or a contract or various other events that are happening in the city, and ctOS tells you about them and where to go do them. However sometimes you don't need ctOS to tell you, I was walking through a park heading towards a guy on his phone, going to listen to his call, when suddenly out of no where some guy starts shooting and then runs off with the shell game guys money, next thing I know I give chase, running through the park, streets and even a shop chasing this guy as he shoots at me (playing vigilante so I try not to shoot back) eventually I tackle the guy, hit him with my asp a few times, take the money he stole and walk back to the shop we ran through and buy some coffee, if you take your time and walk through the world, you will find it is quite alive.
Cons: I really only have a couple of cons here.
Driving, the driving in this game is a little difficult to get used to, Aiden seems to have a led foot, because you tap the accelorator and the car peels out, tap the brake and your tires lock and you slide to a screeching halt, but after I got used to it I was drifting through the city like any other game, though I'm sure the original owners of the cars I steal dont care for how often I crash lol.
The last con isn't all that big of a deal, just a minor annoyance and that would be Uplay, having to download Uplay is slightly annoying but not a deal breaker for me.
So all in all I would give this game a 9/10, I deffinately recommend buying this game, get in-game, make a playlist, listen to music, start walking through the streets, hacking, shooting, driving and overall just enjoying freeroam at the very least.

This feels very awkward, as this is my first time reviewing... anything, at least publicly. So let's read how a socially awkward person writes a review for possibly hundreds to see openly, shall we?
I am a moderate player of magic, I know probably 70-80% of the mechanics to be classified as a decent player, and Magic 2014 has taught me more about a game I've already been playing for the past several years. New understanding to certain mechanics I've been fuzzy about or didn't understand when to do what, when, etc. If you are looking to get into playing magic, but don't want to invest in the paper game, and want to learn, this game is definitely for you, and a lot cheaper to start you off on.
I thoroughly enjoy playing this game, having paid a fraction of the cost of the full price, which is a huge plus in of itself. The amount of decks to play with, I still have a lot of decks to plays through, to see how my skills compare to many of the older "meta" decks that used to be, and still are, very popular. If you are astonished by the amount of different cards in this game, you should see what the card archive on the MTG website has, literally thousands upon thousands, dating a couple decades back. With the amount of selection you have in Magic 2014, unless you are someone who plays this all day, you will have plenty to do on here, a sizeable compaign for the price paid (a little bit extra if you bought the expansion), with several different game modes, it will keep you busy for at least a little while. Having a little over 60 hours, I've only touched 1 deck thus far, out of 21. So if you are looking for quantity over quality, you don't have to choose, you get both for a much cheaper price than starting yourself off with paper cards.
A few minor gripes about this game, aside from your inability to actually build your own custom deck, which appears to be the biggest complaint about every other game, aside from the horribly rated Magic 2015 (the only seemingly good thing about 2015), is some of the decks that already pre-made, are broken in terms of how strong they are (card symmetry, strength of individual cards), where some decks just can't compete with others without drawing a really incredible starting hand. I myself have had to constantly restart duels, simply because the deck you are facing tends to have very powerful starting hands, or you seem to have every single action countered immediately, essentially forcing you to restart to not waste your time with a very bad start. While some decks seem overpowered based on their card mechanics and how well the deck is simply put together, there are others that are just the opposite, having such a slow start with horrible hands that you either have to restart, or just save yourself the stress and pick another deck to try your luck. There are also times, during Two-Headed Giant mode, 2v2 matches, the AI partner I have seems to always have a♥♥♥♥♥♥hand, while facing that same AI controlled deck, they draw beautiful hands that essentially win the game in under 10 turns. Whether it's due to the difficulty settings, I'm not sure, but it gets annoying losing to the same pair of AI opponents over and over, taking a break afterward. I have also noticed that I can unlock all but 10 cards for the one deck I've been playing most frequently. Whether those cards are hidden behind a paywall, I'm not sure on that either, but if that's the case, that is kind of upsetting, considering a lot of the great cards are in that block of 10 that I can't seem to unlock, and I'd rather not pay extra for a few extra virtual cards. I have paper decks to fall back on whenever this gets too much. Also, for me anyways, the game does crash out to the desktop from time to time, although not enough for it to be game-breaking.
Pros:
-Solid gameplay
-Numerous decks to play with
-Multiple game modes
-Tons of cards to get a new person acquainted
-Decent tutorial for beginners
-Lots of content in general for much cheaper than paper starting kits
Con:
-Seemingly overpowered/underpowered decks
-Derpy AI at times
-Inability to create your own decks from cards you unlock
-Occassionally crashes out from time to time (experience may vary)
All in all I give this game a 9/10. Great game to start you off into playing Magic, and much cheaper in the long run, unless you become more interested, and want to play in paper form too. If you can handle the few minor previously mentioned issues that I experienced, then this game might be a 10/10 for you. I know I enjoyed this game for the amount I paid, and I still do, and have no plans on stopping anytime soon. Good luck, and have fun everyone.

La-Mulana is a wonderfully difficult metroidvania-game of riddles, with challenging bosses, and a huge game to explore.
There is so much to discover and unfold in the game, part of the fun is finding out how to obtain a new treasure or find a new area to explore. The platforming physics are a bit wonky at first, and can mess up the gaming logic in your head, but it feels fair as you learn how to adapt to it (For example : In-game, if you jump moving right, you can only move right, but if you jump up without moving left or right, you can control your jump more. Also, touching a wall while jumping in a direction can give you back your aerodynamic control).
The main challenge of the game is solving these huge riddles that can really stump you if you don't have a guide, and at times, you might need to look at every aspect of details, or every word the game conveys, just because it can be very vital for solving these challenging puzzles. Aside from the riddles, the game isn't that difficult until you start reaching certain areas (especially in the early-game), or fight bosses (then again, if you're as skilled in video games as I am, hard mode isn't as hard as it seems, despite the extra deaths (which is all apart of the fun in a game)).
At the time of this review, I feel like I'm near mid-game, but I still feel like I just scratched the surface. The soundtrack is amazing, the satisfaction of solving a overly arching riddle is trumendous, and the bosses are quite challenging to fight. I highly recommend this game to the few that won't give up.
(Also, if you're not sure about this game, there is a free version available looming around the internet with older graphics and slightly more frustrating moments, and equally great soundtrack. Just remember to patch the english translations, otherwise you'll get stumped quite easily)(Another thing I'd like to mention is that the official guide for this game is actually super useful!)

A 2D Non-Linear Exploration Action Platformer, or as many call, a "Metroidvania". La Mulana is one of the few games which could be considered a work of art - that is, we aren't just talking about story and graphics here like many games lauded as art are praised for - the entirety of this piece of work is a masterwork of the craft of game design.
Gameplay will challenge and push players to their limits, and encourage discussion among peers to discover it's many secrets. Graphics and story are basic yet without any glaring flaws. Music is catchy, and captures the mood of every location and event perfectly.
Controls may seem stiff at first, but the even a casual player will be able to get used to them, especially since the levels are designed around them. Some puzzles may be too tough to solve solo, and while taking notes down old school style is encouraged, some may be discouraged by the lack of taking in-game notes (bar the ability to log down a number of clues). However, none of these minor setbacks add up nor will bog a player down for long.
All explorers, Metroidvania fans, and fans of "hard" games will surely enjoy this remake of the classic indie.
This is the game that started the whole "It's like Dark Souls" trend meme despite it's original freeware version existing years before Demon Souls even.

"Obtuse" is a word that another reviewer used to describe this one, and it could very well be a one-word review. Anyhow...
La-Mulana is a beautifully made game (esp. environment art, music, boss design) and has a lot of fun aspects, but in my opinion it ultimately falls victim to its own sense of smugness. I actually didn't mind the control scheme, which is essentially a modified version of Castlevania's, with weapon-specific timing, pushback when getting hit, and unalterable directional jumping (except when descending from a standstill jump). It's pretty easy to get used to if you've played enough games of that era.
I also don't mind many of the "puzzles" (which I think could be more accurately described as riddles). What ended up nudging me toward not recommend the game was the implementation of the riddles. After about the third or fourth areas, you start finding heaps of increasingly cryptic clues that won't be introduced for nearly another whole half of the game and often refer to far-off places (also true for many diases and events which trigger distant environment changes that you subsequently have to hunt for). This is the main design element that necessitates the tedious manual note-taking that the developer gleefully encourages. It also has the effect of (rather artifically) increasing the game's perceived difficulty. To me, this didn't really have the seemingly intended effect of inspiring the required devotion of time and manual energy to figure out most of the game on my own, but instead kinda transformed the experience into what increasingly felt like a menial task. Very glad that there are a variety of guides to reduce the tedium, otherwise my patience would have worn off long before finishing the game.
Glad I got it on a good sale. For now, I'm having more fun just challenging the bosses in the time attack mode.

Tactics 2: War is a great real-time strategy. Putting you on the ground, under the sea, and in the air. Large, destructible, open maps grant the freedom to strategize, as well as 'pick your stand' as it were.
The gameplay is solid, balanced, and is optimized fairly well. I experienced no FPS drops.
Tactics 2: War also allows the player to seamlessly take control of any unit owned on the field.
The ability to go first person a nice touch, giving another element of realism to battles. (Though third person, and the default 'free camera' are great in their own right.)
The AI can be surprisingly difficult, actually challenging the player in huge battles. (There are difficulty settings.) This, along with a good variety of units, adds to the replayability of Tactics 2: War.
However, the one thing I would like to see changed is the menu UI. I was a bit put off at first because of this, but let me assure you, it does not subtract from the excellent gameplay in the slightest.
In addition, the fact there is no multiplayer (Yet, Dev stated it is planned.) is a real bummer.
All in all, Tactics 2: War is a great real-time strategy, rich in fun and replayability.

As an adult gamer, Commandos is still challenging as hell! But it's also fun as hell and very accessible for a modern gamer.

This game is pretty awesome. I bought this on a 'wim' simply because it seemed to have a good story, was sci-fi-esk and had Rutger Hauer in it. Seemed like it had a good start to it, so I decided to try it out. Not often that such a thing happens, so I thought 'why not'?
It's one of the best games I have played, There are some nitpicky things, which I'll get to a bit later.
First the good things:
The game really focusses on the atmosphere, and that's great. It sets up the relationship between Dan and his son Adam pretty early on. You can sense immediately from the start there is something that is not right between the two of them.
That's not the only thing that's being set up and executed well. Another thing is that I was thoroughly spooked through the entire game. It's odd to explain, but while not many things happenedg, at the same time loads of things happened.
It is mostly tension building, and while a few things here and there do happen, you're not in any real danger for most of the time. The feeling of said tension, the atmosphere building is just so well done, it all accumulated to a good experience overall.
Generally I don't like to play horror or spooky games, but I'm very happy to have played this game.
It plays with your mind a lot, bringing up a variety of questions that we experience in today's world and what we might experience in the future as well. What choices will you make throughout this game?
Choices are important, as it turns out there are multiple endings!
For example (and to avoid spoilers): Nearing the end you have a choice to either listen or not listen to someone. You can walk away or do your Observing thing. Not gonna spoil, but I'll say it's darn interesting :wink:
Furthermore I appreciate the autosaving function. It helps quite a lot that you don't have to pause the game to save, keeping you thus in the game's atmosphere the whole time.
However, here is where I also have an issue with it...
So now on to the negative things:
A thing that somewhat bugs me is that you cannot load up a save from a certain point. Meaning: If I wanted to go back to make a different choice to explore all endings, or simply to look around an area because I want to make sure I didn't miss anything (e.g. Patient Cards), I have to replay the whole game to get to that same point.
At the very least one autosave slot and one to three manual save slots. That way you can simply move on with the main game you're playing (maybe saving before making one choice or another), and when you've reached one of the endings of the game, you can choose from one of your manual save points and select the other choice(s).
It's really something nitpicky, but seeing how you can get achievements for these eendings and other choices, it feels a bit -perhaps the incorrect words- 'unfair' to play through the entire game again.
I also came across a bug, or perhaps glitch I should say. It is near the end of the game.
Since I have recorded the game in its entirety, I can easily post the time to the video once it's up. However, until then I shall try to explain as best as I can what and where it happened. I'll put a spoiler up just in case, but even in the spoiler I try to keep it as vague as possible:
Another glitch/bug is when you listen to recordings. You can walk and such, but if you're thinking of doing anything else besides that? Don't. It'll end the recording you've been listening to. It's a shame, I think the recording should just play on while you're exploring the room you would be in. I can understand if it would stop when you would leave the room, but that doesn't happen either. I think I wanted to crouch at the time, but that stopped the recording, which seems like a bit of an odd feature.
Before Observer got an update it was running fine. Since it got updated it's been randomly jittery/stuttery. It's not the game's atmosphere either, it's actually running less smoothly. It's a shame, because it takes me out of the feel of the game a bit. What has been fixed is the resolution issue. While the original issue seems to have been resolved: staying in the 'original' resolution after I shut the game off and start it up again later. As if it completely forgot about what resolution I selected previously. This is something it now remembers.
However I can't seem to share screen anymore since the update. I understand most to nearly no one shares their screen while playing, however I do via Discord. Before I could share the screen via Discord with a friend of mine so he could see what I was doing. Now when the game starts up, whether I'm screen-sharing or not, the game seems to 'stutter' during the Photosensitivity warning, something it didn't do before. While I screen-share it is at this point the screen-share turns entirely black.
Original resolution issue was fixed, but a different one seems to have emerged ^^;
The last issue I have requires another spoiler tag.
The game for me is one of the greatest game-experiences ever.
The only real issue I have is that you have to play through the entire game again to make the different choices.
Besides that though, the game captures the psychological thriller/horror themes extremely well. It provides some intriguing questions and some answers, but it's mostly an all 'figuring-it-out-for-yourself' experience in the end of it all. While some things are pretty self-explanatory, at the same time the game says: What do these things mean to you? That is what is so great about it. You can interpret it how you want to or just be led by the facts the game provides. It gives security and self-doubt at the same time. Combining it with horror elements is what makes this game a true psychological horror.
I'll be looking forward to these guys making another game exploring such elements in different ways.

Pinball Arcade has a single mission: To bring back original classic pinball tables with faithful remakes so that all can enjoy them. Not only do they stick to their promise of authetic tables, they deliver an extremely satisfying experience with them too.
Pinball Arcade is classified as "Free to Play" with an initial free offering with "Tales of the Arabian Nights" table that is in no way limited. You have a full table that happens to be one of the most popular tables ever made! The table in itself is certainly a dream to play on with changing skill-shots and a number of stories that you progress through as you play.
Other tables are available for purchase which will provide for many other experiences. My absolute favorite table, "Cirqus Voltaire" is bundled in with the also-amazing "Funhouse" which is probably the easiest $5 to spend on anything in this set.
The physics feel great, and with the recent addition of vibration through Xbox 360 controllers (or other controllers), it gets as close to playing the original thing as you can get. Visually a lot of these tables are not only faithful, but extremely good looking, the post processing alone giving the harsher glare that I remember from the original table in itself, and even better is that care was made to ensure that the dot-matrix-display was embedded in "Cirqus Voltaire" as it should be.
The one downside at the moment is that there is no "cabinet" orientation, meaning that for the time being the tables will have to be played in a standard aspect ratio (4:3, 16:9, 16:10). It has been said that there will be an update that not only offers a cabinet orientation, but that it will also use dual screens so that the game can be used in dedicated virtual pinball cabinets with one simulating the table, and the other simulate the backboards.
This is an extremely well done simulator for pinball. While competitors may be good with their own works, Pinball Arcade flies by in a stunning fashion with licensed tables that are faithful, beautiful, and always work. There's more to come too, with the possibilities of "The Addams Family" and other major tables coming in as well!

This game is somehow manages to be as addicting (and life sucking) as games of the genre of Clash of Clans, the kind that you make a base online, with other players. Despite there being no real incentive to log on, as the base does not change without you, you still can't stop playing! It's a tremendous amount of fun, and I like the way it uses fairly realistic technology, or at least technology that will be developed within the next 50 years or so. One thing that I do have to say is that the AI's stupidity is just mind boggling. I've heard of engineers getting trapped by building connections around themselves, and in my base, colonists have starved to death walking from canteen to canteen, stopping midway because somebody took their meal. This became such a large problem that I would personally reccomend always making sure that your food infrastructure can support at least 2-3 times the amount of colonists you actually have. I think it wouldn't take anything from the game to work out those kinds of small things. Also, I'd appreciate being able to station guards at airlocks. Another annoying detail is the fact that the AI do not know how to coordinate to eat, work, and rest intelligently, which becomes a problem when I have 30 engineers, 8 actual job slots for them, and yet half those job slots sit empty most the time, or when I've had medics just sit around in hallways while people die in the sick bay. Lastly, I'd really appreciate the option to play this multiplayer. I get that it would be a large change to the game, but you could have two seperate modes, single and multiplayer. It would be interesting how you would account for attacking other players, as, realistically, a single bullet would pierce the airtight sheild and kill everyone inside. I'm sure there would be a way to work this out, just a matter of deciding to do to or not.

My Review
I - Story
You are one of "15" students that are trapped in a school and that are basically given the choices to:
a ) Accept living there forever
b) Kill someone to leave
Once a killing happens you are given some time to gather clues and then you enter a class trial to find the killer. If you pick the wrong person everyone but the killer is executed and the killer gets to leave. If you find the killer they alone are executed and the others continue living in the school. Its unique.
II - Characters
All of the characters have depth within the game. By talking to them and giving them gifts they give you more information about their lives. Even after learning about them and completing all the free time events I wanted to know more which I’d recommend that you play school mode and read the translated Danganronpa light novels if you want more information on some characters. Also both the Japanese and English voices are amazing (but if you intend on watching Danganronpa 3 then I’d recommend you enjoy the Japanese voices because in the anime dub some of the English voice actors don’t return for their roles).
III - Gameplay
There are two different gameplays. In the first one you walk around the school and talk with your friends. You can give them gifts that will help you learn about them (if the character likes the gift). Once a murder has taken place you must find clues. /These parts can drag if you are not interested in the lack of action but the other gameplay makes up for the action/ The Trials will have you shoot "Truth Bullets", which are all the clues you gathered in the investigation mode, at false statements, answer questions, and try to compose small sentences with letters. Truth be told, those are the best moments of the game.
My rating 10/10

is (more or less) a visual novel about a woman named Jill working at a hole-in-wall bar in a distant cyberpunk future. Whatever you think that means, you're probably wrong; this game defied my expectations at every turn, challenging the standards for how games can tell stories.
avoids using its sci-fi setting as a crutch to build a compelling narrative, and instead places the focus entirely on the characters of Jill's world. You only learn about the dystopia-like events unfolding around her through word-of-mouth, and whatever news articles she reads on her tablet between shifts. Corrupt government officials are oppressing the public, terrorism is rampant, innocent people are dying, but all of that is put to one side as Jill just tries to get by and make another month of rent. This in turn changes the story's framing from
to
. While subtle, it makes a big difference in how believable her life is.
As mentioned earlier, the characters are easily the best selling point of the game; I can imagine an entirely different game about each of the customers that stumble their way into
. The absurdity of each character is subverted by how real the game makes them. Dororthy, for example: She's a sentient robotic lolita ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ (seriously why is that censored, she sells sex), it doesn't get much more ridiculous than that. And yet, she just seemed like a normal person that loves her job and wants to make people happy. Let's not forget the part-time talking Shiba, he's a pretty rad dude. Or Streaming-Chan, the natural evolution of Twitch-IRL, who streams her
for thousands of viewers at all times (bathroom and naughty bits cost extra).
Dialogue feels natural for the most part, with a heavy helping of humor and sassy quips from Jill. However, it is clear that the humor is largely a coping mechanism for the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ hands each customer was dealt in life. There is also a lot of "waifu-ism" pushed into the game (sometimes seiously and sometimes as a joke), which can be a plus or minus depending on your tastes.
And of course, let's not forget about the drink serving*, which serves to add some spice and keep you engaged in all the dialogue. Customers will request drinks and you have an interface to look up recipes and mix them. While not exactly dialogue trees, changing up what you serve to the customers (adding more alcohol for example) can sometimes have an impact on how much people are willing to open up to you (or not). Don't be fooled though
The jukebox is a neat feature as well, letting you setup a playlist of beats to spice up each of your bartending days. The music is surpisingly good, mostly chiptune-y music that helps support the retro theme of the game. I especially enjoyed the song
.
Like all visual novels, the game won't appeal to everyone. But, if you want a rich narrative with characters that feel like real people, take a seat at the bar and enjoy the ride.
*
: There are keyboard shortcuts for serving drinks, which makes the process much easier than using the mouse. QWERT for drink components, AS for ice/aging, and spacebar to mix/blend the drink. Also, try pushing some other buttons, something interesting might happen :)

It is really hard to explain why I enjoyed VA-11 Hall-A so much; it is just what the description says it is, "a booze em' up about waifus, technology, and post-dystopia life."
Of course if anyone heard that description, they'd be left with most likely confusion and might even be turned away from the game, thinking its some waifu dating visual novel or something. However, VA-11 Hall-A is so much more than that, and I'll try to describe it as I experienced it.
To me, VA-11 Hall-A is an extremely calming game, that I spent many hours playing comfortably in my chair with a nice cup of coffee, hot chocolate, or whatever drink felt cozy at the time.
Sitting for hours, just listening to the stories of the characters, while feeling connected through the enjoyably creative drink making system, made the whole experience just comfortable and enjoyable.
So while its very hard to accurately convey what this game is like, I will say that I recommend anyone to at least try it; if you don't enjoy the first hour or so, you probably won't enjoy the rest and can refund it there; however, if you do enjoy it, then buckle up, grab a nice drink, and get ready for a wonderful experience with all VA-11 Hall-A has to offer you.
You won't regret it.

I am surprised this game does not have enough attention to be reviewed. I played this game in 2016 and I still view this game as one of the most engaging stories ever. As usual when it comes to visual novel games I can't really spoil the entire plot of the story, but I can summarize enough to let you know why you should own this game.

You are Jill working as a bartender, an average person living in a cyberpunk setting. You are not a superhero, you don't fight enemies, there is no saving the world, there is none of that. You are merely serving drinks to average folk and you are living your life normally...I love it so much. I guess because I play so many games about saving the world and just focus on my team or myself, I never stop to wonder about the average Joe in a normal life. I love it because you get to relax in a somewhat quiet setting serving drinks and talking to people. Being a bartender is such a brilliant idea because usually, the "stereotype" of bartenders is that they usually are the people who know people's stories. You get to meet unique characters from the cyberpunk world who you will grow to love
You will read Jill's thoughts about each character she interacts with and each line of dialogue is either funny or memorable. Now obviously when I said there is no danger at all in this game it doesn’t mean that mean there is’nt conflict, otherwise it would be quite boring in a storyteller setting. The music is by far one of the best soundtracks to listen to and it never gets old, I absolutely love to listen to it every time and try to set up music where it fits the mood of the scenes....even if some are oddly misplaced.
What makes this visual novel unique is that you get to do stuff besides reading. The bar mechanic is a neat way to keep the reader on their toes and active, you get to mix the correct ingredients to make the drink. If you mess it up you have to start over, if you made a drink but not the correct one you will be deducted from your payment. If you keep losing more money you won't have enough money to pay your apartment. The engagement of reading and playing the game is not new,  in fact if I can recall Phoenix Wright did it and I love it because it’s always better to physically do something while reading rather than just reading. Some visual novels pull it off with the story because making a visual novel that is both eye-appealing and story engaging is actually hard. With VA-11 Hall-A it has one of the most beautifully written stories I have ever read. The world that Jill interacts with makes me wish I could be part of it, despite how troublesome Glitch City is. Which leads me to my next point; I wanted to explain why this game succeeds in exposing a good world building, while at the same time showing how a dystopian setting is done right from a writer's perspective.
When I say what makes a good dystopian setting I did
mean that all games that portray the concept are all bad. It can work when you just want to play the good guy and be the savior. However, this idea concept of either an authoritarian have been use often recently in video games. Games that show the world being oppress by an all-powerful figure like City 17 in Half-Life 2. The idea is fun,but have been use common recently. When writing a dystopian setting writers usually inspire themselves from the famous Orwellian setting. Whether is a totalitarian or authoritarian it follows an easy premise to the story. The hero will rise from people feeling oppress and you must restore hope, this is fine if you are willing to write a simple plot from point A to B. Although this creates recycle ideas that ultimately will be oversaturate. Making a different type of dystopian story is challenging when you are most familiar with the Orwellian plot. It isn't the issue of
the issue is, writers will develop a dependent on using this plot point easily laid out on creating a world where you need to fill their souls with hope. Which eventually leads to lazy writing on a boring predictable set piece and slowly discourage new ideas that limits the game to think outside of its usual environment and VA-11 does it perfectly.
To clarify, the game does not really have an antagonist, although I guess you could say the world is your antagonist but it does not directly show that it is against you. The citizens of Glitch City live normally like actual people but they have problems of their own. Actual problems that are similar and portray our real-world situation in reality, where we know the world is not perfect but we just keep calm and carry on with our business. The bar is the place where people unwind their troubles and share their experiences with either Jill or other friends. It creates this sense of
where even if life throws us s*** we wipe it off and move on with our life. The dystopian world they portray is more of an independent problem rather than a common problem to everyone. Yet despite their troubles they seem to create this sense of
where they can relate to a problem and try to coop with it. Do they fix their own problems? Not always, but they can comfort each other when troubles are ahead which creates a tighter bond. This is exactly where a dystopian setting is done differently than the rest because you can make different types of dystopian settings where it is not limited to “oh I’m being oppressed." The people around you are believable which makes you relate to them, their world makes it organic which makes it more believable in a dystopia world rather than to argue that a utopian world is more believable. Now I heard this game has a similar comparison to Papers Please so let me clarify a bit on those two games.
While I do understand that these two share similar features on "the average Joe" trying to earn its living by working in a dystopian world I will say yes both share sort of the same premise of how the dystopian world would look like in real life. However, that ends here because I don't get why they say VA-11 is a copy-paste of papers please which let me say this: no it is not. Papers, please has an atmosphere of dread as you work which is consistent with the setting of their world. Va-11 is a more "relaxing" setting when doing your duties. Papers, please has a timer, Va-11 does not, the way it interacts with people is different, the story plays out differently. All in all, it shares some ideas but ultimately it is in their own unique ways different.
If I did the review in 2016 it would have been game of the year stamp no questions asked. In fact, I think by the time this review is out it will be my one year anniversary playing this game. I can see a bit of complaint where the bar mechanic can get tedious, as it does not add more features or difficulty to the gameplay. But I would argue that it is mostly a game to relax and enjoy the experience it provides, Instead of this mechanic being in the main game I feel it should be a bonus feature where you quickly serve drinks to customers without looking at your handbook. That would create a sense of replayability just like Papers, Please did. I give this a score of 10/10 GOTY.

La-Mulana is a beautifully made game (esp. environment art, music, boss design) and has a lot of fun aspects, but in my opinion it ultimately falls victim to its own sense of smugness. I actually didn't mind the control scheme, which is essentially a modified version of Castlevania's, with weapon-specific timing, pushback when getting hit, and unalterable directional jumping (except when descending from a standstill jump). It's pretty easy to get used to if you've played enough games of that era.
I also don't mind many of the "puzzles" (which I think could be more accurately described as riddles). What ended up nudging me toward not recommend the game was the implementation of the riddles. After about the third or fourth areas, you start finding heaps of increasingly cryptic clues that won't be introduced for nearly another whole half of the game and often refer to far-off places (also true for many diases and events which trigger distant environment changes that you subsequently have to hunt for). This is the main design element that necessitates the tedious manual note-taking that the developer gleefully encourages. It also has the effect of (rather artifically) increasing the game's perceived difficulty. To me, this didn't really have the seemingly intended effect of inspiring the required devotion of time and manual energy to figure out most of the game on my own, but instead kinda transformed the experience into what increasingly felt like a menial task. Very glad that there are a variety of guides to reduce the tedium, otherwise my patience would have worn off long before finishing the game.
Glad I got it on a good sale. For now, I'm having more fun just challenging the bosses in the time attack mode.

But the difficulty doesn't come from the combat, it comes from exploration itself. The entire game is just one massive system of extremely discreet hints and puzzle pieces. La-Mulana is a 2D Action Platformer Metroidvania game. In here, you're playing as Professor Lemeza, he's an archeologist who tried to solve the mysteries of the ruins. This game is huge and vast, and as this is a metroidvania game, expect a lot of backtrack. There will be a lot of unsolved stuff behind, and even though it looks impossible to do, it's not, you'll able to do some crazy feat once you progress. That's one of the beauty of this game. So, now on to the review !
(+) Positive
- The progressive feels real, you starts with totally nothing, but once you unlocks stuff. It actually impacts in a great way.
- Interesting puzzle and riddle, and most of them are fair, logical and there's a hint for them.
- The soundtracks are great, really fits the atmosphere.
- A lot of secret, for those who likes treasure hunting.
- The place is vast and huge, great for those who likes exploring, you may find difficulties at first though !
- The boss fight is really challenging. Man, beating them feels great.
(-) Negative
- At the beginning, this game is kinda dull, since you're really limited. And it's kinda nuisance to go back to the first place just for healing. But later in the game, this will no longer become a problem.
- Beware, while most of the riddle is fair, some of them are not. you might get stuck.
- The death traps, yes, there are some in this game. There's a trap where you'll get killed instantly. Also, there's a trap that get you stucked and you'll most likely dead if you don't have a necessary item to get away. Trial and error i might say.
So, if you like a challenging 2D Action game, and don't mind dying a lot. This game is totally for you ! But just a reminder, it's not for everyone, really.

TL;DR
The game is great for learning how to play MTG, but it suffers some bad AI/RNG issues when playing against the computer. It's also disappointing that deck building is so limited.
Pros:
-Many decks to choose from.
-Many cards to unlock
-Lots of content in the way of campaigns and challenges
-Rewarding Gameplay
Cons:
-AI/RNG can stack against you. They will always get the cards they need 80% of the time, having an answer for whatever you play.
-Sealed Cards are limited. Can only open a few packs, and you can't use your created deck in any other modes.
-Gameplay can hang up on AI making decisions. Sitting there for a few minutes while the computer is stuck on its Main Phase.
Overall, the game is a good experience.  You can work your way through the single player and unlock decks and have a lot of fun playing them.  There's even a few decks I've discovered on here that I want to put together for real life MTG play.
Don't expect too much from this, but its worth the price on sale, and if you want to keep practicing your MTG skills or learning the best card game in the world.

You'll meet a colorful cast of interesting characters with penetrating conversations only a head full of alcohol could reveal.
Citizens with AI or biomechanical mods are fairly ubiquitous, there's a corgi that wears a hawaiian shirt and sunglasses, the main character is a lesbian, philosophical ideas are handled gracefully and with a fresh angle, there's plenty of hilarity (just wait till you meet Streaming-Chan).
You get to choose your playlist from a pretty awesome and varied selection of electronic and chiptune music.
Eventually you'll question reality.
This game is fresh and different.  The small amount of "bartending action" helps to make the graphic novel-esque direction feel interactive, and there are consequences to how much alcohol you give to your customers....
All in all, an excellent and well crafted game.  Get it!

Usually with most dystopian or utopian themed works I often run into the problem of the writers exaggerating how bad or good the future will be, mainly due to the fact that they don't attempt to ground the work into the real world with things that make you say " yea , I see that everyday now." This is not the case at all with va11halla and I couldnt be happier to say that, because their attention to making this dystopia seem believable and recognizable enough to the average person of our time makes this gmae truly something that immerses the player into the world. With the atmosphere grounded in the real world they also nailed the unique framework dystopian worlds provide in that there is also a lot of things that will make you think about what the future holds, things that seem just out of reach for today's world but just in sight of tommorow's.
Past the world building lies an absolutely killer ost aswell as likeable characters, even the most annoying characters in this game illicit sympathy from me and thats something few games seem to accomplish.
Lastly, this game made me do something that no other game has done before, I started to truly evaluate my life and my problems due to the conflicts of the characters in the game. I saw the main characters weaknesses and drew parralels to my own, and i'm in the process of trying to mend those issues thanks to this game and thats something that for me personally is well worth the time and money I put into this game.
In summation, this game is a fleshed out experience truly deserving of its reputation among its community and im so glad I gave a try on a whim a few nights ago.

Don't think you can get away with playing this game blind, unless you're a VERY determined player. You will have to write down nearly everything you scan, explore whatever you can, etc. This game is ridiculous in puzzles and level design and, in my opinion, it's nowhere near to even the best part of the game! It's well worth skipping it using a guide because the rest of the game IS worth it. Items, powerups, etc really help alleviate the difficulty this game has at the beginning.
Also, this game is pretty hard even with a guide. For a good portion of the game you have no defense and very bad platforming; it gets much better later, but if you don't have a guide for powerups, it's understandable how you can get frustrated because the tools to make your life easier aren't available. Also, it is worth mentioning that both whip upgrades are permanently missable; however, reloading a save can let you try again. Just keep that in mind. With that said, the game is amazing. La-Mulana pleasantly surprised me when I first started playing.  Here was a Metroidvania in the strictest sense of the word, with an expansive hand-crafted map just waiting to be explored.  Pivotal items could be found anywhere, so you were constantly rewarded for investigating every nook and cranny.  These upgrades also allowed you to intuitively access new areas--for example,
At this point, my only complaints were that save points are few and far between, and are often not located anywhere near bosses.
As I progressed through the game, I grew more and more frustrated.  Upgrades stopped being intuitive since the obstacles they got past became too obviously artificial.  For example,
This leads to a lot of directionless backtracking.
Eventually, I got stuck, looked at a guide, and was shocked at the number of required items that were hidden in unfairly obscure locations.  Stuff like "once you do X, a ceiling in an unrelated area that you've already explored becomes breakable with your whip".  Maybe a tablet somewhere contains a subtle hint that would point you in the right direction, but I feel this level of opaqueness is bad game design.  Super Metroid had plenty of hidden secrets, but there was almost always something unusual about the area to prompt you to scan it more closely with your X-Ray Scope.
I'm unsure whether I will continue playing La-Mulana, but if I do, I expect to have to rely on a guide.  Despite this, I do see why the game was so influential, and I still think it has quite a lot to offer.

Some things the original does better. Some things this remake does better. If you're at all interested in a game that will not hold your hand, has actual puzzles that require thought and detailed scanning of the ruins, has challenging but fair fights, then I implore you to try the free version for a feel of what the remake has to offer. Oh, if you're afraid of being punished for your mistakes you can just get out now.
You can find everything you need to get started here:
Running the original version on modern windows require some finangling in the compatability settings, but it's fairly straightforward (Run as admin, compatability mode for XP service pack 2, 16-bit color mode.)
That being said, what this version offers over the original is a more streamlined experience. Some of the puzzles were switched out and brand new ones even thrown in. This updated version is a lot less obtuse. While I hated the new graphics at first, they certainly grew on me and it was nice to hear some of the songs in a modernized format.

Visuals: 9/10 - Stays extremely faithful to the original game while keeping to a crisp pixel-art aesthetic. Everything about each area of the ruins looks vibrant and visually appealing while still keeping to the aesthetic of traversing ancient ruins. Quite a lot of the in-game murals are taken from mythology from certain parts of the world, which makes for a fun learning(?) experience.
Gameplay: 9/10 - The game feels smoother and more fair, the Menu layout and Computer Program management is a lot more streamlined and simple to use. There are no 'Cheap Deaths'. The puzzles are not impossible. They actually require some intelligence, and gathered information from the areas you've visited. Don't expect to beat this game in a week, that's for sure. As someone who was guilty of using a walkthrough for the MSX-themed original, coming to the remake with little memory of how to solve each puzzle and working it out by yourself is far more rewarding. Don't give up.
Music: 8/10 - The soundtrack remasters each song from the original and brings it straight up to date with the game's more modern theme. Each track uses leitmotifs well, but I can't help but feel that some of the charm and theming of the original tracks is lost here.
TL;DR: Miss the days where puzzle note-taking was a necessity? Where puzzles were actually difficult? Miss that old-school feeling of being rewarded for killing a tough boss or taking nearly two hours to solve a single puzzle? Pick this game up, straight away, full price.
A fantastic HD remake that fixes many of the issues of the original game, and an absolute must-play in general for any kind of masochist.

This is truly a very unique gameplay experience that I can’t quite say I’ve ever experienced before. Observer takes place in a very dark, gritty cyberpunk setting along with detailed environments, textures, and objects that capture your attention for hours on end. It leaves you completely immersed in a gameworld intricately designed. I’m not very big on horror or thriller games and I usually find their stories to be even more dreadful. This doesn’t apply to Observer.
I found myself going out of the way to get more details, more lore, even trying to find a window just to take in the world a bit more. Each crime scene was an intricate event, documenting & cataloguing clues, following up on possible leads, and then following the main quest lines. The main quest line had me binging this game for hours so I could get to a spot that felt right to pause in. Surprise though, no spot felt like a good time to take a break to go and sleep like a responsible adult! It took me about 7-8 hours to finish but was certainly worth it.  It really felt like I was reading a book and just had a vivid dream about the book. Quite the unusual experience.
I do have a couple qualms with the game, and figured it would be worth noting,
Aside from those issues, I recommend the game for those who have an interest in unusally captivating thriller games based in the cyberpunk world. That sentence doesn’t give the game justice, but it’s a good starting point! I simply don't have any other way of explaining how this game just... immerses you. I have to say I am extremely impressed by this game and I look forward to seeing more from the developer.

I cannot stress enough how boring this game is.
They sank their entire budget into pretty art and flashy effects, and left us with the bare minimum of gameplay. The cluttered designs so clearly inspired by Blade Runner do not work in a video game setting. As a film, the scenery is gorgeous eye candy. As a game-- particularly one where you're playing as a detective-- it's beyond infuriating. There is simply too much going on. All the sets are too busy with no clear idea of what exactly I'm supposed to be looking for. Half of the time, they simply make no logical sense. I couldn't suspend my disbelief high enough to buy that this was an actual building that actually got built and people actually lived in it.
The main pushing point is the idea of "hacking fears," but this only composes a tiny fraction of the gameplay. When it does come up, God help you if you have any kind of photosensitivity. It's a compiliation of Bethesda glitches masquerading as special effects. I'm supposed to be scared of the ominously floating bucket? The exploding chair? I guess Skyrim is the most terrifying game of our time.
There is exactly ONE level that really stands out, but it's towards the very end of the game and only lasts a few minutes.
I got this game on sale and I regret it. This is maybe $5 worth of poorly planned content. All style, no substance. If you want to play a game about exploring people's minds, stick to Nevermind.

----------
The "Free" portion of this game currently needs clarity. What's "Free" is essentially a built in demo system. I didn't know how the payment model worked until launching the game. It's reasonable, but should be more evident up front.
In the hopes that I can save y'all some time...
Tales of the Arabian Nights is the only table that comes fully free with this download. For everything else the trial/pricing system is as follows:
Any table can be played for free on a trial basis. The trial is based on a predefined score for a particular game, and when your reach that score, your game will immediately end. You can trial play a table as many times as you like, but the threshold score is pretty low, and you'll typically get cut off before ball 3.
Tables can be purchased in pairs for $5.
Every table in a "season" can be purchased for $30. There are 22 tables in season 1.
I love Bride of Pinbot. It's a machine I've sunk hundreds of quarters into, thus I'm very familiar with it. This recreation looks and sounds just like the real thing. It's such a trip experiencing this table again! I can only assume that the other tables are as accurate. Presentation aside, the physics are a bit weird. The balls come off the flippers at a lower angle than they should, making it much easier to hit the far left and right ramps. The stellar visual/audio recreations make up for any ball motion issues.
I will certainly be sinking at least $5 into this. Just be warned that this is not as "Free" as advertised... and certainly shouldn't be given the quality.

This is a great game for people who love pinball.
I've toyed around with the idea of buying a pinball machine for the house. I struggled with several things: where would I put it, which one would I get, how would I maintain it, how much would it set me back. None of those questions came with easy answers. Pinball arcade is at worst a fair compromise and likely a better choice. I can play all the games I enjoy without all the issues owning a real table would bring. For one, my wife will never get annoyed with how Pinball Arcade looks in the house.
Pinball Arcade feels pretty real. The controls on the keyboard do seem to play a little differently than a real Pinball table--slight hesitation from pressing and releasing the flippers, but this very slight. I notice this when I try to pass the ball from one flipper to the other. It's a reflex I developed on real tables and it doesn't quite work on Pinball Arcade. I've read that the game reacts better to game controllers, however I haven't been able to configure it to work with my game pad yet.
The things I really appreciate are the detail in the tables and the sounds of the games. Some of it is pure nostalgia. The tables offered are some of the best available. If they could get Fish Tales and Addams Family that would be awesome.
The physics of the game are great, however they do take a toll on my PC. I've noticed that if I put the anti-aliasing up to 16X and turn ball reflection on high at full resolution that the game will slow down in multi-ball. With those options disabled, the game keeps a steady frame rate.
I've seen a lot of negative feedback about how the game is free to download with one excellent pinball table, Tales of the Arabian Nights. That seems like a very fair model to me. I'd prefer that the tables be offered as regular DLC, but buying them in game isn't that bad.
I'm not sure why people are upset that they get to play a table for free and are asked to pay money if they want more. If they don't like it they're out the free that they paid.
In conclusion, buy if you are a pinball fan. I trust the developers will continue to improve the very minor issues in the game.

While experienced players might find the limited deck customizations in the main campaign disappointing, new players like myself won't feel overwhelmed.
That being said, this is a solid introduction to Magic and certainly worth the sub-$10 price tag, especially if you can pick it up on sale.

Luckily I didn't sell everything, so it was only a matter of time before my wife learned to play and now thanks to the online version we can play again on the diner table just like 10 or more years ago.
The game itself is in my opinion purely for enthusiasts, you're either into card games or you're not. Graphics are allright, music too, story and cutscenes aren't remarkable.
The computer does show you a lot better how the game mechanics work and what does what than you can with friends around your playing table though.
If you're a fan of MTG or are in need of nostalgia of your former MTG friends-around-the-table moments...this is a good investment.

Many people will criticize narrative based games because (in some cases) there wasn't really a reason for them to be a video game, they could have just as easily been a book. While this could have in theory been made into a book, and actually WAS made into an anime (which sucks compared to this), it uses the fact that it is a video game to it's advantage in ways that you couldn't really do in a book. For example, during sections of the game, you can go around and have conversations with the different characters and get to know them better, and since you can't possibly figure out everything about everyone in a single playthrough (you can't even come close), this gives you agency and lets you decide what characters you want to look deeper into.
Taking the time to really get to know these characters is more rewarding than it may seem at first, because none of these people are nearly as one-dimensional as they seem (yes, even hifumi . . .)
This game has a lot of wtf moments, but they're the good type . . . most of the time, other times there really just aren't words to describe it.
If you don't like visual novels, or think that they have no place in video games, then this one shouold sell you on them.

"It looked like an easy victory, but after the last battle; we can see it's not as easy as we thought." With the WWII Spam of the early 2000's, you would think they would die out. With the release of Medal of Honor: Airborne WWII Is back and has a few different changes. Should it be a good pickup? Or just another game that's late of the WWII Spam?
Story/Design: Airborne invites players to fly and dive into the skies of multiple famous battles as Boyd Travers. Not much about the guy, but hey, none really did with the other WWII games. With select battles from other MoH titles like Market Garden, and of course Normandy. (Since every WWII game needed a reference to the battle of Normandy.)
There isn't too much story to it, just going to objective to objective and accomplish them. They range from taking out a group of targets to go and blow up some artillery guns to help your other airborne comrades. The game is decent looking, a medium rig could run it but it looks quite nice on a great rig. With it being released in 2007, even some of the other games had a few better sounds. The firearm shot sounds don't ruin the game, but with others at the time it could be a bit better. With the story, there isn't much to it. Objective here, and objective there but luckily you're doing objectives during more famous battles that are usually well done and you can choose how you go to each of the objectives instead of a linear path, which is a spectacular change from go here, cut scene and follow the linear AI path.
Gameplay/Mechanics: No more running and gunning or running out and blasting each brain-dead AI in the face to reach the next objective. MoH Airborne takes things to a new level with some great changes added to the WWII FPS standards. As you dive out of the plane at each start point and choose where you would like to land, it is all up to you. Either landing in safe zones with your team or directly in enemy sights; the enemy AI is brutal and ruthless, able to hit you from rather large distances, and can seem a bit cheap at times; but it's much better than having brain-dead AI who just sit there until you shoot their face.
Of course with the AI being so brutal and checkpoints usually not showing up until you finally clear an objective; this can lead to starting from the plane over and over and over again. It's fine the first few times, but after the 6th time of doing the same thing you'll want to just rage quit. The game is more slowly paced than a few other FPS's.
Aiming down the sights will stop your character from walking around and instead be able to duck, lean, and raise your character instead of just walking around. This is a better choice so you can take it more slowly since the AI will be on your trail the whole time. Shooting hundreds of Nazi's and common soldiers will with the same gun will lead to a level up system to it, causing the game to slow-motion for a few seconds and to tell you what you unlocked for the following gun. Whether it be extended mag, reduced recoil, or better fire rate this can help you choose what gun firearm you love to use most and is a welcome addition to the standard FPS.
The game can offer replay ability for the ones who want everything unlocked, such as landing in certain spots while parachuting. For the gameplay, the AI is brutal and the checkpoints can be rather annoyingly placed. The gunplay is fun and great to control with a great gun level up type system.
Overall this is one of the best WWII games I have played, with smarter AI and a few different takes on a few things; although not being a completely perfect FPS experience, it's definitely a step in the right direction for a WWII game.
8/10 Excellent WWII FPS

La-Mulana does not give even the tiniest crap about you, and it's all the better for it. It wisely understands that playing as an action-archaeologist exploring mysterious ruins means hurtling into a confusing unknown, and everything about its play reinforces that. It's fantastically sprawling, fantastically confusing, and fantastically frustrating, but if you enjoy a taste of those elements, this could be the perfect game for you.
It's closest cousin is probably Super Metroid, but La-Mulana trades out the former's tight action gameplay for much, much,
more focus on puzzles and look-before-you-leap lethality. And not just block-pushing shenanigans. (Though there's no shortage of that, of course.) La-Mulana demands that you approach your adventure like an actual archaeologist. You'll need to pay attention to details, take diligent notes, understand the history of the ruins, and never, ever, stop looking for new nooks and crannies to explore. Metroidvania-style games often feature an element of sequence-breaking, allowing diligent/skilled players to tackle the game in unusual orders. La-Mulana stands alone in being so massive and so uninterested in shepherding you along a default path that it's hard to say if there's a "proper" sequence at all. Even killing major bosses might yield nothing more than a pat on the back. Rare is the game that puts you so thoroughly on your own.
That said, there are some big dings that make it more masochistic cult classic than masterpiece. For one, puzzles do branch into the realm of insane BS from time to time, and the game introduces (or rather, requires but does not introduce) a couple of unique environmental interactions along the way. Even if this kind of game is right in your sweet spot, keep the wiki bookmarked; you
need it at some point or another. Second, solving a puzzle triggers a confirmation sound effect, but the game doesn't show you
was unlocked or changed, which is a huge problem when the result is screens or entire zones away. And finally, things continue escalating in complexity all the way to the finale. While that would be fine in something like a platformer, here it means that you will absolutely be following a guide for the last big puzzle, and that it doesn't feel like you've come full-circle on the mysteries of La-Mulana so much as the it feels like the game just throwing more and more craziness at you.

This is a game that should have been better than it is: a dystopian cyberpunk horror that doesn't quite live up to its promise. Nevertheless, it's an interesting and worthwhile experience, in my opinion.
The biggest failing is that it's more walking-simulator than adventure game. There are some very basic mechanics during investigative parts of the game: you can scan things and you can talk to people, and that's pretty much it. Occasionally you interact with a keypad or press a button, but there's barely anything that could be called a puzzle. Large sections of the game simply have you walking forward through various scenes, leaving you feeling like a passive viewer rather than a player.
Where Observer shines is its atmosphere and world. The main location looks as if it would be very much at home in the film Blade Runner; conversations and reading material, along with the run-down environment, paint a picture of a grim but interesting setting that almost seems wasted on a single game (I hope for a sequel). The more obvious horror elements are weaker. Either I'm getting too old to appreciate horror, or its retreading ground that's been well covered in recent years. At times, the game can be very creepy, but this stuff tends to outstay its welcome, in my opinion. A story twist at the end does justify one of the elements I found a little unnecessary at the time, but it doesn't make those sections more interesting to play.
Speaking of Blade Runner, the use of Rutger Hauer to voice the main character was much appreciated, although not entirely successful. I can't honestly say that I thought his performance was great. My first reaction on hearing him was a rather sad realisation of how old he his now, and it seems to affect his performance. That said, I'm glad he's in the game, because even if the acting isn't quite up there with Roy Batty, it's Rutger bloody Hauer, and that counts for something.
This review seems somewhat negative, but while I don't think the game quite lived up to its initial promise, I don't regret buying it. Rather than finding it bad, I wanted it to be better than it was. Overall I was very immersed in the world and the story, and enjoyed it a lot, even if some sections did drag on a bit. It has its flaws, but the story, and the way it's told, make for one of those experiences that stay with you.
