This game is a conditional recommend as of its current version (V 0.71b). It is important to realize that it is very definitely an Early Access game - there are still a lot of odd crashes, client desync issues, and other network connectivity glitches. In fact, the netcode seems to be a little more unstable than usual in the current version because they have been working to clean it up.
That said, if you are willing to put up with instability, the game is still very fun to play and is driven by a team that is committed to improvements. Having played this game since back in the Desura days, I can look back and see a ton of improvements: we've gone from four Mias and one Monster to three playable avatars and two very different monsters. We've gone from one map up to nine. And even better - the team is engaged in the forum and does hear feedback from the playerbase. There seems to be a good mix of bug crushing and new features coming out.
The gameplay is a little tough to get in to as there is no tutorial or help file of any description. The game definitely works once you get the hang of it, but the learning curve is tough. Example: You can block a door with your body if the monster is trying to push in, but the monster can pull open a door even if you're trying to hold it. Usually. The game issues really hurt here, because getting stuck in a glitch can cause players to develop nasty anti-patterns.
Definitely worth a bash, and just as fun with friends or as a pickup. Just be careful of the lurker who shouts Randian philosophy as he carves a swath of destruction through the level.

I never really got into viual novels until I picked this up off the store, and I probably would have passed over it completely if I had bothered to look at the tags. Luckily for me, I only looked at the trailer and a few reviews. While this was probably a very dumb way to reach a decision, it turned out to be the right one.
Many people will criticize narrative based games because (in some cases) there wasn't really a reason for them to be a video game, they could have just as easily been a book. While this could have in theory been made into a book, and actually WAS made into an anime (which sucks compared to this), it uses the fact that it is a video game to it's advantage in ways that you couldn't really do in a book. For example, during sections of the game, you can go around and have conversations with the different characters and get to know them better, and since you can't possibly figure out everything about everyone in a single playthrough (you can't even come close), this gives you agency and lets you decide what characters you want to look deeper into.
Taking the time to really get to know these characters is more rewarding than it may seem at first, because none of these people are nearly as one-dimensional as they seem (yes, even hifumi . . .)
This game has a lot of wtf moments, but they're the good type . . . most of the time, other times there really just aren't words to describe it.
If you don't like visual novels, or think that they have no place in video games, then this one shouold sell you on them.

Overall, it's good. But not perfect. The two main problems with this game are:
1- Not enough control over what's happening.
There should be some possibility of optional micromanagement. For instance, you should be able to order personnel/robots to do specific tasks. Would be useful if a worker passes just beside a box he could carry on his way to the other end of the base, instead of just ignoring it because another worker (from the other end of the base) is programmed to get it. Also, you should be able to set the construction priority more precisely. Maybe with a construction queue you can modify. This should all be optional, so if you don't like micromanaging, you can keep playing like you do now.
2- The AI seems horrible at times.
Nobody is efficient. Personnel won't wait for a meal maker to finish preparing a meal, even if it's almost done. Instead, they'll try their luck at another one, sometimes in a different room far away. I just saw a worker carrying a box the looooong way around instead of using a very obvious, much shorter alternate path. Robots/workers should be intelligent enough to remove material from one construction machine (any kind) to another one of the same kind right beside. That way, at least one of them could be used, instead they'll leave them both partially filled, and therefore not usable at all. Sometimes, workers will try to satisfy a need but not necessarily the most urgent one.
All that being said, it's still an enjoyable game but I have a feeling the replayability value will rapidly fade away.

Let me point out the things that I hated about this game.
-The jumps. You never know for sure where your jumps gonna land, and it's not that I don't enjoy retro SNES castlevania kinda of jump, but this is not like Castlevania IV, it's more like Castlevania 2, Volgarr the Viking did it good.
-The graphics confuses you. The game is meant to be full of secrets and doesn't explain anything to you, and I'm ok with that, I like to explore and figure things out by myself, but the scenery shouldn't be a puzzle itself, if I look at somewhere and I don't know if I can land on it, or if I can even PASS through it, that really turns down all the fun to search for secrets, thjis is in the category of mistakes that you cannot do on your game, that's poor level design straight outta NES era.
-Farm system. Why does it exist in this game? You are exploring, you suddenly finds the solution for the puzzle, but damn, you're out of "weights" and can't solve the puzzle, actually, you can't do anything, because you use weights on the ruins everytime, time to go back to the village to farm or buy some weights, like, why? Why I have to stop and change my mindset in the middle of a run just because I run out of a stupid item? There is no reason to the weights to exist, there is no item management in the way you use them, because you want to use it everytime, there is no strategy.
-The difficulty. No, I'm not a filthy casual, but this game is just hard for the sake of being hard, it is actually a contradiction by itself, because if it wasn't that hard, the exploration and sense of discovery would be much more enjoyable, the game begs to you to explore and find secrets, but you're not going to be able to do that, because even if you're doing good and playing well, sometimes the game's just going to destroy you, imagine that you're on a pit, there is a ladder to get out of this pit, that's the only way out, but when you climb it, an enemy attacks you and drops you back to the pit, you try again and again, but there is no time to either kill it or dodge it, so you're basically trapped. IT IS A DEATH TRAP THAT CAN TAKE 5 MINUTES OR EVEN MORE, JUST TO KILL YOU.
-The puzzles. No, the puzzles are not good, I've seen people praising this game for its puzzles, but no, the idea of puzzles on this game is like, put a bunch of spikes, if the player fall on those spikes he can use a "weight" to finish the puzzle. There are some oks, but most of them can't be even called puzzles.
-Emails/Tutorial. The game keeps pausing itself to teach you some dumb things, like, at the start of the game it says to you use a "weight" to get an item, but it doesn't say anything about the purpose of the item, which would be something interesting. The problem is, it uses texts to teach things that should be teached by visuals, and doesn't do anything to teach you about things that should be explained by texts. Like, if you want to make your water poisoned, just make her visually poisoned, don't send me a damn text about it.

This is hardcore Metroidvania, a great hardcore Metroidvania.
The game starts you off exploring in a rather limited area, so you will soon stumble upon the first dungeon, which are called fields in this game. This first field also serves as an old school tutorial: you will learn the mechanics of the game within it, to recognize some traps and to doubt others. It's also really great as you can complete almost everything in the first field without ever going elsewhere, even beating its boss.
Once you've beat the first boss and completed most of the field's puzzles, it's time to branch out into the real game. Now you will begin the real exploration! You will need to visit many areas before being able to complete one, only stopped by a lack of tools or by too powerful enemies. The hints, which were pretty self-contained in the first field, will be found pretty much anywhere.
This game is really great and I heartly recommand it. Warning tough: the jumping controls are stiff and need a little adaptation. You might also want to consider a pen and paper to take note of some hints early on - until you find an in-game software you can use for that. Besides the accumulation of orbs, the hot spring is the only way to regain health.
What I think is the most amazing thing is how understanding the lore is primordial to understand and solve the puzzles. Through its tablet hints and other environmental cues, the game has a lore to tell and recurring themes that become more and more the key to find some of the later solutions. The "second" field, Mausoleum of the Giants, introduce the concept quite forcefully, even though most of its lore puzzles can be brute-forced without much trouble.
As usual with this kind of game, you start off really weak but if you commit yourself to find everything, you will become almost overpowered by the game's end, so don't be put off by the initial difficulty (or maybe you should come back with a better weapon or more health).

Do you find games a bit too easy? Want a real challenge? A challenge so hard the game not only kicks you in the balls, but also spits in your eye and laughs at your misfortune?
La-Mulana might just be your answer to all three.
La-Mulana is a Metroidvania-esque puzzle platformer following the adventure of Professor Lamenza in search of his father in the ancient ruins of La-Mulana. It's your job to not only find your father, but uncover the secrets of La-Mulana.
This game features lots of devious, head scratching puzzles, tough and challenging boss battles and enough dubious traps to make you think the game REALLY doesn't like you. This game is by no means for the weak-willed or those easy to anger as this game can and WILL♥♥♥♥♥♥you off, but if you're willing to take on it's various puzzles and traps then perhaps you can truly unlock the truth to La-Mulana.

I will go back and play it when I have more time to invest in it, but I am not sure others would.

This game seemed to have a lot of potential. Cool setting and visual style, simple interface, space.. and it is fun to begin with, but within a matter of a couple of hours, I think you'll see just about all the game has to offer, beyond recoloured planets with harsher conditions. And believe me, even on a planet with no sandstorms, lightening strikes or meteor showers, your colonists will find a way to pointlessly die. I sat here watching them take food from the store, to the meal maker, then stand around a die as someone else took their meal. Things dont get built, regardless of whether you set it as priority, engineers stand around idle while the inevitable worker shortage leaves many of the resource processing machines doing precisely nothing.
TL:DR - Starts off being fun, devolves into micromanagement and frustration at dumb AI.
Maybe I'm "doing it wrong" but it seems like the entire system of the game is designed to be massively unfair and punish anyone who gets over-confident and expands too quickly. Shame too, cause I was hoping this would be good. As it stands, not recommended, but if you can pick it up cheap or on Humble, its worth a few hours of your time.

Medal of Honor: Airborne (MoH: A) is essentially an overlooked game that offers a worthwhile experience especially given its low cost. The gameplay offers an emersive atmosphere with detailed graphics and awesome WWII sounds. However, MoH: A has a few drawbacks that will sometimes have you bashing your head onto your keyboard. The biggest of which is the increasing difficulty that carries on throughout the campaign where new enemies are introduced that are stubborn to your virtual bullets. Still, if you're looking for some good World War II action based upon the famous paratroopers of the era, then MoH: A is a no-brainer.

After their excellent Pacific Assault, the Medal of Honour franchise revisits the European theatre of World War II - this time, concentrating on Airborne operations. Each mission begins with the player being dropped over the target and it's their choice where to steer their chute towards. Would you prefer the safer zones marked by green flares? Or, are you daring enough to land amongst and surprise the enemy? Each map has several objectives before the mission is completed. There's so much happening during these fierce battles: smoke, noise, shouted orders, alarm and confusion. This is a game that really gets the adrenalin going. Skill and conduct are awarded by medals and weapon bonuses, plus unlocking access to 'the making of' videos. After the mission briefing, the player has a choice of primary and secondary weapons (a pistol is automatically provided for emergencies) before heading into combat. Med-kits, ammo, and grenade packs can be picked up along the way.

It's a good game for those who never played Magic before.  And that's where my praise ends.
Duels of the Planswalkers is notoriously known for being a constricting way to actually play Magic.  In-game purchases for pre-made decks that have pre-determined cards for you to 'customize' with, and a predictable AI that doesn't strain any challenge is really discouraging for people that were hoping for a more flexible card game based in the Magic universe.
If you're like me (relatively new to Magic but has some experience with playing in draft sessions and such), skip this.  Either go play Magic irl or buy the original Magic: The Gathering RPG by Sid Mier.  Otherwise, there's no harm getting this if it's on sale,  and if you're curious to learn how to play.  Just know that, once you get the grasp of things, you'll notice very quickly how boring it gets.

My playing hours at Steam are still low, but don't be fooled. I played this game like a madman when i was a kid. Now bought all the three of them to my Steam.
I haven't encountered any game-breaking bugs, or bugs at all actually. Everything plays smoothly on Windows 10.
Now on to the game itself: It's hard. In order to get stars on the level evaluation, you have to pretty much order around the guys at the same time. The levels itself are pretty diverse, and detailed, many ways to complete a level and there's no time limit if you dont want to reach for the stars. It's a great and challenging squad strategy. If you enjoy a hard games that require thinking of proper use of tactics, buy this.

Word of warning; Alpha is alpha. Is not even Beta. It's hardly meant to be playable, but it most certainly is.
Now then; After hours on hours in this, I can only say it's absolutely fantastic for an alpha-stage game. Crashes will happen, but it is to be expected. Counting in the voice chat and scary levels, and an absolutely terrifying monster (Lurker - Phantom's hardly scary, more like annoying.), this is bound to have you both screaming and laughing. No promises, of course. You kind of have to like being scared and maybe be easy to scare to enjoy this fully.
The more and more of your friends dieing around you only intensifies the experience, if you're not one of the few to die first. Knowing -you- are the primary target of the monster is enough to have you go ";_; Halp" and hide in a wardrobe. Which, I might add, is perfectly possible. You can hide in wardrobes. But I'd recommend hiding in a proper room with an inward door, so you can push back against it. Outgoing doors, like those on wardrobes, are bound to get you killed.
Anyway; This game is awesome. The devs are working on it constantly. The community is 'okay'. Worth more than what it sells for, even as Alpha. The only things negative about this game is trivial things that are there only because of the stage of the game. These issues are bound to get fixed. So that leaves only the good parts to go \o/ The amount of fun this gives is endless.

Damned is a really fun Survival Horror game where both the survivors and the monster are players. The (maximum of 4) Survivors run around the map rushing to find the different keys/codes to open doors/safes whilst trying to avoid the Monster, who is trying to kill them (there are only 2 types of monster at the time of this review). This can lead to some pretty tense moments of blubbering in a corner whilst the monster metaphorically sniffs around trying to find you. The surprising thing about Damned is that even though it's in alpha, it's still a really good game! Yes, they have bugs to fix, but lately they have really gotten around to fixing a good majority of them.
At the time of this "review", the game has a relatively small playerbase outside of the swarm of players every major update. If you're going to buy this game, the best way to do enjoy it would be to buy it alongside your friends, or to get the multi-copy pack so nobody gets left out.

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

I got this game because I loved UnEpic and UnEpic's creator said he was inspired by La-Mulana. The game title sounds spanish too - could be one reason ^^
Anyways, my first impressions when I launched La-Mulana was that the controls are kind of rigid : the jumping is not the greatest but not the worst either. Music gave me a little headache since it's a short loop... but still good - just wished the loop was a little bit longer - the double to be precise... Sounds are ok, some are good ; overall it has a feel proper to itself, which is good.
As for the game itself, it's pretty rich, meaning there seems to be a lot of stuff to do, to collect, to investigate - you're a guy that probably has Indiana Jones posters in his bedroom and pray to the Lost Ark before sleeping.
I like the graphics, especially the levels - the difference between zones is good and refreshing since they change a lot from one to another. There are yellow-ish pyramids-like levels or ones more inspired by some temples of water, etc. Some mobs can seem strange in appearance, but like the sounds, it gives a style to the game.
The game is full of surprises : level design and game design make it hard, with low-level puzzles to sort - which is great since it's an action-platformer and I hate it when there's too much puzzling to do... and with the save system you can organize yourself so that you don't have to walk a lot to get back to what you were solving - or trying to solve. Sometimes you get punished for not getting the right jump, or for not killing an enemy while jumping. This can get frustrating but that's part of the game and adds to it. Overall it's a difficult game, but for good reasons.
I'm not far in the game but I feel this won't change, and I like it that way. The only bad thing I have to say is this : when moving from one map to another, the ingame objects (characters etc) stop and the camera slide so that it centers to the map you're moving to... and sometimes, you get hit by an enemy that is too close to the point of arrival on the new map, getting you to move back to the previous map you can from - to me this is not a gamebreaking matter but I would have liked not to see that issue being in.
I would recommend getting in when it's on sale OR full price if you like the genre.

I want to like this game.
But I do not.
The controlls are sloppy, there's no player scaffolding, and the physics are atrocious. Two examples from the physics complaint: jump mechanics and preservation of inertia. There are two things that Super Mario Brothers, the gold standard of physics expectations in 2D platformers, do correctly. If I fall off a ledge running full-tilt, where do I fall? Straight down? No, but in La-Mulana, the answer is "yes."
I'm torn between conquering this and deleting it forever, or just deleting it forever and cursing the developers for burning away some of my money.
I would hope they fix the physics in the two aspects--oh! Another one! As a player, I have the expectation of being able to grab a ladder/rope in mid-fall. Here, I cannot. It turns a game that could be "interesting" into one that is "tolerable ... perhaps."
I cannot possibly recommend this game.
UPDATE: I looked at the Kickstarter page for This Game Part Two. I learned more from the manual there than I did about this game in my entire ownership, and I played the demo and found the physics problems remain. I will not be buying that game, and see now that this was an intentional design decision. Pity, as it's irritating and unenjoyable to be stymied by a game with sloppy controls and unintuitive physics and movement. "Hard" is fine; "broken" is irritating.
UPDATE 2: I now have ten hours of gameplay invested. I have only invested these, an additional eight hours over when I wrote my original review, in order to ensure I wasn't selling this game short. I was not. This is a game that I "tolerate," at best. I do not enjoy it. The controls and art and design all conspire to push the player into prime striking position for enemies, and there is little logical association between a switch and its effect. I have to wonder if the dev put this out there as a lark: a kind of special f-bomb to video game players everywhere: "you like to play games? Well f-you, guys!" This is the only explanation that makes sense with all the design and artistic conventions that have been broken in this game. I really, really, really wish I hadn't waited six months between purchase and play, because now I'm screwed out of $15. Worse, the person who wrote this software is now some percentage of that $15 richer, AND has been given a dollar-vote of, "yes, this game is good." It is not. It needs significant work. It won't get that work, though, as La-Mulana 2 is on Kickstarter and is more of the same; just a re-skin of this game with (presumably) different and equally-f-you-based "puzzles."
UPDATE 3: The game is growing on me, like a fungus. After 33 hours total gameplay and a 6-hour (new) savefile, it's interesting, but continues to be hamstrung by horrible platformer-controls and swimming mechanics. If you fall into lava with fireballs/rocks, you're pretty much done for, as you'll be batted around like a toy mouse in a room full of cats. Ice is similarly slick, but that's expected: it's ice, just ice where mu = 0.0001 or so. You will, in one particular area, be sent back and forth between screens if you forget that an enemy awaits just inside the screen transition, on ice.
Overall, with 33 hours in and really needing--truly, absolutely needing--a direct walkthrough read in the Chamber of Illusions (the whole "on bended knee" thing. Ugh!), I remain correct in my original assertion: I cannot recommend this game at its asking price given its treatment of the above controls/scenarios. Could I recommend it at the $5 mark? Yes. It's frustrating, as it is hamstrung by deliberately-bad controls, but for $5 you can do much worse.
UPDATE 4, 46 hours of play: I would recommend this game at the $5 mark. Comments on controls and physics are unchanged, but the game as a whole has grown on me. Gameplay improved post-Feather.

I think part of the problem is that the user gets overwhelmed by different and vast amounts of data. Sometimes this made it  difficult to decide what to do next.  While the open world will basically allow you to do almost anything, it is easy to lose track of the larger story.  There are simply  tons of  NPCs that can be hacked.  On top of this, all things electric are within your span of control.  For example, while waiting to cross a busy street, I played around with the traffic light controls and managed to change the light to red mid cycle causing a chain reaction multiple car accident.   Later while spying  on a bad guy, I hacked into the city camera system and switched from one camera to another until I had the best / closest view.    The game provides you with the information and tools to track down bad guys and to actually stop some crimes before they happen.  Your character is basically a busy body that butts into everyone’s business attempting to manage the situation to their advantage.  So the question you might be asking at this point is if the game is worth the price.  On reflection I think this is a well-crafted game that is different enough that it takes a bit before you become comfortable with the amount of information and game play.   While I've been reluctant to give it another go, it is one of those games that I'm saving for a rainy day.

I want to like this game, but it's just so frustrating.
There's the aspect that you're creating an "environment to succeed" for the little AIs... but they're so stupid. For instance, there's no way to prioritize tasks amongst the different specialties.... and God help you if you lose all the AIs in that specialty (looking at you, biologists). It wants you to believe that it's smart, but the granualarity and control just leads the dumb AIs to destruction.
For example...let's say you have a food crisis...sure, you got into it, but the game's supposed to be about survival. Unfortunately, the only people who can "man" the biopods are biologists. Why can't a worker or engineer or medic be re-routed to help the biologists? No clue. You'd figure in a survival scenario, you'd do whatever you could to make that lettuce grow. Every other game in the genre has figured this out...any bot can do the job, the ones with specialties can do it better. Simply, let me assign any bot to a job, and give me bonuses for those spec'd in that job.
Another example, the dumb rules about malnutrition. The machines are programmed to build certain "meals". Can you control that, maybe queue it up? Nope. It just ramrods through your resources. Again, if eating mashed potatoes causes death when there's a bunch of fried chicken laying around, maybe allow the engineers to reprogram the meal dispensers?
Nice try, hoping this game evolves a bit and it's not some weird princpled simulation wonks in charge of developing the underlying AI rules engine.

I don't think I like Commandos: BEL just for nostalgia's sake. This is truly a great game.
One unique thing about the game is that even while the missions often times feel impossible at first, there are actually a near-endless number of ways to complete them. Whenever I watch videos of another player completing a mission, I pretty much always find them doing things I never thought of doing.
And when you consider how much time and effort will regularly go into completing a single mission, it's pretty amazing that there are 20 of them, not to mention the stand-alone expansion (Commandos: Beyond the Call of Duty).

I've sunk over 80 hours into this game at this point, so I think I've got a good feel for it.
First off, I really enjoy this game.  There is something very zen and meditative about it.  Doing all the micro-management of the community has a very satisfying feeling once you get the hang of it.
It can be frustrating at first, as you are trying to figure out the best way to expand, and you miscalculate, causing a massive domino effect, ruining your entire colony.  But aside from those frustrations, the game has a distinct charm to it.
I would say it's similar to games like SimCity, in that your job is to balance several factors at once, to keep disaster from destroying everything.  You build your base stronger, and better, so that you can make it bigger, to get more people.  In doing so, you have to make it stronger again, and better, and bigger, so you get more people.  There really isn't an "end" to it, just like games like SimCity.  You can just keep building and expanding, and taking enjoyment in seeing the finely tuned machine hum along, everything working as intended.
If you don't like that kind of game, don't buy this one.  If you do love that type of game, where you are the person responsible for the lives and well being of hundreds of people, then you will probably enjoy this game.

I wanted to like this game so much; I really did. Planetbase presents the really cool if not original concept of building an inhabitable and self-sufficient base on an otherwise uninhabited planet. You are presented with a crew of seven people and a few robots that will help you get started with the construction of your base. Getting started with the basics of the game is really easy with a tutorial that highlights the most important rules and functions of the game. The UI is simple and easy to navigate and placing objects is not TOO problematic.
So, once you make it past the tutorial and get started building your own base, the game's flaws start to slowly, but surely, make themselves known. One problem that I had with the game is how limited base-building really felt. Once you build your oxygen tank, you HAVE to construct every facility around it. There is no way to build multiple structures despite having relative freedom in constructing airtanks and airlocks. I guess this is acceptable to some, but for fans of the city building genre, this is stifling and outright annoying.
Speaking of construction, there is no way to prioritize building certain structures or even producing certain resources (which can be alot of ♥♥♥♥ING fun when your base is falling apart). The AI does whatever it wants with no real sense of survival. Are your wind turbines in need of repair and it's nighttime where they're crucial? Better suck it up and sit in the dark, because the AI is probably going to focus on repairing solar panels and there is NOTHING that you can do about it. You can build certain structures for maintaining production all day, but what the AI decides to do is pretty much RNG-based. This is CRIPPLING and can make the game very unfun once you get more colonists and a larger base. Biologists may or may not produce food, medics are damn near worthless, and workers will create♥♥♥♥♥♥that you don't need over important things even when you have a surplus of workers.
The game is a resource management game that is dependant on the AI. When the AI gives no ♥♥♥♥s and does what it wants until it dies of exhaustion or hunger, then who's to blame. According to some players, though, small bases are stupidly easy to manage. In a builder game, limitations like these are not acceptable.
The game looks really good and has a great soundtrack. I've played this game sober, drunk, and under the influence and thoroughly enjoyed its presentation in all instances. But if you want a better builder game, pick up Anno 1404 or Cities: Skylines, or just wait until this goes on sale.

While 2014 is undoubtedly as fun as any Magic product, it really doesn't play nearly as well as Duels 2013. The Sealed Play mechanic is underwhelming in that it costs you money to play it each time -- a ridiculous concept for a single player game! Two-Headed Giant is alright, but the majority of the game just feels limited and less smooth than Duels 2013. Whether you're a longtime fan of the game or just starting off, go get the previous edition of the game and have more fun there.
